descs.en: He blew open a shipping container expecting guns and found a princess. She won’t go home. She keeps coming back.

synopsis.title: Synopsis
synopsis.content:
Lee Jun Hyuk goes to West Basin at two in the morning to kill the man who signs the papers. He blows the lock on the wrong container, expecting guns, and finds five women who have been in the dark for two days. One of them is standing in the middle of the box, between the door and the others, with her hands open.

He gets them out, leaves them at a hospital, and won't give his name. Evangeline Lin finds him anyway: a noodle menu on a dashboard, three days at a corner table, two bowls ordered every time. She is the Lin family's quiet daughter, the paper twin, and she has been somebody's secret since she was three days old. He is a big, kind, talkative man who hunts the people who move people, and he has a rule about everything.

She follows all of his rules except one. She keeps coming back.

authorNote.title: Author Note
authorNote.content:
Evangeline says almost nothing in Every Flower in the Shop. I always wanted to know what she'd say if somebody waited long enough, and the answer turned out to be: not much, and every word of it on purpose. So I gave her the man who talks more than anyone in the series. He talks to frightened people so they'll follow his voice. She's the first person who ever listened to all of it.

It's a dark book in places. He's done terrible things for what he thinks are good reasons, and the book doesn't pretend otherwise. But it's mostly about small things done in dangerous rooms: towels folded in thirds, a lamp left on, a window box behind bulletproof glass, a man practising a woman's name in the shower. And about what happens when the one person who never asks for anything finally asks.

He's rich, by the way. Very. He just never had anyone to spend it on. That changes in chapter fourteen, and then it really changes.

contentWarn.title: Content Warning
contentWarn.content:
21+ · For adult readers. Mature themes and heated love scenes.

This is a dark romance with a lot of tenderness in it, but it has hard moments:

• Human trafficking: women held in a shipping container, and a lorry where eleven women died (The Container Had a Princess in It, Don't Stop Moving, She Asks Nothing, Someone Else Finishes It)

• Killings by the hero, mostly off the page (Don't Stop Moving, He Goes Hunting)

• An infected knife wound and a high fever, treated at home (The Night He Had a Fever)

• A dying man and morphine (The Target Is a Judge)

• A photograph of a captive sold online (The Traffickers Remember Her)

• A knife held to a father's throat, with no harm done (Jun Hyuk Meets His Father-in-Law (Badly))

• An abduction attempt, a head injury and a shooting (The Abduction Attempt, She Shoots First, After)

• A man found in a refrigerated container (Jun Hyuk Takes a Job He Hates)

• A sniper's choice on a riverbank (He Goes Anyway — Then Turns Back)

• A mother's death in an aid station, remembered by a child (The Borderland Boy)

• Grief for a parent the heroine never knew (A Letter From a Palace, The Throne Lets Her Go)

glossary.title: Names & Terms
glossary.content:
West Basin — The container terminal where it starts. Row K, the old control tower.
Nam's Noodles — Eleven tables on River Bridge Road in the border town. Phones go in a jar between the chilli oil and the soy sauce.
The karaoke flat — Two rooms over a karaoke bar that closed in 2019. Painted windows, three locks, a camp bed.
The menu — Nam's takeaway menu, taped inside the door, with his rules on the back (and two of hers).
The textile building — Eight storeys by the harbour. He owns it. Sixth floor: five windows of glass you can shoot at all day.
The window box — A steel greenhouse bolted to a twenty-centimetre ledge, behind a hatch cut into bulletproof glass.
The rabbit book — His school exercise book of names, boats and payments. There are ten in the end.
The Grey Lanterns — The border unit that took him in at eight. Old Ko's unit.
The court language — The language of the country she was born in, which is never named. She taught herself.
The heron — The gold crest on her baby blanket: a heron over three peaks.
No. 9 Fig Tree Lane — The house with a real address. Thirty-one windows, and every one of them opens.
The Open Door — The foundation she starts for people who come out of boxes.
Rule seven — Don't come back.

chapters.title: The Container Had a Princess in It
chapters.desc: West Basin, two in the morning. He came to kill the man who signs the papers. He opens the wrong box.
chapters.epigraph: “If you want to live, stay behind me.” — Lee Jun Hyuk, row K, West Basin container terminal
chapters.content:
The man Lee Jun Hyuk had come to kill was twenty minutes late.

Jun Hyuk lay on his stomach and thought you’d expect a man to be on time for his own crime. Then again, men like Kuang were never on time for anything. Somebody else always did the waiting.

He was lying flat on the roof of a forty-foot container, four high, in row K of the West Basin container terminal, at ten past two in the morning on a Thursday in October. The steel under his chest still held the day’s heat. Below him the stacks went on in every direction like a city with no doors, red and blue and rust-brown and green, lit orange by the floodlights on their tall masts, and between them the straddle carriers stood parked for the night with their legs apart, like big patient animals. Out past the last row, the harbour moved black and oily under the cranes.

He was a big man, and big men don’t lie comfortably on container roofs. He had been up there three hours.

He went over it again, the way he always did before. Kuang Yaoming. Deputy Port Commissioner. Fifty-four. Played golf on Wednesdays, badly. Had a wife who thought he worked late, and a flat in the eastern district with a different woman in it, who also thought he worked late. Signed his own name on anything that came through row K on a Thursday. Guns, Jun Hyuk thought, mostly. A sideline. That was what the manifests said, if you knew how to read them, and he knew how, because an old woman who made the best noodles on the river had taught him.

The guns could wait. Kuang had signed the papers on eleven boats in four years that should never have come in.

There was a ledger in Jun Hyuk’s go-bag, a cheap school exercise book with a cartoon rabbit on the cover, and in it, in pencil, in his own big careful hand, were the names of the boats and the dates and what had come off them. On two of the pages, what had come off them had been people.

✦ ✦ ✦

At two twenty-three a car came in through the east gate with its lights off.

It was a dark saloon, clean, and it drove slowly along the access road between the stacks and stopped at the foot of the old control tower, which nobody used any more except Kuang. A man got out. Grey coat, grey hair, golf umbrella under his arm though it wasn’t raining. He looked left and right the way men do when they think they’re being careful and went up the outside stairs of the tower. The light came on in the office at the top.

Late, and he’d brought an umbrella. Jun Hyuk nearly laughed.

He did not move yet. He had learned patience from a man called Old Ko, who had said that the second car is always more important than the first, and who had been right about most things except, in the end, his own heart.

The second car came at two thirty-one. A white van with a cleaning company’s name on the side, which would have been more convincing if any cleaning company in the city worked at half past two in the morning in a container terminal. It stopped at the end of row K. Two men got out of the front. One went up the tower stairs to Kuang. The other walked along the row, counting containers under his breath, and stopped at a rust-red forty-foot box at ground level, two along from the one Jun Hyuk was lying on. He checked the doors. He checked his watch. Then he lit a cigarette.

The container had a customs seal on its doors and a heavy new padlock under the seal, the kind with a shrouded shackle that you couldn’t get bolt cutters onto. The number stencilled on its end, which Jun Hyuk had memorised a week ago, matched a line in the ledger with the rabbit on the front, under Kuang’s signature. Machine parts. Transshipment. Hold for collection.

Guns, Jun Hyuk thought. He’d have bet his truck on it.

✦ ✦ ✦

After that it went fast.

He came down the back of the stack the way he’d gone up, on the twist-lock corners, without a sound. People never believed a man his size could do that. The smoking man had his back to him. Then Jun Hyuk was behind him, and then the man was asleep on the ground with his cigarette still burning next to his hand, and Jun Hyuk was saying, low, “Sorry. Sorry. You’ll have a headache. You’ll live,” while he tied the man’s wrists with his own shoelaces.

He looked up at the tower. The light was on. Two shadows moved across the window, Kuang and the van driver, talking.

He looked at the container.

It was not the plan. The plan was the tower, Kuang, and away over the east fence before the night shift came on at four. The container was for later. The container was for an anonymous phone call to a detective who was supposed to be honest. But the padlock was right there, and Kuang’s signature was on the papers, and whatever was in that box was going to leave on a ship at six, and then it would be in somebody’s hands on the other side of the sea, and it would be used. Jun Hyuk had seen what guns were used for. For years he had been one of the things they were used for.

He took the small charge out of his bag. He had brought it for the steel door at the back of the tower. It would do for a padlock.

Quick look, he thought. Photograph the crates. Shut the door. Upstairs.

He set it and stepped round the corner of the next box. On three the lock went, a flat hard crack that bounced off the stacks and came back twice.

Up in the tower, the shadows stopped moving.

Well, he thought. That’s that, then.

He went back, pulled the bar down and swung the right-hand door open.

✦ ✦ ✦

The smell came first.

Heat, and sweat, and a bucket in a corner, and the sour stale air of a box that had been shut in the sun for two days. He knew that smell. He had known it since he was twenty-five years old, and he had spent seven years making sure that every night he went to sleep with it in his nose, on purpose, so that he would not forget it.

He did not breathe for a second.

Then the floodlight from the mast behind him fell into the container in a long orange slab and lit it to the back. There were no crates.

There were five women.

Four of them were on the floor at the far end, against the corrugated wall, holding on to each other. Two empty water bottles lay on their sides beside them. Somebody had drilled a row of holes through the roof, small ones, the size of a finger, and a little grey light from the masts came through them and made spots on the floor. One of the women was young, nineteen or twenty, with her face pressed into the shoulder of the woman next to her. She was making a sound like a kettle on a low flame.

The fifth woman was standing.

She was standing in the middle of the container, between the others and the door. Between the others and him. Tall, straight, barefoot, in what had been a pale grey cardigan and long skirt, with her black hair come down out of a knot and her hands open at her sides. She had put herself there. When the lock went she must have got up in the dark, walked to the middle of the box and stood in front of the others, so that whatever came through that door would come to her first.

She looked at him.

He had been looked at by a great many people with guns in their hands and a great many people about to die. He had been looked at by men who wanted to kill him and women who were afraid he was going to kill them, and he knew what every one of those looks was made of. He did not know what this one was made of.

She was not afraid of him. She looked straight at his face in the orange light: the scar through his eyebrow, the black clothes, the size of him filling the door, the gun he had not known he’d drawn until he saw her look at it. She took all of it in, steadily, as if it were weather coming in. Then she looked past him, at the stacks, at the left side and the right side and the gap at the end of the row, and he realised that she was counting the ways out.

“Oh,” said Jun Hyuk. “Oh, hell.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Footsteps on the tower stairs, coming down fast. A man’s voice, calling a name. Another voice, higher, Kuang’s, saying something about the police, saying go and look, go and look.

Jun Hyuk did not have time. He had about forty seconds. He had planned this night for a week, and none of the plan had five women in it.

He made himself smaller in the door. It was a thing he’d learned to do for frightened people. He crouched, so his head was lower than the standing woman’s, and put the gun down by his knee where they could all see it, pointing at the ground, and spoke in the voice Old Ko had taught him, the low, easy, ordinary voice you’d use for a dog that had been hit by a car.

“Hello,” he said. “Hello. Listen to me. I’m not with them. I’m not with anybody. I came here for something else, and I found you, and now I’m getting you out. That’s all. That’s the whole story. We’re going to go now. Not in a minute. Now.” He looked at the standing woman, because she was the one who would decide. “Can they walk?”

She looked at him for one more second. Then she nodded.

“Good. Good. That’s it. You’re doing well.” He was talking to all of them, and to the one making the kettle sound most of all. “There are some men coming down some stairs. They’re not good men, and they’re slow, and they’ve had too much coffee. We’re going to go the other way. I know the other way. I’ve been lying on top of a box for three hours looking at it.”

The young one had lifted her face. She was staring at him. Her lips were cracked.

“What’s your name, little sister?” said Jun Hyuk.

“Nuo,” she whispered.

“Nuo. Good name. I’m going to get you a bottle of water the size of your head, Nuo. Two bottles. Hold on to the hand of the lady next to you. Everybody hold on to somebody.” The footsteps had reached the bottom of the stairs. “Now listen. This is the only rule. It’s easy. Are you listening?”

The standing woman was listening. She was watching his mouth as if she were going to have to repeat it later in a court of law.

“If you want to live,” said Jun Hyuk, “stay behind me, and don’t stop moving.”

He stood up.

He held his left hand out behind him, low and open, and did not look back to see if anyone would take it. There wasn’t time to look back. He was already watching the end of the row.

Something cold and thin closed round his fingers.

He glanced down. It was the standing woman’s hand. She had taken it without a word, and with her other hand she had reached behind her and taken the hand of the woman behind her, who had taken the next, and the next, so that the five of them stood in a line in the orange light like children on a school trip, joined, waiting, and the tall woman at the front of the line holding on to him.

Her fingers were like ice. They didn’t shake.

He looked up from her hand to her face, once, for half a second, which was all he had. He would be ashamed afterwards of what he noticed in that half-second, with five women in a box and men on the stairs and Kuang’s light still on in the tower: that she was beautiful, the kind that stops a man in a doorway. He noticed it anyway, and put it away, and looked at the end of the row.

“Good,” said Jun Hyuk. “That’s it. Here we go.”

And they went.

✦ ✦ ✦

He would think about it afterwards, more than he wanted to. The running was ordinary and the men were stupid, and the low gap at the bottom of the reefer stacks was where he’d known it would be. He would get to Kuang later.

What stayed with him was the moment in the doorway, before any of it. The smell. The holes in the roof. And a woman with no shoes on standing in the middle of a dark box, between the door and the people she had decided were hers, waiting for whatever was coming, with her hands open.

He had done that once. A long time ago, on a river road, he had been the thing standing in front of a door. And he had stepped aside.

“Keep moving,” he said, to all of them, and to himself. “Don’t stop. Keep moving.”

She didn’t let go of his hand.

chapters.title: Don’t Stop Moving
chapters.desc: The run through the stacks, a gap that hums, four minutes to wait, and the man he came to kill. She memorises everything.
chapters.epigraph: “If I’m not back in four minutes, you’re in charge. You look like you’re already in charge.”
chapters.content:
They had taken her on Tuesday at twenty to six in the morning, at the orchid stalls.

Evangeline Lin had been going to the morning flower market twice a week since she was fourteen, because it was the only place in the city where nobody looked at anybody. Everyone was looking at the flowers. The old men with their trolleys looked at the lilies, the restaurant buyers looked at the price boards, and the girls from the hotels looked at their phones. Nobody looked at a tall quiet young woman in a grey cardigan crouching by a tray of white phalaenopsis, checking the roots.

Two men had looked at her. She noticed them a second too late. A hand over her mouth that smelled of motor oil. A van door. A needle in her arm. And one of them, in the van, laughing, close to her ear, had said Your Highness, the way boys tease a child in a paper crown.

That was how she knew they knew.

She had not said a word to them. Not in the van, not in the warehouse with no windows, not in the container where they put her with four other women who had been promised jobs in hotels across the sea. Two days in the dark. She had not said a word to anybody except, once, to Nuo, who was nineteen and had cried until she was sick, and to whom Evangeline had said, in the middle of the second night, low, “Breathe with me,” and then counted, in and out, for an hour.

Now there was a man holding her hand.

✦ ✦ ✦

He ran the way she imagined a bear would run if a bear had been trained by an army: fast, low, and much quieter than anything that size had any right to be. He didn’t let go of her. He didn’t look back. He kept his left hand behind him and her fingers in it, and every few seconds his grip tightened slightly, once, like a question, and every time it did she tightened hers back.

And he talked.

He talked the whole way. Low, steady, under his breath, in a rough cheerful voice with a border accent in it, the kind of accent the vegetable sellers had who came down from the north on the early buses.

“Left here. Good. Mind the cable, Nuo, there’s a cable, big step, good. You’re all doing fine. Better than me. I’ve done this before and I’m wheezing. I’m too big for this. My knees are thirty-two years old but they think they’re sixty. Right. Right again. Keep holding hands. Don’t look at the light, look at the ground. The ground’s your friend. The ground has never let you down.”

Behind them, somewhere among the stacks, a man was shouting. Another answered him, further off. A torch beam swung across the end of the row they’d just left and swung away.

“They’ve gone the wrong way,” said the big man. “Of course they have. They went the way the noise came from. Amateurs.” He sounded almost disappointed. “Nearly there. Twenty more steps. Count them with me. One. Two. Three.”

He counted. Evangeline found her lips moving with his. Behind her, Nuo’s thin cracked voice was counting too, and then Bik’s. Bik had said for two days that she was thirty and had a son and would not die in a box. Then the other two joined in, and the five of them and the man went down the long orange corridor between the stacks whispering numbers like a strange choir.

At twenty, he stopped.

✦ ✦ ✦

The refrigerated containers were stacked in their own block at the end of the terminal, plugged into the power on tall grey posts, and every one of them hummed. Their compressors blew warm air out of grilles at the bottom, and between the bottom row and the concrete there was a gap, a long low dark space where the cables ran, a little more than knee high.

“In you go,” said the big man. “On your stomachs. It’s warm. It smells of fish and hot dust. You’ll hate it. Nobody’s ever looked under here in the history of the world. All the way along to the third post, there, see it? Go.”

Bik went first. Then the two who held each other and had not said their names. Then Nuo, sobbing without any noise, her cracked feet black on the bottoms. Evangeline let go of his hand to help her down and felt, for a second, the cold of the night on her fingers where his hand had been.

He crouched beside her. Up close he was even bigger. There was a scar through his left eyebrow, an old white one, that made one side of his face look permanently a little surprised. His hair was cut close to his head. He smelled of the harbour and of steel and faintly of instant coffee. He was close enough that she could feel the heat coming off him in the cold, all down her side, like standing next to a stove. She had been cold for two days. She didn’t move away from it.

“Listen,” he said. His voice had dropped further, so low she felt it more than heard it. “I’ve got a job to do. It takes four minutes. You lot stay here, flat, quiet, and nobody will find you. If I’m not back in four minutes—” He pointed past the reefer block, to the far fence, where a blue straddle carrier stood parked against the wire. “There’s a hole in the fence behind the blue one. Big enough for a fat man. I know because I’m the fat man who made it. Go through it, go along the ditch to the road, and keep walking towards the lights. There’s a petrol station. Go in, tell the man at the till to call the police, and don’t let anyone send you anywhere in a van, ever again.” He looked at her. “You’re in charge.”

She looked back at him.

“You look like you’re already in charge,” he said. “So you might as well be.”

She nodded.

He pressed a button on the big plain watch on his wrist and turned it so she could see the numbers start.

“Four minutes,” he said. “Don’t come looking for me. I mean it. Whatever you hear.”

Then he went. She watched him go, a big black shape between the orange stacks, moving towards the old tower at the far end of row K with the light on at the top of it. He didn’t run now. He walked. She lay down on her stomach in the warm fish-smelling dark beside Nuo, and put her arm over Nuo’s back, and watched the place where he’d been.

She counted.

✦ ✦ ✦

At one minute and ten, a man ran past the end of the reefer block with a torch. He didn’t look down. Nobody ever looked down. Evangeline had learned that at nine years old, under the dining table in the house in the Walled City during one of her father’s dinners, listening to men talk about ships. People looked for you at the height of their own eyes.

At two minutes and forty, there was a scuffle somewhere near the tower stairs. A grunt. Something heavy hitting metal. Then nothing.

At three minutes and twenty, there was one shot.

It was not loud. It was a flat, short sound, like someone dropping a book in a library, and it came from the top of the tower, and the light up there did not go off. Under her arm, Nuo flinched so hard that her forehead hit the concrete. Evangeline held on.

She knew what the sound was. She had grown up in a house where men came to see her father at night, and she was not stupid, and she had never once in her life been allowed to pretend she was. She knew what the big man had gone to the tower for. She lay in the dark with her cheek on the ground and the compressors humming over her head, and waited to feel something about it.

What she felt, mostly, was that she wanted him to come back.

At three minutes and fifty-one, he came back.

✦ ✦ ✦

She saw his boots first, stopping by the third post. Then he crouched, and she saw his face.

It was the same face. Calm, wide, ordinary, the scar through the eyebrow. But for a few seconds he did not say anything at all. He crouched by the gap and looked in at them, at the five of them lying in a row, and his mouth was shut and his eyes were dark and far away, as if he had come back from much further than the tower.

Then it was gone.

“Right,” he said, in the easy cheerful voice. “Who’s hungry? Nobody? Liars. Out you come. Mind your heads, it’s low. Up, up. There you go, Nuo. Look at you, you’re filthy. You look like a chimney sweep. We all do.”

He was humming, she realised, as he helped them out. Under his breath, between sentences. Some tune with no beginning or end, the kind men sing to themselves when they’re carrying something heavy a long way.

She stood up last, and he held out his hand to help her and then stopped with it in the air, a little away from her, and waited.

She looked at the hand. The tip of the little finger was missing, cleanly, at the first joint. There was nothing on it, no blood, no powder. He was waiting for her to decide.

She took it.

His hand closed round hers, warm and dry and enormous, and his thumb moved once across her knuckles, as if he were checking she was all there. She felt it all the way up her arm. When he let go of her at the fence, to hold the wire back for the others, she stood in the orange light with her hand still half closed, and could feel exactly where his thumb had been.

✦ ✦ ✦

His truck was on the far side of the fence, through the hole behind the blue straddle carrier, which was big enough for a fat man, as advertised. It was an old grey pickup with a canvas cover over the back and mud thrown up over the number plate, and he opened the back and helped the four of them up into it, onto a pile of old sacks and a folded tarpaulin, talking all the time.

“It’s not a limousine. I’m sorry about that. The limousine’s at the cleaners. There’s water. There’s—here.” He was pulling plastic bottles out of a crate in the corner and handing them up. Big ones, a litre and a half each. “I promised you a bottle the size of your head, Nuo. I’m a man of my word. Have two. Slowly, slowly, little sips, or you’ll be sick on my sacks. I love those sacks.”

Nuo held the bottle in both hands like a baby and drank and cried at the same time.

Evangeline stood by the tailgate and watched. She watched him give out every bottle and check that each of them could open the cap. He opened Bik’s for her when her hands shook too much. He tucked the tarpaulin round the two women who held each other, who were shivering now that the danger had stopped. Then he counted them, twice, touching each of them lightly on the shoulder or the top of the head as he went.

When he had finished, there was one bottle left. He held it out to her.

She took it. She had not drunk anything since the afternoon before. She held it and did not open it until she had looked at all four of them in the back of the truck, and seen that they were all drinking.

When she looked round, he was watching her do it. He wasn’t smiling any more.

“In the front,” he said. “You. With me.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The cab of the truck smelled of coffee and gun oil and wet dog, though there was no dog. There was a lot else. A thermos. Three empty cans of the sweet black coffee from the machines at the border bus station. A child’s exercise book with a cartoon rabbit on the cover, shoved down between the seats. And on the dashboard, held in place by a wedge of folded cardboard, a takeaway menu, greasy, creased, printed in red and yellow.

NAM’S NOODLES. Beef brisket, pork bone, wonton. River Bridge Road. Open till late. No credit cards.

Evangeline read it twice while he started the engine. Then she looked out of the window and did not look at it again.

He drove with the lights off until they reached the road. Then he turned them on and drove like an old man, at exactly the speed limit, with both hands on the wheel. He talked to the four women in the back through the little window behind his head, telling them it wasn’t far now, telling them about a hospital that had nice nurses and terrible tea, telling Nuo she’d be fine, she was tough, anybody who could cry that much for two days and still have water left over was the toughest person in the truck.

He didn’t talk to Evangeline.

She sat beside him with the bottle in her lap and watched his hands on the wheel, and the scar, and the way his eyes kept going to the mirror, and she memorised him, the way she had always memorised things without meaning to: the house, the stairs, the faces of the men who came to her father’s office at night, the crest on a silk blanket in a cedar chest. Height. Hands. Missing fingertip. Scar. Accent. The tune he hummed. The way he had waited, with his hand in the air.

At a red light at the edge of the industrial district, empty, at a quarter past three in the morning, he spoke to her without turning his head.

“You didn’t cry,” he said.

She looked at him.

“Two days in that box, and the little one was falling apart, and you didn’t cry once. Did you?” He was watching the light. “And you stood in front of them. When the lock went. I saw you.”

The light went green. He didn’t move the truck.

“Who are you?” he said.

She looked at the menu on the dashboard, and then at his face, and then at the green light, and back at him. She thought about the man in the van saying Your Highness. She thought about the one shot from the tower.

“Nobody,” said Evangeline.

It was the first word she had said to him.

He looked at her, then, properly, for the first time since the container door: a long, careful, sideways look, as if she were a lock he’d been sent to open and had found, on closer inspection, to be a lot more complicated than the drawings.

“Right,” he said. “Course you are. Me too.”

He drove on.

chapters.title: He Leaves Her at a Hospital
chapters.desc: Harbourside General, half past three in the morning. He won’t give his name. He doesn’t look back. She memorises his face anyway.
chapters.epigraph: “Name.” “No.” — the emergency entrance, Harbourside General
chapters.content:
He stopped the truck fifty metres short of the hospital, in a side road behind a row of shuttered pharmacies, under a streetlight that didn’t work.

“This is as far as I go,” he said, through the little window to the back. “The big doors with the red sign. See them? Emergency. Walk in, sit down, tell the lady at the desk you need a doctor and the police, in that order. They’ll be nice to you. If anyone’s not nice to you, tell them you’ll come back with a very big man.”

He got out and went round and let the tailgate down, and helped them out one by one. Bik, with her jaw set. The two who held each other. Nuo, who had drunk both her bottles and was hiccuping. He held each of them by the elbow until they were steady on the pavement and then let go, carefully, as if one of them might tip over.

Evangeline got out of the cab by herself.

He came round the front of the truck and stopped in front of her. He had a pencil in his hand, a short one, and a page torn out of the rabbit exercise book, and he was writing on it against the bonnet in big square letters.

“Give this to whoever comes,” he said. “Police. Not hospital people, police. And if there’s a detective called Song, give it to him, he’s the only one I’d—” He stopped. “Just give it to the police.”

She took it and read it. A container number. A row. The name KUANG YAOMING, and under it, Deputy Port Commissioner. Look at the papers for row K. Look at the last four years. Nothing else. No name at the bottom.

“Don’t tell them about me,” he said. “Tell them a man let you out and drove you here, and you didn’t see his face because it was dark, and he was very ugly. That bit’s true.” He was already turning away. “Go on. Go inside. You’ll be warm.”

He had his hand on the door of the truck when she caught his sleeve.

She hadn’t decided to. Her hand did it: reached out and took hold of the black cloth at his wrist, and held on.

He stopped. He looked down at her hand on his sleeve, as if it were something that had landed there and he wasn’t sure if it would sting. Then he looked at her.

He was close. She had to tip her head back to see his face, and she did, and for one second his eyes went to her mouth and stayed there, as if he’d forgotten where he was and what he’d just done and who might be coming round the corner. She felt it like a hand on her skin.

“Name,” said Evangeline.

For a second she thought he would tell her. Then his face shut, the way a safe door shuts, without any fuss.

“No,” he said, quite gently.

She let go of his sleeve.

He got into the truck and started the engine. He didn’t look at her again. He pulled away from the kerb at exactly the speed limit, without lights, and turned the corner at the end of the road. Then the street was empty except for the five of them and a cat on a wall and the hum of the big hospital up the hill.

Evangeline stood on the pavement and looked at the corner where the truck had been.

Then she turned round, and took Nuo’s hand, and walked the others up to the doors with the red sign.

✦ ✦ ✦

What he did not see her see, because he wasn’t looking back, was the truck.

She had looked at it carefully, the whole time he was helping the others down. A grey pickup, old, a dent in the back left wing. Canvas cover with a tear in one corner, mended with orange tape. Mud on the plate, but not all of it. Mud runs down, and the bottom half of the numbers is always cleaner than the top. She had read the last three.

What she did not see him do, because he had turned the corner, was stop.

He pulled in at the end of the next road, where he could see the hospital doors in the wing mirror, and turned off the engine, and sat there.

He sat there twenty minutes or more. He watched them go in. He watched a nurse in green come out and look up and down the street and go in again. He watched two police cars arrive with their lights going and no sirens, and then a third. He watched the doors open and shut, open and shut.

She was in. They were all in. The job was done, and it hadn’t even been his job. He should go home.

He didn’t go home.

He was thinking about her hand on his sleeve. It had been cold, and it hadn’t shaken. Name, she had said, as if she had a right to it, as if she’d already decided she was going to have it and was only giving him a chance to hand it over before she took it.

Nobody, she’d said, in that low flat voice. He didn’t believe it for a second.

He was thinking about her mouth when she said it, which was worse, and which he had no business thinking about at all, in a side road at four in the morning with a dead man in a tower behind him. He thought about it anyway. He sat with both hands on the wheel and thought about it until he made himself stop.

At four o’clock, the night shift came on at West Basin, and someone would be going up the tower stairs about now. He started the engine.

He did not look at the hospital again. He watched it in the mirror until the road bent and took it away.

✦ ✦ ✦

The nurses were kind and the tea was terrible, as promised.

They put the five of them in a side room off the emergency department with a curtain instead of a door, and brought blankets, and more water, and sweet tea in paper cups, and a young doctor with tired eyes. He looked at their feet and their wrists and the inside of Nuo’s elbow where the needle had gone in, stopped talking, and then went on in a gentler voice.

Evangeline sat on the end of a trolley and let them look at her. They took blood. They put a drip in the back of her hand. They asked her name and she told them. Lin. Evangeline Lin. Walled City. The nurse writing it down paused at the address and glanced up at her, and then wrote it down without saying anything, which meant that the nurse was from the city and knew what the Walled City was and who lived in it, and had decided to be polite.

Nuo would not let go of her hand.

“Did he—” Nuo whispered, the third time the curtain moved and it was only a porter. “Is he coming back?”

“No,” said Evangeline.

“Was it him? The noise. At the tower.”

Evangeline looked at her.

“Sleep,” she said, and Nuo put her head down on Evangeline’s lap on the trolley like a much younger child, and after a while she slept.

✦ ✦ ✦

Detective Song Wei Long came at five.

She heard him before she saw him: a man’s voice in the corridor outside, low and level, asking the nurse something, and the nurse answering. She knew the voice. She had known it since she was eleven years old and a young policeman had come to the house in the Walled City to ask her father about a warehouse fire, and had sat at the kitchen table with his notebook and drunk her mother’s tea and called her father Mr. Lin in a voice with nothing in it at all, so that her father, who frightened most people, had sweated through his shirt.

He pulled back the curtain.

He was older. Grey at the temples. The same face, long and narrow and composed, like something made of winter. He looked at the room, at the four women asleep or pretending, and at her on the trolley with Nuo’s head in her lap.

He stopped.

“Evangeline,” said Song Wei Long.

She inclined her head.

He came in and pulled the curtain shut behind him and stood at the end of the trolley with his hands in the pockets of his coat. He didn’t take out his notebook. He looked at her for a while, the way he had looked at her father across the kitchen table: patiently, as if he had all night and the truth would come out if he waited.

“The officer downstairs says you were in a container at West Basin,” he said. “For two days.”

She nodded.

“And that a man let you out. And drove you here.”

She nodded again.

“And that you have something for me.”

She took the folded page out of the pocket of her cardigan and held it out. He read it standing up, once, and she watched his face not change, and then watched it not change a little more.

“Kuang Yaoming,” he said.

She waited.

“The night shift found Deputy Commissioner Kuang in the old control tower at West Basin forty minutes ago,” said Wei Long, in exactly the same tone, “with a bullet in him. And a man downstairs from him with a headache and his shoelaces round his wrists.” He folded the paper along its creases and put it in his pocket. “This man who let you out. What did he look like?”

Evangeline looked at him.

She thought about a scar through an eyebrow. The tip of a finger, missing at the first joint. A voice like gravel in a bucket saying good, good, you’re all doing fine. The silence by the third post. No, he had said, and got into his truck.

“Tall,” she said.

Wei Long waited.

“How tall?”

“Tall.”

He looked at her for a little while longer. The corner of his mouth moved. On anyone else it wouldn’t have counted as a smile.

“You haven’t changed at all,” he said. “You used to sit under the stairs in your father’s house when I came. I always knew you were there. You never made a sound.” He took his hands out of his pockets. “All right. Tall. I’ll write that down.” He did not take out his notebook. “I’ll need you all to make statements later today, when you’ve slept. And Evangeline. Whoever took you knew who you were. Didn’t they?”

She didn’t answer.

“That’s what I thought,” said Wei Long, and pulled the curtain back, and went out.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her father came at six.

She heard him on the stairs, too, before anything. Her father had been a big man all his life, broad and heavy, and he had always walked like it, but this morning he was running, and a big man running up hospital stairs at six in the morning sounds like furniture falling down them. Then the curtain was pulled back so hard that one of the hooks came off the rail, and Lin Jian was standing there in his old brown coat over his pyjamas, with his grey hair standing up on one side, and Raiden behind him in a T-shirt inside out, white-faced, for once not smiling at all.

“Evangeline,” said her father.

He came across the room in two steps and put his arms round her.

She went still. She always did, when anyone touched her first; she couldn’t help it, any more than you can help shutting your eyes when something comes at your face. Her father knew it. He held on anyway. He was shaking. She could feel it through the coat, a deep slow shaking that went all through him like a ship’s engine, and she stood inside it with her drip arm held out to the side and Nuo awake now and staring, and after a moment she lifted her free hand and put it flat against his back, between his shoulders, and left it there.

“I’m here,” said Lin Jian, into her hair. “I’m here. I’m here. They told me—I didn’t know. Two days. I didn’t know. I had men looking. I had every man I have looking.”

Over his shoulder, Raiden met her eyes. He looked as if he had been crying in the car and had stopped just before the door. He lifted his hand, a small helpless wave, and tried to smile, and didn’t manage it.

Two days, paper twin, his face said. Two days, and none of them found you.

She looked back. I know.

✦ ✦ ✦

Elowen came at half past six, with Zhao Zhendong behind her like a wall that had decided to follow her.

Her sister didn’t run. Elowen never ran. She walked into the little curtained room in her work clothes with soil on her cuffs and her face perfectly composed, and looked at Evangeline on the trolley, and at the drip, and at her bare black-soled feet under the blanket, and the composure went out of her face all at once, like water out of a broken vase.

She didn’t touch her. She knew better. She stood beside the trolley and held out her hand, palm up, and waited.

Evangeline took it.

Elowen held on hard and said nothing.

Behind her, Zhao looked at the four other women in the room for four seconds each. Then he turned and went out into the corridor, and Evangeline heard him say something low to someone, and heard someone answer yes, Mr. Zhao, and footsteps going away fast.

In the corridor, her father was on the phone.

He had gone out to make the call so that she wouldn’t hear it. He had always done that: gone out of rooms, closed doors, stood at the end of corridors with his back turned. And she had always heard. Every house has a place where the sound carries, and she had found them all by the time she was seven.

“No,” her father was saying, low. “No. Nobody can know. Nobody. If they knew who she is, they’ll sell it again, do you understand? Find out who. Find out who talked. I don’t care what it costs. Find out what they were going to get for her.”

Elowen’s hand tightened on hers.

On the little television on the wall in the corner, with the sound turned down, the early news had started. A reporter in a raincoat was standing outside the gates of West Basin container terminal in the first grey light, with police tape behind her and the tall cranes going up into the clouds. The words along the bottom of the screen said Deputy Port Commissioner found dead. Then Police appeal for witnesses.

Nuo was watching it. She turned her head and looked at Evangeline.

Evangeline looked at the screen.

She was thinking about a takeaway menu on a dashboard, greasy, red and yellow. River Bridge Road. Open till late. No credit cards.

And she was thinking about the way he had said no. He hadn’t said he couldn’t. He had just said it, and driven off, as if that settled things.

chapters.title: Evangeline Does Not Go Home
chapters.desc: Her father sends a car to the hospital. She sends it away. Then she asks Zhao Zhendong one question at five in the morning.
chapters.epigraph: “No.” — Evangeline Lin, to her father, for the first time in twenty-four years
chapters.content:
The car came for her at noon.

It was her father’s own car, the old black Mercedes with the cracked leather in the back that he had driven for fifteen years because he trusted it, and his own driver, Uncle Mok, who had driven her to school every morning from the age of six to the age of seventeen and had never once said more than good morning. He stood at the end of the trolley in his grey jacket with his cap in his hands.

“Your father says to bring you home, Miss Evangeline,” he said. “He’s had your room aired. He says there are two men on the door and three on the street, and nobody will come near you.”

Evangeline was sitting on the edge of the trolley in a borrowed hospital gown and the grey cardigan, which a nurse had washed for her in a sink and dried on a radiator, and which still smelled faintly of the container. Her feet were bandaged. The drip was out. Nuo had been taken away an hour ago by a social worker and a woman from a church, and had cried, and had made Evangeline promise to visit, and Evangeline had promised.

She looked at Uncle Mok.

She thought about her room at the top of the tall house in the Walled City. The narrow bed, the orchids on the sill, the door she left open a crack every night so she could hear the stairs. Two men on the door. Three on the street. The cedar chest in the attic with the blanket in it, still there, still folded, where it had been for twenty-four years. Nobody will come near you.

Nobody ever had.

“No,” said Evangeline.

Uncle Mok blinked.

“Thank you,” she said. “Tell him no.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Her father came himself at two.

He came without his coat this time, in his office clothes, with his tie loosened, and he stood at the foot of the trolley the way Uncle Mok had, and looked at her with his heavy grey face, and she could see him trying to understand what had just happened in this room. In the twenty-four years of her life, Evangeline had never once told her father no. Not about school, not about clothes, not about the photographs she was never allowed to be in or the parties she was never allowed to go to or the way he had always, at dinners, said and this is my daughter Elowen, and then, and Raiden, and never her name at all. She had not said yes, either. She had done what she was told, gone upstairs, and left her door open a crack.

“Evangeline,” said Lin Jian. “You’ve had a shock. You need to come home. It’s not safe.”

“It wasn’t safe at home.”

He flinched as if she’d hit him.

“I know,” he said, and his voice cracked. “I know. The detective told me. It was Feng.” He said the name as if it tasted bad. “From prison. He sold the story to a man, and that man sold you. I am finding out who. I will find all of them. I’ve got every man I have looking, every—”

“You had every man you have looking for two days.”

He stopped.

She hadn’t meant to say it. She didn’t say things. She looked down at her bandaged feet and felt her face go hot, and waited for him to shout, because once, long ago, when she was small, he had shouted.

He didn’t shout. He sat down, heavily, on the plastic chair by the trolley, and put his face in his hands.

“I know,” said her father, behind them. “I know.”

She looked at him. His grey hair, thinning at the crown. His big hands, the knuckles swollen now. A man who had frightened half the Walled City for thirty years, sitting on a hospital chair, crying without any sound.

She did what she always did. She reached out and put her hand on his back, between his shoulders, and left it there.

But she didn’t go home.

✦ ✦ ✦

She went to Elowen’s.

Not the shop. The house on the hill, Zhao’s house, which had more locks than any building in the city except the prison, and two dogs who had arrived with no names and now had several each, none of which they answered to. Elowen drove her there herself in the shop’s new van, with Zhao’s car following so close behind that every time Elowen braked he had to brake too, and Elowen said, “If he rear-ends us I’m going to divorce him,” without looking in the mirror, and Evangeline nearly smiled.

Elowen gave her the guest room at the end of the corridor, the one with the window over the garden. She put clean towels on the bed, folded in three and then rolled, the way their mother had done it. She put a glass of water on the bedside table. She stood in the door.

“Stay as long as you like,” she said. “Forever, if you want. Zhendong won’t mind. He’ll pretend to mind. He minds nothing that I want.”

Evangeline sat on the edge of the bed and looked at the towels.

“Ev.” Elowen’s voice changed. “Tell me what you need.”

Evangeline thought about it, carefully, because it was a real question and Elowen deserved a real answer.

“Shoes,” she said.

Elowen laughed. It came out of her too loud, and then her face crumpled, and she stood in the doorway with one hand over her mouth, laughing and crying at the same time.

“Shoes,” she said. “Right. Yes. Shoes. I can do shoes.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t sleep that night.

She lay in the guest room with the door open a crack, and listened to the house. It was a quiet house. A man walked round the outside of it every hour; she heard the gravel. The dogs breathed at the bottom of the stairs. At two in the morning, Zhao came along the corridor, stopped outside her door for a few seconds, and went away again. She knew it was him because no one else in the world walked like that, as if every floor might be mined and he’d decided to cross it anyway.

She lay and looked at the ceiling and thought about a box in the dark.

It came back in pieces. The heat. The smell of the bucket. Nuo’s voice going thin and high like a kettle. The holes in the roof, the grey spots of light that she had watched for two days as they moved across the floor, morning, evening, so that she could count the hours. The sound the lock made when it went, a flat crack like the sky breaking. The door swinging open, and the orange light coming in, and a man in it so big that for a second she had thought he wasn’t a man at all.

Hello, he’d said. Hello. Listen to me.

She thought about his hand. The size of it round hers, and the heat of it, and his thumb moving once across her knuckles in the dark between the stacks. She thought about the way he’d looked at her mouth by the hospital, for one second, as if he’d forgotten himself. Nobody had ever forgotten themselves over her. She lay in her sister’s guest room and closed her hand on the sheet, and her face went hot in the dark, and she didn’t know what to do with any of it.

She turned on her side and pulled her knees up.

She did not cry. She had not cried in the box and she did not cry now. But she lay awake until half past four, when the window began to turn grey, and then she got up and put on the cardigan and went downstairs.

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhao Zhendong was in the kitchen.

He was sitting at the long table with a bowl of congee, which Elowen made in the evenings and left on the stove for him, because he got up at four. He sat now. Elowen had taught him to; he used to eat standing up. He was in a black T-shirt with a gun in a holster under his left arm, and he looked up when she came in and looked at her for four seconds, which was what he did with everyone, the way other people said hello.

Then he got up and got another bowl down from the shelf, and filled it, and put it on the table across from his, and sat down again.

Evangeline sat.

They ate. Neither of them said anything for a while. Zhao Zhendong was the only person she had ever met who talked less than she did, and they had always got on very well, in the sense that in three years of family dinners they had exchanged perhaps a hundred words and been comfortable with all of them.

When he had finished, he put his spoon down.

She put hers down too.

“Who kills men who sell people?” said Evangeline.

“Hm,” said Zhao.

She waited.

He went on looking at her. It was the longest she had ever seen him look at anyone except Elowen. Then he turned his empty bowl a quarter turn on the table, with one finger, the way some men turned a glass.

“There’s a man,” he said. “From the border. Nobody knows his name. Big. Talks too much.” A pause. “He’s killed four of the people who move people. In five years. An official in the customs. A man who ran boats. A man who ran the trucks on the river road.” Another pause. “Last night, a deputy port commissioner.”

Evangeline kept her face still.

“The people he kills,” said Zhao, “are not good people. I’ve sold to some of them.” He said it without any change in his voice, as a fact, as if he were telling her the price of rice. “He’d kill me too, I think, one day. He doesn’t care for men like me. That’s fair.”

He looked at her.

“Stay away from him,” said Zhao.

✦ ✦ ✦

Elowen came down at five and found them sitting there, opposite each other, with two empty bowls.

She looked at her husband. She looked at her sister. She had been married to one and related to the other for long enough to read a silence as well as most people read a page.

“What did you tell her?” she said.

“Hm,” said Zhao.

“Zhendong.”

“She asked.” He got up and took both bowls to the sink and ran water into them. “I answered. She’d have found out. She’s a Lin.” He turned off the tap. “She’s the worst one.”

Elowen looked at Evangeline.

“Ev,” she said. “Whatever it is you’re thinking. Don’t.”

Evangeline looked back at her.

She loved Elowen. She had loved her all her life, the way you love the person who held your hand on the stairs when you were four and had never once let go. Elowen had been the only one, in the tall house in the Walled City, who said her name at dinners. Who came up to her room at the top of the house and sat on the end of her bed and talked to her about nothing, flowers, school, boys, and never needed her to answer. Who had cried at the hospital and laughed at the word shoes.

“I know,” said Evangeline.

She knew exactly what Elowen meant. She just wasn’t going to do it.

✦ ✦ ✦

She stayed nine days.

She bought shoes with Elowen. She made her statement to Wei Long in a small grey room at the station with a box of tissues on the table that she didn’t touch, and told him everything, exactly and in order, except the face. She visited Nuo at the church hostel, with a bag of oranges and a phone with credit on it and Elowen’s number in it, and sat on the end of Nuo’s bed while Nuo cried and talked and cried, and listened to all of it. She went to the tall house in the Walled City for dinner, once, and her father didn’t talk about her coming home, and she saw that it cost him everything he had not to.

On the tenth day, at a quarter to six in the morning, she went down to the bus station by the old ferry pier with a canvas bag over her shoulder, and bought a ticket on the first bus north.

She had looked it up. There was only one River Bridge Road in the north. It was in the border town, the last stop, three hours on the old road, where the river came down out of the hills and the bridge went over it to the other side, the side that had no flag.

She sat at the back, by the window. The bus was full of vegetable sellers going home and men with tool bags and an old woman with a chicken in a basket, and nobody looked at her, because nobody ever did.

The city slid away. The towers got lower, then fewer, then stopped. There were hills, green and steep and close, and fish farms, and villages with laundry on poles, and then more hills.

Evangeline watched them go by. She had her hands folded in her lap.

She was not frightened. She checked, and it was true. She had spent her whole life in a house where she was a secret, careful and quiet, and she had been frightened every day of it for so long that she had stopped noticing.

Now she was on a bus to a town she had never seen, looking for a man who had told her no and killed somebody in the time it takes to boil an egg.

The bus came over the top of a pass, and the river was below them, brown and wide, with a bridge across it.

chapters.title: The Woman Who Kept Showing Up
chapters.desc: Three days at a corner table in a noodle shop by the river bridge, two bowls ordered every time. On the fourth day he sits down at the cold one.
chapters.epigraph: “She orders two bowls. Every time. One for her and one that goes cold. I’ve stopped charging her for the cold one.” — Old Nam, River Bridge Road
chapters.content:
Nam’s Noodles was eleven tables, one counter, a glass cabinet with roast ducks hanging in it, and Old Nam.

Old Nam was seventy-three, or seventy-six, or eighty, depending on who was asking and whether she liked them. She was small and bent and wore the same quilted purple jacket in every season, and she had run the shop at the foot of the river bridge for fifty-one years, since before the bridge had a checkpoint on it and before the other side of the river stopped having a name. Two cats lived under the counter and were called, as far as anyone could tell, Cat and Other Cat. Old Nam did not smile at customers. She looked at them. The ones she liked she fed twice as much as they’d ordered, and the ones she didn’t like she fed exactly what they’d ordered and watched while they ate it, and they didn’t come back.

On the first day, the quiet girl came in at eleven in the morning and sat at the corner table by the window, the one with a view of the bridge and the door and the kitchen at the same time, and ordered two bowls of pork bone noodles.

She ate one. The other went cold.

She sat there until four, with a pot of tea, not reading, not looking at a phone, doing nothing at all except watching the door with her hands folded on the table. Then she paid for both bowls and left.

On the second day, the same.

On the third day, at about two in the afternoon, while Old Nam was wiping the table next to hers, the quiet girl spoke.

“Does a big man eat here?”

Old Nam stopped wiping.

She looked at the girl. Tall, straight-backed, a good grey cardigan, good shoes, new ones. A face like something carved out of pale wood and then left out in the rain. City money, and old money, and something else underneath the money that Old Nam had not seen in a long time: a person who had been quiet for so long that it had turned into a kind of strength. She had seen it in women who came across the river with nothing. She did not expect to see it in a girl with shoes like that.

“Lots of big men eat here,” said Old Nam.

“He talks,” said the girl. “A lot.”

Old Nam went on wiping the table.

That night she made a phone call on the old black phone behind the counter, the one with the cord, to a number she had never written down anywhere.

“There’s a girl,” she said. “Three days. Two bowls.”

On the other end, there was a long pause.

“What does she look like?”

“Like a heron,” said Old Nam, “that’s decided to stand in your river until you give it a fish.”

There was a sound on the line like a big man putting his forehead against a wall.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the fourth day, Lee Jun Hyuk came in at ten past eleven, out of the rain, and walked straight across the shop to the corner table, and stood over her.

She looked up at him.

She was holding a cup of tea in both hands. There were two bowls on the table: hers, half eaten, and the other one, full, steaming, with the spoon laid across the top. Her face did not change at all, but her eyes did. He saw it anyway, a small steady brightness that hadn’t been there a second ago.

“No,” said Jun Hyuk.

She waited.

“No. Absolutely not. No.” He pulled out the chair opposite her and didn’t sit in it. He stood behind it with his hands on the back, and the chair creaked. “I don’t know how you found this place and I don’t want to know. Actually I do. How did you find this place? No, don’t tell me. The menu. It was the menu, wasn’t it. On the dashboard. I knew it. I thought, she’s looking at that menu, I should move that menu, and then I thought, she’s been in a box for two days, she’s not reading menus. Stupid. Stupid. I’m stupid.”

He was aware that he was talking too fast. He was aware that Old Nam had come out from behind the counter and was standing with her arms folded, watching him with an expression of enormous satisfaction, and that the cats had both come out to watch too.

“Listen,” he said. “Listen to me. You don’t know what this is. You don’t know who I am. I’m not a nice man. You think I’m a nice man because I gave you some water. I’m not. I’m a man who was at West Basin for a reason, and you know what the reason was because you heard it. Didn’t you? You heard it. And you came anyway. On a bus. On your own. To a town where people go missing for a living. And you’ve been sitting in a window, in a window, for three days, where anyone on that bridge can see you, with your face—with that face—” He stopped. He took a breath. “Why? What do you want? Money? I’ve got money. I’ll give you money. You want me to say sorry about the tower? I’m not sorry about the tower. You want—what do you want?”

She looked at him.

Then she reached out with one hand and pushed the second bowl across the table, a few centimetres, towards the empty chair.

“Hungry?” said Evangeline.

✦ ✦ ✦

He sat down.

He didn’t decide to. His legs did it, the way her hand had done it at the hospital, and then he was sitting at the corner table in Nam’s Noodles with a bowl of pork bone noodles in front of him that she had ordered for him three days running, and it was hot, because Old Nam had swapped it for a fresh one every hour, and he was starving.

He ate. She drank her tea.

Old Nam brought a plate of roast duck that nobody had ordered and put it down between them with a bang and went away.

“You came back four days in a row,” he said, between mouthfuls, still angry, quieter now. “You don’t know me.”

She shook her head slightly, as if he’d asked the wrong question.

“What’s your name?” he said. “Your real one. Not nobody.”

She thought about it. He could see her thinking about it, weighing it. He had seen a lot of people decide whether to tell him things. He had never seen anyone do it so openly, as if they didn’t care whether he knew they were deciding.

“Evangeline,” she said.

He put his spoon down.

“Evangeline,” he said, carefully, like a word in a language he didn’t speak. It was too long for his mouth, all those pieces. It sounded like the name painted on the front of an old ship. “That’s not a name. That’s a sentence.”

She didn’t answer. But her eyes changed again, and he realised she was laughing. Somewhere deep inside, where nobody could see it, she was laughing at him.

He looked down at his noodles and didn’t like how much he liked it.

✦ ✦ ✦

He saw the car at a quarter to twelve.

A silver saloon parked on the far side of River Bridge Road, by the pharmacy, with its engine running. Two men in the front. One reading a newspaper, the other not even pretending.

He went on eating and didn’t look at it again. When he’d finished his bowl he wiped his mouth and said, conversationally, “Don’t turn round. There are two men in a silver car across the road who’ve been watching this window since I sat down. Do you know them?”

She didn’t turn round.

“Yes,” she said.

“Are they the same people who put you in a box?”

“My father’s.”

He breathed out. “Your father sends men after you.”

She lifted one shoulder. Always.

“Who’s your father?”

She looked at him. She didn’t say.

“Right,” he said. “Course.” He stood up. He put money on the table, too much. Old Nam pushed half of it back at him and he pushed it back again and she took it, neither of them looking, the way people do something they’ve done ten thousand times. “Come on. Through the kitchen. Don’t look at the window.”

She stood up. She didn’t ask where.

“I’m not taking you anywhere you’ll like,” he said, as they went past the hanging ducks and the steam and the startled cook and out of the back door into an alley full of crates and rain. “I’m taking you somewhere you won’t get yourself killed sitting in a window. For one night. And in the morning I’m putting you on a bus. And you’re going home. To your father and his silver car. And you’re never coming back here. All right?”

She walked beside him through the rain and didn’t answer.

✦ ✦ ✦

The flat was over a karaoke bar on Third Street that had closed in 2019, when the owner went across the river and didn’t come back.

You went in through a steel door at the side, and up a stairwell with no light that smelled of old beer and older cigarettes, and through a second steel door at the top that had three locks on it, and then you were in two rooms with their windows painted over black on the inside. A camp bed. A table, two chairs. A kettle, a gas ring. A row of plastic crates against one wall with lids on them. A go-bag by the door. Nothing on the walls or the floor, nothing anywhere to say a person lived here or ever had.

Evangeline stood just inside the door and looked at it.

He watched her look. He felt, for some reason, ashamed of it, which was ridiculous. It was a safe house. It wasn’t supposed to be anything.

“It’s not much,” he said. “It’s not anything. It’s four walls. Nobody knows it’s here except me and Nam, and Nam doesn’t count, because she knows everything. You can have the bed. I’ll be in the chair. I sleep in the chair anyway.”

She looked at the chair. It was by the door, facing it, a hard wooden kitchen chair with a blanket over the back.

She looked at him.

“I sleep sitting up,” he said. “Old habit. Don’t worry about it.”

He made tea. Instant coffee for him, three sugars, and for her, because he didn’t have tea, he went back down the stairs and across the alley to Nam’s back door and came back with a paper bag of tea leaves and a lecture, in two languages, about what sort of host keeps a girl like that in a place like this without tea, which he had not asked for and which Nam had delivered in full while he stood in the rain.

She drank it at the table. He sat across from her and talked, because the room was quiet and he didn’t know what else to do in it.

He talked about the bus. He talked about the rain. He talked about Old Nam, who had fed him for eleven years and threatened to poison him for nine of them. He talked about the cats, and the bridge, and the checkpoint, and the man who sold spring onions on the bridge every morning and had been there so long that both sides of the river let him through without papers because nobody could remember a time when he wasn’t. He talked about the weather on the other side of the river, which was different, he said, you wouldn’t think a river could make that much difference, but it did.

She listened.

She listened to all of it. He noticed it after a while and couldn’t stop noticing it. People didn’t listen to him. They endured him. They waited for him to stop, or they talked over him, or they laughed at him, or they were frightened of him and nodded at everything he said with their eyes on his hands. She listened as if every word he said was going into a box she was keeping somewhere, carefully, with the lid on. When he told her about the spring-onion man, she turned her teacup a little on the table, and he knew she was seeing him.

He stopped talking.

She looked up.

“You should sleep,” he said. His voice had gone rough. “Bus is at seven.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She slept on the camp bed in her clothes, with her shoes beside it, side by side, and her face turned towards the door.

He sat in the chair and didn’t sleep. He sat with his hands loose on his knees and watched the door, the way he always did, and then he found he wasn’t watching the door. He was watching her. The long shape of her under his one blanket. Her hair come out of its knot over the edge of the bed. The hand she’d left open on top of the blanket, palm up, as if she were waiting for something to be put in it.

He told himself no. He told himself several times.

At three he got up anyway. He crossed the two steps of floor between the chair and the camp bed and crouched beside it, the way he’d crouched in the door of the container, and looked at the open hand on the blanket. He could have put his own in it. He thought about how it would feel. He thought about it so hard that his hand had come up off his knee before he noticed.

Her eyes were open.

She was lying on her side, watching him, and he didn’t know how long she had been. She didn’t move. She didn’t close the hand, and she didn’t take it away. She looked at him in the dark from a foot away, and he looked back, and neither of them moved.

He stood up and went back to the chair. He sat down in it with his heart going as if he’d run up the stairs, and didn’t look at the bed again until it was light. When it was light her eyes were shut. He didn’t believe for a second that she was asleep.

In the morning he walked her to the bus station by the bridge, and bought her ticket, and stood on the pavement while she got on. She sat at the back, by the window. She didn’t wave. She looked at him through the glass, steadily, until the bus pulled away.

That was that, he told himself, all the way back up the alley.

✦ ✦ ✦

Then he went and got the truck, and followed the bus.

He followed it all the way. Three hours, down the old road, through the hills and the fish farms and the villages with laundry on poles, two cars behind it, with his cap pulled down. He watched her get off at the ferry pier in the city. He watched her get on a tram and followed it to the edge of the Walled City. Then he parked and went after her on foot up the steep narrow streets, well back, until she went in through the door of a tall old house with too many stairs. A light came on at the very top.

He stood in the street and looked at the light until it went out.

Then he drove three hours back to the border and sat up in the chair by the door, telling himself it was only to make sure she was safe.

He did it every time, after that. Every bus she ever took home. She never once looked round.

She came back three days later.

She came back with a flask of soup, which she put on the table in the flat without a word, because Old Nam had let her in. Old Nam had let her in because she had brought Old Nam a bag of oranges and a pot of white orchids, and Old Nam had looked at the orchids a good while and then given her the key.

“Nam,” said Jun Hyuk, at the bottom of the stairs.

“She brought me oranges,” said Old Nam, from her back door, not sorry at all. “In eleven years you’ve never once brought me oranges.” And she shut the door.

He went upstairs. Evangeline was sitting at the table with the flask of soup in front of her and two bowls, and two spoons, and her hands folded.

He stayed in the doorway.

“You don’t ask for anything,” he said at last. “Do you notice that? You turn up, you sit, you don’t ask for anything. You don’t want anything from me. What do you want?”

She looked at him. She took the lid off the flask. The smell of ginger and pork bone came up out of it and filled the dead little room, and for a moment it smelled like somebody’s kitchen.

She poured two bowls, and pushed one across the table, and didn’t answer.

She came back the week after that. And the week after that.

chapters.title: Lee Jun Hyuk Does Not Own Towels
chapters.desc: He dries himself with yesterday’s T-shirt. She notices. The next time she comes up the stairs, she is carrying three white towels. And on a Sunday, over a towel folded wrong, he asks.
chapters.epigraph: “You own something, you have to go back for it. Old Ko said that. Old Ko owned one spoon.”
chapters.content:
The shower in the karaoke flat was a cupboard.

It had been a storeroom once, for crates of beer, and somebody had put a tray on the floor and a plastic curtain on a rail and an electric water heater on the wall that took forever to warm up and no time at all to go cold again. Jun Hyuk never waited for it. He came out of it on a Tuesday evening in late November with the water still running off him, in a pair of black trousers, picked yesterday’s T-shirt off the back of the chair, rubbed himself down with it from his head to his arms, and dropped it on the floor.

Then he noticed she was looking at it.

She was at the table, where she always was. She had come up the stairs at six with Old Nam’s key and a bag from the market, and was shelling broad beans into a bowl, fast, without looking at her hands. She had stopped. She was looking at the T-shirt on the floor.

“What?” he said.

She looked at the T-shirt. Then at him. Then at the T-shirt.

“It’s clean,” he said. “Was clean. Yesterday. It’s a T-shirt. It dries things. That’s what it’s for, partly.”

She went back to the beans.

He didn’t know why he felt he’d lost an argument. Nobody had said anything.

✦ ✦ ✦

She had been coming for five weeks.

Twice a week, sometimes three times. On the first bus up from the city, or the second. She came up the dark stairs with Nam’s key and let herself in through the three locks, and sat down at the table, and did things. That was the only way he could describe it. She did things. She brought soup in a flask and made him eat it. She brought tea, proper tea, in a tin with a picture of mountains on it, and a teapot, and two cups that didn’t match. She brought a lamp, a small one with a paper shade, and plugged it in on the table, so that the dead black room had one warm yellow corner in it, and when he came in late from wherever he’d been, he could see the light under the door from the top of the stairs.

She never asked where he’d been.

She never asked anything. That was the part he couldn’t get past. He’d ask her questions—Does your father know you’re here? Do you have a job? Where do you tell people you go?—and she’d answer the ones she wanted to with one word, or two, and the others she’d just look at him until he stopped. But she didn’t ask. Not once. Not what do you do, or who are you, or who was the man in the tower. Not even his name.

He hadn’t told her his name.

He’d thought about it. He thought about it every time she came up the stairs. He opened his mouth to say it, sometimes, and then didn’t, because if she had his name she had a piece of him, and if she had a piece of him then one day someone would take it off her, and he knew how people took things off other people. He’d watched it done. He’d done it.

So he talked about everything else instead. And she listened.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the Tuesday of the fourth week, at twenty to six in the morning, she was crouching by a tray of white phalaenopsis at the flower market in the Walled City, checking the roots, when somebody stopped beside her.

She knew it was him before she looked up. Nobody else in the world was that big and that quiet.

He was in his black jacket with his cap pulled down and his hands in his pockets, and he wasn’t looking at her. He was looking at the market: the old men with their trolleys, the restaurant buyers, the girls from the hotels with their phones, the vans backing in at the far end with their doors open. He was looking at the vans.

“This is where they took you,” he said, low. He wasn’t asking.

She stood up with a pot in her hands.

He still wasn’t looking at her. He was watching a white van at the far end of the row, steadily, until its driver got out and started unloading lilies, and then he looked at the next one. “You come here twice a week. Tuesdays and Saturdays. On your own. In the dark.”

“Yes.”

“Not any more,” said Jun Hyuk.

He turned his head then and looked at her, and his face under the cap was one she hadn’t seen on him before, harder and much hotter than the cheerful one. It made her stomach turn over.

“Not on your own,” he said. “I’ll be here. Tuesdays and Saturdays. Twenty to six. I’ll stand by the orchids and look at vans. You won’t even know I’m here.”

She stood there holding the pot.

“I’ll know,” said Evangeline.

He was there every Tuesday and every Saturday after that, without fail, in the dark, at twenty to six, by the orchids. He drove three hours from the border to do it, and three hours back, and went to work. She never asked him to. He never asked if she minded. Some mornings he carried her trays. Some mornings he only stood there. And every time a van backed in at the far end of the row with its doors open, she felt him go still beside her, close enough that his arm was against her shoulder, and watch it, until it was only lilies. He never moved the arm away afterwards. Neither did she. They stood like that by the orchids in the dark, touching at one place, and it was all she thought about on the bus home.

✦ ✦ ✦

She came back on Friday with three towels.

They were white and thick, the best ones on the shelf at the back of the supermarket by the bus station. She took them out of her canvas bag one at a time and put them on the end of the camp bed. Each one was folded the same way: in thirds lengthwise, and then rolled, tight, like a cake.

He stood in the doorway of the shower cupboard and looked at them.

“What are those?” he said.

She looked at him as if he had asked what water was.

“I know what they are,” he said. “I know what towels are. I’ve seen towels.” He came over and picked one up. It was heavy and soft and it smelled of washing powder, the flowery kind, and very faintly of something else, something green, like leaves after rain. He held it as though it might do something. “I don’t—I don’t need these. I don’t own towels.”

She waited.

“It’s a rule,” he said. “You don’t own things. Old Ko said that. You own something, you have to go back for it. You leave a room with nothing in it and you never have to go back. You can walk out of it in the middle of the night and you’ve lost nothing.” He was still holding the towel. “Old Ko owned one spoon. He kept it in his top pocket. When he died, they buried it with him. That was everything he had in the world, a spoon.”

She looked at the towel in his hands.

“Who was Old Ko?” she said.

It was the first question she had ever asked him.

He didn’t answer right away. He sat down on the end of the camp bed, which complained, with the towel in his lap, and looked at it.

“A sergeant,” he said. “In a unit on the border. When I was a kid. He took me in.” He turned the towel over. “He wasn’t a good man, exactly. Nobody in that unit was a good man. But he was good to me. He taught me to read. He taught me to talk. You know why I talk so much? He told me to. He said, when people are scared, you keep talking, so they hear a voice that isn’t scared, and they follow the voice. He said a quiet man with a gun frightens people. A man with a gun who won’t shut up about the weather—people stop being frightened of him, and they do what he says.” He laughed, a little. “It works. Mostly. It worked on you. A bit.”

She didn’t say anything.

“He died years ago,” said Jun Hyuk. “Heart. In a truck. He was fifty-eight and he’d been shot four times and stabbed twice and blown off a bridge once, and his heart just stopped, on a Tuesday, on the way to buy cigarettes.” He folded the towel back up, badly, all wrong. “So. That was Old Ko. And I don’t own towels.”

He put it back on the bed.

She got up from the table, and came over, and picked up the towel he’d folded wrong. She shook it out. She folded it in thirds, lengthwise, and then rolled it, tight, the way it had been, and put it back with the others.

Then she went back to the table and sat down.

He looked at the three white rolls on the end of his bed.

✦ ✦ ✦

He used them.

Not that night. That night he showered and came out and reached for the T-shirt on the chair out of habit, and she was at the table, and she didn’t look up, and he stood there with his hand on the T-shirt and the water running down his back. Then he said a word he’d learned at ten from a man who’d later been eaten by a crocodile, and went and picked up one of the towels.

It was soft.
