He stood in the middle of the room in the black trousers with a white hotel towel round his shoulders and his hair dripping, and felt ridiculous, and felt something else he didn’t have a name for, like putting his hand on a radiator in a cold house.

It was just a towel, he thought. At the table, she turned a page of the book she wasn’t reading, and he could have sworn she was smiling at it.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next week, he left the towel on the back of the chair, wet, in a heap.

When he came back the next night, late, it was gone. It was on a hook. There had not been a hook. Now there was a hook, a small brass one, screwed into the wall beside the shower cupboard with a screwdriver that he also had not owned until that week and that was now in the drawer of the table, beside a box of plasters and a roll of tape and a packet of sewing needles and three candles and a box of matches, none of which he had owned either.

The towel was hanging from the hook, straight, folded once over it. The other two were on the end of the bed, rolled.

She was filling the place up, one small thing at a time, and he was letting her.

There was a lamp on the table, and the lamp was on, and under it was a plate with a bowl turned upside down over it to keep it warm. Under the bowl was rice, and salted fish, and a fried egg with the edges gone crisp, and greens, and a pair of chopsticks laid neatly across the side of the plate.

He stood and looked at it.

He thought: if I have to leave tonight, I’ll have to leave the towels.

He thought: I’d come back for them.

He sat down and ate.

✦ ✦ ✦

She caught him on a Sunday.

She had come up early, the first bus, and let herself in at nine, and he was sitting on the end of the camp bed with his back to the door, which he never did, with a pile of laundry on the bed beside him. It was the first time she’d ever seen him not facing the door. He had the three towels laid out on the blanket. He was folding them.

He was doing it badly.

He was frowning at the first one with enormous concentration, the way she imagined he frowned at locks. He folded it in half the wrong way. He looked at it. He unfolded it. He folded it in thirds, but the thirds weren’t even, and when he tried to roll it, the end stuck out sideways like a tongue.

“Thirds,” he was muttering. “Then roll. She does it in two seconds. Thirds, then roll.”

Evangeline stood in the doorway with her bag over her shoulder.

He unrolled it again. He laid it flat. He smoothed it with his big hands, the one with the missing fingertip and the one with the old white scar across the knuckles, carefully, the way she’d seen him touch the shoulder of a frightened nineteen-year-old in the back of a truck. He folded it in thirds again. Better. He started to roll.

“There,” he said, under his breath, pleased with himself.

He heard her.

He didn’t jump. He went still, the way a big animal goes still in long grass. Then he turned his head and saw her in the doorway, and went red.

It went all the way up, from the neck of his T-shirt to the scar in his eyebrow.

“It’s a rule,” he said. “Folding. Old Ko. He said—you keep your kit square. Everything square. It’s discipline. It’s nothing to do with—I wasn’t—”

She put her bag down.

She came across the room and sat down on the end of the camp bed beside him, not touching, with the pile of towels between them. She picked up the one he had been rolling. She unrolled it. She laid it flat on her knees.

Then she took his hand.

She had never done that, not since the container. She took his right hand by the wrist, and he let her. She put it flat on the towel, at the near edge, and put her own hand on top of it, and moved it a third of the way across. She lifted, and folded. She moved his hand again. Lifted, and folded. Then she put his hand at the end, and her hand over his, and rolled, her fingers on his knuckles, until there was a white roll on her lap, tight, perfect, like a cake.

She let go.

He didn’t move his hand. It was still lying on the towel on her knees where she had left it.

He was looking at her. She could feel him looking. He had stopped talking. In five weeks she had never once heard him stop talking for this long; there was always something, the weather, the bus, the cats, a man on a bridge who sold spring onions. Now there was nothing. The room was so quiet she could hear the water heater ticking as it cooled.

She didn’t look up. She knew if she looked up something would happen, and she didn’t know yet what it would be, and she wasn’t ready to find out.

So she picked up the next towel, and laid it on her knees, and waited.

After a while, his hand moved.

He folded the second one himself, in thirds, with her watching. He rolled it. It wasn’t perfect. The end was a little loose.

She didn’t fix it.

“You’ve got it,” said Evangeline.

She looked up.

She hadn’t meant to look. She wanted to see if he’d heard, and he was right there, a foot away on the end of the camp bed, with his face still red to the scar and his eyes gone dark, and he wasn’t looking at the towel at all.

He lifted his hand off the towel, the way he’d lifted it by the third post at West Basin, and held it in the air near her face without touching her. His fingers weren’t steady.

“I want to kiss you,” said Jun Hyuk. It came out of him low and rough, as if it had been sitting in his chest for weeks and had finally pushed its way up. “I’ve wanted to since the hospital. Since before. I’m not going to, unless you—” He stopped. “I’m asking. That’s all. I’m asking.”

She looked at his hand in the air.

Then she leaned forward an inch, until her cheek was against his palm.

He made a sound she had never heard from him. His hand closed round the side of her face, gently, as if it might come apart, and he bent his head and kissed her.

The first time he barely kissed her at all. His mouth on hers for one breath, warm and careful and asking again, and then lifting away an inch to look at her, the way he’d counted the women in the back of the truck, to make sure.

She didn’t let him make sure. She took a handful of his T-shirt and pulled him back.

The second time wasn’t careful. The towel slid off her knees onto the floor and the pile between them went over, and his other hand came up into her hair and the knot came down, and she heard herself make a sound against his mouth that she hadn’t known she had in her. He kissed her the way he did everything that wasn’t talking, with his whole attention. The water heater ticked. The camp bed creaked under the two of them. She kept her fist in his shirt.

When he drew back, he didn’t go far. He stayed with his forehead against hers, breathing as if he’d carried something up six flights, and for once he didn’t say a word.

Neither did she. She sat on the end of his camp bed with her hair down and her mouth burning and three white towels on the floor, and found that she was smiling, properly, where he could see it.

He saw it. He lifted his head and stared at it as if it were something he’d been told about all his life and never believed in.

She leaned in and kissed him again herself, short, once, so he’d know it hadn’t been an accident. Then she bent down and picked the towels up off the floor, one by one, and laid the first one flat on her knees, and waited for his hand.

chapters.title: Rules of a Safe House
chapters.desc: He comes home at three in the morning with someone else’s blood on his sleeve and finds the lamp on. So he writes seven rules on the back of a noodle menu. She follows six of them.
chapters.epigraph: “7. Don’t come back.” — the back of a menu from Nam’s Noodles, taped to the inside of a door
chapters.content:
He came up the stairs at ten to three in the morning on the first Saturday in December and saw the light under the door, and for one long horrible second he thought someone had found the flat.

Then he remembered the lamp.

He stood on the dark landing with his hand inside his jacket and his heart going like a truck engine, and made himself breathe. It was the lamp. The little lamp with the paper shade, on the table, that she left on. She had started leaving it on when she went, so that he would come home to it. He had told her not to. She had looked at him. It was on every time.

But it was three in the morning, and she always caught the six o’clock bus back to the city, and the lamp was on, and he could hear, faintly, through the steel door, a page turning.

He unlocked the three locks and went in.

She was at the table, in her coat, with a book open in front of her that she had not been reading, and a teapot, and two cups. She looked up. She looked at his face first, the way she always did. Then she looked down at the sleeve of his jacket.

He looked down too. He’d forgotten about the sleeve. There was a dark stain on it, stiff, from the wrist almost to the elbow.

“It’s not mine,” he said.

She waited.

“It’s not mine,” he said again, and his voice came out much louder than he meant, and he heard it bounce off the painted windows. “What are you doing here? It’s three in the morning. You get the six o’clock bus. You always get the six o’clock bus. Why are you here?”

“You said ten.”

“What?”

“You said you’d be back at ten.” She didn’t raise her voice. She never did. “It’s three.”

He stood in the doorway with the blood on his sleeve.

He had said ten. On Thursday, he’d said, I’ve got something on Friday night, I’ll be back by ten, don’t come up. And she had come up, at five, with soup, and found the flat empty, and waited, and ten had come and gone. Eleven. Midnight. The last bus. One. Two. And she had sat at this table in the dark room in her coat and not known whether he was alive, and turned pages in a book she wasn’t reading, and left the lamp on.

“You waited,” he said.

She didn’t answer.

“Anyone could have come up those stairs,” he said. “Anyone. You don’t know who knows about this place. Neither do I, not really. If someone had come up those stairs, if someone had—” He couldn’t finish it. “You’d have opened the door. Wouldn’t you? If someone knocked. You’d have thought it was me.”

She looked at him.

“No,” she said.

“How would you know?”

“You don’t knock,” said Evangeline. “You’ve got a key.”

He shut his mouth.

✦ ✦ ✦

He went into the shower cupboard and took off the jacket and the shirt under it and stood under the water until it went cold. He watched it go down the drain, pink and then clear. He didn’t think about the man whose it was. He’d stopped thinking about them, mostly, years ago. You couldn’t do this and think about them, any more than you could be a surgeon and think about every patient’s mother.

He thought about her instead, sitting at the table since five o’clock with the lamp on.

He’d kissed her on the end of his camp bed six days ago, with a towel on her knees. He’d kissed her again on the Tuesday, at twenty to six in the morning, behind the orchid trays at the flower market, until the old woman who sold them coughed. He’d thought about nothing else all week. And tonight he’d come up the stairs with a man’s blood on his sleeve and seen the light under the door, and the first thing he’d thought was that someone had found her there. Because of him. Because he’d let her stay long enough to be found.

When he came out, with a white towel round his neck, because he used the towels now, he had stopped pretending he didn’t, she had made fresh tea. She had put his jacket and shirt in a bucket of cold water in the corner, with salt. She had not asked whose blood it was.

He sat down at the table opposite her.

Then he got up again and went to the counter and found a pencil, and the menu from Nam’s Noodles that had been on his dashboard, and which he had brought upstairs after the hospital, for reasons he hadn’t examined. He turned it over to the blank side. He sat down again.

“Right,” he said. “Rules.”

She raised her eyebrows slightly.

“You keep coming here,” he said, writing. “Fine. I can’t stop you. I’ve tried. Nam won’t help. She’s on your side. Everyone’s on your side. Even the cats. So if you’re going to keep coming here, there are rules, and you follow them, or I’ll—” He didn’t know what he’d do. “I’ll be very upset. Rules.”

He wrote. He wrote in big square capitals, the way Old Ko had taught him to write, pressing hard, so that the pencil nearly went through the cheap paper.

1. DON’T OPEN THE DOOR. EVER. I HAVE A KEY.

2. NO PHONE IN HERE. LEAVE IT AT NAM’S.

3. LIGHTS OFF BY THE WINDOW.

4. IF I’M NOT BACK BY THE TIME I SAY, YOU LEAVE. NAM KNOWS WHERE.

5. DON’T TOUCH THE BAG.

6. DON’T WAIT UP.

He stopped. He looked at the list. He looked at her across the table, in the lamplight, with her coat still on and her hands round her cup. There was a mark on the back of her left hand, small and faded, where the drip had been in the hospital, in October. It had been two months.

He looked at her mouth, and thought about Sunday, and the towels on the floor, and the light under the door an hour ago.

He wrote the last one.

7. DON’T COME BACK.

He turned it round and pushed it across the table to her.

She read it the way she read everything, all the way through and then again. Her eyes went down the list and stopped at the bottom.

Then she looked up at him, and he saw her eyes change, the way they had in the noodle shop.

“Seven,” she said.

He nodded.

She looked at it a moment longer. Then she took the pencil out of his hand, and folded the menu once, neatly, and got up, and went to the door. There was a roll of tape in the drawer now, because she had put it there. She taped the menu to the inside of the steel door, at eye height, her eye height, where she would see it every time she came in.

She came back to the table and sat down and drank her tea.

✦ ✦ ✦

She followed the rules, every one of them, exactly and without complaint, the way she did everything. That was what got him.

She left her phone at Nam’s. Every time. She came in through the back door of the shop and put it in a jar on the shelf behind the counter, between the chilli oil and the soy sauce, and Nam put a saucer over it, and she came up the stairs with nothing that could be traced. She never opened the door. He tested her once, the second week. He knocked from the landing and stood there five minutes, and she didn’t open it. When he let himself in with his key she was sitting at the table, and she looked at him so hard that he apologised.

She kept the lights off by the window. She didn’t touch the bag. She never once, in all the weeks, touched the go-bag by the door, or the plastic crates along the wall, or anything in them, or asked what was inside.

And when he said a time, and wasn’t back by it, she left. She went down to Nam’s. Nam made her tea in the back room and sat with her, and when he came in, late, wrecked, through the back door of the shop, she’d be there at the little table among the sacks of flour, with her coat on, waiting, which was not technically waiting up, because she was not up in his flat. She was up in Nam’s. He pointed this out. She looked at him. Nam laughed so hard she had to sit down.

She followed one to six.

She broke seven every time.

She came in through the steel door, and closed it, and turned the three locks behind her, and every time, before she took her coat off, she looked at the menu taped at her eye height, and touched it, once, lightly, with one finger, on the seventh line. Then she looked round at him.

He started waiting for it. He’d be in the chair, or at the table, or in the shower cupboard with the curtain half open, and he’d hear the locks, and he’d find he was holding his breath until she touched it.

✦ ✦ ✦

He caught himself at the window on a Thursday.

It was a quarter past nine in the morning, and the first bus from the city got in at nine. He was standing by the painted-over glass in the back room, where there was a scratch in the black paint the size of a coin that he had made years ago, so he could see the bridge and the bus stand without being seen. He was standing with his eye to the scratch, watching the bus stand, and the bus had come in, and people were getting off, the vegetable sellers, the men with tool bags. She wasn’t one of them.

He stood there until the last person had got off.

Then he stood there some more.

What are you doing, Lee, he thought. She didn’t come on Thursdays. She came on Tuesdays and Fridays and sometimes Sundays. It was Thursday.

He didn’t move from the window.

She came on the eleven o’clock bus. He saw her get off it, the last one, tall in her grey coat with her canvas bag, and stand on the pavement for a moment and look up and down River Bridge Road, left, right, at the cars, at the pharmacy, at the men on the bridge. Then she walked the wrong way. She went past Nam’s, and round the corner, and into the market, and he lost her among the stalls, and a quarter of an hour later she came out of the far side of the market in a dark blue coat instead of a grey one, with her hair under a scarf, and went down the alley to Nam’s back door.

He realised he was smiling, with his eye pressed to a scratch in some black paint.

She’d been doing it every time. Of course she had. The silver car from her father, the men on the bridge, the people who’d sold her once and could sell her again. Every time she came here she came the long way round. She changed buses. She changed coats. She lost whoever was behind her, and she did it so well that he had never once seen anyone following her up River Bridge Road, not in seven weeks.

She’d sat three days in a window with her face to the glass for anyone to see. All this care was for the flat, and for him in it.

Nobody had ever done anything to keep him safe.

He went and sat down in the chair by the door, heavily, and put his face in his hands.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Princess,” he said that afternoon, when she’d made him eat a second bowl of rice. It came out of him without his thinking. “This isn’t a palace, Princess. You don’t have to feed me like I’m going to the slaughterhouse.”

She went still.

He saw it happen. He had been watching her face for seven weeks, and it hardly ever moved, and now it moved: not much, a flicker, the kind of flicker you see in a person’s face when you’ve touched a bruise you didn’t know was there. Her hand stopped on the rice pot. Her eyes went somewhere else.

“Hey,” he said. “Hey. I didn’t mean—”

“Don’t,” she said, low.

“All right.” He held up both hands. “All right. No Princess. It’s a joke. It’s a word. It’s what you call girls with good shoes. I won’t—”

She looked at him. She took her hand off the rice pot. Whatever it was had gone back behind her face, and the door was shut, and he didn’t know what he’d seen.

He didn’t say it again that day. He thought about it all night, sitting in the chair. He didn’t know why it mattered.

But when she’d gone for the six o’clock bus, he went to the steel door and looked at the menu. Under his seven rules, in pencil, in small, neat, upright letters, there was an eighth one that he hadn’t written.

8. Use the towel.

He stood there with his hand flat on the door.

Then he took the pencil out of his pocket and wrote, underneath it, in his big square capitals:

9. GET THE BUS BEFORE DARK.

On Friday, when she came in and closed the door and turned the three locks, she looked at the menu. She touched seven, the way she always did. Then she touched nine. Then she looked round at him, sitting at the table pretending to read a newspaper that was three days old.

This time he didn’t pretend.

He put the newspaper down. He’d been thinking about it since Thursday at the window, and all night in the chair, and he’d decided somewhere around four in the morning that he was done. Done writing her rules he hoped she’d break. Done kissing her as if she might change her mind halfway through, and then walking her to the bus, and standing at a scratch in the paint for the rest of the day like a dog at a gate. He was thirty-two. He’d walked into worse rooms than this.

He got up and crossed it.

She stood by the door with her coat still on and watched him come. She didn’t move. When he stopped in front of her, close, closer than he’d ever stood, she had to tip her head back to keep looking at him, and she did.

“I’m going to kiss you,” said Jun Hyuk. His voice was low and not steady at all. “Properly. Not like Sunday. Not like I’m sorry about it. I’ve been kissing you all week as if I was going to have to give you back.” He was so close now that she could feel the words.

He didn’t wait for her to answer. He took her face in both his hands and kissed her.

He did it as if he’d been thinking about nothing else for two months, which he had. He kissed her the way a man drinks water after a long road, and backed her up against the steel door, and she made a small astonished sound against his mouth. She didn’t break, or vanish, or change her mind. She put a hand on the back of his neck and pulled him down the rest of the way and kissed him back. The steel door was cold against her shoulders and his hands were warm on either side of her face. Somewhere down in the alley Nam’s radio was playing the song about the girl on the ferry.

When she drew back, she didn’t go far. She stood with her forehead against his chin and her hand still on his chest, where his heart was pounding.

“Yes,” she said. A little late, to a question he hadn’t asked.

He laughed, shakily, into her hair.

She caught the half-past six bus, because rule nine was rule nine. He walked her to it. At the bus stand by the bridge, in front of the spring-onion man and two vegetable sellers and a woman with a chicken in a basket, he bent down and kissed her again, quickly, the way people do at bus stops, as if he’d been doing it for years.

The woman with the chicken said something approving. The spring-onion man raised one of his hats.

Then he stood on the pavement and watched the bus all the way to the end of River Bridge Road, and didn’t bother with the scratch in the paint at all.

chapters.title: She Watches the Exits
chapters.desc: Footsteps on the stairs, the lamp off, and a back window he thought nobody knew about. She was there first. Then, in Nam’s back room, she tells him what she was raised to be.
chapters.epigraph: “Every house has a place where the sound carries. I’d found them all by the time I was seven.”
chapters.content:
It was the second week of January, and cold, the wet grey border cold that got into the walls of the karaoke flat and stayed there, and he was cleaning his things at the table.

He did it every night. It didn’t matter where he was or how late it was or how tired. He laid an old grey cloth on the table, not one of her towels, a rag the size of a towel he’d kept in the truck for years, and took out what he carried, and cleaned it, piece by piece, the way Old Ko had taught him at eleven years old by the light of a hurricane lamp in a tent. He didn’t talk while he did it. It was the only time of day that he didn’t. Old Ko had said that a man who talks while he does this is a man who doesn’t respect it, and Jun Hyuk had respected very little in his life but he respected that.

She sat across from him with her tea and watched.

She’d watched him do it before, a dozen times. She never said anything. She didn’t look away, either, the way he’d seen other people look away, as if he were doing something obscene at a dinner table. She watched his hands the way she watched everything, steadily, missing nothing.

Sometimes, when he reached for the cloth, she’d already pushed it across the table to where his hand would be.

That was the night they heard the stairs.

✦ ✦ ✦

He heard it half a second after she did. Later, that was the part he kept coming back to.

The street door at the bottom of the building opened. It had a squeak in the bottom hinge that he had never oiled, on purpose. Then feet on the first flight. More than one pair. Heavy. Not trying to be quiet, and then, at the turn of the stairs, trying.

He was on his feet with his hands already moving, putting things away into the bag, fast, without looking. He turned to the table to tell her to get down.

The lamp was off.

He hadn’t seen her move. The table was empty. The teacup was gone, the book was gone, the chair was pushed in. The room was dark except for the thin grey line under the door from the landing.

“Evangeline?” he said. Nothing above a breath.

“Here.”

It came from the back room. He went through, fast, low, with the bag over his shoulder, and found her by the window. Not the window with the scratch in the paint. The other one, the small one at the end, over the sink, that looked out onto the back of the building and the iron fire escape that had rusted half off its brackets in 2015 and that nobody ever used. He had loosened that pane himself, years ago. He’d taken out the old putty and put in new putty that he could cut with a knife, and painted over it, and told nobody, because it was the way out, and the way out was a thing you told nobody.

She had it open. She had the pane lifted out of the frame and leaned against the wall, and she was standing beside the gap with her coat on and her bag over her shoulder, holding it, waiting for him.

The cold air came in. Somewhere below them, on the stairs, a man said something, low, and another man laughed.

Jun Hyuk looked at the window. He looked at her.

“How,” he said.

She just looked at him. Later.

He went first, because he’d go first even if the building was on fire and she was the one holding the door. He went out onto the rusted fire escape, which groaned under him, and up, not down, because down was the alley and the alley was where people waited, and up was the roof. He reached back. She was already there, climbing out after him, quick and neat, her long skirt gathered in one hand. She put the pane back in the frame from outside. He hadn’t known you could. She did it by feel, fast, and pressed the edges, and it held.

They were on the roof by the time the men reached the top of the stairs. They heard them knocking, then not knocking, then something heavier. They didn’t wait to hear what. They went across the roof of the karaoke building, and over the low wall onto the roof of the pharmacy, and across that, bent double in the dark, with the lights of the bridge orange below them and the river black, and down the iron ladder at the far end into the yard behind Nam’s kitchen, where Other Cat was sitting on the bins and looked at them with no surprise whatsoever.

At the bottom of the ladder, in the dark of the yard, he turned round and pulled her into him.

He didn’t say anything. He held her against him with both arms so hard her feet came off the ground, with his face in her hair and his heart slamming against her cheek, and then he put her down and kissed her, hard, in the yard behind the noodle shop, with the bins and the cat and the men somewhere above them on the stairs, as if he’d only just found out she was alive.

“You were there first,” he said against her mouth, roughly. “At the window. Before me. Don’t ever—” He couldn’t finish it. He kissed her again instead.

✦ ✦ ✦

Nam put them in the back room, among the flour sacks, and didn’t ask anything. She brought tea. She brought a bowl of noodles for him that he hadn’t asked for, and a bowl for Evangeline, and went back out to the shop and stood behind her counter and watched the street through the steam on the window with her arms folded, like a small purple general.

He couldn’t sit. He stood by the back door, with his shoulder against the frame, where he could see the yard.

“Who were they?” said Evangeline.

“Doesn’t matter. Men.” He was looking at the yard. “Somebody whose trucks I set on fire last year, probably. They’ve been asking round the town. They’ll have the wrong building. They’ll have the right building and the wrong floor. I’ll find out.” He breathed out. “It doesn’t matter. I’m not going back there for a week. That’s all. It doesn’t matter.”

It did matter. He knew it did. He kept seeing the lamp off, and the chair pushed in, and the empty table. She’d done it all in the half-second before he heard the door.

He turned round.

“How did you know about the window?” he said.

She was sitting on a sack of flour with the bowl of noodles on her knees. She looked up at him.

“Second time I came,” she said.

“The second time you came, you were there for an hour. You sat at the table. You didn’t go in the back room.”

“I went to fill the kettle.”

He stared at her.

“The paint’s different,” said Evangeline. “On that pane. Newer. And there’s no dust on the sill. There’s dust on every other sill.” She looked down at her noodles. “And it’s the only window that faces the fire escape.”

He sat down.

He sat down on a sack of rice across from her, in Nam’s back room, with the bag between his feet, and looked at her. He had been in this business since he was nine years old. He had been in units with men who’d fought in four wars. He had worked with people the governments of three countries paid very good money to know where the doors were. He had never, in his life, met anyone who noticed the putty on a window the second time they filled a kettle.

“Who taught you that?” he said.

She didn’t answer. She held the bowl in both hands and looked into it.

He waited. He was good at waiting, when he had to be. He didn’t talk. It was hard. He sat on the sack of rice and kept his mouth shut, and the steam came up out of her bowl, and in the shop Nam’s radio was playing an old song about a girl on a ferry.

“Nobody,” said Evangeline at last.

“Nobody. Right. Nobody again.”

“Nobody taught me.” She turned the bowl a little in her hands. “I taught me.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She told him then. Not all of it, he worked out later, but more words than he had ever heard her say. She said them looking at her bowl, in her low flat voice, without stopping, as if she wanted to get to the end before she changed her mind.

“I grew up in a house where I was a secret,” she said. “I wasn’t allowed in photographs. Not school ones, not family ones. If there was a camera, someone took me out of the room. At dinners, when people came, I wasn’t at the table. I was upstairs, or I was under the stairs, or I was under the table. My father would say, this is my daughter Elowen, and this is my son. He never said my name.” She turned the bowl. “Nobody told me why. I didn’t ask. I thought it was something I’d done.”

He didn’t move.

“So I learned the house,” said Evangeline. “Every house has a place where the sound carries. A stair. A pipe. A corner of the kitchen. I’d found them all by the time I was seven. I knew every way out. The coal door. The roof over the scullery. The window on the second landing that doesn’t lock. I sleep with my door open so I can hear the stairs. I’ve always done it. I can’t sleep with it shut.” She looked up. “I watch the exits. I watch the people. I don’t make any noise. I was very good at it. Nobody ever saw me.”

“I saw you,” said Jun Hyuk. It came out before he could stop it.

She looked at him.

“In the container,” he said. “I opened the door and you were standing in front of them. You weren’t hiding. You put yourself there.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

She thought about it. He watched her think.

“I’d been hiding behind doors all my life,” she said. “I was tired of it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t ask why she’d been a secret. He wanted to. He could feel the question sitting in his mouth like a stone. But he’d sat across a lot of tables from a lot of people who had a thing they didn’t say, and he knew what it looked like when the thing was so big that if you said it out loud the room would change shape, and she had that look.

So he asked something else.

“The Princess thing,” he said. “In the flat. When I said it. Is that why?”

She went still, though not as much as before.

“My father was paid,” said Evangeline, “to make me disappear. When I was three days old. He kept me instead.” She held his eyes. “He thought I might be worth something.”

He sat still.

“Who paid him?”

“People who wanted a problem moved.”

He thought about the van at the flower market, which she had told him about once, in four sentences, in December. He thought about the man in the van saying something to her, which she had not told him, and which he had known, from the way she didn’t tell him, that she had heard. He thought about her father’s silver car on River Bridge Road.

He thought about a word. Princess. You don’t have to feed me like I’m going to the slaughterhouse.

“Oh,” he said. “Oh, hell.”

She looked back down at her bowl.

“I’m not a princess,” said Evangeline. “I’m a daughter. I wanted to be a daughter.”

He didn’t say anything. For once in his life he couldn’t think of a single thing. He sat on Nam’s sack of rice with his big hands hanging between his knees, and looked at her, and the song on Nam’s radio ended and another one started, and he didn’t hear it.

Then he got up off the rice sack and sat down beside her on the flour, which made a cloud, and put his arm round her shoulders, and pulled her in against his side. She let him. She put her head on his shoulder and went on holding her bowl, and after a while she started eating her noodles again, as if nothing had happened, with his arm round her.

He didn’t call her Princess again. Not ever.

✦ ✦ ✦

Lunar New Year was the twenty-second.

He moved, for that week, to the room over the tyre shop by the river, the one with no windows at all, and she didn’t come, because he didn’t tell her where it was, and because it was New Year and she would be in the Walled City with her family. Nam told him she had come into the shop on Friday and put her phone in the jar and sat at the corner table for one bowl of noodles and gone away again, and that she had asked nothing, and that she had looked, Nam said, like a heron that’s been told the river’s closed.

He spent New Year’s Eve in the room over the tyre shop with a packet of instant noodles and the radio. He’d spent most of them like that. It didn’t bother him. New Year was for families, and he didn’t have one, and you didn’t miss things you’d never had.

He told himself that twice. The second time he said it out loud, which didn’t help.

On the second day of New Year, the twenty-third, at a quarter to eleven in the morning, Nam called him on the phone with the cord.

“Get over here,” she said, and hung up.

He went through the back door of the shop and into the room with the flour sacks. Evangeline was sitting at the little table, in a red jumper, which he had never seen her wear, with her hair in a plait over one shoulder. In front of her was a plastic box with a lid, and a bottle of black vinegar, and two pairs of chopsticks.

She looked up at him.

“You didn’t come on the six o’clock bus,” he said. It was the first thing he could think of. “You came on the nine. There wasn’t a six o’clock. It’s New Year.”

She took the lid off the box.

Dumplings, thirty or so, in neat rows, with the frilled edges all going the same way. Somebody had made them by hand, the way somebody else had once taught her. They were still warm. She must have carried the box inside her coat on the bus.

“I made them,” she said.

He sat down.

She put a pair of chopsticks in his hand and pushed the vinegar towards him and sat back with her own hands folded and watched him eat. He ate six without stopping. They were pork and cabbage and ginger, and they were the best thing he had ever put in his mouth, and he was trying to think of how to say that without sounding like a madman when he bit into the seventh and his teeth hit something hard.

He stopped. He took it out.

A small silver coin, the old kind, washed clean. At New Year somebody always puts one in a single dumpling, and whoever gets it has a lucky year.

He looked at it in his palm.

He looked at her.

Her face did not move at all. Her hands were folded on the table. But she was looking at the coin in his hand, and her eyes had gone bright, and he understood that she had known exactly which one it was.

She’d marked it somehow, a pleat or a fold he’d never spot, and let him eat six first so he wouldn’t guess.

“You did that on purpose,” he said.

She picked up her own chopsticks.

He closed his hand round the coin. It was warm.

“Nobody’s ever—” he said, and stopped, because Nam was in the doorway, and because his voice had gone, and because there wasn’t an end to that sentence that he knew how to say.

He put the coin in his top pocket, where Old Ko had kept his spoon.

Then he leaned across the little table, past the vinegar, and kissed her, in front of Nam, in front of the flour sacks and the cats, for long enough that Nam said something rude in the dialect from across the river and went back to her counter.

chapters.title: The Night He Had a Fever
chapters.desc: A knife wound he stitched himself, a week of lying about it, and forty degrees. For once in his life he can’t talk. So she does, all night.
chapters.epigraph: “When people are scared, you keep talking, so they hear a voice that isn’t scared, and they follow the voice.” — Sergeant Ko Baek-san, who never met her
chapters.content:
He lied to her for six days.

He was bad at it. She knew on the Saturday, when he came up the stairs at eleven at night and stopped on the landing outside the door for a count of ten before he put the key in the first lock, which he had never once done. She knew when he came in and sat down at the table instead of going to the shower, and when he reached across the table for the teapot and stopped halfway and sat back, and when he laughed at something he’d said about the cats and the laugh stopped halfway, as if somebody had shut a door on it.

“I’m fine,” he said, before she’d said anything at all. “I’m tired. Long day. Big man, long day.”

She looked at the way he was sitting. Upright, too straight, his left arm held close against his side.

“It’s nothing,” he said. “Pulled something. Getting out of the truck. I’m old. Thirty-three next month. Practically dead.”

She waited.

On Monday he wore a jumper, though the flat was warm for once, and kept it on. On Tuesday he moved the camp bed so it was against the wall, and she watched him do it, and watched him stop halfway and stand with one hand flat on the wall and his eyes shut, breathing through his nose. On Wednesday he wasn’t there when she came, and there was a note on the table in his big square capitals, BACK THURSDAY 8PM. RULE 4. and under it, smaller, DON’T WORRY.

She worried.

She did it the way she did everything, without any noise. She went home on the six o’clock bus. She sat in her room at the top of the tall house in the Walled City with the door open a crack and did not sleep, and in the morning she went down to the kitchen before anyone was up and took the first-aid box out of the cupboard under the sink, the big one, the one her mother had kept stocked for twenty years because Lin Jian’s men came home with things they couldn’t take to hospitals. She took out what she thought she would need. She put it in her canvas bag, under a jumper.

She got on the first bus north.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was a quarter past four on Thursday afternoon when she came up the dark stairs, and the lamp wasn’t on.

She stopped on the landing.

He’d said eight. Rule four was for if he wasn’t back by eight. It was four. She should go down to Nam’s, and drink tea in the back room among the flour sacks, and wait.

She put her ear to the steel door.

At first she heard nothing. Then she heard something so low through the steel that she wasn’t sure it was a sound at all: his voice, going on and on in a mutter, without stopping, like a radio left on in an empty room.

She didn’t knock. He had a key and so did she.

She opened the three locks and went in.

✦ ✦ ✦

The room was dark and smelled wrong.

It smelled of sweat, and of something sweeter and worse under it, a smell she knew from her father’s men, from the kitchen table in the Walled City at two in the morning when she was twelve and had come down the back stairs and seen what was on it. She found the lamp by touch and turned it on.

He was on the camp bed.

In four months she had never once seen him lie down. He slept in the chair by the door, sitting up, facing it. Now he was on the bed against the wall, on his right side, with his knees drawn up and the blanket kicked off onto the floor, in his jumper and trousers, and he was shaking, the whole length of him, so hard that the frame of the camp bed rattled against the wall, steady, like a train going over a bridge.

And he was talking.

“—open it,” he was saying, low and fast, with his face to the wall. “Open it. Open it, open it, it’s fine, just open it, just look, just look, it’s eleven, it’s not my job, it’s eleven, Ko, Ko, it’s not my—open it—”

She knelt down beside the bed.

She put the back of her hand on his forehead, the way her mother used to. It was like putting her hand on the side of a kettle.

He didn’t know she was there. His eyes were half open and they weren’t looking at anything. His lips were cracked. He was still talking, the same words, round and round, the way water goes round a drain.

“Jun Hyuk,” said Evangeline.

She had never said his name. He had never told it to her. Nam had, in December, in the back room, without being asked: His name’s Lee Jun Hyuk, if you want it, and he’ll kill me for telling you, and he won’t, because he can’t cook. Evangeline had kept it in the box with everything else and never taken it out.

She took it out now.

“Jun Hyuk. It’s me.”

He stopped talking.

For a second the room was completely quiet except for the rattle of the bed frame. His eyes moved. They found her face, close to his, in the lamplight. They didn’t know her.

“Princess,” he whispered. Then his face crumpled. “No. No. Not that. Sorry. Sorry, I said I wouldn’t.”

“It’s all right,” said Evangeline.

“It’s not.” He was shaking harder. “It’s not all right. It’s eleven. I opened it. I opened it after. Two days after. I should have opened it at the—”

“I know,” she said, though she didn’t. “I know. Let me look.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She cut the jumper off him with the scissors from her sewing kit, because he couldn’t lift his arms. The T-shirt underneath was stuck to his left side, and it was dark there, and wet, and the smell was worse.

She soaked it off with warm water from the kettle. It took twenty minutes. He talked the whole time, but not to her: to Ko, to somebody on a river road. She didn’t listen to the words. She listened to the voice for when it changed, the way her father’s drivers listened to an engine.

Under the T-shirt there was a wound along his left side, low, below the ribs. Eight centimetres, maybe more. A knife, a long straight cut. He had stitched it himself. She could see that at once, because the stitches went in from one direction only, the direction a right-handed man would go if he was doing it in a mirror. Black thread. Eleven stitches. Neat. He’d done it well.

It hadn’t been enough.

The skin all round the wound was red and tight and shiny, and swollen up in a ridge so the stitches were straining in it like a fence with too much behind it. It was hot to the touch, even hotter than his forehead. At the lower end, a thin red line ran out from the cut and down towards his hip, across the white skin, like a crack in a plate. And there was a yellowish place at the bottom of the wound where the stitches had already started to pull through, and a smell coming out of it.

She sat back on her heels and looked at it.

She knew enough to know it was bad. Not enough to know how bad.

She got up. She put the blanket over him, though he kicked it off at once. She went to the door, and down the dark stairs, and out through the alley to Nam’s back door, because rule two was no phone in the flat, and she had never broken it, and she wasn’t going to now.

✦ ✦ ✦

Elara answered on the fourth ring.

“Ev?” Her little sister’s voice was thick with sleep. Elara was in her final year of medical school, on placement at Harbourside General, and slept at odd hours, in odd places. “Ev, it’s—what is it? Where are you? Whose phone is this?”

“I need you to tell me what to do,” said Evangeline.

There was a pause on the line. Then Elara’s voice changed completely. Evangeline had never heard her little sister sound like that: clear and fast and level, all the sleep gone out of it.

“Tell me what you see.”

Evangeline told her. The fever. The shaking. The wound, eight centimetres, self-stitched, eleven sutures, the redness, the heat, the swelling, the pus at the lower end, the red line running down towards the hip. The talking. The way he didn’t know her.

“How long since the injury?”

“Six days. I think.”

“Is he breathing fast? Is his heart going fast?”

Evangeline thought about it. “Yes.”

“Is he confused? Does he know where he is?”

“No. He’s talking to someone who isn’t there.”

Elara breathed out.

“Ev,” she said. “He needs a hospital. That’s an infected wound and it’s spreading. That red line is the infection going up the lymph channels. He’s got a fever, his heart’s racing, he’s confused. That’s how sepsis starts. People die of this. Young strong people. He needs IV antibiotics, he needs fluids, he needs a proper surgeon to open that wound and wash it out—”

“He can’t.”

“Ev—”

“He can’t,” said Evangeline. “If he goes to a hospital, they’ll ask. Then they’ll find out.”

There was a long silence on the line.

“Who is he?” said Elara.

Evangeline didn’t answer.

Another silence. She could hear her sister breathing. In the shop, beyond the door, Nam’s radio was playing, and the cats were arguing under the counter.

“Okay,” said Elara at last, in the clear level voice. “Okay. Listen to me. I’m going to tell you exactly what to do, and you’re going to do all of it, and if any of the things I tell you to watch for happen, you put him in a car and take him to a hospital whether he can or not, and you call me from the car. Do you promise?”

“Yes.”

“Do you have something to write on?”

Evangeline took the pencil from beside Nam’s phone and turned over the order pad.

“Go,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

The stitches had to come out. Elara said it twice. The wound was full of infection with nowhere to go, and it had to be opened so it could drain. Take them all out. Every one. Then wash it out, a lot, with clean water that had been boiled and cooled, with salt in it, a teaspoon to two cups, and use more than you think, keep going until what comes out is clean. Don’t stitch it again. Leave it open. Pack it, gently, with clean gauze soaked in the salt water, loose, not tight, so it can drain from the bottom. Cover it. Change it twice a day.

Antibiotics. Elara named two. Nam’s cousin had a pharmacy on the other side of the market, and Nam’s cousin asked no questions of anyone who came through Nam’s back door. Nam took the order pad out of Evangeline’s hand without a word and went.

Paracetamol for the fever, on the hour Elara said, not more. Water, as much as he’d take, a sip at a time, with a little sugar and salt in it. Cool cloths on his forehead and his neck and under his arms. Not ice on the skin. Wrapped.

Watch for: if he gets more confused. If he can’t stay awake. If his skin goes blotchy, or cold at the hands and feet while his body’s hot. If he stops passing water. If the red line keeps climbing past where it is now. Mark where it is now, Elara said. With a pen. Then you’ll know.

“Any one of those,” said Elara, “and you go. Promise me again.”

“I promise.”

“Ev.” Her sister’s voice wobbled, just once. “Ev, do you love him?”

Evangeline stood in the back room of Nam’s Noodles with the phone in her hand and the order pad gone and the radio playing.

She thought about a white towel folded badly in thirds. About a coin in a dumpling, in a big hand. About the way he talked to Nuo in the back of the truck, and listened to the weather on the other side of the river, and waited, with his hand in the air, for her to decide.

“Call me at three,” said Evangeline, and hung up.

✦ ✦ ✦

She took the stitches out with the nail scissors from her sewing kit, boiled for ten minutes in the kettle, and the tweezers from her mother’s first-aid box.

She did it by lamplight, kneeling beside the camp bed, with one hand flat on his hip to hold him still. He fought her at the first one. He was strong even with forty degrees in him, much stronger than she was, and his arm came round and knocked the lamp, and the light swung wildly round the black walls.

She stopped.

She thought about what he had told her, in November, with a towel in his lap. When people are scared, you keep talking, so they hear a voice that isn’t scared, and they follow the voice.

She had never in her life talked to make anyone feel better. She hadn’t talked to make anyone feel anything. She had spent twenty-four years making no sound at all.

She put the lamp straight. She put her hand back on his hip.

“I’m going to take out the stitches,” said Evangeline.

Her voice sounded strange in the dark room, low and flat and much too loud.

“There are eleven,” she said. “You did them yourself. They’re good. Very straight. You did them well. They’re just in the wrong place now. They’re holding in something bad. I’m going to take them out, one by one, and it’s going to hurt, and then it’s going to be better.” She cut the first one. He flinched. She drew it out. “That’s one. Ten more.”

He had gone still. The muttering had stopped. His eyes were half open, looking at the wall.

“That’s two,” she said. “You’d be talking now, if you were me. You’d tell me about the weather. It’s raining. It’s been raining since four. Nam says it’ll stop on Saturday. Nam’s always wrong about the weather. That’s three. The cats are under the counter. Other Cat stole a prawn off the cook’s board this afternoon. Nobody saw but me. That’s four.”

She kept going.

She talked through all eleven stitches. She talked about the cats and the rain and the prawn. She talked about the man who sold spring onions on the bridge, whom she had seen that morning, and who had been wearing two hats, one on top of the other. She talked about the orchids on the sill in her room in the Walled City, which were white, and which she had grown from a single plant her mother gave her when she was nine. Then, without meaning to, she talked about her mother: her hands, her soup, the way she had folded towels.

She took out the eleventh stitch. She washed the wound with boiled salt water from Nam’s biggest jug, cup after cup, while he shook and she talked and the water came out of it, pink and yellow and then, at last, clear.

She packed it. She covered it. She drew a line on his hip with a biro where the red streak ended, and wrote the time beside it, in small neat letters.

Then she sat on the floor beside the camp bed with her back against the wall and his head close to her shoulder, and put a cool wet cloth on his forehead, one of her white towels, and held it there, and kept talking.

✦ ✦ ✦

He woke at ten to three.

At first he didn’t know where he was, and afterwards that was the part that stayed with him. He had always known. He had woken up in more places than he could count, in trucks and tents and cellars and hospital corridors, and he had always known, before he opened his eyes, exactly where the door was and who was in the room and how far it was to the nearest thing he could use.

He opened his eyes and there was a lamp, low, with a paper shade. And a ceiling he knew. And a voice, low and flat and steady, close to his ear, going on and on about soup.

“—and she always put the ginger in first. Before the bones. She said if you put it in after, the soup knows. It tastes like you weren’t paying attention. Elowen does it the other way and it’s wrong, and I’ve never told her. I’ve never told anybody. You can’t tell her. She’d—”

He turned his head.

She was sitting on the floor by the bed, against the wall, with her knees drawn up and a bowl of water beside her and a pile of gauze, and her hands were wet, and there was something on the front of her red jumper that might be blood. Her hair was coming out of its plait. Her face was grey with tiredness under the lamp. She was holding a towel to his forehead with one hand, and with the other she was peeling back a dressing on his side, gently, a little at a time, to look.

She was changing his bandage at ten to three in the morning, on the floor, in a room that smelled of salt water and fever and blood, with her hands steady, talking to him about soup.

She was not afraid of the wound, or the smell, or the blood on her jumper, or the gun on the table, or the bag by the door, or anything he had done or would do. She was looking at the inside of his side as if it were an orchid root that needed checking.

For four months he had told himself he let her keep coming because the world was full of men in vans and he was the one standing between them and her. Lying there with the fever going out of him like a tide and her hand on his forehead, he saw that she had been standing in a doorway too, every time she came up those stairs. What she kept out was the river road, and the box he went to sleep with in his nose, and the eleven.

“Evangeline,” he said. It came out as a croak.

She stopped talking.

She looked at his face and saw he knew her. Her mouth shook, once, and then it was steady.

“You’re awake,” she said.

“You know my name,” he said. “You said it. I heard you.”

“Nam told me,” said Evangeline, and when he croaked that he was going to kill Nam, she said he could do it later, and put the dressing back. “Drink this.”

She held a cup to his mouth, water with sugar and salt in it, and he drank, a sip at a time, the way she told him to, watching her over the rim.

At three o’clock exactly, she got up and went down the stairs to Nam’s, and he heard her voice faintly through the floor, low, on the phone, saying better, I think, yes, the line hasn’t moved, yes, I promise, and then she came back up and sat down on the floor beside him again and put the towel back on his forehead.

He wanted to say something. He didn’t know what. He didn’t have a single word for it, and he had words for everything.

“You can talk,” he said instead. “You can really talk.”

She looked at him.

“Only when it’s an emergency,” said Evangeline.

The fever broke at a quarter past five. He felt it go, all at once, like a hand opening, and the sweat came out of him and soaked the blanket, and he started, for no reason at all, to laugh, weakly, with his eyes shut.

She didn’t ask why. She changed the towel.

chapters.title: Four Syllables
chapters.desc: Three weeks of healing, a spoon for his birthday, and a man who has gone quiet for the first time in his life. He’s been practising four syllables in the shower. She decides the rest.
chapters.epigraph: “That’s not a name. That’s a sentence.” — Lee Jun Hyuk, November, before he learned it
chapters.content:
A wound left open heals from the bottom up.

Elara explained it on the phone, on the second day, in the clear level voice. You don’t close it. You let it fill in by itself, from the inside, a little more every day, and you keep it clean and keep it packed and change the dressings twice a day, and in two or three weeks there’s new pink skin across the top, and a scar, and it’s done. It takes longer than stitches. It leaves a worse mark. But it doesn’t go bad again, because there’s nowhere for the bad to hide.

“Tell him to lie still,” said Elara. “Tell him if he lifts anything heavier than a teacup I’ll come up there and stitch him to the bed.”

Evangeline told him.

“She sounds terrifying,” said Jun Hyuk, from the camp bed, where he had been lying for two days because he couldn’t do anything else. “I like her. Does she want to come up and terrify me in person? I could do with the company. You don’t talk.”

Evangeline didn’t answer.

She changed the dressing at eight in the morning and eight at night. She learned to do it quickly, peeling the old gauze back a little at a time, washing the wound with the boiled salt water, packing the new gauze in loosely, the way Elara said. She checked the line she’d drawn on his hip with the biro. On the first morning the red streak had gone back a centimetre from it. On the second, three. On the fourth there was no streak at all, just the line, and the time beside it in her small neat letters, and he lay looking down at it while she worked.

“You wrote the time,” he said.

“Elara said.”

“You wrote it very neatly. For four in the morning. In the dark.” He was quiet a moment. “Most people’s handwriting goes, when they’re frightened.”

She pressed the edge of the dressing down.

“I wasn’t frightened,” said Evangeline.

He looked at her. She didn’t look up.

“Liar,” he said gently.

✦ ✦ ✦

She stayed.

It wasn’t a decision, exactly. On the first night she slept on the floor beside the bed, sitting up against the wall, in case. On the second night she slept on the floor lying down, with one of the towels for a pillow, in case. On the third, he said, “This is ridiculous,” and tried to get up and give her the bed and got halfway before the wound pulled and he had to lie down again, grey in the face, swearing at the ceiling in two languages. She went down to Nam’s and came back with a second camp bed, which Nam had produced from somewhere without explanation, and put it up against the opposite wall, and lay down on it, with her door open, as it were, to the stairs.

Rule nine said get the bus before dark. She didn’t get the bus. He didn’t say anything about it.

He didn’t say much about anything, and that was what she couldn’t place. She turned it over on the third day and the fourth and the fifth like a mahjong tile that didn’t fit any hand. He had always talked. Since the container, since the first word, he had never stopped. About the weather, the cats, the bridge, Old Ko, the noodles, the rain on the other side of the river. He talked when he was happy and when he was angry and when he was frightened and when he was eating. He talked, she had thought, the way other people breathed.

Now he lay on the camp bed with his hands folded on his chest and watched her.

He watched her make tea. He watched her change the dressing. He watched her sit at the table in the lamplight with her mending, sewing a button back onto his good shirt, which she had found in the bottom of the go-bag, though she had not touched the bag. He’d handed her the shirt himself. He watched her and said nothing, for minutes at a time, and when she looked up he looked away, or shut his eyes, or said something about the cats, too fast, and then stopped again.

She thought he was angry.

She thought about it for two days and decided it must be the window. Or the bag. Or the stitches, which she had taken out without asking. Or the name, which she had said when he hadn’t given it to her, in the dark, to make him come back. Or the fact that she had seen him like that, shaking, talking to a dead man about eleven of something, on a camp bed with his knees drawn up like a child. Men like her father did not forgive you for seeing them like that.

On the sixth night, when she had changed the dressing and was packing the gauze away, she said, without looking at him, “I can go.”

He opened his eyes.

“What?”

“Back to the city. You’re better. Nam can do the dressings.” She snapped the lid of the first-aid box shut. “You don’t have to have me here.”

He didn’t answer at first.

“Is that what you think,” he said at last, “this is?”

She looked at him.

He looked back at her. Then he looked up at the ceiling, and put one big hand over his eyes, and laughed, a short helpless laugh, with no breath in it.

“Go to sleep, Evangeline,” he said, behind his hand.

She lay down on the second camp bed, with her face to the door, and didn’t sleep.

He had said her name, the whole of it, all four pieces, in the dark. And then he had laughed as if somebody had hit him.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the first of March he was thirty-three.

She knew because Nam told her. Nam had known him eleven years and said he had never once had a birthday in all of them, because he didn’t know when it was. The first of March was the date on the first papers anyone had ever made for him, when he was eighteen, by a man in a back room in a border town who’d needed a date to put on the form and had picked one out of the air.

“So it’s not his birthday,” said Nam, in the back room, chopping spring onions. “It’s the birthday of a piece of paper. He thinks that’s funny. It’s not funny. Nothing he thinks is funny is funny.”

On the morning of the first of March, when Evangeline came back up the stairs from Nam’s with the breakfast, she put a small paper parcel on the table beside his bowl.

He was sitting up now, in the chair, not the bed. The wound had closed over at the top, pink and new and shiny, a long raw line under the dressing that she still changed every night. He looked at the parcel.

“What’s this?”

She sat down and poured the tea.

He unwrapped it. His big hands were careful with the paper, as if it might be the important part.

It was a spoon.

An old one, silver, small, the kind you’d use for sugar or for a soft-boiled egg, with a plain handle worn thin at the neck by a great many years of other people’s hands. She had found it in the market in the Walled City, on a tray of old cutlery at the back of a stall that sold broken clocks. She had gone through a whole tray of them before she found it.

He held it up in the lamplight.

He didn’t say anything. He looked at it, turning it over. The bowl of it caught the light from the paper shade and threw it, small, across his face.

“Old Ko had one spoon,” said Evangeline.

His hand stopped turning it.

“You said,” she said, “you own something, you have to go back for it.” She put the teapot down. “So now you have to go back for something.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He was quiet for so long that she thought she’d made a terrible mistake.

He sat in the chair with the spoon in his hand and looked at it. He didn’t look at her. His face had gone still, the way it had by the third post at West Basin, in October, when he came back from the tower. His eyes were dark. His mouth was shut. She watched him, and waited, and the tea got cold.

Then he put the spoon in the top pocket of his shirt, carefully, where he kept the coin from the dumpling. He buttoned the pocket.

He picked up his bowl and started to eat his breakfast.

He didn’t say thank you. He didn’t say anything at all, for the whole of breakfast, and the whole of the morning, and most of the afternoon. But every so often, she saw, his left hand went up and touched the pocket, lightly, as if he were checking that it was still there.

She began to see it then. Everything else he talked about: the weather, the cats, the rain, the dead men, the river road. He talked so that nobody would hear what was underneath. When something got all the way down to where there wasn’t any talking, he went quiet.

She thought about the six days since the fever, and the way he had watched her, and looked away, and said nothing.

She sat at the table that afternoon with her mending, and did not sew a single stitch.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the eleventh of March, a Saturday, he had a shower.

He had been forbidden, until then. Elara had said sponge baths only, and nothing near the wound, and he’d endured it for three weeks with a patience that had astonished Nam and had nearly killed him. Now the wound was closed. Elara said, on the phone, yes, fine, a quick one, don’t scrub it, pat it dry, and if he’s an idiot about it I’ll know. So at six o’clock in the evening he went into the shower cupboard and drew the plastic curtain, and the electric heater ticked and hummed on the wall.

Evangeline was at the table. She was shelling peas into a bowl, fast, the way she did beans.

She heard the water start. She heard it run while the heater warmed up, which he had never once waited for before. Then she heard him step in.

Then she heard him say something.

Under the noise of the water, low, to himself, the way he talked to himself when he thought nobody was listening. She couldn’t hear the words. She could hear the shape. A word, and then a pause, and then the word again. A word with pieces. He was saying it slowly, and then a little faster, and then slowly again, the way people say the name of a town over and over before they get on a train.

Four pieces.

Her hands stopped on the peas.

She sat still at the table with a pod open in her fingers and listened, through the plastic curtain and the water, to Lee Jun Hyuk practising her name.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came out with a white towel round his neck, the way he always did now, in a clean black T-shirt, with his hair wet. He’d patted the wound dry, as instructed. He was carrying himself straight for the first time in a month.

He sat down at the table across from her.

He didn’t say anything. He picked up a pea pod out of the pile and opened it with his thumb, badly, and the peas went everywhere, across the table and onto the floor, and he looked at them.

“I’m not good at that,” he said.

She said nothing.

He picked up another. He opened it more slowly. The peas stayed in. He ran his thumb down the inside, the way he’d seen her do, and they fell into the bowl, five of them, one by one, with five small sounds.

He looked at the bowl. Then he looked up at her.

“Evangeline,” he said.

He said it carefully, all four pieces in order, like a man carrying a full bowl across a room. In November he’d told her it wasn’t a name, it was a sentence. On the night of the fever it had come out of him rough and broken. Now he said it in the lamplight, at the table, with the peas, as if he’d practised it in the shower to get it right, which he had.

She looked at him.

He looked back.

He didn’t say anything else. He didn’t say that’s a nice name, or it’s still too long, or anything about the cats. He’d said what he came to say, and he sat there with his big hands on the table and a pea pod in one of them, and waited, the way he had waited at West Basin with his hand in the air.

She put down the pod she was holding.

She got up. She came round the table. He watched her come, and didn’t move, and his face went still and dark, the way it had over the spoon.

She stood beside his chair. He was so big that sitting down, his head came nearly to her shoulder.

She put her hand on his face.

She’d touched his face a hundred times since the towels. At the bus stop, in the doorway, across the table at Nam’s. This was different, and they both knew it. She put her palm flat against his cheek, rough with a day’s stubble, warm from the shower, and felt him go still under it, and kept it there.

Then she bent her head and kissed him.

He kissed her back the way he had since the steel door, as if he’d been waiting all day to, and she didn’t let him slow down. She kissed him until his hand came up into her hair and his breath went ragged, and then she drew back an inch, and took his hand, the one with the missing fingertip, and stood up straight, and pulled.

He didn’t move.

“Evangeline,” he said, not steadily. “The wound—”

“You’re allowed a teacup,” said Evangeline. “I’m lighter than a teacup.”

He stared at her. It was the closest thing to a joke he’d ever heard her make, and she’d made it with her hand in his, standing over him, and her face perfectly serious except for her eyes.

He stood up.

✦ ✦ ✦

He could see she’d decided, the way she decided everything, without any fuss. And the moment he saw it, he stopped waiting.

He picked her up.

Wound and all, the whole length of her, off her feet, against him, and she gasped and put her arms round his neck, and he kissed her on the way across the dark little room, and laid her down on the camp bed as if he’d been carrying her towards it since November.

The lamp was still on, on the table, low, with its paper shade. She reached out from the bed and turned the shade so the light fell on the wall instead of on them, and left it on. She wanted to see him. He understood that and his heart nearly went.

He touched her as if he was checking she was real. His fingertips went over her face first, the way they always did, eyebrows, nose, cheekbone, jaw, and then they didn’t stop at her jaw. They went down the side of her throat to her collarbone, lightly, as if he were reading something written there, and stopped at the hollow at the base of her neck, where her pulse was. He pressed two fingers there and held them. Feeling it go.

It was going fast.

“Still you,” he said. Barely a sound.

She undid her own cardigan. He watched her do it, every button, without breathing. When it fell, he didn’t look down. He looked at her face, the whole time, as if her face were the part he’d been waiting for.

She lifted his T-shirt, carefully, over the pink new line along his side that she’d made out of a wound, and put her mouth on the scar beside it, an old one, across his ribs. The breath went out of him. Then he wasn’t careful any more, and neither was she, and the camp bed took the weight of both of them with a long complaining creak that neither of them heard.

He was slow. She’d thought he would be. He was slow the way he’d been slow with the towels, as if it were the most important thing he’d ever been asked to do and he’d die before he got it wrong, and every time he found something new, the inside of her wrist, the curve of her waist, the place under her ear that made her catch her breath, he stopped and looked at her face to be sure. And every time she pulled him back down, so he’d know she had decided all of it.

He didn’t say a word. Not one. The man who talked to everyone about everything ran out of words somewhere between her collarbone and the lamp, and didn’t find them again, and didn’t look for them. He listened to her instead, with his hands and his mouth and the whole of his attention, as if every breath she took was a sentence he was writing down.

She held on to him with her hands on the stars of old shrapnel scars across his back, which she found in the dark and didn’t ask about, and felt him shake under her fingers, and held on harder.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards, he didn’t go back to the chair.

She felt him think about it. She was lying with her head on his chest and her hand over his heart and the lamp still on, low, against the wall, and she felt every muscle in him remember the chair by the door, the way it had been remembered every night for twenty-four years.

She pressed her hand down flat.

He breathed out. He stayed.

“I like you here,” said Evangeline, low.

He laughed. It came out of him helpless and shaking, the laugh from the end of the fever, and his arm tightened round her, and he turned his face into her hair and didn’t let go.

On the table under the lamp, the bowl of peas sat half full, and on the floor around his chair were all the ones he’d dropped, scattered, green, like something spilled on purpose.

chapters.title: A Silver Ring With Coordinates Inside
chapters.desc: He’s going across the river for two weeks. The night before, cleaning the rifle at the table, he puts a plain silver band down beside her teacup instead of a proposal.
chapters.epigraph: “If I don’t come back, this ring has the coordinates to a life where no one can find you. If I do come back, you’re mine.”
chapters.content:
After the eleventh of March, he couldn’t stop touching her face.

He couldn’t stop touching her at all, if he was honest, and he’d stopped pretending otherwise. He’d done all the waiting he was ever going to do, and now she’d told him in every way she had that she didn’t want him to wait for anything. So he didn’t. When she came in through the steel door and turned the three locks and touched rule seven on the menu, he was already crossing the room. When she stood at the gas ring, he came up behind her and put his arms round her waist and his chin on top of her head, and she’d once thought that would make her scream, a man coming up behind her, and instead she leaned back against him and went on stirring. When she sat at the table with her mending, he pulled her chair round, legs scraping, until it was beside his, and put his arm along the back of it, and read his three-day-old newspaper like that, with his thumb moving on her shoulder.

Some nights it went the other way. He’d be at the table with his newspaper, and she’d get up from the table without a word and cross the room and climb into his lap, a knee either side of him, and take the paper out of his hands and kiss him. She never said anything first. She never explained it afterwards. He’d lose his place in the paper for the rest of the night and not mind.

And at least once a day he’d stop whatever he was doing, and lift his hand, and touch her face.

He did it as if he were reading it. His fingertips went over her eyebrows, one and then the other, and down the line of her nose, and across her cheekbone to her ear, and along her jaw, slowly, the way she imagined a blind man might learn a face. Sometimes he’d stop at the corner of her mouth and leave his thumb there and just look at her, and she’d stand still and let him, with her eyes half shut, and her stomach would go over and over like a fish in a bucket.

“What are you doing?” she asked him, once, the first week of April.

“Checking,” he said.

“For what?”

He thought about it. His thumb was on her bottom lip.

“That it’s still you,” he said. “That I didn’t make you up.”

She kissed his thumb, and then his palm, and then his wrist, where the pulse was. He shut his eyes.

✦ ✦ ✦

He talked again now. Whatever had shut off in him after the fever had come back on, and he talked the way he used to, more, about everything, all the time, with his feet on the second chair and his tea going cold and her at the table across from him shelling something or mending something or doing nothing at all except listening.

He told her about the river. About the other side, where there were hills so steep the villages were built on stilts, and the people grew tea in terraces and kept bees, and the war had been going on so long that the children played at it in the lanes the way children in the city played at shops. He told her about Old Ko’s unit, the Grey Lanterns, sixty men in old trucks with paper lanterns painted on the doors, who’d fought for whoever paid on whichever side and had, mostly, been paid to guard things. Roads. Bridges. Mines. He told her about the first time he’d seen the sea, at nineteen, from the back of a truck. He told her about a woman in a hill village who’d mended his boots for free because he’d carried her goat across a river.

He didn’t tell her what he did now. What he’d done at West Basin. Who he went to see, on the nights he said a time and came back late with something on his sleeve.

She didn’t ask.

He noticed that she didn’t ask. She saw him notice. Sometimes, in the middle of a story about bees or goats or Old Ko’s terrible cooking, he’d stop and look at her across the table with an expression she couldn’t read at all, as if he was waiting for her to ask, and was afraid she would, and was more afraid she wouldn’t.

She asked about the goat.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the twentieth of April he told her he was going away.

“Two weeks,” he said. “Maybe a bit more. Over the river. There’s someone I’ve been looking for a long time, and I’ve heard where he might be, and if I don’t go now, he’ll move, and I’ll lose him again.” He was looking at his tea. “I’ll go on Sunday. Early.”

She put down the jumper she was mending.

“Who?” she said.

It was out before she could stop it, the one question she never asked.

He looked up.

She looked back at him. She felt her face go hot. She didn’t take it back.

He looked at her for a while. Then he put his tea down.

“A man,” he said, “who moves people across the river. In boats, and in trucks, and in boxes. He’s been doing it for twenty years. Thousands of them. Most of them get where they’re going and end up somewhere worse than where they started. Some of them don’t get where they’re going.” He paused. “They call him the Ferryman.”

She didn’t move.

“The container you were in was his,” said Jun Hyuk. “Kuang signed the papers. The Ferryman owned the box.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He did it on Saturday night, the twenty-second, at the table.

She’d come up on the five o’clock bus, because he was going early on Sunday and she wanted the whole evening, and she had cooked, on the gas ring, the pork rib soup with ginger that her mother used to make for her father before he went anywhere. Ginger first. Then the bones. She’d made him eat two bowls. Then she’d cleared the plates, and he’d put the old grey towel on the table, and taken the long canvas case out from under the camp bed and opened it, and started.

She sat across from him with her tea and watched.

It was the rifle. She had seen it twice before. It came apart in his hands into its pieces and he laid them out on the grey towel in a row, in order, and cleaned each one with a rag and a little bottle of oil and a set of small brushes in a roll of leather, and put each one back. He didn’t talk. He never talked while he did it. She had learned that the way she’d learned the window and the stairs: from watching. It was the only time of day that he was silent of his own accord, and she sat with it like she’d sit with someone praying.

When he’d finished, he laid it in its case and closed the lid.

He didn’t get up. He sat with both hands flat on the case for a moment. Then he reached into the top pocket of his shirt, where he kept the coin from the dumpling and the spoon she’d given him for his birthday, and took something out, and put it on the table beside her teacup.

It was a ring, a plain silver band, not wide and not narrow, with no stone. It sat on the scratched wooden table in the lamplight beside the cup, and it was so simple that for a second she didn’t understand what it was.

She looked at it. She looked at him.

He wasn’t looking at her. He was looking at the ring.

“Pick it up,” he said. “Look inside.”

She picked it up. It was warm from his pocket. She turned it to the lamp and looked inside the band.

There were numbers.

Two lines of them, engraved, small, neat, going round the inside of the ring. Degrees, and minutes, and seconds. She’d seen numbers like that before, on the charts in her father’s office, on the edges of the maps where the ships went.

“That’s a place,” said Jun Hyuk.

His voice was low and even. It was the voice he’d used in the door of the container. He’d used it on Nuo in the back of the truck.

She didn’t think she was the frightened one.

“There’s a house there,” he said. “A small one. Stone. Old. There’s a fig tree. Nobody knows it’s there except me and the man who sold it to me, and he’s dead. There’s money there, in the wall, behind the stove. Enough. There are papers, in a name that isn’t yours, that will hold. There’s a boat that goes there twice a week from a harbour nobody watches.” He was still looking at the ring in her hand. “I’ve been getting it ready for nine years. For me. In case I ever needed to stop being me.” He took a breath. “I don’t need it now.”

He looked up at her at last.

“If I don’t come back,” said Lee Jun Hyuk, “this ring has the coordinates to a life where no one can find you.”

She held the ring in her fingers. She couldn’t feel her hands.

“And if I do come back,” he said, “you’re mine.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t say anything.

He waited. He was good at waiting now. He’d learned it from her. He sat across the table with his hands flat on the rifle case and his face still and his eyes on hers, and he didn’t say a single word, and she could see what it was costing him not to.
