She could see every word he wasn’t saying going past behind his eyes like cars on a bridge at night. It’s not a proposal. It’s not anything. You don’t have to. It’s a key, that’s all. Throw it in the river if you want. I just wanted you to have somewhere to go. I just wanted—

She looked down at the ring.

She thought about the house in the Walled City. The cedar chest. The camera she’d been taken out of the room for, and the dinners she wasn’t at, and her father’s voice in the hospital corridor in October saying nobody can know. Twenty-five years of being something to keep. Something worth more than a house. Something you could put in a box, in the dark, with holes drilled in the roof, and send across the sea.

He’d built her a door, a way out in case he couldn’t be the way out any more.

And the other half. If I do come back, you’re mine.

Her father said my daughter the way he said my ships, like a line in a ledger. Looking at Jun Hyuk’s face across the table, she knew this was something else. He meant he would come back for her. She was the thing he’d go back for.

He’d never gone back for anything in his life.

She put the ring on.

She put it on herself, on the third finger of her left hand, and pushed it down past the knuckle. It fitted. Of course it fitted. He had looked at her hands for six months the way he looked at everything.

She held her hand out flat on the table between them, in the lamplight, with the ring on it.

He looked at it.

He didn’t say anything at all. His face went still. He reached out and put one finger on the ring, on the back of her hand, and left it there.

“Yes,” said Evangeline.

He put his head down on his arms on the rifle case, and for a while he didn’t lift it.

✦ ✦ ✦

He left at four in the morning.

She was awake. She heard him get up from the other camp bed, and pick up the bag, and the rifle case. She heard him stop. She lay on the second camp bed with her face to the door and her eyes open in the dark, and felt him standing over her.

He crouched beside the bed.

He didn’t say anything. He touched her face, the way he did: eyebrows, nose, cheekbone, jaw. Then he found her left hand, on top of the blanket, and turned it over, and put his thumb on the ring.

“Two weeks,” he whispered. “Maybe a bit more.”

She found his face in the dark with her free hand and held it.

“Go on,” she said.

He went.

She listened to him go down the stairs. Every step. The street door, with the squeak in the bottom hinge. The truck, starting, in the alley. The engine going away down River Bridge Road towards the bridge, and the checkpoint, and the other side of the river, where there were hills so steep the villages stood on stilts.

She lay with her thumb on the ring until it was light.

✦ ✦ ✦

Elowen saw it at Sunday lunch, the week after.

It was at the tall house in the Walled City, at the long kitchen table, the way it was every Sunday now, since Elowen had made it a rule. Their father at the head. Raiden being loud. Eliana with her laptop on her knees under the table, where she thought nobody could see it. Elara asleep sitting up after a night shift with a dumpling halfway to her mouth. Zhao at Elowen’s elbow, eating steadily, saying nothing, looking at everyone in turn.

Evangeline reached for the soy sauce.

She saw Elowen’s eyes go to her hand.

She took the soy sauce and put her hand back in her lap, under the table, and went on eating. She didn’t look up. Elowen didn’t say anything. Elowen went on talking to Raiden about a wedding order, two hundred white roses, in exactly the same voice, and passed the greens to her husband, and laughed when Raiden did something stupid with a spring onion.

But afterwards, at the front door, when everyone else was in the kitchen and Zhao had gone to get the car, Elowen stopped her on the bottom stair.

“Ev,” she said.

Evangeline looked at her.

Elowen looked at her sister’s left hand, which was at her side. She didn’t take it. She knew better. She looked at it, and then at Evangeline’s face, and her own face was composed and cool and her eyes were not composed at all.

“Is he kind to you?” said Elowen.

Evangeline took her time over it.

She thought about a man folding a towel badly on the end of a camp bed. About a hand held in the air, waiting. About water running in a cupboard while he practised her name. About a fig tree she had never seen, and money behind a stove, and a boat that went twice a week from a harbour nobody watched. All of it built for nine years, and given away across a table, so that she would have somewhere to go if he didn’t.

“Yes,” said Evangeline.

Elowen looked at her.

“Then I won’t ask anything else,” she said. “Yet.”

Zhao’s car pulled up outside. Elowen put her hand, lightly, on her sister’s arm, above the elbow, and went down the steps.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came back on the fifth of May, after thirteen days, at eleven at night.

She heard the street door. The squeak in the bottom hinge. The stairs. She knew his feet on those stairs better than her own name now. They were slower than usual. They stopped on the landing outside the steel door.

The key in the first lock. The second. The third.

He came in.

He had a cut on his bottom lip, healing, and a bruise along his jaw that was going yellow at the edges, and he was thin, thinner than when he’d left, and he smelled of woodsmoke and river and two weeks of not sleeping. He hadn’t found the man he was looking for. She knew it from his shoulders before he’d shut the door.

He was holding a jar.

Honey. A big glass jar of it, dark gold, the kind from the hill villages, with a cloth tied over the top with string, and a pressed flower stuck to the side.

He stood just inside the door, and looked at her sitting at the table under the lamp, and held out the jar, awkwardly, the way a boy holds out something he’s made at school.

“I brought you this,” he said. “From a village. They keep bees. I said I’d—I thought you’d—” He stopped. “I’ve never brought anyone anything.”

She got up.

She came across the room. She took the jar out of his hands and put it on the table without looking at it.

Then she took his face in both her hands, cut lip and bruise and all, and pulled it down to hers.

“You came back,” she said, against his mouth.

He nodded. He couldn’t manage more.

She held up her left hand between their faces, so he could see the ring.

“Then I’m yours,” said Evangeline.

He didn’t say anything. He couldn’t. She’d known he wouldn’t be able to. He picked her up instead, the whole length of her, off her feet, carefully because of the cut on his lip and the place on his side that was still pink, and held her against him in the middle of the dark little room, with her arms round his neck and her face in the woodsmoke of his collar, and stood there, swaying slightly, like a man on a boat that has finally come in.

chapters.title: The Target Is a Judge
chapters.desc: In 2016 a judge let the Ferryman walk out of court in a week. Seven years later Jun Hyuk climbs the stairs to his flat to finish it, and finds an old man waiting for him in the dark.
chapters.epigraph: “I wondered when you’d come. I’ve been leaving the door unlocked since March.” — Judge Lo Wing-hang
chapters.content:
She made him lie down again in May.

He’d come back from across the river thinner and jumpier, after thirteen nights of sleeping sitting up in the cab of a truck, and on the third night home he got up out of the camp bed at one in the morning, without a sound, and went and sat in the chair by the door, the way he’d slept every night of his life since he was nine, before March. She lay there for an hour in the dark, listening to him not sleep. Then she sat up and said his name.

“Jun Hyuk.”

“Mm.”

“Come and lie down with me. I can’t sleep with you over there.”

He came, and crouched by the bed, and she found his hand in the dark and pulled. He let her. He lay down on the narrow canvas beside her, on his back, with his feet hanging off the end, and she put her head on his chest and her hand flat over his heart.

Then she lifted her head again and kissed him in the dark, the way you’d pull a blanket up over someone. He kissed her back. Some of the stiffness went out of his shoulders. The rest of him stayed rigid. She could feel him listening to the door.

“I can’t see it from here,” he said.

“I can hear it,” said Evangeline. “I’ve done it all my life.”

He breathed out. She felt his chest go down under her cheek. She lay still, and let him listen, and listened herself, to the building settling and the water heater ticking and the trucks going over the bridge, until his heart slowed down under her hand, beat by beat, like a clock being wound back.

She fell asleep first.

He didn’t sleep at all. He lay on his back with his feet hanging off the end of the camp bed and her asleep on his chest, and looked at the ceiling, and didn’t move a muscle until it was light, in case she woke up and he had to stop.

He did it every night after that.

✦ ✦ ✦

The judge was in June.

He told her he’d be away one night. In the city, not across the river. He’d be back the next evening. Rule four. She nodded and didn’t ask. He went down the stairs at six o’clock with the bag on his shoulder and the long canvas case left under the camp bed, because he wouldn’t need it for this, and she watched him go from the table with her hands round her cup and her thumb on the ring.

He’d been carrying Lo Wing-hang around in his head for seven years.

He’d sat in the public gallery in 2016, at the back, in a borrowed jacket, and watched it happen. Gu Shanlin in the dock in a grey suit, small, neat, soft-voiced, with an ivory toothpick he turned in his fingers. The prosecution with four boxes of evidence. A witness who had been in one of the trucks. And Judge Lo, sixty-two years old, with his silver hair and his reading glasses on a chain, listening to all of it with his chin on his hand, and then, on the sixth day, ruling that the witness was unreliable, and the evidence was improperly obtained, and the case was dismissed.

Gu Shanlin had walked out of court at four in the afternoon and been across the river by nine.

Jun Hyuk had sat in the gallery until they cleared it. Then he’d gone back to the border and sat in Nam’s back room for two days without speaking, which Nam said afterwards was the only time in the eleven years she’d known him that he’d been quiet for more than an hour. And on the third day he’d started the exercise book with the rabbit on the front.

Lo was on the first page.

✦ ✦ ✦

Lo lived alone now, in a flat on one of the old roads below the Peak, the ones that wound round the hill under the big houses, with the trees growing over them. His wife had died in 2019. His son lived abroad and didn’t call. A woman came in the mornings to clean and to cook and to do the other things. Jun Hyuk knew all of this because he had spent six weeks learning it, sitting in his truck at the bottom of the road, and in a café across from the hospital where Lo went on Thursdays.

He didn’t know what Lo went to the hospital for. It hadn’t seemed important.

He went in at two in the morning, over the wall at the back, through the garden, which had gone to seed, and up the iron stairs to the kitchen door.

The kitchen door was unlocked.

He stood on the step with his hand on the handle and didn’t move. In his experience, doors that should be locked and weren’t were the start of something bad. He stood there for two minutes, listening. Nothing. The trees moving. A car on the road below. A clock somewhere inside, ticking.

And something else: a faint steady hiss, then a pause, then the hiss again, like breathing but not quite.

He went in.

✦ ✦ ✦

The flat was dark and tidy and smelled of medicine, the sweet heavy kind that collects in rooms where someone has been ill for months. He went through the kitchen and along a corridor with photographs on the walls, a woman in a wedding dress, a boy in a school blazer, the same boy older in a graduation gown, and the hiss got louder, and there was a light under the last door.

He pushed it open with two fingers.

It was a bedroom. A hospital bed, the kind with rails and a remote control, where the double bed must once have been. A machine beside it on a trolley, with a tube that went to the bed, hissing and pausing, hissing and pausing. A lamp on the bedside table. A glass of water. A tray of pill bottles, a lot of them. A small plastic box with a syringe in it and a label from a pharmacy.

And in the bed, propped up on four pillows, an old man.

He was tiny. The judge Jun Hyuk remembered from the court had been tall and solid, with silver hair and a voice that filled the room. This man was a bundle of bones under a blanket, with a thin tube under his nose and the hair gone to white wisps, and his skin was yellow, like old paper or a nicotine stain, and the whites of his eyes were yellow too, in the lamplight.

The yellow eyes were open. They were looking at the door.

“Ah,” said Judge Lo Wing-hang.

His voice was a dry thread. There was nothing in it but tiredness.

“I wondered when you’d come,” he said. “I’ve been leaving the door unlocked since March.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Jun Hyuk didn’t move.

He stood in the doorway with his hand inside his jacket. He’d planned this for six weeks. He’d planned it, if he was honest, for seven years. He knew exactly what he was going to say. He had a speech. He’d practised it in the truck. It started with a date, the eleventh of August 2015, and a stretch of the river road, and a refrigerated truck, and eleven names, which he had found out one by one over two years and written in the back of the rabbit book. It ended with the judge knowing exactly why.

He couldn’t remember a word of it.

“Sit down,” said the old man. “Please. You’re very large. It hurts my neck to look up.”

Jun Hyuk sat down.

There was a chair by the bed, a hard one, with a cardigan over the back. The cleaner’s, probably. He sat in it with his hands on his knees.

“You know who I am,” he said.

“I know what you are.” The yellow eyes moved over his face. “You’re the man who killed Kuang. And the river captain. And the man with the trucks. You’re the one they talk about on the border. The big one, who talks.” A breath. The machine hissed. “I didn’t expect you to be so quiet.”

“I’m usually not.”

“No.” Something like a smile moved the thin mouth. “I imagine not.”

They looked at each other.

“It’s cancer,” said Lo, as if Jun Hyuk had asked. “The pancreas. They found it in January. It was already everywhere. They gave me until the summer.” He moved one hand a little on the blanket. It was all bones and blue veins. “It’s the summer.”

Jun Hyuk looked at the machine. At the pill bottles. At the box with the syringe in it.

“You left the door unlocked,” he said.

“Yes.”

“For me.”

“For whoever came.” The old man closed his eyes. “I thought it would be you. Or someone like you. I hoped it would be soon. The cleaner comes at eight. All night I lie here and look at the door.” He opened his eyes. “Do you know what it’s like? Lying in the dark, waiting for someone to come and kill you, and they don’t come?”

Jun Hyuk thought of a box with holes drilled in the roof.

“Yes,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t kill him.

Afterwards he’d tell himself it was because the man was dying anyway and there was no point, and it would have been a kindness, and he hadn’t come to be kind. That was true as far as it went. What stopped him was that Lo Wing-hang wanted it. Had wanted it since March. Had lain in the dark for thirteen hours a night with the door unlocked, hoping. And Jun Hyuk sat in the hard chair by the hospital bed with the cleaner’s cardigan behind his back and the machine hissing, and understood that if he did it, it would be the old man’s choice and not his. It would be a service. And he would not give this man that.

“I’m not going to kill you,” he said.

The yellow eyes flickered.

“I’m going to sit here,” said Jun Hyuk, “and you’re going to tell me everything. Gu Shanlin. Who paid you. How much. Who else he pays. Every name. Every case. Every year. And I’m going to write it down, and you’re going to sign every page.” He took a pencil out of his pocket, and the rabbit book, and opened it to a clean page. “And then I’ll go. And you can lie here and look at the door.”

The old man looked at him.

Then he started to talk.

✦ ✦ ✦

It took four hours.

Lo talked slowly, in the dry thread of a voice, stopping often. Sometimes he stopped for so long that Jun Hyuk thought he’d fallen asleep, or died, and then he’d start again in the middle of a sentence. The machine hissed and paused. The clock in the corridor ticked. Jun Hyuk wrote.

He wrote names. Dates. Sums of money, in different currencies, paid into accounts in different countries by companies with names like Harmony Pacific and Blue River Holdings. Nine cases between 2008 and 2018. Not only the Ferryman. A shipping company. A man who ran a chain of massage parlours in the eastern district. A police superintendent, now retired, whom Jun Hyuk had met once in 2017 and had liked. Two other judges. A man in the Department of Justice. It went on.

He didn’t talk. Not once, in four hours, except to say spell that and how much and what year. He sat in the chair and wrote in his big square capitals, pressing hard, and his hand ached, and the pages filled up.

At a quarter to six, the old man stopped.

“That’s all,” he said. “That’s everything I know.”

Jun Hyuk held out the book and the pencil. Lo took the pencil in his bony yellow fingers and signed the bottom of every page, one by one, Lo Wing-hang, in a hand that had once signed sentences, and that shook now so much the letters wandered.

When he’d finished, he let the pencil fall on the blanket.

“Why did you do it?” said Jun Hyuk. “You had him, and you let him go.”

Lo looked at the ceiling.

“He paid me,” he said. “Very well. And I had a son at a university abroad, which was very expensive, and a wife who liked a certain kind of life. And I told myself that the evidence really was improperly obtained, which it was, in part. And the witness really was unreliable, which she was, because she was terrified.” A pause. A hiss. “And I told myself that if I didn’t let him go, someone else would. Another judge. On appeal. That it would make no difference.” He turned his yellow eyes to Jun Hyuk. “That’s what you tell yourself. That it makes no difference. That you’re one man on one road, and if you don’t wave the truck through, somebody else will.”

Jun Hyuk went still.

The old man didn’t know. He couldn’t know. He was talking about himself.

“My son doesn’t call,” said Lo. “He found out. Somehow. Years ago. He doesn’t call.”

Outside the window, the sky was going grey over the trees.

“Will you stay,” said the old man, “until I fall asleep? The morphine’s due at six. I can do it myself. I’d just—” His voice cracked, a small dry crack, like a twig. “I’d rather not be alone when I do.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He stayed.

He didn’t know why. He sat in the hard chair with the rabbit book on his knee and watched the old man fumble with the plastic box, and in the end he took it from him and did it himself, because the hands were shaking too much, and he’d done it before for men in tents. He watched the yellow face ease. He watched the eyes close.

“Thank you,” said Lo Wing-hang, faintly.

Jun Hyuk didn’t answer.

He sat there until the old man’s breathing was slow and even, and the machine hissed and paused, and the light came up grey and then white behind the trees. He sat there until he heard the cleaner’s key in the front door at eight. Then he went out the way he’d come, through the kitchen, down the iron stairs, over the wall.

He sat in his truck at the bottom of the road for an hour and didn’t start the engine.

✦ ✦ ✦

He went back twice.

He didn’t tell anyone. He went in through the kitchen door at two in the morning, on the Tuesday and the Saturday after, and sat in the hard chair, and the old man was awake both times, looking at the door, and didn’t seem surprised. They didn’t talk about the cases. They didn’t talk about much. Lo told him about his wife, who had grown orchids on the balcony, white ones, and who had died in her sleep in the next room. Jun Hyuk told him about the honey from the hill villages, and the woman who had carried a goat across a river, or rather the goat that he had carried, for the woman, and the old man laughed, once, a dry papery sound, and said that he had never laughed at two in the morning before.

Jun Hyuk didn’t tell him about Evangeline. He thought about her, the whole time, sitting in the chair. He thought about white orchids.

Lo Wing-hang died on the twenty-first of June, nine days after the first night, in the morning, while the cleaner was making his tea.

Jun Hyuk found out from the newspaper. A paragraph on page eleven. Retired High Court judge dies at 69. A photograph from 2010, silver hair, reading glasses on a chain. Survived by a son.

On the twenty-second, an envelope arrived at police headquarters, addressed by hand in big square capitals to Detective Song Wei Long. Inside it were forty-one pages torn out of a school exercise book, each one signed at the bottom in a shaking hand. There was no note.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t talk for nine days.

It started the evening he came home from the first night, the thirteenth, and it didn’t stop when the old man died. He came up the stairs and in through the three locks, and Evangeline was at the table, and she looked at his face, and he couldn’t say anything. He sat down in the chair by the door. He sat there all evening. She made tea, and put it by his hand, and he didn’t drink it. She made soup, and put it by his hand, and he ate it without tasting it, because she was watching.

He didn’t tell her where he’d been. He didn’t tell her anything. He couldn’t find the words, and it frightened him a little.

She didn’t ask.

Twice that week he went out at one in the morning and came back at dawn, and she didn’t ask where. She sat across from him at the table every night with her mending. She didn’t touch him unless he reached for her, and he didn’t reach. She lay on the camp bed every night and he lay down beside her, the whole creaking length of him, and lay on his back and looked at the ceiling, and she put her hand flat on his chest over his heart and kept it there until he slept, if he slept.

Nobody had ever been quiet with him before. People went quiet near him, frightened, waiting for him to finish. She was quiet the way the river was at night, a quiet with room in it.

On the twenty-second, the night after the paragraph on page eleven, in the dark, with her hand on his chest, he opened his mouth.

chapters.title: She Asks Nothing
chapters.desc: In the dark, with her hand on his chest, he tells her about a truck on the river road in 2015. Two nights later the typhoon takes the power, and she lights the three candles from the drawer.
chapters.epigraph: “You opened mine.” — Evangeline, in the dark, on the twenty-second of June
chapters.content:
“I’m going to tell you something,” he said, into the dark. “And then you can go.”

She didn’t move her hand.

“I mean it.” His voice was rough from nine days of not using it. “After this you’ll want to. And you should. I’ll put you on the bus myself. I’ll give you money. I’ll tell Nam to give you your phone and not let you back up the stairs. You can keep the ring, and go to the house with the fig tree, and never—”

“Tell me,” said Evangeline.

He was quiet for a while. The water heater ticked. Outside, the wind was getting up; the typhoon that had been sitting off the coast for two days had started to move, and the radio at Nam’s had been saying since the afternoon that the signal might go up by Saturday.

“Eight years ago,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

He told it lying on his back, looking up. She lay with her head on his chest and listened to it come up through him, as much as heard it.

He’d been twenty-five. Three years after Old Ko died. He’d been working for whoever paid, the way the Grey Lanterns always had, and that summer a man had paid him and four others to guard a checkpoint on the river road, a stretch of tarmac between two villages with a barrier across it and a hut with a tin roof. Nothing went down the river road that the man who paid didn’t want to go down it. That was the job. You checked the papers, you lifted the barrier or you didn’t.

“I didn’t know who he was,” said Jun Hyuk. “The man who paid. I didn’t ask. You didn’t ask, in that work. I know now. I’ve known for eight years.”

On the eleventh of August, at four in the afternoon, in forty-one degrees of heat, a refrigerated truck had come down the river road towards the barrier. White. A fish company’s name on the side. The driver had papers. The papers said frozen prawns.

“I looked at the papers,” he said. “They were fine. They were very good papers. Better than they needed to be.” He breathed in. “And I looked at the truck. And the refrigeration unit on the front was off. It wasn’t running. It was forty-one degrees and a truck full of frozen prawns had its fridge off. And I thought, that’s odd. I thought, I should open the back. I had my hand on the door. I had my hand on the handle.”

Her hand on his chest didn’t move.

“And the driver said, the boss says don’t open it, it breaks the seal, the buyer won’t take it. And I thought about the man who paid. And I thought, it’s not my job. It’s not my truck. If I don’t wave it through, somebody else will. It makes no difference.” His voice had gone flat. “So I took my hand off the handle. And I lifted the barrier. And I waved it through.”

The wind threw something against the painted-over window. A bit of paper. A leaf.

“They found it two days later,” said Jun Hyuk. “In a lay-by twenty kilometres down the road. The driver had left it. Run. Nobody knows why. Something went wrong, a deal, a payment, I don’t know. He just parked it and walked away. I heard about it on the radio in the hut, and I got on a motorbike and I went, and I was the first one there, and I opened the back.”

He stopped for a while.

“Eleven,” he said at last. “Women. Girls. The youngest was sixteen. They’d been in there since before it came through my barrier. They’d been in there when I had my hand on the handle. If I’d opened it, if I’d just—it would have been hot, but they’d have been alive. Some of them. Most of them. They’d been banging on the walls. You could see. The marks.” He stopped. “I’ve got their names. In the back of the book. I found them out one by one. It took two years.”

She thought about the container at West Basin. The holes in the roof. Nuo making the kettle sound. Bik saying she would not die in a box.

She thought about the man in the door, in October, crouching down so his head was lower than hers. Hello. Listen to me. I’m not with them.

“The truck was the Ferryman’s,” he said. “He was the one who paid for the checkpoint. He was arrested the next year and a judge let him go in a week. This month I went to kill the judge. I didn’t. He was dying. I sat with him. I made him write it down. He died yesterday.” His voice cracked. “I sat with him, Evangeline. I gave him his morphine. I held the man’s hand. And I don’t know what that makes me.”

He was shaking slightly. She could feel it through his chest, under her cheek.

“I’ve killed five men since then,” said Jun Hyuk. “Five that I went looking for. Men who sold people, or helped. I’ll kill more. I’ve been doing it for eight years. I don’t do it because it’s right. I don’t know if it’s right. I do it because I lifted a barrier, and I’m trying to put it back down, and it doesn’t go back down. It never goes back down.”

He stopped.

“So,” he said. “That’s what I am. That’s what you’re lying on. Now you can go.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t go.

She lay with her head on his chest and her hand over his heart and was quiet. He waited for her to move. For her to sit up. For her to get up off the camp bed in the dark and put on her coat and go down the stairs and not come back, which was what she should do, which was what anyone would do.

She didn’t move.

After a while, she lifted her head, and he felt her looking at him in the dark.

She didn’t say it wasn’t your fault. She didn’t say you were young, or you didn’t know, or you’ve paid for it. People had said those things to him. Nam had said some of them, once, years ago, in the back room, and he’d walked out and not come back for a month.

She found his face with her hand, and put her palm flat against his cheek, the way she had at the table with the peas.

“You opened mine,” said Evangeline.

He went still.

“At the right time,” she said.

Something went out of him all at once, the way the fever had gone, and his whole body shook once under her, hard, and then he turned his face into her palm and pressed it there, his mouth against her wrist, and didn’t make a sound.

She didn’t say anything else. She’d said it.

She lay back down with her head on his chest, and her hand on his face, and he put his arm round her, all the way round, and held on as if the camp bed were a boat on the typhoon sea. She stayed awake until he slept, which took hours, and then she slept too.

✦ ✦ ✦

The signal went up on Saturday afternoon.

By six the wind was screaming down River Bridge Road and the rain was coming sideways off the river like gravel thrown at the windows, and the bridge was shut, and Nam had pulled her shutters down and sent the cook home. At ten past eight, with a bang that came from somewhere down by the river and shook the building, the power went.

The lamp went out. The water heater stopped ticking. The whole flat went black, a total black, the black of a room with painted windows in a town with no lights.

She heard him move. She heard him stand up from the chair by the door, fast, and stop.

“It’s the substation,” he said. “It goes in every typhoon. It’s fine. It’s—stay where you are, I’ll—”

She was already at the drawer.

She’d put things in that drawer since November. Plasters. Tape. Needles. The screwdriver. And three candles and a box of matches, which she had put there in the first week, because her mother had always kept three candles and a box of matches in the kitchen drawer, because the power went in typhoons and you had to be able to find light in the dark without looking.

She found the box by touch. She struck a match.

The flame jumped up, small and yellow, and the room came back round it: the table, the chairs, the camp bed, the painted windows, the menu on the door. And him, standing by the chair, huge, with his hands at his sides, looking at her across the little light.

She lit the first candle. She stood it on a saucer on the table. Then the second, from the first. Then the third.

Three small flames, in a row, on the scratched table. The light moved on the black walls. Outside, the typhoon went on screaming.

He hadn’t moved.

She looked at him over the candles. He was looking at her the way he’d looked at her in the container door, in October, with the orange light behind him, as if he didn’t know what she was made of. The candlelight was on his face, on the scar through his eyebrow, on his mouth, on his throat where the black T-shirt began. He was breathing hard, and it wasn’t fear. She knew what he sounded like frightened.

She’d been going to come round the table. He didn’t let her.

He crossed the room in three steps, round the table, past the candles, and stopped in front of her, close, and she had to tip her head right back to see his face. Two nights ago he’d told her about the truck and the handle and the eleven, and lain on his back in the dark waiting for her to go, and she hadn’t gone.

He didn’t wait for her hand on his chest. He put his own hands on either side of her face, and held it, and looked at her in the candlelight as if he’d never been allowed to look properly before.

“I’m not asking this time,” he said. His voice was rough.

She was already up on her toes. He kissed her.

He kissed her as if he’d been holding a door shut against something for nine years and had finally let go. She wound her arms round his neck and kissed him back with everything she had, and the candles leaned and flickered on the table as if someone had opened a window.

He undid her cardigan himself, quickly, his big fingers clumsy on the small buttons, swearing under his breath at the third one, and she laughed against his mouth, low, and helped him with the fourth.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the candlelight his back was a map.

She’d felt the marks in March, in the dark, and never asked. Small pale scars, dozens of them, scattered from his shoulders to his waist like stars. Now, when he turned to drop his T-shirt on the chair, she saw them for the first time, and put her fingers on them, and he stopped with his hand still on the chair.

“Shrapnel,” he said, without turning round. “I was nineteen. A truck in front of ours hit something on the road. Old Ko picked bits out of me for a week with tweezers and a bottle of rice wine. He made me count them.” A breath. “Forty-four.”

She touched them one by one, counting under her breath the way she’d counted the stitches. Somewhere around thirty he started to shake. At forty-four she pressed her mouth to the place between his shoulder blades where they were thickest, and a low broken noise came out of him, like something giving way.

He turned round and picked her up.

The whole length of her, off her feet, the way he had on the fifth of May. He carried her the three steps to the camp bed and knelt and put her down on it, and didn’t lie down beside her straight away. He knelt on the floor in the candlelight and kissed her hand, and the ring on it, the plain band with the coordinates inside, and then her wrist, and the inside of her elbow where the needle had gone in, in the van, last October. He kissed his way up her arm, taking his time, and she lay on the camp bed with the typhoon screaming at the painted windows and let him, and didn’t make a sound, and then did.

He talked, this time. Not much. Not about the weather. Against her skin, between kisses, things she’d never heard anyone say to anyone, in his rough border voice: her name, and that she was beautiful, and that he’d thought so in the container door with the orange light on her, and been ashamed of thinking it, and wasn’t any more. That he’d watched her shell beans for five months and thought about her hands. That he’d never wanted anything in his life the way he wanted her, and he’d wanted to stay alive quite badly, on occasion. She listened to every word. She put her hands in his short hair and held his head and listened, and her heart went like something trying to get out.

When he finally came down onto the camp bed beside her, it made a sound like a gunshot, and they both froze, and then she laughed out loud into his shoulder. He’d never heard her laugh out loud. He lifted his head and stared at her as if she’d done a magic trick, and she laughed harder, and he put his face in her neck and laughed too, helplessly, shaking, and the bed held. Somehow, the bed held.

She drew him down to her.

After that the candles burned down one by one on the table, and the typhoon screamed itself out against the painted windows, and neither of them noticed when the last flame went. They had no use for it by then. They’d learned the shape of each other in the dark, the way she had learned the house in the Walled City, every stair and every doorway, every place where the sound carried. He held her as if she were the only solid thing in a world that had been moving under him all his life, and she held on to him just as hard.

✦ ✦ ✦

At some point, in the black, long after, with her head on his chest and his arm round her and the camp bed sagging under the two of them almost to the floor, she lifted her head.

She found his face with her hand, in the dark, the way he always found hers. Eyebrows. Nose. The scar. Cheekbone. Jaw. The corner of his mouth.

“I love you,” said Evangeline.

She’d never said it to anyone. She said it plainly, once, the way she’d said name at the hospital, so there could be no mistake.

He didn’t say anything. Under her hand she felt his face go still. She waited. She’d learned to wait for this.

“I love you,” he said at last. It came out of him cracked down the middle. “I love you. I’ve loved you since the fever. Since before. I’ve been carrying it round for months like the coin in my pocket and I didn’t know how to give it to you.” His arm tightened. “Say it again. Please. I want to hear it again.”

She said it again.

Outside, the wind was dropping. Somewhere down on River Bridge Road, a shutter that had been banging all night stopped.

She fell asleep with her ear over his heart, listening to it slow down.

chapters.title: Elowen Visits, Carrying Groceries
chapters.desc: Four bags of shopping, a dozen lemons from her mother’s tree, and the coolest look in the Walled City. Downstairs, an arms dealer waits in a car and a man who hates arms dealers goes down to talk to him.
chapters.epigraph: “I married a man who says one word. You found one who says all of them.” — Elowen Zhao
chapters.content:
“No,” said Jun Hyuk. “Absolutely not.”

“She’s my sister. She wants to meet you.”

“She’s married to Zhao Zhendong.” He was standing at the gas ring with his back to her, stirring a pan of rice that didn’t need stirring. “Do you know who Zhao Zhendong is? Do you know what he sold, for fifteen years? I’ve seen what he sold. I’ve seen what it does. I’ve dug what it does out of people with a pair of pliers in a tent.” The spoon went round and round. “I’m not having Zhao Zhendong’s wife up those stairs. She’ll tell him. He’ll tell somebody. Men like him always tell somebody.”

“He’s stopping.”

“Men like him don’t stop.”

“He’s stopping,” said Evangeline, “because she asked him.”

The spoon stopped.

He turned round. She was at the table, as always, with a bowl of beans, and she wasn’t looking at him. She was looking at the beans. But her face had the look it got when she’d decided something and was only giving him a chance to catch up.

“She asked him,” he said.

“He cancelled the biggest deal of his life,” said Evangeline, “because she said one word.” She split a pod with her thumb. “She’d die before she told anyone where I was. She’d die before she told him.”

He looked at her.

“One visit,” he said. “One. Alone. Phone at Nam’s. She changes buses twice. She doesn’t bring him.”

Evangeline went on shelling beans.

“She’ll bring him,” he said. “Won’t she.”

“He’ll wait in the car.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Elowen came on the eighth of July, a Saturday, on the ten o’clock bus, which she had changed onto from the nine o’clock at the market town halfway, which she had changed onto from a taxi at the ferry pier, which she had got into from the back door of her own shop. She came up River Bridge Road in a linen dress and flat sandals with her hair pinned up and her sunglasses on and four heavy shopping bags, two in each hand, and walked into Nam’s Noodles as if she had been coming there all her life.

Nam looked at her from behind the counter.

Elowen took off her sunglasses and looked back.

Something passed between them that Jun Hyuk, watching from the back door to the kitchen, didn’t understand at all. It took about two seconds. At the end of it Nam nodded and held out her hand, and Elowen put her phone in it, and Nam put the phone in the jar between the chilli oil and the soy sauce, beside Evangeline’s, and put the saucer over both.

“Up the alley,” said Nam. “Steel door. He’s behind it pretending he isn’t nervous.”

“I’m not nervous,” said Jun Hyuk, from the kitchen.

“He’s nervous,” said Nam.

Elowen looked across the shop at him. It wasn’t a long look by Zhao standards, but in it Jun Hyuk felt himself weighed, measured, priced, and wrapped, the way he imagined she did with a bucket of roses at six in the morning, and he had the strong impression that he had come out of it at a discount.

“Mr. Lee,” said Elowen.

“Mrs. Zhao.”

“Carry these,” said Elowen, and held out two of the bags.

He carried them.

✦ ✦ ✦

The car was at the far end of the bridge, on the city side, by the checkpoint. A black saloon, very clean, with the engine off. He saw it from the alley as he took the bags. He’d seen it from the window with the scratch in the paint an hour ago, when it pulled in and parked and didn’t move, and nobody got out.

He took the bags up the stairs. He put them on the table. He looked at Evangeline, who was standing by the table in a pale blue dress he hadn’t seen before, with her hands folded, looking at her sister in the doorway with an expression he’d never seen on her either. Nervous. Evangeline was nervous.

He looked at the two of them.

“I’ll make tea,” he said. “No. You make tea. I make terrible tea. I’ll—I’m going to go downstairs for a minute.”

“Where?” said Evangeline.

“To say hello,” said Jun Hyuk, “to your brother-in-law.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He walked across the bridge.

It was a hot morning, and the river was low and brown under it, and the spring-onion man was in his place in the middle with his basket, in one hat today, and nodded to him. The car didn’t move as he came. He walked up to the driver’s side and stood by the window with his hands in his pockets.

After a while, the window came down.

Zhao Zhendong looked at him.

Jun Hyuk had seen him before. Twice. Once across a harbour, at night, through a pair of binoculars, in 2018, when Jun Hyuk had been watching a ship and Zhao had been selling it. Once in a photograph on the front page of a newspaper, under a headline about a Red Notice. He had never been this close. Close up, Zhao was smaller than he’d expected and much more frightening, in the way a still dog is more frightening than a barking one. He had a face like a shut door.

“Hm,” he said.

“Morning,” said Jun Hyuk. “Nice car. Very clean. Bulletproof, I’d say, from how it sits. Bit heavy at the back. You’d want to check the rear suspension. I’m Lee. You know that. You’ve had someone asking about me since October. Big man, from the border, talks too much. That’s me. All true. Especially the last bit. I’m told you don’t. Talk, I mean. I’m told you say one word a day and it’s that one. Hm.” He nodded at the city side of the bridge. “I’ve got your sister-in-law upstairs. She’s very nice. I’m not a nice man. You know that. You’ve got a file. I’ve got a file on you too, as it happens. Two, actually. One from before your wife and one from after. The second one’s much shorter.”

Zhao didn’t say anything.

“Velde,” said Jun Hyuk. “That was a lot of rifles. The ones you didn’t send.”

Zhao’s eyes narrowed a fraction.

“I was there,” said Jun Hyuk. “In the highlands. Not for the militia. For the people the militia would’ve used them on. I was waiting for the shipment. I was going to find out where it landed and—well.” He shrugged. “It didn’t come. I waited eleven days on a hill and it didn’t come. And I found out later why it didn’t come.” He looked at the man in the car. “So I don’t like you. I don’t like what you were. I’ve dug what you sold out of people with pliers. But I’ll say this once and then I’ll never say it again, because I don’t like you. Thank you for listening to your wife.”

Zhao looked at him. He kept looking.

“Stray dog,” said Zhao.

Jun Hyuk grinned at him, which nobody had done in years, by the look on Zhao’s face, and walked back across the bridge. The window went up behind him.

✦ ✦ ✦

When he came back up the stairs, the two of them were sitting at the table with the teapot between them, and the shopping bags unpacked onto the counter: rice, oil, soy sauce, eggs, greens, a whole roast duck from a shop in the Walled City wrapped in brown paper, a box of the almond biscuits that Evangeline liked and had never told him she liked. And lemons. A dozen lemons, small and knobbly, with leaves still on some of them, in a paper bag.

Elowen looked up at him as he came in.

“Is my husband still alive?” she said, and when he told her what Zhao had called him, she nodded as if he’d brought good news. “That means he likes you,” she said. “He called my father nothing at all for three years.” She pushed a cup across the table towards the third chair. “Sit down, Mr. Lee.”

He sat.

She looked at him over her teacup. She had her sister’s stillness, he thought, but not her sister’s silence. Elowen’s stillness had an edge on it.

“I have one question,” said Elowen.

He waited.

“If she wants to leave,” said Elowen. “If she wakes up one day and wants to go. Back to the Walled City. Or somewhere else. Somewhere that isn’t here, and isn’t you. Will you let her?”

He looked at Evangeline. She was looking at her teacup. Her left hand was on the table, beside it, with the plain silver band on the third finger.

He looked back at Elowen.

“I built her a house,” he said, “so she could.”

Elowen’s face didn’t change. But she put her cup down.

“Show me,” she said.

Evangeline held out her hand across the table. Elowen took it carefully and turned it over, and looked at the ring. She tipped it a little to the window, to the light coming in through the scratch in the black paint, and he saw her read the numbers inside.

She sat there, holding her sister’s hand.

“Where is it?” she said.

“I’m not telling you,” said Jun Hyuk. “I’m not telling anyone. That’s the point.”

Elowen looked up at him. Then, for the first time, the corner of her mouth lifted.

“Good,” she said.

He jumped. He actually jumped. It was Evangeline’s word, in Evangeline’s tone, and he looked from one sister to the other and saw where Evangeline had got it, and Elowen saw him see it, and the corner of her mouth went further.

✦ ✦ ✦

She sent him downstairs to Nam’s for more hot water, because there was plenty of hot water, and he knew that, and went anyway.

When he’d gone, Elowen sat back in her chair and looked round the room. At the painted windows, and the camp bed, which had become two camp beds pushed together with a blanket over both, and the little lamp, and the brass hook by the shower cupboard with a white towel hanging from it. At the other towels, on the end of the beds, folded in thirds lengthwise and then rolled tight.

She looked at those.

“Ma folded them like that,” she said. “You taught him.”

“He taught himself,” said Evangeline. “I showed him.”

Elowen looked at her.

“He talks a lot,” said Elowen. “And you smile when he does. Don’t say you don’t. Inside. I can see it. I’ve been watching you do it since you were four.” Elowen picked up her cup again. “You used to do it at Raiden. When he did his stupid voices at dinner. Your face wouldn’t move, and you’d be laughing so hard inside I could see it from across the table.”

Evangeline looked at her sister and didn’t deny it.

“I married a man who says one word,” said Elowen. “You found one who says all of them.” She drank her tea. “Ma would have laughed for a week.”

Evangeline looked down at the table.

“Ev.” Her sister’s voice changed. “Are you happy?”

Evangeline didn’t answer straight away. She thought about the camp bed sagging to the floor. The candles. A man on his knees in the candlelight kissing the inside of her elbow where the needle had gone in. His voice, in the dark, the next morning, when he’d woken up and found her still there, saying nothing, saying her name, saying it again, as if he couldn’t stop.

“Yes,” said Evangeline.

Elowen put her cup down and put her hand over her eyes.

“All right,” she said, behind it, unsteadily. “All right.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At three o’clock, Elowen went down the stairs with her empty shopping bags folded under her arm.

At the bottom, in the alley, she stopped, and turned round, and looked at Jun Hyuk, who had walked her down, because he walked everyone down.

“If anything happens to her,” she said, in the cool level voice, “I’ll know. I always know. And then I’ll come here, and I’ll find you, wherever you are. And you’ll find out what my husband is afraid of.”

“Your husband isn’t afraid of anything.”

“He’s afraid of me,” said Elowen Zhao, and put her sunglasses on, and went to get her phone out of Nam’s jar.

He stood in the alley and watched her walk down River Bridge Road to the bridge, straight, in her linen dress, with the folded bags under her arm, and watched the black car at the far end start its engine as she came. Zhao got out to open the door for her. He looked across the bridge, over the top of the car, at the man standing in the alley mouth.

Four seconds.

Jun Hyuk lifted one hand.

Zhao got back in the car.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening Evangeline made a soup with the roast duck and the greens. She squeezed one of the lemons over it at the end. Then she cut the rest of them in half and put them in a big jar with salt, layer after layer, pressing each one down with a wooden spoon, and sealed it, and put it on the shelf above the gas ring.

“What’s that?” he said.

“Salted lemons,” said Evangeline. “From Ma’s tree. For when you’re ill.”

He looked at the jar on the shelf. Nothing else in the flat had ever been bought to last more than a week.

He didn’t say anything. He reached across the table and put his hand on hers, the left one, with the ring.

She turned her hand over under his, palm up, and held on.

chapters.title: Evangeline Wants a Window Box
chapters.desc: A sixth-floor flat in an old textile building, a real stove, and windows made of glass you could shoot at all day. They don’t open. She mentions basil once.
chapters.epigraph: “Basil would grow here.” — Evangeline, not asking for anything
chapters.content:
They moved in August, because the border was getting hot.

Not the weather, though the weather was hot too: a wet white heat that sat on the river like a lid and made the karaoke flat, with its painted windows, into an oven by ten in the morning. The other kind of hot. People were asking about him. Nam said so, in July, at the counter, without looking up from her chopping board. Two men in a car with city plates, asking the man who sold spring onions on the bridge about a big man who talked. A woman Nam didn’t know, asking the cook. Somebody who’d been to the tyre shop by the river and asked the owner who rented the room upstairs.

“Who?” said Jun Hyuk.

“I don’t know who,” said Nam. “If I knew who, I’d have told you who. I’m telling you that. People.”

He thought about it for three days. Then he told Evangeline they were going to the city for a while.

“There’s a place,” he said. “In the eastern industrial district. I’ve had it for years, for when I work down there. It’s better than this. It’s got a kitchen. Real windows. Well.” He scratched his jaw. “Windows.”

She didn’t ask why. She looked at him across the table for a moment, and then she got up and started taking things down off the shelf and wrapping them in newspaper. The teapot. The two cups that didn’t match. The jar of salted lemons, carefully, in three sheets, because the salt hadn’t finished its work.

He watched her pack it.

“I’ve moved a dozen times in four years,” he said. “I’ve never had to wrap anything before.”

She put the jar in a box. She put a towel round it.

Then he started on the crates.

There were six of them, along the wall, blue plastic with lids, the kind fishmongers use. They’d been there since the first night. She had never touched them, because of rule five, and because she didn’t touch things that weren’t hers. She’d sat beside them on the floor for ten months and never once asked.

He knelt and took the lid off the first one, to check the catches before he carried it, and didn’t think about it.

She looked in.

It was money. Bundles of it, in plastic, stacked tight, every one the same thickness, in three or four different colours from three or four different countries. Under the bundles, wrapped in oilcloth, something heavy and flat that she knew, from her father’s office, was gold. He took the lid off the second crate. The same. The third had small cloth bags tied at the neck with string, and he opened one to check it, and it was full of little stones that caught the window light and threw it back in sparks.

She sat back on her heels.

“Oh,” said Evangeline.

He looked up. He looked at her face, and then at the open crates, as if he were seeing them through her eyes for the first time.

“Ah,” he said. “Yes. That.”

She looked at the crates. Then at him: at the man who ate instant noodles out of the pot and had dried himself with yesterday’s T-shirt for as long as she’d known him.

“It was a principle,” he said, and rubbed the back of his neck. “Look. I worked for very rich people for a very long time. Mines. Ports. Men with oil fields who were frightened of their own brothers. They pay a lot, people like that, for a big man who’ll stand in front of them and never ask questions. Old Ko taught me to put it away and not spend it. So I didn’t. Fifteen years, I didn’t spend any of it.” He looked at the stones in the bag. “And after the river road, when I started—the other work. The men I went to see always had a safe. Always. Men like that never trust a bank.” He tied the bag shut. “Most of what was in the safes went to the people they’d sold. Hospitals. Hostels. A fund at the church, that pays for courses. But there was a lot. There’s always a lot.”

She looked at the six crates.

“How much?” she said.

He thought about it, honestly, the way she thought about things.

“I don’t know,” he said. “I stopped counting years ago. There are four more places like this. And the house with the fig tree. And some land, across the river, with tea on it. And the textile building.”

“The flat in the textile building.”

“The building,” said Jun Hyuk. “I bought the building. The printing works pays me rent. So does the handbag man. He doesn’t know it’s me. He thinks it’s a company in a country with a lot of sheep.”

She looked at him for so long that he began to go red again, from the neck up.

“I never had anything to spend it on,” he said. “That’s all. I never had anybody to spend it on.”

She didn’t say anything. She got up and went to the shelf and took down the last of the cups, and wrapped it, and put it in the box with the jar of salted lemons, carefully, in a towel.

But he saw her face, as she turned. And he saw what was in her eyes, and he thought, she’s going to be unbearable about this, and found he didn’t mind at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

The textile building was on a street of old factories near the harbour, eight storeys of grey concrete from the nineteen-sixties with the name of a shirt company still painted along the top in letters nobody could read any more. The bottom three floors were a printing works now. Floors four and five were empty. The seventh and eighth were a man who made fake designer handbags and didn’t ask questions of anyone in the building, because nobody asked questions of him.

The sixth floor was one long room with a kitchen at one end, a bathroom at the other, and a row of tall windows down the whole south side.

She stood in the door and looked at it.

It was full of light. After ten months in the karaoke flat, with its black-painted glass, it was like walking out of a cinema in the afternoon. The windows went from waist height almost to the ceiling, five of them, in steel frames, and through them she could see the harbour, grey-blue, with the cranes along the far side and the ferries going back and forth and the sky enormous over all of it.

She walked to the nearest window and put her hand on the glass.

It was cold, even in August. And thick. She could feel how thick it was. When she pressed, it didn’t give at all, not the way glass gives, even a little.

“Laminated,” said Jun Hyuk, behind her. “Five layers. Glass and plastic and glass. You could stand on the street and shoot at it all day and you’d just make it look cloudy.” He put his hand on the frame beside hers. “Somebody in the sixties made very expensive shirts here, and somebody in the nineties made something else, and they both had enemies. I put the glass in myself. It doesn’t open. None of them open. There’s air conditioning. It’s very loud.”

She looked out at the harbour.

She looked at the window frame. Steel, painted grey, bolted into the concrete. There was no handle, no hinge, no catch. She ran her finger along the bottom of it, where on any other window there’d be a sill, and found a narrow concrete ledge outside the glass, maybe twenty centimetres deep, with pigeon droppings on it and a bottle cap.

She looked at the ledge.

“What?” he said.

“Nothing,” said Evangeline.

✦ ✦ ✦

He’d been right about the kitchen.

It was a real one. Not a gas ring on a counter. A proper stove, four burners and an oven, old and white and enamelled, that somebody had cooked on for years before him and that he had never once used except to boil water. A sink you could get a pot in. Cupboards. A fridge, humming, with nothing in it but three cans of coffee and a bottle of soy sauce that had gone solid.

She stood in front of the stove a while.

Then she turned on every burner, one after another, and watched the blue flames come up in a row, and turned them off again. And the oven. She opened it and looked inside and shut it.

He was leaning in the kitchen door watching her.

“It works,” he said. “I think it works. I’ve never—”

She turned round and looked at him.

He stopped talking. He’d never seen her look like that. Her face hadn’t moved; it never did. But it was shining, as if somebody had taken a cloth to it.

“You’ve never cooked on a stove,” he said.

“At home,” said Evangeline, “the cook cooked.”

“But the soup. The ginger. The dumplings, at New Year—”

“Ma taught me. In the cook’s kitchen, at night. When the cook had gone.” She turned back to the stove and put her hand flat on the cold white enamel. “She said I should know how to feed someone. In case.”

“In case of what?”

She thought about it.

“In case someone was hungry,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

She cooked for three days.

He’d never seen anything like it. She went out to the wet market at the end of the street at six in the morning, the first day, with a canvas bag and a list in her head, and came back with fish, pork, chicken, a bag of clams, eggs, tofu, four kinds of greens, garlic, ginger, spring onions, a bag of dried mushrooms, a bag of dried shrimp, star anise, rock sugar, three kinds of soy sauce, and a cleaver.

She’d got the cleaver from a knife man by the fish stalls, she said, when he asked. She was taking it out of its newspaper. It was enormous and sharp and she held it the way he held the things he cleaned at night. “He sharpens them on a wheel. He sharpened it while I waited. I said it was for my husband.”

He sat down at the long table by the windows.

She hadn’t noticed what she’d said. She’d also, he saw, paid for all of it herself. Her purse was on the counter, open, flat, and there was a little paper slip from the knife man folded inside it, and he knew whose money that was. It was her mother’s. Elowen had told him, in July, on the stairs: their mother had left each of them an account, and Evangeline had never touched hers until the autumn she started taking buses north.

He got up, and went to the go-bag, and came back, and put a black card on the counter beside her purse. Then another one, from a different bank, in a different name. Then a bundle of cash, still in its plastic.

She looked at them.

“For the market,” he said. “For the knife man. For anything. For everything. You don’t spend your ma’s money on me. Not ever again. That’s a rule. Number ten.”

She looked at the card. Then at him.

“Put it on the menu,” said Evangeline.

He went and found the menu, which she’d brought from the border and taped inside the new door, and wrote it, in big square capitals: 10. SHE NEVER PAYS.

She watched him write it. Then she put the cards in her purse, and shut it.

She was rinsing the clams. He watched her rinse them, one by one, under the tap, and put them in a bowl of salt water, and he didn’t say anything.

On the first night she made steamed fish with ginger and spring onion, and clams with black bean, and greens with garlic, and rice. On the second night she made braised pork belly, which took four hours, and which she checked every twenty minutes, lifting the lid and looking in and putting the lid back, the way she’d checked his wound. On the third she made a chicken soup with the dried mushrooms that he ate four bowls of, and then sat back and looked at the ceiling.

“I’m going to get fat,” he said.

She looked at him.

“I’m going to get so fat,” he said, “that I can’t get through the hole in the fence at West Basin. I’ll have to make a new hole. A bigger hole. People will see the hole and say, look, a fat man made that, and I’ll be caught, and it’ll be your fault.”

She took his bowl and filled it again.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the fourth morning in the textile building, he heard her humming.

He was at the long table by the windows with his coffee, three sugars, and she was at the stove with her back to him, in her nightdress and a cardigan, frying eggs. And she was humming. Low, under her breath, not well. He’d never heard her hum before. He’d never heard her make any sound she didn’t have to.

It took him a moment to place the tune. Then he put his cup down.

It was his. The work song he hummed when he was carrying something, or driving, or cleaning his things, the one with no beginning and no end that the men in the Grey Lanterns had sung on the long roads, that Old Ko had sung, badly, in the cab. She’d heard it a thousand times. She’d picked it up without noticing, the way you pick up an accent, and here it was coming out of her at the stove, all wrong in the middle where he always went wrong too.

He didn’t say anything. He didn’t want her to stop.

He sat at the table and listened to her get through it twice, and slide the eggs onto two plates, and turn round. She saw his face and stopped.

“What?” she said.

“Nothing,” said Jun Hyuk. He couldn’t stop smiling. “Your eggs’ll get cold.”

He didn’t tell her for a week. When he finally did, she went red from the collar up, for the first time since he’d known her, and didn’t hum again for days. Then one evening, at the sink, she did, and caught herself, and glanced over her shoulder at him, and went on.

That evening he didn’t stay at the table.

He came up behind her at the sink and put his hands on the edge of it, either side of her, not touching her, close enough that she could feel the heat of him all down her back. He bent his head until his mouth was a breath from the side of her neck, just below her ear, where he’d found out in March that she couldn’t stand to be kissed without her knees going. He didn’t kiss it. He stayed there, an inch away, breathing.

She stopped humming. Her hands went still in the water.

“I’ve been thinking about that spot all day,” he said, low, against the air beside her skin. “At the docks. In the truck. The whole way up the stairs.” He still didn’t touch her. “I’ll stand here all night if I have to. I’m very patient.”

She stood there with her hands in the washing-up and her eyes shut.

“You’re not patient,” said Evangeline. “You’re terrible at it.”

“No,” he agreed, and his mouth was on her neck before she’d finished saying it, there, exactly there, and her knees went the way they always did, and she dropped a plate into the sink and didn’t care, and turned round in his arms with her wet hands on his face and kissed him back until the water went cold.

✦ ✦ ✦

She went to see Nuo on the Thursday.

She’d been going every month, as she’d promised in the hospital. Nuo wasn’t at the church hostel any more. She had a room in a shared flat in the old town with three other girls, and a job at a bakery on the corner, and her hair cut short, and a phone that she held up to show Evangeline photographs on, of cakes, of her roommates, of a cat that lived on the bakery roof.

They sat on the bench outside the bakery in the heat and ate egg tarts.

“I’m going to do a course,” said Nuo. She said it shyly, looking at her tart. “At night. At the college. To be a nurse. There’s money for it, for people like—for people like me. A woman from the church helped me fill in the form.”

Evangeline looked at her.

“Like the ones at the hospital,” said Nuo. “That night. They were so nice. One of them sat with me in the toilet when I was sick. She held my hair.” She turned the tart round. “I want to be the one who holds the hair.”

“Good,” said Evangeline.

Nuo laughed. She’d learned to laugh again since October; it came out of her easily now, though it stopped sometimes, halfway, the way his did.

“You always say that,” said Nuo. “Good. Just good. Like a teacher.”

Evangeline ate her tart.

“Do you ever see him?” said Nuo.

Evangeline didn’t answer right away. She looked at the street. A truck went past. A woman with a pram. Two of her father’s men, in a silver car, parked a little way down, pretending to read a newspaper; she’d lose them in the market afterwards, through the fish, out the back by the knife man.

“Yes,” she said.

Nuo put her tart down.

“Tell him,” she said. Her voice wobbled. “Tell him—tell him I’m going to be a nurse.”

“I’ll tell him.”

“Tell him I’m going to hold people’s hair.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She told him that night.

He was at the table, cleaning his things, and she sat across from him the way she always did, and waited until he’d finished, and put the cloth back on the towel, because she knew now that you didn’t talk while he did it, and then she told him. All of it. The flat in the old town and the three roommates and the bakery and the cat on the roof and the college and the form, and the fund at the church that would pay for all of it, and the woman who’d held her hair in the hospital toilet. She said it in about forty words, which was a speech, for her. At the part about the fund, she looked up at him, and held his eyes, and went on.

He listened without moving.

When she’d finished, he sat looking at the towel on the table with his things on it.

His face went quiet. She watched it and waited, and outside the five tall windows that didn’t open the lights of the harbour came on, one by one, all along the far side, and the ferries went back and forth with their lamps lit.

Then he got up and went into the bathroom and shut the door.

She heard the tap run. It ran.

When he came out, his face was wet, and he didn’t explain, and she didn’t ask. He came and sat down at the table across from her and folded his big hands on top of the towel.

“A nurse,” he said. His voice was rough.

She waited.

He nodded. He kept nodding, looking at his hands.

She looked past him at the window.

The light from the room fell out through the thick glass onto the narrow concrete ledge outside, twenty centimetres deep, with the pigeon droppings and the bottle cap. Behind it were the harbour and its lights and the big dark sky. She’d looked at that ledge every day for a week. She’d measured it with her eyes. South-facing. Sun from ten in the morning until four in the afternoon. Out of the wind, mostly, because of the building next door.

“Basil would grow there,” said Evangeline.

He looked up.

She was looking at the ledge. She wasn’t looking at him. She’d said it the way she said things about the weather, or the cats, or the price of fish: a fact, mentioned, and then put down. She didn’t say I want. She didn’t say could we. She never did. She’d said it looking out of the window, and now she was drinking her tea.

He looked at the ledge. He looked at the thick grey frame with no handle and no hinge and no catch, bolted into the concrete, that he had put in himself, in 2019, so that nothing could come in.

He looked at her.

“Basil,” he said.

She didn’t answer. She’d already said it. She wouldn’t say it again.

He didn’t sleep that night. He lay on the mattress on the floor of the long room beside her, the mattress they’d brought from the border instead of the camp beds, and listened to her breathing, and looked at the dark row of windows, and thought.

At three in the morning he got up and took the measuring tape out of the go-bag, and went and stood at the nearest window in his bare feet, in the light of the harbour, and started measuring.

chapters.title: He Builds One Anyway
chapters.desc: A steel box bolted to a concrete ledge, a hatch cut into five layers of glass, and nine pots of herbs. Then a pair of earrings from Harbour Road, a flower-shop wedding, and a man on the roof across the street all night.
chapters.epigraph: “Good mend.” — Evangeline Lin, at a wedding, to Aurelia Chen
chapters.content:
He started at three in the morning and didn’t tell her.

She knew anyway. She knew because she woke at ten past four, the way she always woke when the room changed, and his side of the mattress was cold, and there was a light at the far end of the long room, by the windows. A small one. A torch, held in his teeth.

She lay still and watched.

He was standing at the nearest window in his bare feet with a measuring tape and a pencil and a pad of graph paper, measuring the steel frame. Again. He’d measured it four nights running. He measured the frame and wrote down a number, and measured the glass and wrote down a number, and then he crouched and put his face close to the bottom of the window and looked out through it at the concrete ledge, twenty centimetres deep, with the pigeon droppings and the bottle cap, for a good while, with the torch in his teeth, like a man reading a map of a country he meant to invade.

She didn’t say anything. She shut her eyes.

When he came back to the mattress at five and lay down carefully, so as not to wake her, she put her hand flat on his chest, and felt him jump.

“Come back to bed,” she said. “It’ll still be there in the morning.”

“I am asleep,” he said. “This is me asleep.”

She kept her hand there until he was.

✦ ✦ ✦

It took him three weeks.

He didn’t explain any of it. He went out in the mornings and came back with things. Steel sheet, cut to size by a man in a workshop by the docks who he said owed him a favour, and who he paid anyway, in cash, more than the favour was worth. Angle iron. A box of bolts. A drill the size of a small dog. Then, on the second Saturday, a man came: a thin, nervous glazier with grey hair, who had been fitting glass in banks and jewellers’ for thirty years and had been told he would be paid four times his rate if he did one small job on a Saturday and forgot the address afterwards.

The glazier looked at the windows.

“You want,” he said, “to cut a hatch. In that.”

“A small one,” said Jun Hyuk. “Here. At the bottom. Forty by thirty. With a frame and a lock. Laminated, same as the rest, five layers. It has to open from inside and only from inside. And it has to hold. The whole pane. If someone puts a round through it, it has to hold like it holds now.”

The glazier looked at him. He looked at Evangeline, at the long table, with her tea.

“What for?” he said.

“Basil,” said Jun Hyuk.

The glazier looked at him for a moment longer. Then he took his glasses off and cleaned them on his shirt and put them back on, and took out a notebook of his own, and they bent their heads over the graph paper together like two surgeons over an X-ray. They talked about lamination and frame tolerances and edge bonding for two hours. Evangeline drank her tea and didn’t understand a word of it, and didn’t mind.

✦ ✦ ✦

He built the box himself.

He did it on the ledge, outside the glass, at night, roped to a steel ring he bolted into the concrete beside the window, on the sixth floor, with the harbour wind coming up the side of the building and the lights of the ferries going back and forth below. She stood inside the window and watched him, with her hands flat on the cold glass, and barely breathed.

It was steel, painted grey, the colour of the frame, so that from the street you wouldn’t see it. Long, the length of the window. Narrow, to fit the ledge. Deep enough for roots. He drilled holes in the bottom for drainage, and put a tray under the holes so the water wouldn’t run down the side of the building onto the printing works’ sign. He cut slots along the back, low, for air. And over the top of it, sloping down from the glass to the front edge, he fitted a lid: laminated glass, in a steel frame, the same as the windows, so that whatever grew in the box would grow under glass you could shoot at all day.

“It’s a greenhouse,” he said, when he came in through the hatch at two in the morning, with grease on his hands and a cut across his thumb. “Sort of. An armoured one. The lid keeps the rain off and the heat in, and the slots let the air through, and if anyone ever—if anyone ever shoots at the window, the box is fine. The plants are fine.” He was sucking his thumb. “Nobody shoots at basil. Probably. But in case.”

She took his hand and looked at the cut.

It wasn’t deep. She washed it at the sink anyway, and dried it on one of the white towels, and put a plaster on it from the drawer, which had come with them from the border, with the needles and the tape and the three candles.

He watched her do it.

“You haven’t looked at it,” he said. “The box. You haven’t said if it’s—”

She put the box of plasters away and shut the drawer.

Then she went to the window and knelt down in front of the hatch, the forty-by-thirty hatch in the five layers of glass, and turned the little steel key in the lock, and pushed. It swung outward on its hinge, silently, the way the glazier had promised. The harbour wind came in. It smelled of salt and diesel and, under that, faintly, of the night.

She put her hand through the hatch and touched the steel edge of the box, the way he’d touched the ring on her finger, the first night.

She stayed there on her knees.

He came and knelt down behind her, because he couldn’t not, and she turned round on her knees and took his face in her hands, plaster and grease and all, and kissed him.

He kept his hands off her. They were black to the wrist. He held them out to the sides like a man who’d been told not to touch the paint, and she kissed him anyway, with the harbour wind coming in through the open hatch, until he forgot about the grease altogether and put both hands flat on her back and pulled her in against him.

She didn’t wash that cardigan for a week. It had two black handprints on the back, one either side, and she wore it to the market twice before he noticed, and went red, and she didn’t explain.

✦ ✦ ✦

She planted it on the Sunday.

He took her to the plant market himself, the one near the stadium, in the truck, at seven in the morning, and walked behind her with a trolley. She walked along the stalls the way she’d walked along the orchid stalls in the Walled City since she was fourteen: slowly, looking at the roots, not the leaves, turning the pots in her hands. He said nothing at all. He pushed the trolley. Every time she looked at something for longer than three seconds, he put it in.

By the fourth stall the trolley was full.

“It’s a window box,” she said, looking at it.

He put a pot of lemon thyme in, because she’d glanced at it, and said only, “Rule ten.”

She looked at the trolley. Basil, two kinds. Mint. Coriander, which would bolt in the heat, and she knew it, and he didn’t. Chives. Thyme, and lemon thyme. Rosemary. A small bay tree, which would never in a hundred years fit in a twenty-centimetre box. A tray of strawberry plants. A pot of white orchids.

She took the bay tree out and put it back on the stall. She took out the strawberries. She left the orchids.

He put the strawberries back in when she wasn’t looking.

She planted the box that afternoon, kneeling at the hatch, reaching through, in the light coming off the harbour. Nine pots in the long steel box, in compost she’d mixed herself in a bucket, with grit for the rosemary, and bark for the orchid at the end the building next door kept in shade. He sat on the floor behind her and handed her things. The strawberries she put in a hanging pot he hadn’t known he’d bought, hooked inside the glass, in the sun.

When she’d finished, she shut the glass lid of the box from inside, with the long handle he’d made for it, and shut the hatch, and turned the little key.

They looked at it together through the window. A row of green, small, on a grey steel box on a grey concrete ledge on the sixth floor of a textile building nobody looked at, behind five layers of glass.

“It’s not much,” he said.

She leaned back against his chest. He put his arms round her from behind, and she let him, and didn’t go still. She hadn’t gone still with him for months now. She hadn’t noticed when it stopped.

“Basil would grow here,” she said, and he laughed into her hair, because she’d said it in August, looking out of a window, as a fact, and now it was going to be true.

✦ ✦ ✦

The invitation to Elowen’s wedding had been on the long table since June.

Not the registry office. That had been three and a half years ago, on a Tuesday, with soil under Elowen’s nails and a red background in the photograph. This was the other one. The real one, Elowen said, with the air of a general announcing an invasion: in September, in the flower shop, with every Lin and every friend and two dogs and an arch from the shipyard and Elara doing the cake.

Evangeline’s name was on the envelope, and under it, in Elowen’s cool slanted hand, and guest.

She’d looked at it, in June. Then she’d put it face down on the table.

“I can’t,” said Jun Hyuk, in August, when he found it. “You know I can’t. Zhao’s men on the door, Chen Si’s men on the street, half the Syndicate, every policeman who’s ever wanted a photograph of Zhao Zhendong with a camellia in his buttonhole, and Song Wei Long, probably, at the back, with his face. I can’t walk into a room like that. I can’t be in a photograph. I’m not a person who can be in a photograph.” He put the card down. “I’m sorry.”

She didn’t say anything. She wasn’t allowed in photographs either. She’d never been in one in her life.

She’d been going to stand at the back.

“I’ll be there,” he said.

She looked up.

“Not in it. Near it. Where I can see.” He was looking at the card. “Every door, every window, every car on the street. All night. Nobody will get within a hundred metres of that shop that I don’t know about. I’ll be there the whole time.” He paused. “You won’t see me. But I’ll be there.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He took her to Harbour Road a week before the wedding.

He didn’t say where they were going. He drove the truck into the city on a Thursday afternoon and parked it behind the old ferry terminal and walked her up the hill, in his one good shirt, the one she’d sewn the button on, with his cap pulled down, and stopped outside a shop with a black front and gold letters, AURELIA, and a necklace in the window.

The necklace had been broken, once, and mended. You could see the mend. It ran through the middle of it in a seam of gold, and that was the point of it. She had seen it before, from the bus, a hundred times.

“I don’t know anything about jewellery,” said Jun Hyuk. “I asked your sister what you’d like. She said you’d never tell me. She said to come here and look at your face.”

The woman behind the counter was tall and dark and immaculate, in cream, with a broken necklace of her own at her throat, and she looked up when the door opened, and looked at Evangeline, and recognised her. Elowen’s sister. The quiet one. They’d been in the same room at a dozen dinners.

Then she looked at the man behind Evangeline, all one hundred and ninety-three centimetres of him in a cap and a mended shirt, and her eyebrows went up.

“Hello,” said Evangeline.

Aurelia Chen looked at her for a moment.

“Hello,” she said. “I don’t believe you’ve ever said that to me before.”

Evangeline inclined her head.
