Aurelia’s eyes went to the plain silver band on her left hand. Then to the man. Then back to Evangeline’s face, and the cool shop manner gave way to real interest.

“Well,” she said. “What can I show you?”

He told her: earrings, for a wedding, and pale blue, because Evangeline always wore pale blue and he’d only just noticed. Aurelia didn’t ask anything else. She went into the back and came out with a tray. She laid them out on the black velvet one pair at a time and watched Evangeline’s face, not her hands, the way he’d said Elowen told him to.

Evangeline’s face didn’t move. Not for the sapphires, or the topaz, or a pair of diamonds that cost more than the truck.

On the eighth pair, it moved.

They were small. Aquamarines, pale, almost grey, the colour of the sky at five in the morning over the harbour, before anyone was up. Each one hung from a short drop of gold, plain, and the gold had a seam in it, the same seam as the necklace in the window, as if each earring had been broken once and mended.

Aurelia saw it. Of course she saw it.

“Those,” she said to Jun Hyuk, without taking her eyes off Evangeline. “Those ones.”

He didn’t ask the price. He put a card on the counter, a black one, and Aurelia ran it, and handed it back, and wrapped the earrings in black tissue in a small black box with gold letters on the lid, and tied it with a ribbon.

“Thank you,” said Evangeline.

Aurelia looked at her with an expression he couldn’t read at all.

“Three words,” she said. “In one afternoon. I’m going to have to sit down.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The wedding was on the twenty-third of September, a Saturday, and it went on until two in the morning.

She stood at the back.

She’d known she would. She stood at the back of the flower shop in the Walled City, in a pale blue dress, with her hair pinned up and the aquamarines in her ears, beside the second row of buckets, with her arms folded, and watched everything. Her father walking Elowen down the aisle in his funeral suit, and stopping halfway, and saying something to Zhao that made Zhao go still. The thousands of lights Eliana had strung across the ceiling coming on all at once at nine forty-one, gold, like the sky had come indoors. Raiden in a silver waistcoat beside a tall woman in a leather jacket with grease under her nails, whom he introduced to everyone as Jinx, and who looked at Evangeline once, across the room, and nodded, as if they’d recognised something in each other. Elara’s cake. The dogs.

She’d brought Elowen an orchid that morning. A white one, a cutting from the plant she’d given her sister the week Elowen moved into the house on the hill, three and a half years ago, when the marriage was a contract and everyone was frightened. Elowen had looked at it on the counter beside the till and burst into tears.

I kept a piece, Evangeline had said.

She stood at the back now and watched the door. She knew he was out there. Somewhere across the street, in the dark, where she couldn’t see him. On a roof, she thought. He liked roofs. She watched the door and the windows and the black gap between the buildings opposite where the streetlights didn’t reach, and every so often she thought she saw something, a shape against the sky, and then it was gone.

At half past eleven, at the little bar by the cooler, Aurelia came and stood beside her.

They stood there together, not speaking, for about a minute. Aurelia had a glass of champagne. Evangeline had a glass of water. Across the room, Chen Si was dancing with Elowen, correctly, and Zhao was watching them both with his arms folded, and Aurelia was watching all three with an expression of deep private amusement.

Evangeline looked at the broken necklace at Aurelia’s throat. The gold seam where it had been mended.

“Good mend,” she said.

Aurelia went still beside her. Then she turned her head and looked at Evangeline’s ears, at the two small mended drops of gold with the pale stones in them. Her mouth moved at the corner.

“Yes,” she said. “I think so too.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At ten past two, when the last of the lights were going off and her father was asleep in a chair by the door and Raiden was carrying the dogs out to the car, Evangeline cut two slices of Elara’s cake onto a paper plate, and put her coat on over the pale blue dress, and went out of the back door of the shop into the alley.

The building opposite was an old tea merchant’s, four storeys, with an iron ladder up the back to the roof for the water tanks. She’d watched it all night. She went up it in her good shoes, with the plate in one hand, the way she’d gone up the fire escape at the border in January.

He was there.

He was sitting with his back against the water tank on the far side of the roof, where the shadow was deepest, with a pair of binoculars on his knees and a thermos beside him, looking down at the street. He’d been there since six in the evening. He didn’t look round when she came over the edge of the roof. He’d heard her on the ladder. He’d have heard her if she’d been a cat.

She sat down beside him on the warm tar of the roof and held out the plate.

He looked at the cake. He looked at her.

He took it. He ate a slice in four bites, with his fingers, without taking his eyes off the street, and then he stopped, and turned his head, and looked at her properly for the first time.

The streetlight from the alley came up over the edge of the roof and caught the side of her face. Her hair pinned up. The pale blue dress under her coat. The aquamarines in her ears, the colour of the sky before anyone was up, moving slightly when she breathed.

He didn’t say anything. He just looked.

“Every door,” she said. “Every window. Every car on the street.”

“Every one,” he said. His voice was rough. “All night.”

“I know.” She leaned her head on his shoulder. “I couldn’t see you. I watched you anyway.”

He put the binoculars down on the roof. He put his arm round her. She sat with her head on his shoulder on the warm roof of the tea merchant’s with the city going quiet all round them, the last taxis going home, the lights going off one by one in the flower shop across the street, and the sky over the harbour beginning, faintly, at the edge, to turn the colour of her earrings.

“You’re the most beautiful thing I’ve ever seen,” said Jun Hyuk. “I wanted to say it at the shop. In front of everyone. Every time you came past the window, I wanted to say it. So I’m saying it now. On a roof. Where nobody can hear.”

She turned her face into his neck.

“I can hear,” said Evangeline.

He turned his head. Her mouth was right there, at his jaw, and he stopped pretending he was watching the street.

He kissed her on the roof of the tea merchant’s with the binoculars on the tar beside them and the paper plate sliding off his knee, slow at first, and then not, his hand going in under her coat to the small of her back and pulling her across him until she was in his lap in her pale blue dress, with the water tank at his back and her shoes kicked off on the tar. She kissed him as if she’d been standing at the back of a flower shop for eight hours waiting to, which she had. Somewhere below them a taxi door slammed. Neither of them looked.

“Every door,” she said against his mouth, when she could. “You said.”

“I’m still watching,” said Jun Hyuk, and he was, over her shoulder, with one eye, because he was who he was. He kissed her again anyway, and didn’t stop until the last taxi had gone, and the street stayed empty.

chapters.title: The Traffickers Remember Her
chapters.desc: There is exactly one photograph of Evangeline Lin in the world. It was taken with a flash in the dark of a container, and in October someone puts it up for sale.
chapters.epigraph: “Price on request. Serious buyers only. Palace interest welcome.” — a listing, deleted at 4:00 a.m.
chapters.content:
The basil came up in nine days.

She’d known it would. Basil was easy, if it had sun and heat and you didn’t drown it, and the steel box had all three. But she knelt at the hatch every morning anyway, at seven, with a cup of tea, and turned the little key, and looked. On the ninth day there were two rows of seed leaves, round and bright, like small green coins, pushing up through the dark compost in the corner where she’d sown it as well as the pots.

She looked at them for so long that he came and knelt beside her to see what was wrong, and saw, and put his arm round her shoulders. “Look at that,” he said. “Nine days. You said nine days.”

She leaned against him and looked at the seed leaves. Then, for no reason she could have explained, she laughed.

It still surprised him, every time. It came out of her so rarely, and so completely, like water coming up out of the ground, and when it stopped, she always looked a little startled herself, as if she’d forgotten she had it. He’d started keeping a count. That made eleven since the typhoon.

He didn’t tell her he was counting. He kissed her instead, on the side of the head first, and then, when she turned her face up, properly, kneeling on the concrete by the hatch with the tea going cold beside them, until she put her hand flat on his chest and pushed him off so she could look at the basil again.

✦ ✦ ✦

He spoiled her in October. He didn’t call it that. He wouldn’t have known what to call it. He’d just never had anyone to buy things for, and now he did, and he was making up for twenty years.

He bought a rice cooker, a good one, Japanese, because she said once that the one at home in the Walled City had been the same for twenty years and made rice like a sponge. He bought a set of knives from the knife man by the fish, all of them, and the knife man wept. He bought a teapot from a shop in the old town that sold only teapots, a small round one in dark clay that the old man in the shop said would remember every tea she ever made in it and get better each time, and Evangeline held it in both hands in the shop and didn’t put it down. He bought her a coat. He didn’t know anything about coats. He went into a shop on Harbour Road that had one coat in the window and nothing else, and looked at the woman behind the counter, and said, “She’s this tall, and she’s always cold, and she likes pale blue but she’d never say it,” and walked out forty minutes later with a coat in a bag the size of a suitcase that had cost more than his first truck.

She stood looking at the coat when he gave it to her. He could see her starting to say it was too much, and he held it open before she could, and said, “Put it on. I’ve never bought anyone a coat. I bought Old Ko a hat once and he used it to carry eggs.”

She put it on.

It was soft and warm and exactly the pale blue she would never have asked for, and it came down to her ankles, and she stood in the middle of the long room in it, by the windows, with the harbour behind her, and didn’t move.

He sat down on the end of the mattress.

“Good,” he said, hoarsely, before she could.

She looked at him sitting on the end of the mattress. Then she came across the long room to him in the coat and stood between his knees, and he put his hands on her waist through the soft blue wool and looked up at her as if she’d come down a staircase.

“Say it’s too much,” he said. “Go on. I can see you want to.”

She bent and kissed him instead.

He pulled her down into his lap, coat and all, the whole ankle-length armful of it, and kissed her back until she’d forgotten whatever she’d been going to say about the price, and some time after that. When she finally sat up, the coat had slid off one shoulder and her hair was coming down and he was grinning at her like a boy who’d got away with something.

“Keep it on,” he said.

She kept it on.

✦ ✦ ✦

Eliana found the photograph on the seventeenth of October.

She’d been looking for a year. Nobody had asked her to. She had told nobody she was doing it. In October 2022, the week after the hospital, she had sat up in her room at the top of the tall house in the Walled City, in the dark, with three screens, and set up something she called a fence. She didn’t explain to anyone what it was. It watched the places where things were sold that couldn’t be sold in shops, the ones you got to through three other places, and it watched them for Evangeline’s name, and for the Lin name, and for the address of the house, and for a picture of her sister’s face, which Eliana had had to make herself, from memory and from a drawing Raiden did, because there were no photographs of Evangeline anywhere in the world.

Except one.

The fence caught it at nineteen minutes past three in the morning. Eliana looked at it, got out of bed, was sick in the bathroom, and rang Elowen.

✦ ✦ ✦

Elowen brought her to the textile building at eight.

Jun Hyuk had given Elowen the address after the wedding. Nobody else. He’d written it on a piece of paper on the roof of the tea merchant’s, at three in the morning, and handed it to Evangeline, and said, give it to her, she’s the only one, and Evangeline had given it to her sister at breakfast with the rest of the cake.

Elowen came up the stairs first, fast, with her face set like a blade. Behind her came a girl of twenty in a black hoodie with the hood up and a laptop held against her chest in both arms like a shield, who stopped in the doorway of the long room and stared up at Jun Hyuk with her mouth open.

“You’re huge,” said Eliana.

“I know,” said Jun Hyuk. “Everyone says. It’s a lot of work. Come in. Sit down. There’s tea, there’s congee, there’s a very good teapot, it remembers things—”

“I found it,” said Eliana. She didn’t sit down. She was looking past him, at Evangeline, at the long table by the windows. Her eyes were red. “Jie. I found it. I’m sorry. I’m sorry. I found it and I took it down and I took the copies down, all the ones I could find, and I don’t know if I got them all, I don’t know who’s seen it, I don’t—”

“Show me,” said Evangeline.

✦ ✦ ✦

Eliana put the laptop on the long table and opened it and turned it round.

It was a page on a site with a black background and grey writing, in three languages, and in the middle of it there was a photograph.

It had been taken with a flash. You could see that: the white glare in the middle, and the hard black shadows behind, and the way everything at the edges fell away into the dark. A corrugated wall. A floor. The edge of something that might be a bucket. In the background, out of focus, a huddle of shapes against the wall that were women, holding on to each other, their faces turned away from the light.

And in front of them, in the middle of the picture, in the white of the flash, looking straight at the camera, Evangeline.

Her hair had come down. Her cardigan was grey with dirt. There was a mark on her cheek. Her face was perfectly still, the way it always was, carved, pale, and her eyes in the flash were enormous and black and looking straight down the lens, at whoever was holding it, without blinking, without fear, without anything at all.

Under the photograph, in English and in two other languages, there were four lines of grey text.

Female. 24. Healthy. Royal blood, documented. Location: the city. Currently unprotected.

Price on request.

Serious buyers only.

Palace interest welcome.

✦ ✦ ✦

Nobody said anything.

Eliana was crying without any noise, in her hood, with her hands over her mouth. Elowen had her hand on the back of her youngest sister’s neck and was looking at the screen with a face like a closed door. Behind them, the harbour was grey, and the ferries went back and forth, and a gull came down and sat on the steel box on the ledge outside and looked in through the glass.

Evangeline looked at the photograph.

She remembered it. Of course she did. The first day. Before the dark set in properly, before she’d learned to count the hours by the holes in the roof. The door had opened, a crack, and a man had leaned in with a phone, and there’d been a flash so bright it hurt, and she’d been standing, because she’d got up when she heard the door, the way she would get up again two days later. And the man had laughed, and said smile, Your Highness, and shut the door.

She hadn’t smiled.

She looked at her own face on the screen. She had seen it in mirrors and in windows and in the backs of spoons, but she had never seen a picture of herself in her life. She’d been taken out of every room with a camera in it since before she could walk.

This was the only one.

She looked at the girl in the white glare, with the mark on her cheek and the women behind her, and thought: so that’s what I look like when I stop hiding.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t look at Jun Hyuk.

She knew where he was without looking. He was standing behind her chair. He’d been standing there since Eliana turned the laptop round. He hadn’t moved and he hadn’t spoken, and she could feel him not speaking, like the pressure before a storm.

“Who,” said Elowen.

Eliana wiped her face on her sleeve and pulled the laptop back towards her and typed. Her hands were steady now, steadier than her voice; she was always steadier with her hands on a keyboard.

“The account’s new,” she said. “Two months old. But the way it’s written, the words, the way the price is put, it’s the same as eleven other listings on that site over three years. Same person. I traced the uploads. Most of them go through four countries and come out nowhere. This one didn’t. He was lazy. He uploaded it from a phone, and the phone was on a network in the eastern district, at a place that’s a mahjong club above a car wash on Kiln Street.” She swallowed. “And the account’s got a name on it. Not a real name. A handle.”

“What?” said Elowen.

“Hwang,” said Eliana.

Behind Evangeline’s chair, Jun Hyuk breathed in.

It was the only sound he made, one long slow breath, like a man about to go under water.

“I know him,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

Elowen took Eliana home at ten.

At the door, Eliana stopped, and turned, and looked up at Jun Hyuk with her red eyes in her black hood. She looked young.

“I took it down,” she said. “I want you to know I took it down. Every copy I could find. And I put something in the site so that if he puts it up again, it’ll—” She stopped. “It’ll go wrong. For him. Very wrong.”

He looked down at her.

“Good,” he said. “Thank you. That’s very good.”

Eliana’s face crumpled. She put her arms round him, as far round as they would go, which was not far, with the laptop squashed between them, and held on, hard and quick. Then she let go and went down the stairs fast, and Elowen looked at him once, from the landing, a long cool look, and followed her.

He shut the door. He turned the locks.

✦ ✦ ✦

Evangeline was still at the table.

The laptop was gone, but she was sitting looking at the place where it had been, with her hands folded, straight, in the pale blue coat she’d put on that morning because the long room was cold and hadn’t taken off.

He came and sat down across from her.

He didn’t say anything. She’d known he wouldn’t. There was nothing in his face at all. His hands were on the table, open, and they were dead still, and she had never in her life seen anything so frightening as how still they were.

“I was standing up,” said Evangeline.

He looked at her.

“In the picture.” She looked at the table. “When they opened the door. I’d got up when I heard it. Like at West Basin. I don’t remember deciding to. They opened the door and I was already up.” She turned her hands over, palms up, on the table. “I’d never seen a photograph of myself. Not one. Ever.” Her voice was low and level. “So that’s the only one. That’s what I look like.”

He reached across the table and put his hands over hers.

They were warm. Hers were cold. He held them, both of them, the ring under his thumb.

“I know what you look like,” he said. His voice came out of him like something being dragged over gravel. “I’ve looked at you every day for a year. I know what you look like asleep, and when you’re cooking, and when you’re cross with the basil for being slow, and on a roof in a blue dress at two in the morning. That’s not what you look like.” He tightened his hands. “That’s what they made you look like. For one second. With a flash. In the dark.”

She looked at him.

“I’m going to go and see Mr. Hwang,” said Jun Hyuk.

She didn’t say don’t, or be careful, or what will you do to him. For a year she had watched him go down the stairs and come back with things on his sleeve, and she had never asked who or why. He’d told her in June what he was, and she had stayed.

Her face didn’t move. But she turned her hands over under his and held on, hard.

Then she let go.

“Have something to eat before you go,” said Evangeline, and got up to heat the congee.

chapters.title: He Goes Hunting
chapters.desc: A mahjong club above a car wash on Kiln Street, a man called Hwang, and four days. She follows every rule. She doesn’t sleep.
chapters.epigraph: “If I’m not back by Sunday, go to your sister. Don’t wait up.” “I won’t.” — the sixth floor, Thursday night
chapters.content:
He left on Thursday night at eleven.

He did it the way he always did. He cleaned his things at the long table on the grey towel, in silence, while she sat across from him with her tea. He packed the bag. He put on the black jacket. He stood by the door, and she got up and went to him, and put her hand flat on his chest, over his heart, and he put his hand over hers.

“Sunday,” he said. “If I’m not back by Sunday night, you go to your sister. Not your father. Your sister. She knows what to do. Don’t wait up.”

“I won’t,” said Evangeline.

He looked at her. They both knew she was lying, and they both let her.

He touched her face. Eyebrows, nose, cheekbone, jaw, the corner of her mouth. Checking.

Then he bent his head and kissed her, hard and slow, with his hand at the back of her neck and his other arm right round her, lifting her onto her toes, as if he were taking something with him that he’d need. She held on to the front of his jacket until he let her go, and then for a second after.

He turned the three locks and went out, and she heard him on the stairs, all six flights, until the street door shut at the bottom.

She turned the locks behind him.

✦ ✦ ✦

Thursday night she didn’t sleep.

She went to bed at ten past twelve, because rule six said don’t wait up, and she followed the rules. She lay on the mattress on the floor of the long room on her side, facing the door, with the blanket over her and her eyes open. She didn’t wait up. She lay down. That was different.

The harbour lights came in through the five tall windows and made long pale shapes on the floor. The air conditioning roared and stopped and roared. Down in the printing works, on the bottom floor, the night shift was running something, and the whole building hummed with it, faintly, through the concrete, like a cat purring in another room.

At three o’clock she got up and checked the locks. All three. She went back to bed.

At five she got up and knelt at the hatch and turned the little key and looked at the basil. It was a week older than the basil she’d shown him. It had its first true leaves now, the second pair, pointed, with the smell in them. She touched one lightly through the hatch and smelled her finger.

She shut the hatch.

✦ ✦ ✦

Kiln Street was in the eastern district, behind the old brickworks, where the roads were narrow and the buildings were tall and close and covered in signs. Car wash on the ground floor. Above it, on the first and second floors, behind windows taped over with yellowed newspaper, the Golden Harvest Mahjong Club, which had been there since 1987 and had not, as far as anyone knew, ever closed.

Jun Hyuk sat in a noodle shop across the road for seventeen hours.

He didn’t mind. He’d sat in worse places for longer. He sat at the counter by the window with a bowl in front of him that he refilled every two hours so the owner wouldn’t throw him out, and a newspaper he turned the pages of without reading, and watched the door beside the car wash, and the stairs inside it, and the men who went up them and came down.

He talked to the noodle shop owner, because he talked to everyone. About the weather, and the noodles, and the owner’s son, who was at university studying something with computers and never called. The owner was a small worried man with a burn on his wrist, and by the ninth hour he had told Jun Hyuk about his wife’s knees, his brother’s debts, and the man who ran the mahjong club, whose name was Mr. Hwang, who came down at four every afternoon for a bowl of wonton, no spring onion, and who had once, in 2019, pushed the owner’s nephew down those stairs for being slow with the change.

“Is he a regular, then?” said Jun Hyuk. “Mr. Hwang?”

“Every day,” said the owner. “Four o’clock. You could set your watch.”

Jun Hyuk said that was very useful to know, and ordered another bowl.

✦ ✦ ✦

Friday she went to the wet market.

She went at six, in the pale blue coat, with her canvas bag and his black card in her purse, which she didn’t use, because the fish woman didn’t take cards. She bought fish. She bought greens. She bought ginger and pork ribs and dried mushrooms, and she went home and made the soup her mother made for her father before he went anywhere, ginger first, then the bones, because if you put the ginger in after, the soup knew.

He wasn’t there to eat it.

She made it anyway. She ate one bowl at the long table by the window and put the rest in the big pot in the fridge, where it would keep.

At eleven in the morning Elowen rang.

Not on her phone. She didn’t have her phone; it was in a drawer in the kitchen, switched off, the way he liked. On the old black landline that came with the building, which had rung exactly twice since August, both times a wrong number.

“Ev,” said Elowen. “Is he back?”

“No.”

“Do you want me to come?”

Evangeline considered it.

“No,” she said.

There was a pause on the line.

“You don’t have to do this on your own,” said her sister. “You know that. You’ve never had to. I’d have sat on the stairs with you, at home. Any night. You only had to say.”

“I know,” said Evangeline. “I’m not on my own.”

“Ev, he’s not—”

“He’s on Kiln Street,” said Evangeline. “In a noodle shop. Waiting. He’ll talk to the owner about the weather.”

Another pause.

“How do you know that?”

“Because I know him.”

Elowen said goodbye in a voice gone flat and careful, and rang off, and didn’t ring again that week. Evangeline knew what she’d done. She did it to everyone who came close: gave them nothing, so politely that they couldn’t argue, and let them go away hurt. She’d done it to her father for twenty-four years. She didn’t ring back. It cost her two Sunday lunches of Elowen passing her the rice without looking at her, and she paid them without a word.

✦ ✦ ✦

At four o’clock on Friday afternoon, Mr. Hwang came down the stairs beside the car wash for his wonton.

He was fifty, perhaps, soft and heavy, with a shaved head and a gold chain and a phone in each hand, and he came across the road without looking, the way men cross roads when they have never once in their lives thought that a car might not stop for them. He came into the noodle shop and sat down at his table at the back, under the calendar, and the owner went pale and went to get his bowl.

Jun Hyuk folded his newspaper.

He picked up his own bowl, which had a little broth left in it, and walked to the back of the shop, and sat down at Mr. Hwang’s table, opposite him, on the stool facing the door.

Mr. Hwang looked up.

“Hello,” said Jun Hyuk. “Good afternoon. Don’t get up. Please. You’re having your wonton. Very good wonton here. I’ve had nine bowls of the noodles, I haven’t tried the wonton, I’m told it’s better without the spring onion. Is that true? You’d know.” He put his bowl down. “I’m Lee. You’ve heard of me, I think. Big. From the border. Talks a lot. That’s me. And you’re Mr. Hwang, of the Golden Harvest, and you’ve got a phone in each hand, and in one of them, I think it’s the left one, there’s a photograph of a woman in a container.”

Mr. Hwang had stopped moving.

“I’d like to talk to you about her,” said Jun Hyuk pleasantly. “I’d like to talk to you about who you sold her to last year, and who answered your little advertisement this week, and how many copies you’ve got. And then I’d like you to come for a walk with me. Not far. You can bring your wonton.”

The owner came out from the back with the bowl, and saw them, and stopped.

“It’s all right, uncle,” said Jun Hyuk, without looking round. “Put it down. Mr. Hwang’s going to need his strength. And you might want to close for the afternoon. I’d go and visit your son, if I were you. The one with the computers. I bet he’d love to see you.”

The owner put the bowl down carefully. He took off his apron. He went out of the front door without his coat, and turned the sign on the door to CLOSED, and walked away down Kiln Street fast.

Mr. Hwang looked at the door. Then at the big man across the table.

“Who are you?” he said. His voice had gone thin.

“I told you,” said Jun Hyuk. “I’m Lee. I’m the man who opened the box.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Saturday she cleaned the flat.

All of it. Every surface. The long table, the kitchen, the stove, inside the oven, the bathroom, the tall windows, inside, the five of them, with newspaper and vinegar, the way her mother did, until the glass was so clear that the harbour seemed to come right into the room. She washed every towel. She folded them all, in thirds and then rolled, and put them in a row on the shelf in the bathroom, and stood and looked at them.

She did not touch the bag. It was gone, with him. She did not touch the crates, which were stacked in the corner under a tarpaulin, and which she had never once opened.

At two in the afternoon she sat down at the long table as if her legs had been cut, and put her face in her hands.

She didn’t cry. She sat like that for twenty minutes, without moving, with her elbows on the table and her face in her hands and her eyes shut. She thought about the flash. Smile, Your Highness. She thought about the thing she’d seen in his face across the table on Tuesday night when he said I’m going to go and see Mr. Hwang. She thought about what he was doing. Right now. This minute. Somewhere in the city, on a street she didn’t know, to a man she’d never met.

She didn’t know what she felt about it, and she made herself sit with that, the way she’d made herself sit with the one shot from the tower at West Basin, lying on her stomach in the warm dark. She didn’t know. She’d grown up in a house where men came to her father’s office at night, and she wasn’t stupid, and she knew what Mr. Hwang was and what he’d done to her and what he’d done to the eleven other women in his eleven other listings. And she knew what Jun Hyuk was. He’d told her in the dark. That’s what you’re lying on.

She didn’t know if it was right. He didn’t either. He’d said so.

She knew she wanted him to come back.

She took her hands off her face and got up and went to the hatch. The basil was fine. The strawberries were not; something was wrong with their leaves. She spent the rest of the afternoon working out what, with a magnifying glass from the drawer and a library book about pests, and found it, a tiny pale insect on the undersides. She washed every leaf by hand with soapy water until it was dark.

✦ ✦ ✦

Sunday she sat at the long table by the window all day with the pot of tea, in her coat, and didn’t move.

She didn’t wait up. It was daytime. You can’t wait up in the daytime.

At six o’clock in the evening the light went. At seven the harbour lights came on along the far side. At eight a ferry went past with music on the top deck, a party, coloured lights, faint through the five layers of glass. At nine she ate a bowl of the soup from the fridge, standing at the stove, because he said that was what you did when you had to eat and didn’t want to.

At ten, rule four. If I’m not back by the time I say, you leave.

She looked at the door.

She thought about Elowen, in the house on the hill, sitting up, waiting for the phone. You don’t have to do this on your own.

She looked at the clock on the kitchen wall. Ten past ten.

She picked up her bag. She put on her shoes. She stood by the door with her hand on the first lock.

She stood there a while.

Then she took her hand off the lock and went back to the table and sat down. She took her shoes off and put them side by side under the chair.

She’d follow the rules. All of them. She always had. But Sunday night, he’d said. And Sunday night lasted until it was Monday.

✦ ✦ ✦

At eight minutes past three in the morning, she heard the street door.

Six flights down. The faint double knock of it shutting, which you could only hear if you were listening for it with your whole body, and she was. Then nothing. Then, faintly, through the concrete, feet on the stairs.

Slow.

She stood up. She didn’t go to the door. Rule one. She stood beside the long table in her coat with her hands at her sides, and listened to him come up, flight after flight, the way she’d listened to the stairs in the tall house in the Walled City every night of her life. The fourth floor. The fifth. The landing outside.

He stood there before he put the key in the first lock.

The second. The third.

He came in.

He shut the door behind him. He turned the locks. He stood with his back against the door, and looked across the long dark room at her standing by the table in the light of the harbour, and didn’t say anything at all.

He wasn’t hurt. She saw that first, the way she always did. He was standing straight. He wasn’t holding anything close to his side. There was nothing on his face. His jacket was gone; he was in his black T-shirt, in October, and he was shaking slightly with cold, or with something, and his hands were hanging at his sides.

She looked at his hands.

They were clean. He’d washed them, somewhere. But not well enough. Under his nails, all ten of them, there was a dark line, rust-brown, the colour of the stain on his sleeve in December, the first night she waited.

He saw her see it.

He didn’t move. He stood against the door in the dark with his hands hanging and his face emptied out, and looked at her, and waited for her to go.

chapters.title: She Washes His Hands
chapters.desc: Warm water, a nail brush, and ten fingers, one at a time. She doesn’t ask whose it is. In the morning he tells her the only part she needs: who answered the advertisement.
chapters.epigraph: “Why don’t you ask?” “Because you’d tell me.”
chapters.content:
She didn’t go.

She crossed the long room to him, in the dark, in her pale blue coat, barefoot on the concrete. He watched her come. He didn’t move from the door. When she reached him, she didn’t put her hand on his chest, the way she always did. She looked down at his hands, hanging at his sides.

Then she took the right one, by the wrist, the way she had taken it to fold a towel, and turned round, and walked him to the bathroom.

He came. He didn’t say anything. He let himself be led, the whole enormous length of him, like a horse that’s been out in a storm all night and doesn’t know any more which way is home.

✦ ✦ ✦

The bathroom in the textile building had a deep old sink, white, chipped at one corner, with two brass taps. She put the plug in and ran the hot tap until it steamed and then the cold until it was right, and tested it with the inside of her wrist, the way her mother tested the bath when they were small.

She found the soap. The plain white kind, unscented, that she’d bought because he said scented soap made him sneeze. She found the nail brush, which was new, which she’d bought on Friday at the market without knowing why.

She took his right hand and put it in the water.

He flinched. It wasn’t hot. He flinched anyway, all through his body, as if the water had been something else, and she held on to his wrist and waited until he was still.

Then she washed his hand.

She took her time over it. She soaped his palm with her thumbs, and the back of his hand, and between each finger, one by one. She took the nail brush and worked it under the nails, the thumb first, then each finger in turn, small careful strokes, and the water in the sink went faintly pink, and then faintly brown, and she let it out and filled it again and kept going.

She didn’t look at his face. She looked at his hand.

The missing fingertip. The old white scar across the knuckles. A new graze on the side of the palm, not deep, that she washed around gently and didn’t mention. She held his hand in both of hers under the water, and turned it over, and turned it back, and brushed under each nail until the line was gone, and then brushed again, in case.

He was shaking. She could feel it in his wrist. Not the cold any more.

She took his left hand and did the same.

✦ ✦ ✦

It took a long time. She didn’t know how long. She didn’t look at the clock, and the bathroom had no window. When the water in the sink stayed clear for the third time, she let it out and dried his hands on one of the white towels, finger by finger, the way she’d dry a child’s.

Then she looked up at him.

He was looking at her. He had been looking at her the whole time. His face had gone still, and his eyes were wet, and he didn’t seem to know.

She didn’t ask whose it was, or what had happened on Kiln Street, or where Mr. Hwang was now. She stood in the little white bathroom holding his dried hands in the towel and looked up at him.

“Why don’t you ask?” he said.

It came out of him like a stone out of a well. The first thing he’d said. His voice was cracked all the way through.

“I came in with this on my hands,” he said. “And you washed it off. You washed it off like it was paint. And you don’t—you’ve never once—why don’t you ask?”

She took a moment.

“Because you’d tell me,” said Evangeline.

He stared at her.

“You’d tell me,” she said, “if I asked. Everything. You wouldn’t lie. You never lie to me.” She folded the towel over his hands. “And then you’d have to say it. Out loud. In here. And then it would be in here with us.” She looked at the towel. “You don’t need to say it. I know what you went to do. I knew on Tuesday. I let you go.”

His breath caught.

“You told me what you are,” she said. “In the dark. I didn’t go then. I’m not going now.”

He took his hands out of the towel, and put them on her face. Both of them. Clean, and warm from the water, and shaking. He held her face between them as if he didn’t know what else to do with them.

“It’s mine,” he said. “On my hands. Not you. Not ever. You don’t have to carry any of it. I’ll carry it. All of it. You don’t have to—”

“I know,” said Evangeline.

She reached up and took his wrists, and held them, where they were, against her face.

Then she turned her face into his right hand and kissed the palm of it. The new graze on the side. The place where the fingertip was missing. He stood in the little white bathroom and let her, shaking, with his eyes shut.

When he bent and kissed her, it wasn’t careful at all. He backed her against the chipped white sink with his clean hands on her face and kissed her hard, the way a man drinks after a long road, as if he needed to know the hands were still allowed to hold this. She took two fistfuls of his T-shirt and kissed him back just as hard, and when he let her go he was shaking worse than before.

✦ ✦ ✦

She undressed him. It was only what needed doing, like the night of the fever. He stood in the middle of the little bathroom and let her. She lifted the black T-shirt over his head, and he had to bend almost double for her to reach, and he bent, and she dropped it in the corner. It smelled of smoke and of somewhere she didn’t know. She’d put it in a bucket of cold water with salt in the morning, like the first one, in December. Or she’d throw it away. She didn’t know yet.

She turned on the shower. The one in the textile building, which ran hot straight away. She put him under it.

He stood under the water with his head bowed and his hands flat on the white tiles, and the water ran off him, and she stood outside the curtain with a towel over her arm and listened to him. For a long while he didn’t make a sound. Then he did, low, from somewhere deep in his chest. It wasn’t words. It was the noise a man makes when he has carried something a long way and been allowed to put it down, and doesn’t know how to stand up without it.

She drew the curtain back and stepped into the shower in her clothes.

He turned round. He looked at her standing in front of him under the water, in her dress, in her coat still, the pale blue one he’d bought her, soaked through, going dark.

“Your coat,” he said. “Your coat, Evangeline, it’s—”

She put her arms round him.

He bent down, all the way down, and put his face in her neck, and held on, and the water ran over the two of them, and he cried. Not for long. A minute, maybe two. Great heaving silent breaths, his shoulders shaking under her hands, his arms locked round her so tight that her feet came up off the floor of the shower. She held on to the back of his neck and didn’t say anything.

When he stopped, he didn’t let go.

✦ ✦ ✦

She put him to bed at a quarter to five, in the dark, on the mattress on the floor of the long room, in a clean T-shirt, with the blanket pulled up. He lay on his back. She lay down beside him, in a dry nightdress, with her wet coat hanging over the back of a chair by the radiator, dripping onto a towel.

She put her hand flat on his chest, over his heart.

“I’ve ruined your coat,” he said, into the dark. His voice was so tired it was barely there.

“You’ll buy me another one.”

He breathed out. Not quite a laugh.

“I will,” he said. “I’ll buy you ten. I’ll buy you the shop.”

“Go to sleep,” said Evangeline. “I’m here.”

He slept.

He slept on his back on the mattress on the floor, with her hand on his chest, and he didn’t wake when the sky went grey over the harbour, or when the printing works started up on the ground floor at seven, or when the ferries began, or when she got up at nine and made tea and sat at the long table and drank it, watching him. He didn’t wake at noon. He didn’t wake at two. He didn’t move. He lay exactly as she’d left him, with his face turned towards her side of the mattress, and his hand open on the blanket where hers had been.

She had never seen him sleep for more than four hours at a time.

She sat at the table and watched him all day. She didn’t do anything else. She didn’t go to the market or kneel at the hatch or read or mend. She sat with her tea and watched a man sleep, eleven hours, twelve, with the light moving across him from the five tall windows, and didn’t want to be anywhere else.

✦ ✦ ✦

He woke at a quarter to four in the afternoon.

He didn’t know where he was. Then he did. She watched it happen: his eyes opening, and the ceiling, and the windows, and the light, and then his head turning, fast, to her side of the mattress, and finding it empty, and then turning again, faster, and finding her at the table.

His whole body let go.

He lay there and looked at her across the long room. He didn’t say anything for a while.

He asked her what time it was. When she told him a quarter to four in the afternoon, he stared at her, and then at the light in the window, and then at the ceiling.

“I don’t sleep,” he said, bewildered. “I don’t. I haven’t slept like that since I was nine. I haven’t—” He stopped. He put his arm over his eyes. “What did you do to me?”

She got up and went to the stove and turned the gas on under the soup.

He lay there with his arm over his eyes for a while. Then he got up, slowly, like a much older man, and came across the long room to the stove where she was standing, and put his arms round her from behind, and his face in her hair, and stayed there while the soup heated.

When it started to bubble she reached past him to turn it down, and he caught her hand and turned her round instead, and kissed her against the stove. Slow, still half asleep, his whole weight leaning into her, his hands spread on her back, as if he’d woken up starving and she was the only thing in the building. The pot boiled over behind her and hissed on the flame. She turned the gas off by feel without opening her eyes.

When he finally let go, he went to the window and knelt at the hatch, and looked at the strawberries in their hanging pot, and frowned. The leaves had been spotted on Thursday. They were clean now, every one, as if somebody had washed them by hand.

He looked round at her. She was stirring the soup and didn’t look up.

✦ ✦ ✦

He told her one thing, that evening, at the table, after two bowls of soup.

Only one. She hadn’t asked for it. He told her anyway, because it wasn’t the kind of thing that would be in the room with them; it was the kind of thing she needed to know.

“There are no more copies,” he said. “Of the picture. Anywhere. There was the one on his phone, and four on a computer at the club, and one on a memory card in a drawer, and one he’d sent to a man in a country across the sea, and I spoke to that man on the phone, on Saturday, for a while, and he’s deleted it, and he’s very sorry.” He turned his spoon over on the table. “And Mr. Hwang won’t sell anything again. To anyone. Ever.”

She didn’t say anything.

“Two people answered the advertisement,” said Jun Hyuk. “Before your sister took it down.” He looked at the spoon. “One was a broker in the southern ports. I know him. He buys for men who collect things. He’s been told not to collect you.”

She waited.

“The other one,” he said, “came from an address I don’t know. A long way away. Not a broker. Not a buyer. It didn’t offer any money. It just asked a question.” He looked up at her. “It asked if she was well.”

Evangeline went still.

“And at the bottom,” said Jun Hyuk, “there was a little picture. The kind people put at the bottom of emails, when they work somewhere important. A crest.” He watched her face. “A heron. In gold. Over three mountains.”

She looked at him across the table.

She didn’t say anything. Outside, the harbour lights came on. The ferry with the coloured lights went past again, the other way. In the steel box on the ledge, under the glass, the basil and the mint and the strawberries she had washed by hand were going dark with the evening.

“I found the blanket when I was fifteen,” said Evangeline at last. “In the cedar chest. In the attic. Silk. With a crest on it in gold thread.” She turned her teacup. “A heron. Over three mountains.”

He didn’t say anything.

“They know,” she said. “Don’t they. Where I am.”

He reached across the table and put his clean hand over hers.

“They know you’re alive,” he said. “They know you’re in the city. That’s all. That’s all they know.” His thumb moved on the ring. “And they asked if you were well. Nobody’s ever asked me that in an email.”

She looked down at his hand on hers.

“Am I?” she said.

He took the question seriously. She watched him do it.

“Yes,” said Jun Hyuk. “You are. I check every day.” He tightened his hand on hers.

chapters.title: Jun Hyuk Meets His Father-in-Law (Badly)
chapters.desc: A tracker in a birthday phone, a lawyer’s letter in a locked drawer, and a knife held very still at the throat of the most frightening man the Walled City ever had. She is in the doorway when he says it.
chapters.epigraph: “She is no longer your asset. She is my wife. If you use her again, I’ll erase you.” — Lee Jun Hyuk, the fishing-net building, 18 November
chapters.content:
The tracker was inside the phone case.

He found it on the sixteenth of November, a Thursday, because he was bored, and because he was the kind of man who took things apart when he was bored, and because her phone had been in the kitchen drawer since August, switched off, the way he liked, and he’d never once looked at it. It was a good phone. New. Her father had given it to her on her birthday, in April, in a white box with a ribbon, and she’d told him so, in three words, when he asked: Baba. Birthday. He chose.

He took the back off the case to look at how it was made, and there it was. A flat black disc the size of a coin, tucked under the lining, with its own battery. It didn’t need the phone to be on. It didn’t need anything. It had been sitting in a drawer in his kitchen for three months, quietly telling someone exactly where the drawer was.

He sat at the long table and looked at it.

Then he went and looked out of the window with the scratch in the paint that wasn’t there, because there was no paint on these windows, and looked down at the street, six floors below. At the cars parked along it. At a silver saloon, parked across from the printing works, with its engine off, that had been there, he now remembered, on Tuesday. And on Friday the week before. And on the Sunday she’d come back from the plant market with nine pots of herbs.

“Oh, you bastard,” said Jun Hyuk, under his breath.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t tell her on Thursday. He didn’t tell her on Friday.

On Friday night he went out at eleven, without the bag, and came back at four, and on Saturday morning at nine he put on his good shirt, the one she’d sewn the button on, and the black jacket, and stood by the door.

She was at the long table. She looked at the shirt.

“Where,” she said.

It wasn’t a question, quite. It was the nearest she came.

He thought about lying. He’d never once lied to her. He wasn’t going to start on a Saturday.

“I’m going to see your father,” he said.

She put her cup down.

“There’s a tracker in your phone,” he said. “In the case. It’s been there since your birthday. There’s a car outside that’s been outside since August. And I went to his office last night, and I opened a drawer that was locked, and there’s a letter in it.” He looked at her. “From a law firm in a country across the sea. Sent after the advertisement. Acting for an interested party who would be very grateful for information about the present whereabouts and situation of a young woman who may be of interest to a certain family. Very grateful. With a number. A big number.” His jaw tightened. “He hasn’t answered it. But he hasn’t thrown it away. He’s kept it in a locked drawer, with a copy of your birth certificate, both of them, the real one and the paper one, and a photograph of a silk blanket. And a note in his own handwriting. Value? With a question mark.”

Evangeline didn’t move.

“So I’m going to see him,” said Jun Hyuk. “Just to talk.”

She looked at him. She looked at his good shirt, and at his hands, and at the inside of his jacket, where something was.

“Just to talk,” he said again.

He went down the stairs.

She sat at the table for about a minute. Then she got up, and put on her coat, the new one, the second pale blue coat, which had come the week after the shower in a bag the size of a suitcase, and her shoes, and went down the stairs after him.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her father’s office was where it had always been, on the top floor of the old fishing-net building at the edge of the Walled City, above the godowns, with the river on one side and the market on the other and a view from the window of every boat that came in.

There was a new secretary in the outer room. A neat nervous young man in glasses, at the desk where Feng used to sit with his feet up eating sunflower seeds. He stood up when Jun Hyuk came through the door.

“I’m sorry, sir, Mr. Lin isn’t seeing anyone this morning without—”

“He’ll see me,” said Jun Hyuk pleasantly. “Sit down. It’s all right. You’re new, aren’t you? You’ve got the look. Don’t worry. I’m not here for you. I’m here for him. Have you had breakfast? You should have breakfast. Go downstairs and have some congee. The place on the corner does a good one. Take forty minutes.” He put a note on the desk. “My treat.”

The young man looked at the note. Then at the size of the person who had put it there.

He went to get congee.

Jun Hyuk opened the inner door without knocking.

✦ ✦ ✦

Lin Jian was at his desk.

He was bigger than Jun Hyuk had expected. Broad and heavy and grey, with a face like a slab of old stone, in a cardigan. He looked like what he was: a man who had run the cargo of the Walled City for thirty years, and had been, once, the most frightening man in it. He was reading something. He looked up when the door opened, and saw who it was, and his face didn’t change, except at the eyes.

“You’re him,” said Lin Jian.

“Yes,” said Jun Hyuk, and shut the door.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t hurt him.

He would want that understood, later, by everyone who asked, and a great many people did. He didn’t hurt him at all. He walked round the desk, quite slowly, the way you’d walk round a table at a dinner to pour someone’s tea, and Lin Jian watched him come and didn’t move, which was either very brave or very tired. And when he was standing beside the chair, Jun Hyuk took the knife out of his jacket, an ordinary knife, one he used for rope, and put the flat of it against the side of Lin Jian’s throat, just under the jaw, and held it there, flat and still, not pressing.

Lin Jian didn’t flinch.

“I’m going to talk,” said Jun Hyuk, “and you’re going to listen. I’m good at talking. Everyone says. You’re good at listening, I think. You’ve had to be.”

He laid the tracker on the desk, on top of the papers. The little flat black disc.

“Her birthday,” he said. “In April. In a white box with a ribbon. She told me you chose it. She was so pleased you chose it. She doesn’t get things chosen for her. You know that. You made sure of it.”

Lin Jian looked at the tracker.

“And the car,” said Jun Hyuk. “Since August. Silver. Outside my building. My building. Where she grows basil.” He didn’t raise his voice at all. “And last night I opened your drawer. The locked one. The bottom left. You should get a better lock. That one’s from about 1980.”

Lin Jian closed his eyes.

“Value,” said Jun Hyuk. “With a question mark. In your handwriting. On a piece of paper with her birth certificate.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“I didn’t answer it,” said Lin Jian.

His voice was low and rough, like gravel in a pan. His eyes were still shut.

“I know you didn’t.”

“I didn’t answer it. I was never going to answer it. I put it in the drawer because I didn’t know—” He stopped. “I didn’t know what it meant. If they were going to sell her again. If it was the people who sold her the first time, pretending. If it was her—” He swallowed against the knife. “If it was her real family. If they wanted her back. If she’d want to go. If she’d be safer there. With them. In a palace. With guards. Than here, in the Walled City, with an old man who couldn’t find her for two days. Or with—” He opened his eyes and looked sideways, up, at the face above him. “With you.”

“And the note?”

“I write that on everything,” said Lin Jian. “Every letter. Every contract. Every ship. For thirty years. Value? I don’t—it’s a habit. I didn’t think about it. I didn’t think about what it would look like.” His face moved. “I didn’t think.”

“No,” said Jun Hyuk. “You never do. Do you. You don’t ask, and you don’t think.”

He leaned down.

“She was in a box,” he said quietly, close to Lin Jian’s ear. “For two days. In the dark. With a bucket. With holes in the roof. Because a man sold a story about her, and the story was about what she was worth. And you’ve got a piece of paper in your drawer with her name on it and the word value.” He held the knife still. “I don’t care why. I don’t care if it’s a habit. You don’t write that word next to her name. Ever again. Not on a note. Not in your head. Not in your sleep.”

Lin Jian didn’t say anything.

“She is no longer your asset,” said Lee Jun Hyuk. “She’s not your secret. She’s not your insurance. She’s not your leverage against a throne. She is my wife.”

The word went into the room and stayed there, like a stone dropped into a still pond.

“And if you ever use her again,” said Jun Hyuk, “for anything, for one second, for a phone call, for a letter, for a car outside her window—I will erase you. I’m very good at it. I’ve done it to better men than you. You won’t be in a file. You won’t be in a photograph. Nobody will ever be able to prove you were here.”

✦ ✦ ✦

From the door, low, someone said his name.

He didn’t move. He didn’t take the knife away. But every muscle in his body changed. Lin Jian felt it, through the steel; he saw the big man’s face, above him, go still all the way down.

Evangeline was standing in the doorway.

She’d come up the stairs. Of course she had. She’d come up every staircase he’d ever gone up, since November. She was standing in the door of her father’s office in the long pale blue coat with her hair down and her hands at her sides, and she was looking at the two of them: her father in his chair, and the man beside him, and the knife.

She’d heard. He knew from her face that she’d heard all of it.

My wife.

He’d never said it to her. Not once. He’d given her a ring and said you’re mine and she’d said then I’m yours, and they’d never once said the word. He’d said it, for the first time, to her father, with a knife in his hand.

Nobody spoke.

Then Evangeline came into the room, and walked round the desk, slowly, the way he had, and stopped beside him. She looked at the knife at her father’s throat.

She put her hand on Jun Hyuk’s wrist.

Not pulling. Just there. The way she put her hand on his chest when she came in through a door.

He took the knife away.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t look at him. She looked at her father.

Lin Jian was sitting still in his chair, with his hands flat on the desk on either side of the tracker. His face was grey. His eyes were wet. He looked up at his daughter, standing over him beside the man who had just held a knife to his throat, and his face crumpled, all at once, like paper.

“Ev,” he said. “I’m sorry. I’m sorry. I didn’t—the phone was because I couldn’t find you. In October. For two days. I couldn’t find you, and I had every man I have looking, and I couldn’t find you, and I swore I’d never—” His voice broke. “I just wanted to know where you were. That’s all. I just wanted to know you were somewhere.”

She looked at him.

“And the letter,” said her father. “I didn’t know what to do. I didn’t know what you’d want. Whether you’d want to go to them. I didn’t know—”

“You didn’t ask,” said Evangeline.

He stopped.

“You never ask,” she said. Her voice was low and level. She’d never said so many words to him in her life. “You didn’t ask Raiden. You didn’t ask me. You decide what we’re worth, and what we need, and where we should be, and you don’t ask.” She looked at him. “So ask.”

Lin Jian looked up at her.

The office was quiet. Down below, in the market, someone was shouting the price of crabs. A boat came in on the river and sounded its horn.

“Evangeline,” said her father, like a man speaking a language he’d never learned. “What do you want?”

She looked at him for a moment longer.

Then she turned her head and looked at Jun Hyuk.

“Him,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

Lin Jian put the tracker in his own top drawer, and the lawyer’s letter, and the note with the word on it, and burned the note in the ashtray on the desk in front of them, with a match from a box with a ship on it, while they watched.

He didn’t put the letter in the ashtray. He looked at it and then held it out to Evangeline.

“It’s yours,” he said. “Whatever it is. It was always yours. I’m sorry I kept it in a drawer.”

She took it, and folded it, and put it in her coat pocket.

At the door of the office, as they went, Lin Jian said, “Mr. Lee.”

Jun Hyuk turned round.

The old man was standing behind his desk now, big, grey, in his cardigan, with his hands at his sides. He looked at the man in the door the way you might look at a typhoon that has come through your house and left it, against all expectation, standing.

“You said wife,” said Lin Jian. “You’re not married.”

“Not yet,” said Jun Hyuk.

Lin Jian looked at his daughter, standing beside the big man in the doorway with her hand on his sleeve.

“Hm,” said Lin Jian. It sounded remarkably like Zhao.

✦ ✦ ✦

They walked back through the market.

It was eleven in the morning and full of people: the crab sellers and the fish women and the old men with their trolleys, the orchid stall she’d gone to since she was fourteen, the man who sold broken clocks and old spoons. Nobody looked at them. Nobody ever looked. She walked beside him with her hand on his sleeve, and he walked slowly, for him, so she could keep up, and he didn’t say anything.

At the orchid stall she stopped.

He stopped too.

She stood looking at the white phalaenopsis in their trays, checking the roots without touching them, out of habit. Then she said, without looking at him, in her low flat voice, “You told my father I’m your wife.”

“I did.”

“Before you told me.”

He was quiet. The orchid seller, an old woman in an apron who had sold Evangeline orchids for ten years and had never heard her say more than a word, was watching them with frank interest over the top of the trays.

“I didn’t mean to say it like that,” he said. “With a knife. In an office. To him. I meant to—I don’t know what I meant. Something better. A boat, maybe. Somewhere with lights. I’ve got money. I could do anything. I could hire a whole harbour. I could get the fireworks people. I’d have done it properly.” He rubbed his face. “It just came out. Because it’s true. It’s been true since the ring. Since before the ring. Since you washed my hands. Since the dumpling. I don’t know. Since you stood in the middle of a box and looked at me.” He took a breath. “It’s true and I said it to the wrong person first.”

She turned and looked up at him.

He made himself say it out loud, in the market, in front of the orchid seller.

“Will you?” said Lee Jun Hyuk.

She looked at him.

“Yes,” said Evangeline.

Behind the trays, the orchid seller put her hand on her heart.

He didn’t say anything. He couldn’t. He bent down, in the middle of the morning market in the Walled City, with the crab sellers shouting, and put his forehead against hers, and stayed there, and she put her hands on his face.

“Not a harbour,” she said, against his mouth. “Not fireworks. Six people. And a garden.”

He kissed her, with the crab sellers shouting and an old man with a trolley having to go round them, the way he’d wanted to all the way through the market with her hand on his sleeve. He lifted her up onto her toes with it, and she held his face and let him, and somebody by the crab tanks whistled, and somebody else told him to shut up and leave them be.

When he set her back on her heels, the orchid seller was holding out a pot of white phalaenopsis across the trays.

“Ten years she’s been coming here,” said the old woman, “and never said more than a word. Take it. No charge.”

They didn’t have a garden. They had a steel box on a ledge on the sixth floor. He didn’t point that out. He was already, standing there in the market with the crab sellers shouting, thinking about where he’d find her one.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night, on the mattress on the floor of the long room, with the old woman’s orchid on the sill and the harbour lights moving on the ceiling, he asked her again. Properly. Lying beside her in the dark with his hand on her face, in the voice he didn’t use for anyone else. Will you. Really. Not because I said it to your father with a knife.

She answered him without a word. She pulled him down and kissed him, and undid his shirt herself, button by button, looking at his face the whole time, until he understood that this was the answer and stopped asking. He didn’t talk after that. He kissed the ring on her hand, and the inside of her wrist, and her mouth again, and her throat, and the night went the way the typhoon had, slow and then not slow at all, with nothing between them and the dark but the lights off the water.

In the morning she was still wearing the ring and nothing else, asleep on his chest, and he lay and looked at her until the printing works started up six floors down.

chapters.title: A Letter From a Palace
chapters.desc: A man she never met has died in a country she has never seen, and left her something in his will. The letter is in two languages. She reads the one she was never taught first.
chapters.epigraph: “His late Majesty acknowledges a daughter, born on the seventh day of April 1998, and commends her to the care of his House.” — a letter, hand-delivered, 14 March 2024
chapters.content:
He went to Lunar New Year at the Lins’ in February, and he talked to everyone.

He hadn’t meant to go. He’d meant to sit on a roof across the street, the way he had at the wedding, and watch the doors. But Lin Jian had sent a card, in the second week of January, addressed in his own hand to Mr. Lee Jun Hyuk, care of a noodle shop on River Bridge Road, because he would not use the address his tracker had given him. Old Nam had brought it down from the border herself, on the bus, and handed it over at the textile building with an expression of enormous suspicion.

Inside the card it said: New Year’s Eve. Seven o’clock. Bring her. Please. And underneath, smaller, in a different pen, as if he’d come back to it later: I’m asking.

So he went.

He went in the good shirt and a new black jacket, with a basket of oranges and two bottles of something very old and very expensive for Lin Jian, and a bag of almond biscuits for Eliana, and a potted kumquat tree for the step that was so big he had to carry it up the hill from the car on his shoulder. He stood in the doorway of the tall house in the Walled City, with the kumquat tree, and every Lin in the world looked at him, and Raiden said, “Oh my God, she’s found a wardrobe,” and Elowen said, “Raiden,” and Lin Jian came out of the kitchen in his funeral suit and stopped.

They looked at each other.

“Mr. Lee,” said Lin Jian.

“Mr. Lin,” said Jun Hyuk. “Happy New Year. Where do you want the tree?”

After that he talked. He couldn’t help it. He talked to Raiden about safe rooms, and to Jinx about the engine in her bike, and to Elara about wound packing, at length, until Elara said he had better technique than half her registrars and he went red. He talked to Eliana about the fence she’d built in October, and she showed him things on her laptop under the table, and he understood about a third of them, and told her so, and she was so delighted that she showed him more. He talked to Lin Jian about boats. About the old river ferries, and the tides at the border, and the way the godowns had been built in the fifties with their backs to the water. They talked for an hour, by the window, standing up, two big men with their hands in their pockets, and when Elowen came to call them in for dinner they both looked startled, as if they’d forgotten whose house it was.

Aurelia Chen was there with her husband, at the end of the long table, in red.

She looked at Jun Hyuk for most of the first course. Then she leaned across to Evangeline and said quietly, “Your fiancé talks a great deal.”

Evangeline didn’t answer. She turned her teacup a quarter turn on the table and looked down the long table at him, where he was explaining something about tides to her father with both hands, and Aurelia saw the look and sat back, the corner of her mouth twitching, and went back to her soup.

Between the soup and the fish, he caught her on the second landing.

She’d gone up for more chairs. He followed her, two stairs at a time, and when she came out of the linen cupboard with a folding chair in each hand he was standing on the landing by the window that didn’t lock, the one she’d watched Raiden throw her ribbons into the canal from, filling the narrow space from wall to wall.

He took the chairs out of her hands and leaned them against the banister.

“Your father,” he said, “has just spent an hour telling me about tides. Your brother has called me a wardrobe four times. Your sister’s husband has looked at me for four seconds about eleven times.” He put one hand flat on the wall beside her head. “I’ve been very good. I’ve been the best guest your family has ever had. And I have wanted to do this since I came up the hill with a tree on my shoulder.”

With the whole family laughing in the kitchen two floors down and every sound in the house carrying, the way it always had, he didn’t wait to see what she’d say. He kissed her on the second landing of the house where she’d spent twenty-four years being a secret, against the wall, slow and deep, with both hands in her hair, and she took the front of his good shirt in her fist and held him there until somebody shouted up the stairs about the chairs. Then he picked up both chairs in one hand and her hand in the other and walked her down to dinner, and Elowen took one look at her sister’s face and put her napkin over her mouth.

✦ ✦ ✦

The letter came on the fourteenth of March.

It came to the fishing-net building, to Lin Jian’s office, by hand, at ten in the morning: a man in a grey suit and grey gloves, very polite, who would not give his name to the new secretary, and who would not sit down, and who handed over a long envelope of heavy cream paper sealed with gold wax, and bowed, and left.

Lin Jian did not open it.

He sat and looked at it for an hour, the new secretary said afterwards. Then he put on his coat and drove himself, which he hadn’t done in fifteen years, across the city to the eastern industrial district, to the textile building, and climbed six flights of stairs slowly, because he was sixty and heavy and had never climbed them before, and knocked on the steel door.

He knocked. He didn’t have a key.

Jun Hyuk opened it.

Lin Jian stood on the landing, grey and breathing hard, with the envelope in both hands.

“It came to me,” he said. “It’s for her. I haven’t opened it.” He held it out. “I wanted to ask her. If she wanted to. Or if she wanted me to send it back.”

Jun Hyuk looked at him.

Then he stood aside and let him in.

✦ ✦ ✦

She was at the hatch, kneeling, with a cup of tea, looking at the rosemary, which had come through the winter under its glass lid and was flowering, small, blue.

She stood up when her father came in.

She looked at the envelope in his hands. At the gold wax.

He crossed the long room to her and held it out, the way he’d hold out a dish at the table, carefully, both hands.

“I didn’t open it,” said Lin Jian. “It’s yours.”

She took it.

She looked at the seal. It had been pressed with a ring, and the shape in the gold was clear. A heron, standing, its neck curved, over three peaks. The same as the crest at the bottom of the email in October. The same as the gold thread on a silk blanket in a cedar chest in an attic, which she’d found when she was fifteen, and looked up in the library, and never told anyone.

She didn’t open it.

She sat down at the long table by the windows, with the envelope in front of her, and looked at it. Her father sat down across from her as if he weren’t sure he was allowed. Jun Hyuk stood behind her chair.

Nobody said anything.

“Do you want me to go?” said Lin Jian.

She looked up at him.

“No,” said Evangeline.

She broke the seal.

✦ ✦ ✦

There were two letters inside, folded together.

The first was in English, on cream paper, typed, with a heading in gold that said Office of the Lord Chamberlain and no country under it. Jun Hyuk could read it over her shoulder. Lin Jian could read it upside down.

The second was in another language.

It was handwritten in ink, on thicker paper, in a script that Jun Hyuk had never seen before: tall, looping, joined, with little marks above and below the line like birds on a wire. It went on for three pages. At the bottom there was a signature, and under the signature, pressed in gold, the heron again.

Evangeline put the English letter down on the table, face down, without reading it.

She picked up the other one.

He watched her eyes. He watched them go to the top of the first page, to the first line of the tall looping script with the birds on the wire. And then he watched them move along the line to the end, and back to the start of the next.

She was reading it.

Across the table, Lin Jian was holding his breath.

She read the first page. She turned it over. She read the second. Her face didn’t move. Her hands didn’t shake. She read the way she read the instructions on a packet of seeds, or the label on a medicine bottle, carefully, every word, and at the bottom of the third page she stopped, and looked at the signature, and the gold heron under it.

Then she put the letter down on the table, and put her hands flat on top of it.

“How,” said her father. His voice was barely there. “Ev. How can you—”

“The library,” said Evangeline.

Lin Jian stared at her.

“When I was fifteen,” she said. “After the blanket. I looked up the crest. Then I looked up the country. Then I found a grammar book, in the reference section. A very old one, from the nineteen-sixties, for missionaries.” She looked at the letter under her hands. “I went every Saturday. For nine years. I never took it home. I never said it out loud. I didn’t know how it was supposed to sound.” She was quiet for a moment. “I wanted to know what language I was born in.”

Behind her, Jun Hyuk put his hand on the back of her chair.

He didn’t touch her. He just put his hand there, on the wood, beside her shoulder, so that she would know where he was. She leaned back, slightly, until her shoulder touched his knuckles.

“What does it say?” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

She told them in pieces, with long gaps, in the low flat voice. Her father and Jun Hyuk sat at the long table in the light from the five windows and listened, and neither of them said anything, and the ferries went back and forth on the harbour behind her.

The King was dead.

Not the King. A King. The man who had been the King, of a country she had never seen, the man who had had a child, twenty-six years ago, with someone who wasn’t the Queen. He had died on the twenty-second of January, at seventy-one, of his heart, in his sleep. His son, the Queen’s son, was the King now.

And in the old King’s will, which had been read to his family and his council in the second week of February, there was a paragraph. Just one. The Lord Chamberlain had copied it into the letter, word for word, in the old formal language of the court, and she read it to them twice, first in that language, so they could hear it, slowly, the tall strange sounds coming out of her mouth for the first time in her life, and then in their own.

“His late Majesty acknowledges a daughter,” said Evangeline, “born on the seventh day of April, in the year nineteen ninety-eight, to a woman of his household, and removed from the kingdom in her first week of life, for reasons that his late Majesty regretted for the remainder of his days. He commends her to the care of his House. He leaves to her the house at the lake and all that it contains, which were her mother’s, and a sum from his private estate, to be held for her until she is found.”

She stopped.

“And he asks,” she said quietly, “that she be told he was sorry.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Lin Jian had put his face in his hands.

Jun Hyuk didn’t move. He stood behind her chair with his hand on the wood and looked at the back of her head, at her hair coming loose from its knot, and didn’t say anything, because there wasn’t anything in the world to say.

“The seventh,” said Evangeline.

They both looked at her.

“Of April,” she said. “The ninth is my birthday. On the paper. That’s Raiden’s. That’s the day he was born. I was born on the seventh.” She turned the letter over. “I’m two days older. I knew that. From the blanket. There was a date sewn into the corner, but it was in their numbers, and I couldn’t read them until I was sixteen.” She almost smiled. “I never told him. He’s always said he was older. Since we were four. Because he’s louder.”

Lin Jian made a sound behind his hands that was half a laugh and half something much worse.

“There’s more,” said Evangeline. She picked up the English letter at last and turned it over and read it, quickly, once. “The King. The new King. My—” She stopped at the word. “He wants to receive me. That’s the word. He’s sending someone. An envoy. To discuss arrangements.” She put it down. “On the sixth of April. At the house in the Walled City. If convenient.”

“Arrangements,” said Jun Hyuk.

“Yes.”

“For what?”

She looked at the letter in the court language, under her hand. The tall looping script. The signature at the bottom, which was the Lord Chamberlain’s, not the King’s. The old King was dead and had never written to her. He had written a paragraph in a will and asked someone else to say he was sorry.

“For what I’m worth,” said Evangeline.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her father left at four.

At the door he stopped, and turned, and looked at her, standing by the long table with both letters folded in her hand.

“Ev,” he said. “Whatever you want. Whatever you decide. If you want to go there, to them. If you want to see the house at the lake. If you want to send the envoy away and never—” He stopped. “I’m asking. I’m asking you.”

She looked at him.

“I know, Baba,” she said.

He went down the stairs slowly. They listened to him all the way down, six flights, a big old man on concrete stairs, stopping at every landing to breathe.

Jun Hyuk shut the door and turned the locks.

When he turned round she was still standing by the table with the letters in her hand. She was looking at the window. At the hatch, and the steel box, and the rosemary flowering blue under the glass in the last of the afternoon light.

He came across the room and stood behind her.

“Evangeline,” he said.

She didn’t turn round.

“He was sorry,” she said. “He was sorry for twenty-six years. And he never wrote to me. He didn’t need to find me. He knew where I was. My father’s name was on the—he paid my father. He knew. He could have written. One letter. In twenty-six years.” Her voice was perfectly level. “He wrote it in his will. So he wouldn’t have to see what I said.”

He put his arms round her from behind.

She didn’t go still. She leaned back into him, all her weight, the way you’d lean against a wall at the end of a long day, and let him hold her up.

“I wanted to know,” she said, “what language I was born in.”

“And now you do.”

“It said sorry,” said Evangeline. “And nobody said it to me.”

He held her. He didn’t say anything for a while.

Then he bent his head and said, low, against her hair, in his own rough border voice, the only language he’d ever had, “I’m sorry. I’m sorry he didn’t write. I’m sorry nobody said it. I’m sorry you went to the library every Saturday for nine years on your own. I’m sorry you had to find a blanket in a box to know your own birthday.” His arms tightened. “There. Somebody’s said it. To your face. Out loud.”

She turned round in his arms and put her face against his chest.

She didn’t say anything. When she did, it was muffled against his shirt, and it was in the other language: four or five words, low, in the tall strange sounds he’d heard her read aloud that afternoon for the first time.

“What does that mean?” he said.

“I’ll teach you,” said Evangeline. “Later.”

chapters.title: The Envoy at the Door
chapters.desc: A polite man in grey gloves, a diplomatic passport, two guards on the step, and an offer with a husband already chosen. She asks him one question he won’t answer.
chapters.epigraph: “His Majesty would be pleased to receive you. Everything has been arranged.” — the Envoy, the Walled City, 6 April 2024
chapters.content:
The envoy came at eleven, in a long grey car with a small flag on the front that nobody in the Walled City had ever seen before.
