Raiden watched it come up the hill from the window on the second landing, the one that didn’t lock, with a pastry in his hand. “There’s a flag,” he said, over his shoulder. “An actual flag. On a car. In our street. Mrs. Yim from the fish shop has come out to look. She’s brought a stool.”

Nobody answered him. He hadn’t expected them to.

They were in the front room of the tall house, the good one, that their mother had kept for visitors and nobody had used since she died. Lin Jian in his funeral suit by the cold fireplace, with his hands behind his back. Elowen on the sofa by the window, straight-backed, in grey, with Zhao standing behind her because he wouldn’t sit in a room with strangers coming into it. Raiden at the window. And Evangeline, in the middle of the room, in a plain dark blue dress and the aquamarines in her ears, sitting in her mother’s old armchair with her hands folded in her lap.

Jun Hyuk was on the front step.

He’d decided that at breakfast. “I’ll do the door,” he’d said, and Evangeline had looked at him over her tea, and he’d said, “Not because I don’t want to be in there. I want to be in there very much. I want to sit next to you and hold your hand and glare at him. But he’ll bring guards. They’ll stand on the step. And somebody should talk to them.” He’d buttered his toast. “People tell you things on steps.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The envoy got out of the car.

He was perhaps sixty, slim, silver-haired, in a grey suit so well cut that it made Zhao’s look slightly careless, and pale grey gloves, which he did not take off. He had a narrow, pleasant, patient face, the face of a man who had spent forty years standing in rooms where things were decided and had made sure, in every one of them, that he was the last person anybody would blame. Two men got out of the car behind him. Big, young, close-cropped, in dark suits, with the small hard bulge under the left arm that Jun Hyuk could have found on a man in the dark.

They came up the steps. Jun Hyuk was standing at the top of them, by the open door, in his good shirt and black jacket, with his hands in his pockets.

The envoy stopped two steps below him and looked up. He had to look up quite a long way.

“Good morning,” said Jun Hyuk. “You’ll be the gentleman from the palace. Go on in. Front room, on the left. They’re expecting you.” He nodded at the two guards. “You two can wait with me. There’s tea. There’s a bench. Raiden’s brought pastries, though he’s eaten two.”

The envoy’s eyes went over him the way a jeweller’s go over a stone.

“And you are?” he said.

“The door,” said Jun Hyuk.

The envoy looked at him a moment longer. Then something in his pleasant face shifted, as if he had found a word in a document that he would need to come back to. He went in.

The two guards stayed on the step. One of them looked at the bench. The other looked at Jun Hyuk’s hands, still in his pockets, and then at his face, and then very carefully at nothing at all.

“Sit down,” said Jun Hyuk. “Really. Nobody’s going to shoot anybody on Mrs. Lin’s front step. She’d come back from the dead and kill us all.” He held out the plate. “Egg tart?”

✦ ✦ ✦

In the front room, the envoy bowed.

He bowed to Lin Jian first, briefly, the bow you’d give a man who had once been paid by your employer. Then to Elowen, more deeply. Then he turned to the armchair in the middle of the room and looked at the woman sitting in it for a while, and bowed a third time, slower and lower, with his gloved hand flat against his chest.

“Lady Evangeline,” he said.

She didn’t move. She looked at him.

He sat down when Lin Jian gestured to the chair across from her. He put a leather folder on his knees and did not open it.

“I am here on behalf of His Majesty,” he said. He spoke English with a soft clipped accent, very correctly, like a man who’d learned it at a good school long ago and looked after it since. “I bring you his greetings, and his condolences on the loss of your father, whom he understands you did not know. And I bring you an invitation.” He paused. “His Majesty would be pleased to receive you.”

Nobody said anything.

“Everything has been arranged,” said the envoy. “You would be acknowledged formally, at court, as a daughter of the late King’s House. Not as a princess. That would not be possible, given the circumstances of your birth, and I think you would not wish it. But as a lady of the House, with the title and the precedence that carries. You would have apartments in the east wing of the palace, which are very fine, and look over the gardens. You would receive an allowance from the privy purse, which would be generous. And you would come into your inheritance: the house at the lake, and its contents, and the sum from your late father’s private estate, which I am authorised to tell you is—” he named a figure, in the currency of his country and then in theirs, and at the second figure Raiden, at the window, choked on his pastry, “—held in trust for you now.”

He opened the folder at last and took out a single sheet of paper and laid it on the low table between them.

“And there is a family,” he said, “of very great standing. Very old. Very close to His Majesty. With a son of thirty-one, who is a diplomat, and educated, and kind. His Majesty believes that a marriage into that family would give you a secure and honourable place at court. And would settle certain questions, which have arisen since your father’s will was read, as to your position.” He smiled slightly. “Your future, Lady Evangeline, has been very carefully considered.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Elowen moved first. She put her hand flat on the arm of the sofa, and Zhao, behind her, put his hand on her shoulder, and she stopped.

Lin Jian didn’t move at all.

Evangeline looked at the sheet of paper on the table. She didn’t pick it up. She could read it from where she sat; it was in the court language, in the tall looping script, and it had a name on it and a photograph clipped to the corner of a young man in glasses with a pleasant face and a good suit.

She looked at the envoy.

“What questions?” she said.

The envoy’s eyebrows lifted, slightly. He had not expected her to speak, she saw. He had been told about her, then. Almost silent. Somebody had told him.

“I’m sorry?”

“You said certain questions,” said Evangeline. “Have arisen. As to my position.” Her voice was low and level. “What questions?”

He looked at her for a moment. Then he folded his gloved hands on the folder.

“Your late father had a brother,” he said. “His Highness. A man of strong views, with a great many friends in the north of the kingdom, where the old families are. His Highness has never been entirely reconciled to his nephew’s succession. And since the will was read, and it became known that there is a daughter of the late King’s blood, alive, unmarried, abroad—” He spread his hands. “There are people who might find such a daughter useful. As a figure. As a claim. As a wife for one of their own sons. His Majesty would prefer that she be at court, under his protection, married into a family loyal to him, where nobody can make use of her.”

“Except him,” said Evangeline.

The envoy looked at her.

He didn’t deny it. A man who had spent forty years making sure he would never be blamed for anything looked at her across her mother’s front room and didn’t deny it, because he could see she’d know if he lied.

“Except His Majesty,” he agreed, quietly.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the front step, the younger guard had eaten three egg tarts and was telling Jun Hyuk about his mother.

He hadn’t meant to. Nobody ever meant to. Jun Hyuk had sat down on the bench beside him and asked if it was his first time abroad, and the young man had said yes, and Jun Hyuk had said he remembered his first time abroad, he’d been nineteen, in the back of a truck, and he’d been sick the whole way, and the young man had laughed, and then somehow it was twenty minutes later and Jun Hyuk knew that the young man’s name was Teo, that his mother kept bees, that he’d been in the palace guard for four years and liked it, and that the palace had been strange since January.

“Strange how?”

“People coming and going,” said Teo. “From the north. His Highness’s people. They come to see the King, and they’re very polite, and then they go away, and the King’s in a bad mood for a week.” He lowered his voice. “And last month there were two of them in the corridor outside the Chamberlain’s office, and I was on the door, and one of them said to the other, if she won’t come home by the front door, she can come home by the back. And they laughed.” He looked at the egg tart in his hand. “I didn’t like the way they laughed.”

Jun Hyuk sat still on the bench.

“Did you tell anyone?” he said.

“I told my sergeant. He said not to listen at doors.” Teo looked up at the house. “Is she nice? The lady? People say she doesn’t talk.”

“She talks,” said Jun Hyuk. “When she’s got something to say. It’s the rest of us who go on.”

The older guard, at the end of the bench, who had said nothing for twenty minutes, said, without turning his head, “Teo. That’s enough.”

Teo went red and ate his tart.

Jun Hyuk looked at the older guard for a while. The older guard looked at the street.

“His Highness,” said Jun Hyuk pleasantly, “the uncle. Does he employ people over here? In this city? People who move things across rivers?”

The older guard’s jaw tightened, and that was enough.

“Then tell them something for me,” said Jun Hyuk, in the same pleasant voice, with the plate of egg tarts still on his knee. “When you go home. Tell them the back door’s got me behind it. I’ve put men in that river for less than a laugh in a corridor.”

The older guard didn’t move. Beside him, Teo had stopped chewing.

“Have another tart,” said Jun Hyuk to Teo, kindly, and held out the plate.

✦ ✦ ✦

“You haven’t answered,” said the envoy.

Evangeline was looking at the photograph on the sheet of paper. The young man in glasses. Thirty-one. A diplomat. Kind. She thought he probably was kind. She thought he probably had no more say in this than she did, and was sitting somewhere in a fine room in a palace she’d never seen, looking at a description of her, almost silent, and wondering.

She thought about a man on her mother’s front step, eating egg tarts with two guards, finding out everything they knew.

“There’s something you can tell me,” she said.

The envoy inclined his head.

“My mother,” said Evangeline. “What was her name?”

The room went quiet.

The envoy looked at her, and for a second she thought what crossed his face was pity.

“That,” he said gently, “is for His Majesty to tell you. If you come.”

Lin Jian made a sound by the fireplace. Elowen’s hand had closed on the arm of the sofa so tightly that the knuckles were white.

Evangeline didn’t move.

So that was the price. They’d known what she would ask, and they’d brought the answer with them, folded up in a man’s grey glove, to hand over across a table in a palace after the wedding.

“I’ll answer you tomorrow,” she said.

The envoy looked surprised. “Tomorrow?”

“The seventh,” said Evangeline. “My birthday. My real one.” She stood up. “I’d like to answer on my birthday.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He bowed at the door, the deep bow, with his hand on his chest. Then he went down the steps to the car, past the man standing at the top of them.

He stopped on the second step and looked back up.

“You are her fiancé,” he said. It wasn’t a question. “That will be regarded as a complication.”

“I usually am,” said Jun Hyuk.

The envoy looked at him for a moment longer, and then, to Jun Hyuk’s surprise, almost smiled. He got into the car. The guards got in after him. Teo, at the back door, looked up at the step and lifted one hand, a little guiltily, and Jun Hyuk lifted his.

The car went down the hill with its small flag. Mrs. Yim from the fish shop picked up her stool and went inside.

✦ ✦ ✦

He found her upstairs, in her old room at the top of the house, sitting on the narrow bed with the door open a crack.

He came in and shut it, because she was with him now and didn’t need to hear the stairs. He sat down beside her. The bed sagged alarmingly. The orchids on the sill, the ones her mother had given her at nine, white, moved a little in the draught from the window.

He took her hand. He didn’t wait for her to give it to him. He took it, and held it on his knee, and turned the ring with his thumb, the way he did.

“The uncle’s people are already here,” he said. “In the city. One of the guards told me without telling me. They’ve been asking around the people who move things across rivers. The Ferryman’s people.” He felt her hand go still in his. “If she won’t come home by the front door, she can come home by the back. That’s what one of them said, in a corridor at the palace. Last month.”

She looked at him.

“So whatever you say tomorrow,” said Jun Hyuk, “say it because you want to. Not because you’re afraid of the back door. I’ll take care of the back door.” He tightened his hand. “That’s my job. I’ve been doing it for a year and a half. I’m good at it.”

She looked down at their hands on his knee.

“I know what I’m going to say,” she said.

“I know you do,” he said. “I’ve known since he said everything has been arranged. I was watching you through the door.”

She looked at him. Then she turned on the narrow bed, the one she’d slept in from the age of four with the door open a crack, and took his face in her hands and kissed him.

He made a sound against her mouth and pulled her into his lap, and the old bed groaned under the two of them as if it had never been asked to hold anything like this, and it hadn’t. Twenty-four years she’d lain in this room listening to the stairs. Now she had her hands in his hair and her knees either side of him and the dark blue dress rucked up over them, and she wasn’t listening to anything. He kissed her as if he were angry with every one of those years. As if he could get them out of the room that way.

Downstairs, a door went. Raiden’s voice came up the stairwell, loud, asking if anyone had seen the egg tarts.

She stopped. She didn’t move off him. She stayed in his lap with her forehead against his and her breath coming fast, and listened, out of habit, to her brother’s feet go into the kitchen and not come up.

“Every sound in this house carries,” said Jun Hyuk, low.

She kissed him again, and didn’t care who heard.

chapters.title: Evangeline Says No to a Country
chapters.desc: On her real birthday, in her mother’s front room, she answers the envoy in the language she taught herself in a library. Then he has the afternoon to arrange a birthday, and a great deal of money, and one new fact.
chapters.epigraph: “Tell His Majesty I am not a question to be settled.” — Evangeline, 7 April 2024, in the court language
chapters.content:
She was up at five, on the morning of her birthday, and so was he.

He found her at the long table by the windows in the textile building, in the grey light, with a pot of tea and a pad of paper. She wasn’t writing on it. She’d written on it, sometime in the night, and now she was reading it, over and over, with her lips moving.

He came and stood behind her chair and looked over her shoulder.

It was in the other script. The tall looping one, with the marks above and below the line like birds on a wire. Half a page of it. Some of it crossed out and written again above.

“Is that what you’re going to say?” he said.

She nodded.

“Out loud? To him?”

She nodded again.

“You’ve never said it out loud,” he said.

“I read you the will,” said Evangeline.

“Reading. That’s different.”

She looked up at him over her shoulder. She looked tired and calm, and she was holding the pen so tightly that the knuckle of her first finger had gone white.

He took the pen out of her hand, gently, and put it down on the pad. Then he pulled out the chair beside her, and sat in it, and turned it so he was facing her, knee to knee.

“Say it to me,” he said.

She looked at him.

“I won’t understand a word,” said Jun Hyuk. “That’s the point. Say it to me first. Then you’ll have said it out loud once, and the second time’s always easier. Old Ko said that about everything. Jumping off a bridge. Asking a girl to dance. Telling a sergeant he’s an idiot.” He took both her hands. “Go on. I’m a very bad audience. I’ll just look at you.”

So she did.

She said it to him at half past five in the morning, at the long table, with her hands in his and the harbour going grey and then pink behind her. Slowly at first, stumbling on some of the words, the strange tall sounds catching in her throat as if they’d been folded up in there for nine years and creased. Then less slowly. He didn’t understand any of it. He watched her face. He watched it do things he’d never seen it do: frown, and stop, and go back, and go on, and harden, and once, near the end, something that might have been anger and might have been grief.

When she finished, he didn’t say anything for a while.

“I don’t know what any of that meant,” he said at last. “But I wouldn’t argue with you.”

She leaned forward until her forehead was against his chest.

“Happy birthday,” he said, into her hair. “Your real one. Twenty-six. I’m going to make a terrible fuss later. I’m warning you now.”

She lifted her head off his chest and kissed him. At half past five in the morning, knee to knee at the long table, with the half page of court language crumpled between them, and he tasted the tea on her mouth and forgot what he’d been warning her about. He took her face in his hands and kissed her back until the harbour behind her had gone from pink to gold, and she had to put her hand on his chest and push to remember she had somewhere to be.

✦ ✦ ✦

The envoy came at noon.

Same car, same small flag, same two guards. Mrs. Yim from the fish shop had brought her stool out early and was sitting on it with a flask. Teo saw Jun Hyuk at the top of the steps and nearly waved and then didn’t, because the older guard was looking at him.

The front room was the same too. Her father by the cold fireplace. Elowen on the sofa, Zhao behind her. Raiden at the window, not eating anything today. Eliana had come as well, in her hoodie, and was sitting on the stairs outside the door with her laptop on her knees, because she wouldn’t come in and wouldn’t go away.

And Jun Hyuk, this time, inside.

Evangeline had told him at breakfast. Not the door. In the room. By me. He’d looked at her, and she’d looked back, and he’d understood that this wasn’t a request, and had been so pleased about it that he’d burned the toast.

So he stood behind her mother’s armchair with one hand on the back of it, beside her shoulder, where she’d know where he was. The envoy came in and bowed to her and saw him there and paused for half a second, and then sat down, and laid his leather folder on his knee.

“Lady Evangeline,” he said. “Many happy returns of the day.”

“Thank you,” said Evangeline.

And then she answered him, in his own language.

✦ ✦ ✦

Nobody else in the room understood a word.

They told her that afterwards, each of them, separately, as if it were the most important thing about it. Her father said it in the car. Elowen said it on the phone that night. Raiden said it about eleven times, at dinner, with his mouth full. We didn’t understand a single word, Ev. Not one. And it didn’t matter.

Because they watched the envoy’s face.

He had been sitting with his gloved hands folded on his folder and his pleasant patient expression in place, the face he’d sat in a thousand rooms with. When she began, his eyebrows went up. That was all, at first. A man surprised that a woman who’d been described to him as almost silent was speaking, and in his language, which she had told no one she knew.

Then they saw him listen.

They saw him go still. The pleasant expression came off his face like a coat being taken off, and what was underneath was older and much more tired. He leaned forward a little, without seeming to know he was doing it. At one point, about halfway through, his gloved hand came up off the folder and moved in the air, as if he wanted to say something and had stopped himself.

She spoke for perhaps four minutes. It was the longest any of them had ever heard her speak, in any language, about anything.

When she stopped, nobody moved.

✦ ✦ ✦

What she said was this. She told Jun Hyuk that night, in their own language, in bed, with the lamp low against the wall and his arm round her. She’d translated it already, in her head, a hundred times.

She told the envoy that she thanked His Majesty for his greetings, and for his condolences, and for the trouble he’d taken. She said that she understood why he wanted her at court, and married, and safe from his uncle, and that she didn’t blame him for it, because she had grown up with a father who also thought she was something to be kept safe in a drawer. She said that she would not be coming.

She said that she wasn’t a lady of anybody’s House. She said she had a family already, and a name, and she’d chosen both. She had a father who’d been paid to lose her and kept her, and hadn’t always kept her well, and was learning. She had three sisters and a brother who’d never once in twenty-six years asked her to be useful. And she had a man she’d chosen for herself, who was standing behind her chair, and whom she was going to marry in a garden, with six people, when she was ready, and not before.

She said that she was not a question to be settled.

She said that if His Majesty was worried his uncle would use her, she would sign anything His Majesty needed, any paper, any renunciation, so that nobody could ever stand her up in front of a crowd as a claim to anything. She didn’t want a crown. She didn’t want a wing of a palace. She didn’t want the kingdom’s money. She’d lived twenty-six years without any of it.

And she said: If my brother wants to tell me my mother’s name, he can tell me as a brother. Not as a price. I will not buy her from him.

✦ ✦ ✦

The envoy sat without moving after she’d finished.

Then he took off his gloves.

He did it slowly, one finger at a time, the right and then the left, and laid them together on the leather folder. His hands were old, and thin, and there was a ring on one of them with the heron on it, worn almost smooth.

He looked at her, and said something, in the court language. Not much. A sentence, maybe two.

Evangeline went still in the armchair.

Behind her, Jun Hyuk felt it go through her. He couldn’t see her face. He could see the back of her neck, and her hands in her lap, and he saw her fingers close on each other, hard.

The envoy stood up. He bowed, the deep bow, with his bare hand flat on his chest. Then he did something none of them expected. He turned to Jun Hyuk, standing behind her chair, and bowed to him too: a small, precise bow, from a man who had decided something.

“I will carry your answer to His Majesty,” he said, in English, to all of them. “Exactly as you gave it.” He picked up his gloves. “I think he will want to see you himself. I think it may take some time.” He looked at Evangeline. “Many happy returns, my lady.”

He went out. They heard the car go down the hill.

✦ ✦ ✦

“What did he say?” said Elowen. “At the end. Ev. When he took his gloves off.”

Evangeline didn’t answer at first. She was looking at the empty chair.

“He said,” she said, “you speak exactly like her. You have her accent. The old one, from the lake country. I haven’t heard it in twenty-four years.” She swallowed. “He knew her. He said: She played the viola, in the King’s household orchestra. She was the best of them.”

Nobody said anything.

“He wasn’t supposed to tell me that,” said Evangeline. “It wasn’t in the folder.”

Lin Jian sat down heavily on the edge of the fireplace, in his funeral suit, and put his face in his hands. From the stairs outside the door, Eliana said, in a small voice, “Jie. Jie, that’s—” and stopped.

Jun Hyuk didn’t say anything at all. He put his hand on Evangeline’s shoulder, and she put hers over it, and held on.

Then he took his phone out of his pocket and went out into the hall.

✦ ✦ ✦

He had six hours.

He’d been planning her birthday for three weeks, since the letter came, since she’d said the seventh across the table in the textile building with her hands flat on the court-language pages. He’d had it all arranged. It was a good plan. It had a boat in it.

He stood in the hall of the tall house in the Walled City, by the window on the second landing that didn’t lock, and cancelled the boat.

Then he made eleven phone calls.

The first was to the director of the botanical gardens, a man he had never met, who did not want to talk to anyone at two o’clock on a Sunday afternoon and who, once he’d heard a number, very much did. The second was to a woman Elowen knew who did flowers for weddings, and who said tonight? in a voice of pure horror, and then how many candles? The third was to the head of the music department at the university, who gave him a name. The fourth was to the name.

The name was a woman of about fifty called Mrs. Lai, who taught viola at the conservatory and played in the city orchestra, and who listened to him explain, for some time, standing in a hall in the Walled City with his hand over his other ear, and then was quiet on the line.

“Her mother played,” said Jun Hyuk. “That’s all she knows about her. Her mother played the viola. It’s her birthday. She’s never heard anyone play it. Not once. Not in her whole life. I don’t think she knows what it sounds like.”

There was a long silence.

“What time?” said Mrs. Lai.

The other seven calls were food, a car, a man with lights, more candles, a cake, which he ordered from a bakery in the old town, from a girl with short hair who burst into tears on the phone when he said who it was for and said she’d make it herself, and Old Nam, who he rang last, for no reason, just to tell her.

“About time,” said Old Nam, and hung up.

✦ ✦ ✦

The orchid house at the botanical gardens was called the Glass Pavilion, and it was a hundred years old, iron and glass, shaped like an upturned boat, on the hill at the top of the gardens, and at eight o’clock that evening it was closed to the public, and empty, and full of light.

She didn’t know where they were going. He’d put her in a car at seven and told her to wear the blue coat and not to ask, and she hadn’t asked, because she never did. He walked her up the hill through the dark gardens, past the sleeping flowerbeds and the fountain, holding her hand, and stopped at the door of the pavilion, and opened it.

The orchids were everywhere. They always were, in the Glass Pavilion; it held one of the biggest collections in the region, white and yellow and spotted and striped, hanging from the iron ribs of the roof and climbing the old tree ferns and spilling out of the beds. But tonight there were candles too. Hundreds of them, in glass jars, along every path and on every ledge and in among the roots, so that the whole pavilion glowed gold from inside like a lantern, and the orchids hung in the warm air above them, lit from below, white and pale and still.

There was a table for two in the middle, under the biggest of the tree ferns.

And there was a woman, sitting on a plain wooden chair at the end of the path, in a black dress, with an instrument on her shoulder.

Evangeline stopped in the doorway.

Mrs. Lai lifted the bow and began to play.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t know what she played. He asked, afterwards, and Mrs. Lai told him, and he forgot. It was something old. Slow. Low and warm and sad, the sound of it, deeper than a violin, like a voice in the next room that you know and can’t quite hear. It filled the Glass Pavilion and went up into the iron roof among the hanging orchids and seemed to come back down again.

Evangeline stood in the doorway in her blue coat and didn’t move.

She didn’t cry. He’d thought she might. She stood with her hands at her sides, and her face perfectly still, and listened, and her eyes were brighter than he had ever seen them.

When Mrs. Lai finished, the pavilion was quiet except for the drip of the misters among the ferns.

Evangeline crossed the path to her and stopped in front of the chair.

“Again,” she said. “Please.”

Mrs. Lai looked up at her. She looked at her, at her face, and then at Jun Hyuk, standing in the doorway, and something in her own face gave way. She nodded. She lifted the bow.

Evangeline sat down on the edge of the nearest bed, among the white orchids, close, so close she could have touched the instrument, and listened to her mother’s music for the first time in her life.

Jun Hyuk stayed in the doorway. He’d planned dinner, and the cake, and a great many other things. They could wait. He stood in the door of the Glass Pavilion with his hands in his pockets and watched her listen, and thought that whatever else he did in his life, whatever he had done, he would remember that he’d done this.

✦ ✦ ✦

Much later, at home, in bed, with the lamp low and his arm round her and the taste of birthday cake still on both of them, she told him what she’d said in the court language, into his shirt, three weeks before.

“You are my home,” said Evangeline. “That’s what it means.”

He was quiet.

“Teach me,” he said. “How to say it.”

She said it, slowly. He said it back. He said it terribly, every sound wrong, in his border accent, and she laughed so hard she had to put her face in the pillow, and he said it again, worse, on purpose, to make her do it again, and she did.

Twelve, he thought. Then thirteen.

He said it a third time, properly, nearly, against her mouth, and she stopped laughing.

She kissed the rest of the word out of him. He let her. Then he rolled her under him in the lamplight, with the taste of cake still between them and her birthday not quite over, and kissed her back, slow, down her throat and along her collarbone and back up again, the court words and his own all mixed up together in his mouth, until neither of them was saying anything in any language at all.

chapters.title: Zhao and Jun Hyuk Share a Table
chapters.desc: Dinner for four at the house on the hill. Two sisters in the kitchen, two men on the terrace who would happily kill each other, and one sentence from Zhao Zhendong that changes the next month.
chapters.epigraph: “I sold rifles to the man whose boats took her. I didn’t know. I know now.” — Zhao Zhendong, on the terrace, 11 May 2024
chapters.content:
“It’s dinner,” said Elowen, on the phone. “Saturday. Seven. Just the four of us. He’s agreed.” When Jun Hyuk asked what exactly Zhao had said, she admitted it was hm, and that in her house, that counted.

✦ ✦ ✦

The house on the hill was big and quiet, and had more locks than any building in the city except the prison, and Jun Hyuk counted eleven of them between the gate and the front door before he gave up, out of respect.

It was also, he noticed, a house somebody had made into a home. He’d seen the file photographs, from before. Bare floors, blank walls, a kitchen nobody had cooked in. Now there were rugs, and books, and a long table in the dining room with flowers on it that Elowen had done herself, and a lemon tree in a pot by the terrace doors with three lemons on it, and a smell of something braising, and two large dogs who came to the door, looked him over, and decided, as dogs always did, that he was all right.

Zhao was standing in the hall.

He looked at Jun Hyuk. Jun Hyuk looked back. Neither of them held out a hand.

“Hm,” said Zhao.

“Good evening,” said Jun Hyuk. “Nice house. Lot of locks. I counted eleven and stopped. Your gate sensor on the left is pointing about ten degrees too high, by the way. A man my size could crawl under it. A man your size could walk.”

Zhao went on looking at him.

Then he turned and went into the dining room, and Elowen, behind him in the doorway, put her hand over her mouth.

✦ ✦ ✦

Dinner was difficult for the first hour.

Not unpleasant. Difficult, the way it’s difficult to eat soup sitting between two dogs that have been told not to fight and are thinking very hard about it. Zhao sat at the head of the table and ate steadily and said nothing. Jun Hyuk sat across from Evangeline and talked, because silence made him talk, and the silence at Zhao’s table was the deepest he had ever encountered. He talked about the textile building, and the handbag man upstairs who didn’t know who his landlord was, and the window box, and the basil, which had come through the winter. He talked about the botanical gardens. He talked about Old Nam.

Elowen and Evangeline watched them both, and occasionally caught each other’s eye, and looked away.

Halfway through the braised beef, Jun Hyuk said, “You sold rifles to the Velde militia in 2019. Before the deal you cancelled. Five hundred. Through a broker in the southern ports.”

The table went still.

Zhao put his chopsticks down.

“Zhendong,” said Elowen.

“I’m not starting anything,” said Jun Hyuk. “I’m making conversation. It’s what people do at dinner. I was there. I saw them used. That’s all. I wanted you to know that I know.” He picked up his own chopsticks again. “This beef’s very good, Mrs. Zhao.”

Zhao looked at him. Much longer than four seconds.

“Terrace,” said Zhao, and stood up.

✦ ✦ ✦

“They’re going to kill each other,” said Elowen, at the sink.

They were in the kitchen, the two of them, because Elowen had decided that the men should be left alone on the terrace and had said so, and both men had looked at her, and gone. The kitchen in the house on the hill had been redone two years ago, Elowen said, because when she moved in it had a microwave and a kettle and nothing else, and Zhendong had come home one day to find her cooking on a camping stove in the empty pantry and had had builders in by the Monday. It had a range with six burners now and a window over the sink that looked out onto the terrace, where two large men were standing at the balustrade, a careful metre apart, looking at the harbour.

“No,” said Evangeline. She was drying a plate.

Elowen looked at her.

“Jun Hyuk talks to people,” said Evangeline, “when he wants to know what they’re made of. He’s been talking to Zhao all evening. And Zhao hasn’t said anything. So he’s going to have to.” She put the plate on the rack. “That’s why he said the rifles. So that Zhao would have to say something back.”

Elowen stood at the sink with her hands in the water and stared at her.

“Ev,” she said. “That’s the most I’ve ever heard you say about anybody.”

Evangeline picked up another plate.

“You talk now,” said Elowen. “Do you know that? You talk. Not a lot. But you do. You said three sentences at dinner. To me. Unasked.” Her eyes had gone wet. “You told me the basil came through the winter. You told me about the lady with the viola. You told me.”

Evangeline looked at the plate in her hands. She hadn’t noticed. She thought about it, and realised it was true.

“He talks so much,” she said, “that I had to start, to get a word in.”

Elowen laughed, and then cried, a little, into the washing-up, and Evangeline put down the plate and the tea towel and, for the first time in her life, without being asked, put her arms round her sister from behind and held on.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the terrace, Zhao said nothing for three minutes.

Jun Hyuk let him. He’d been talking all evening on purpose, and now he stopped, on purpose, and stood at the balustrade with his hands on the cold stone and looked at the harbour, all the lights along the far side and the ferries going back and forth and somewhere among them the textile building, six floors up, with a steel box on its ledge.

He was good at silence, when he chose it. He’d just never met anyone who was better.

“I sold rifles,” said Zhao at last, “to the Ferryman.”

Jun Hyuk didn’t move.

“Not the Velde ones. Before. 2016. 2017.” Zhao was looking at the water. “Two hundred. Through a man in the south. For his boats. For the river. I didn’t know what the boats carried. I didn’t ask.”

The ferry with the coloured lights went past, far below, with music on its top deck.

“I sold rifles to the man whose boats took her,” said Zhao. “I didn’t know. I know now.” He turned his head, and looked at Jun Hyuk, and his face was the shut door it always was, and his eyes were not. “I wanted you to know that I know.”

Jun Hyuk looked at him.

He’d expected a threat, after a remark about rifles over the braised beef. Or a look, or Hm. He hadn’t expected that.

“Right,” he said. His voice came out rough. “Right. Well.”

He couldn’t think of anything else. For once in his life.

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhao told him the rest standing at the balustrade, in short flat sentences with long gaps between them, the way you’d unload a truck.

The uncle’s people were in the city. Four of them, Zhao thought, maybe five, in a rented flat in the north of the eastern district, with diplomatic plates on one car and no plates on another. They’d been to see the broker in the southern ports, the man Zhao had used in 2016, who had told them politely that he didn’t buy people. So they’d gone further down the river. To the Ferryman’s people. Zhao’s own men had heard it from a ferry captain who’d heard it from a man in a bar.

“When?” said Jun Hyuk.

“June. They’re moving something across the river in June. A boat. A big one. Paid for already.” Zhao paused. “The broker said the man who paid asked how many people it could carry in the hold. He said one. One person. With a lot of room.”

Jun Hyuk’s hands closed on the stone.

“She goes to the border,” said Zhao. “Your old flat. The noodle shop. She visits the old woman.”

“Every two weeks.”

“Hm.” Zhao looked at him. “They’ll know that. If I know it, they know it.”

Jun Hyuk was quiet for a while.

“Why are you telling me this?” he said. “You don’t like me. I don’t like you. You think I’m a stray dog. I think you’re—” He stopped, because what he thought of Zhao had changed in the last ten minutes and he hadn’t had time to find out what into. “Why?”

Zhao looked back at the house. Through the kitchen window, under the warm light, the two sisters were standing at the sink, and Evangeline had her arms round Elowen from behind, and Elowen was laughing and wiping her eyes with a wet hand.

“Because she’s crying,” said Zhao. “The good kind.” He looked back at the harbour. “I’d give a great deal for that to stay the only kind.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He offered men. Jun Hyuk said no. He offered money, and Jun Hyuk laughed out loud, for the first time that evening, and told him about the six blue fish crates, and Zhao looked at him and then smiled, slightly, at the corner of the mouth, which Elowen said afterwards she had seen perhaps nine times in four years.

Then he offered Bao.

“He drives her,” said Zhao. “When you can’t. To the border, to her father’s, anywhere. He doesn’t talk. He doesn’t stop. He’s been shot twice for my wife and he’d do it again.” A pause. “He likes your woman. He says she’s the only one in that family who’s never asked him a stupid question.”

Jun Hyuk thought about it.

He thought about the silver car outside the textile building, from August, that he hadn’t seen until November. About the river road in June, and a boat with one place in the hold and a lot of room. About Evangeline on the bus to the border every second Saturday with Old Nam’s oranges in her bag, changing coats in the market, losing whoever was behind her, so good at it that he’d stopped worrying. He’d stopped worrying. That was the part that went cold in his stomach.

“Yes,” he said. “Thank you. Yes.”

Zhao nodded once.

They stood at the balustrade a while longer, a metre apart, not speaking, looking at the harbour, until Elowen opened the terrace door and said it was cold, and there was dessert, and if either of them was dead she’d like to know before she cut the cake.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the car going home, Bao driving, smoothly, saying nothing, Evangeline sat in the back with her head on Jun Hyuk’s shoulder and her hand in his.

“What did he say?” she said.

He thought about telling her everything. The boat. The hold. One person, with a lot of room. He’d never lied to her and he didn’t mean to start. But it was ten at night and she’d held her sister at a sink and laughed at dinner, and the boat wasn’t until June.

“He said he sold rifles to the Ferryman,” said Jun Hyuk. “Years ago. Before Elowen. He said he didn’t know what the boats carried. He said he knows now.” He turned the ring on her finger. “And he gave me Bao.”

She was quiet for a while. The lights of the city went past the windows.

“And the rest?” she said.

He looked down at her. She was looking up at him from his shoulder, steadily, in the dark of the car, the way she’d looked at the menu on his dashboard on the first night. She knew there was more. Of course she did.

“Tomorrow,” he said. “At the table. With tea. I’ll tell you all of it. I promise.”

“All of it,” said Evangeline.

Then she reached up and pulled his head down and kissed him, in the back of Zhao’s car, with Bao’s eyes on the road and the lights of the city going past. It wasn’t short. He forgot about the river road for the whole of it, and put his hand in her hair and kept her there when she would have stopped, and kissed her again, deeper, until her fingers were tight on his collar. When she let him go she put her head back on his shoulder and shut her eyes, as if she’d settled something.

In the front, without a word, Bao reached out and turned the radio on.

He looked out of the window at the city all the way home, and didn’t stop thinking about the river road.

chapters.title: The Abduction Attempt
chapters.desc: Old Nam’s seventy-fourth birthday, which she refuses to celebrate. A plan with Bao and two of Zhao’s men on the bridge. Then four men in a noodle shop at two in the afternoon, a pipe, and a choice she makes in about one second.
chapters.epigraph: “If you want to live, don’t stop moving.” — rule nought, which was never written on the menu because it didn’t need to be
chapters.content:
He told her everything on the Sunday morning, at the long table, with tea, the way he’d promised.

The uncle’s people. The flat in the north of the eastern district. The car with diplomatic plates and the car with none. The broker in the southern ports who didn’t buy people, and the men further down the river who did. A boat in June, already paid for, with room in the hold for one.

She listened without moving. When he’d finished, she poured him more tea.

He wanted to tell her to stop going to the border until June was over. He could feel the sentence sitting in his mouth. He’d have said it to anyone else.

“I could take Nam her oranges,” he said instead. “If you wanted. Just for June.”

“No,” said Evangeline.

He put the cup down.

“The fifteenth is her birthday,” she said. “She’ll be seventy-four. She says she doesn’t have birthdays. She’s said it every year for fifty years, and nobody has ever made her a cake.” She turned her own cup. “I’m making her a cake.”

“Evangeline—”

“I’m not going to stop living,” she said, “because of a boat.”

He looked at her across the table. She looked back. Her face had the look he’d learned, a long time ago, not to argue with.

He didn’t argue. He sat with his hands round his cup for a minute. “Right,” he said. “Then we do it properly.” And they made a plan.

✦ ✦ ✦

The plan was good. He’d made a great many plans in his life, and he knew a good one.

Bao would drive her up, in the black car, which had glass like the textile building and doors that weighed as much as a small motorbike. Jun Hyuk would go up the night before and be in Nam’s back room when she arrived. Two of Zhao’s men, who Zhao had offered without being asked and Jun Hyuk had accepted without arguing, which surprised all three of them, would be on the bridge from noon, one at each end, pretending to fish. Eliana had put something on Evangeline’s phone that would tell four people where she was every ten seconds, which made it the opposite of the thing her father had put in the case, and which Evangeline had agreed to without a word, because it was hers to agree to.

And in Evangeline’s canvas bag, under the cake tin, in a soft cloth case, there was the small pistol he’d given her in February.

She’d asked for it. That was the part he still thought about. She’d never asked for anything in her life, and in February, after New Year at her father’s and before the letter from the palace, she’d sat across the table from him while he cleaned his things, and waited until he’d finished, and said, teach me. And he’d taught her. On a range in the hills that belonged to a man who owed him a favour, every Sunday for six weeks. She’d been bad at it and she was still bad at it. She held it correctly and stood correctly and breathed correctly and missed, steadily, with total concentration, about two times out of three.

“You won’t need it,” he said, on the Friday night, watching her pack the bag. “You’ll be in Nam’s shop for two hours with me in the back and Bao outside and two men on the bridge. You won’t need it.”

“I know,” said Evangeline, and put it in.

He watched her do up the bag. Then he got up from the table and came round behind her and put his arms round her, and his chin on the top of her head, and held her against him with his hands flat over hers on the canvas.

“I hate this,” he said into her hair. “I hate all of it. I want that on the record. When you’re in Nam’s shop on Saturday with a cake and a gun in your bag, I want you to remember that I said I hated it—”

She turned round in his arms and kissed him, to stop him saying the rest. He let her. He backed her up against the long table, gently, and then not gently, his hands on her hips and her hands in his shirt, and kissed her until the bag slid off the edge onto the floor and neither of them picked it up. He didn’t say the rest that night at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

Old Nam did not want a cake.

She said so, at length, in two languages, standing behind her counter in her purple quilted jacket at a quarter to two on a hot Saturday afternoon in June, while Evangeline took the cake out of the tin on the corner table. It was a sponge, three layers, with mango, because Nam liked mango and had once said so, in 2022, in passing. Nuo had helped her make it.

“I don’t have birthdays,” said Nam. “I’ve told you. I’ve told everybody. Fifty years. I don’t—who told you it was today?”

“You did.”

“I never.”

“In January. To the cook. You said, I’ll be seventy-four in June and I’ll still be cutting your spring onions because you can’t.”

Old Nam opened her mouth and shut it.

Evangeline put a candle in the cake. One. She lit it with a match from the box she always carried.

Old Nam stood behind her counter and looked at the cake, at the one small flame on top of it, in the corner of her empty shop in the hot afternoon, and her mouth began to shake. Then she came round the counter, slowly, and sat down at the corner table across from Evangeline, and put her old hands flat on either side of the cake.

“Well,” she said, in a voice that wasn’t her voice at all. “Well. Look at that.”

In the back room, behind the kitchen door, Jun Hyuk was watching through the crack and had to sit down on a sack of flour.

✦ ✦ ✦

The shop was nearly empty. That was normal for two o’clock on a Saturday in June, when it was too hot to eat noodles and everybody was asleep. The cook was in the kitchen, chopping. A man at the counter by the window was finishing a bowl of wonton. Outside, at the kerb, the black car with Bao in it, engine running. On the bridge, two men with fishing rods.

At two minutes past two, a truck came down River Bridge Road and stopped beside the black car.

It was a delivery truck, the kind that brought gas cylinders to the restaurants along the river. It stopped close beside the car, so close that its side was almost against Bao’s door, and the driver got out and went round the back and started unloading cylinders onto the pavement, slowly, one at a time, in front of the car’s bonnet.

Bao leaned on his horn.

In the back room, Jun Hyuk stood up off the flour sack.

The door of the shop opened, and three men came in.

✦ ✦ ✦

They didn’t look like anything. They looked like men who’d come in out of the heat for noodles. Two of them were young, in T-shirts and caps. One was older, in a pale shirt, with his hands in his pockets. They didn’t look at her. They looked at the menu on the wall, the way customers did.

The man at the counter by the window put down his spoon and stood up.

He wasn’t a customer either.

Then everything happened at once, and afterwards she could only remember it in pieces, the way she remembered the container.

The man from the counter grabbing for her arm. Her chair going over backwards. Old Nam on her feet, faster than any seventy-four-year-old woman had any right to be, with the big ladle from the soup pot in her hand, bringing it round in an arc of hot pork bone broth into the face of the nearest young man in a cap, who screamed. The kitchen door slamming open. Jun Hyuk.

He came through it the way she’d seen him come down a stack of containers at West Basin, without any noise at all, and much faster than anything his size could move, and the man from the counter, who had her by the arm, saw him and let go.

She did what she’d been taught, the rule that had never been written on the menu because it didn’t need to be: don’t stop moving. She went low and sideways, the way she’d gone under the dining table at nine, towards the back of the shop, towards the kitchen door and the yard and the iron ladder to the roofs, the route she’d known since January 2023, the one they’d walked together a dozen times since, just in case.

Behind her, a table went over. The cake went with it.

She heard Old Nam shout. She heard a sound like a sack of rice hitting the floor, and Old Nam stopped shouting.

She heard Jun Hyuk’s voice, low and level, talking, the way he always talked, the whole time, easy now, easy, you don’t want to do that, friend, you really don’t, and she heard the young man in the cap who’d been hit with the soup stop screaming quite suddenly, and she heard the older man in the pale shirt say something in a language she knew. The court language. Not the city kind. The northern kind, with the hard edges, that she’d only ever read in the notes at the back of the grammar book in the library.

Not him. Her. Take her.

She was at the kitchen door.

She looked back.

✦ ✦ ✦

She’d always looked back. That was the trouble with her. At the hospital, in the street, at the bus window. She’d never once in her life been able to walk away from something without looking back to see it.

The shop was wrecked. Tables over, bowls smashed, broth across the floor, the cake upside down in it. Old Nam was on the floor by the counter, small and purple and still, with the cook kneeling beside her. One of the young men was on the floor too, not moving. The man from the counter was against the wall, holding his arm at a wrong angle.

Jun Hyuk was standing in the middle of it.

He was standing between her and the other two. Of course he was. Between her and the older man in the pale shirt, and the second young man in the cap, who had something in his hand now, a length of steel pipe, the kind that held up the awnings on River Bridge Road. Jun Hyuk was talking to them. He had his hands up, open, low, the way he’d held them in the door of the container, and he was talking, come on now, come on, let’s all calm down, and he was watching the pipe.

He wasn’t watching the man from the counter.

The man from the counter had let go of his broken arm and had something in his good hand, and was coming off the wall, behind him.

She opened her mouth to say his name.

The pipe came round. Jun Hyuk stepped inside it, the way she’d seen him step inside things, and caught the young man’s wrist, and the pipe went clattering away across the floor, and then the man from the counter hit him from behind, across the back of the head, with whatever was in his hand, and she heard the sound it made.

He went down.

He went down all at once, the way a tree goes, on his knees first and then forward onto his hands in the broth, and then onto his side, and he didn’t get up. He didn’t try. There was blood in his short hair at the back. His eyes were open and they weren’t looking at anything.

The man in the pale shirt looked at him on the floor. Then he looked across the wrecked shop at Evangeline, standing in the kitchen door.

“Your Highness,” he said, in the hard northern court language, quite politely. “Please. Come with us. Nobody else needs to be hurt.”

The young man in the cap had picked the pipe up again. He was standing over Jun Hyuk. Looking at the back of his head.

✦ ✦ ✦

She had about one second.

She knew that. She’d learned to count seconds in the dark of a container by the spots of light through the holes in the roof. She knew what one second was.

The kitchen door was behind her. The yard. The iron ladder. The roofs. She knew the way. She’d be on the pharmacy roof before they reached the yard. She’d be at the bridge before they reached the ladder. Zhao’s men were on the bridge. Bao was outside, behind a gas truck, leaning on his horn. Eliana’s thing on her phone was telling four people every ten seconds exactly where she was. If she ran, she would live. That was the rule. That was the only rule. If you want to live, stay behind me and don’t stop moving.

He was on the floor.

She’d been behind him for twenty months. Behind him in the container, behind him through the stacks at West Basin, behind him on the roofs, behind him at her father’s office and on the steps of her mother’s house and at the door of every room he’d ever walked into ahead of her so that whatever was in it would get to him first. She’d followed every rule he ever wrote. She’d broken one.

The young man lifted the pipe.

Evangeline put her hand into her canvas bag, past the empty cake tin, and found the soft cloth case, and stopped moving.

chapters.title: She Shoots First
chapters.desc: Three shots in a noodle shop. The first two hit the duck cabinet. She is still very bad at it. It is enough.
chapters.epigraph: “Stay behind me.” — Evangeline, River Bridge Road, 15 June 2024
chapters.content:
The first shot hit the duck cabinet.

It was loud, much louder than at the range in the hills, where there had been ear defenders and open air and a man who owed Jun Hyuk a favour standing at the back with his arms folded. In the small hot shop, with its tiled walls and its low ceiling, it was like the sky breaking, the way the lock had broken at West Basin, and the glass front of the cabinet where Old Nam’s roast ducks hung on their hooks went white and then fell out of its frame in a sheet and shattered across the counter.

The young man with the pipe flinched and turned.

He looked at her. At the kitchen door, and the tall woman standing in it in a pale blue dress with a small black pistol held out in front of her in both hands, exactly the way she’d been taught, arms straight, feet apart, breathing. He looked at her face. She saw him see that it hadn’t changed at all.

She fired again.

The second shot went into the wall above his head, a hand’s width above his cap, and brought down a calendar from a fish wholesaler, 2019, which Old Nam had never taken down, and a shower of white tile.

The young man dropped flat.

He didn’t drop the pipe. He went down on one knee beside Jun Hyuk with the pipe still in his hand and his other hand over his head, and then, because he was young and frightened and had been paid, he started to get up again, and lifted the pipe, and turned back towards the man on the floor.

She was three metres away. She’d counted it, without meaning to, the way she counted everything. Three metres. At the range he had stood her at three metres, at the end, when she couldn’t hit anything at ten, and said three is enough, three is a room, three is all you’ll ever need.

The third shot hit him in the shoulder.

✦ ✦ ✦

He screamed and the pipe went out of his hand, end over end, and hit the floor and rolled through the broth to the foot of the counter. He went down on his side holding his shoulder, and blood came through his fingers, bright red, onto his white T-shirt, and he kept screaming, high and thin, like a much younger boy.

She didn’t look at him.

She’d already turned. The man in the pale shirt had moved when the cabinet went. Not towards her. Sideways, towards the wall, towards the man from the counter, whose arm was broken and who had dropped whatever he’d hit Jun Hyuk with and was standing very still now, against the tiles, with his good hand up and open.

The man in the pale shirt had his hand inside his jacket.

She pointed the pistol at his chest.

“Stay where you are,” said Evangeline.

She said it in the hard northern court language. It came out that way. It was the language he’d spoken to her in, the northern kind, with the hard edges, and until that moment she had only ever read it, in the notes at the back of a grammar book on the third floor of a library. Stay where you are. Take your hand out of your coat. Slowly. Empty.

He stared at her.

He took his hand out of his coat. Slowly. Empty.

✦ ✦ ✦

She walked forward.

She didn’t run. Running was for when there was somewhere to get to, and the place she needed to be was four steps away. She walked across the wrecked floor of Nam’s Noodles, through the broth and the broken bowls and the upside-down cake and the glass from the duck cabinet, with the pistol held out in front of her in both hands and pointed at the man in the pale shirt the whole way, and stopped beside Jun Hyuk.

Then she stepped past him.

She stood in front of him. Between him, on the floor, on his side, with the blood in his hair and his eyes half open, and the man in the pale shirt, and the man from the counter, and the door to the street, and whatever else might come through it.

“Stay behind me,” said Evangeline, in her own language this time, low and flat, to the man on the floor.

✦ ✦ ✦

He heard it.

He’d hear it for the rest of his life, at four in the morning when he woke and didn’t know for a second where he was. He heard it from a long way down, from under something heavy and dark and ringing, the way you hear a voice from the bottom of a swimming pool.

Stay behind me.

He opened his eyes.

The floor was wet and smelled of pork bone and blood. There was a ringing in his head like a bell in a church a long way off. The light was wrong, too bright, sliding. He couldn’t make his hands work. He could see, sideways, along the tiled floor at the height of a cat, a pair of feet in flat grey shoes, standing very close to his face, planted, apart, the way he’d taught her on the range in the hills.

Above the shoes, a pale blue dress. Above the dress, her back, straight as a door. Her arms out in front of her. Her hair coming loose from its knot. And past her, in the bright sliding light, a man in a pale shirt with his hands up and open and his face gone grey.

She was standing in front of him.

He’d spent nine years standing in front of doors. Every room. Every stair. Every container. He’d made it a rule. He’d written it on a menu, as good as. Stay behind me. And she’d followed every one of his rules for twenty months, except the one about coming back, and now she’d broken this one too, and was standing in Nam’s wrecked shop in her good shoes, with three bullets gone and the gun steady, between him and the thing that had come through the door.

He tried to say her name. It came out as something else.

She didn’t turn round.

“Don’t get up,” she said. “You’re bleeding.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The front door came in at nine minutes past two.

It came in, rather than opening, because Bao had given up on the gas truck, which had been parked so close to his door that it wouldn’t open, and gone out through the back seat and the opposite door and over the bonnet and through the cylinders and round, and Bao was not a man who knocked when he had heard three shots in a building with his employer’s sister-in-law in it. He came through the door shoulder first with the frame splintering round him and a gun in his hand, and stopped.

He looked at the room. The broken cabinet, the calendar on the floor, the boy screaming with his shoulder, the man with the broken arm against the wall, Old Nam on the floor with the cook bent over her, the big man on his side in the broth.

The man in the pale shirt, with his hands up.

And Evangeline Lin, standing over Jun Hyuk with a small black pistol, straight.

Bao looked at her, and his eyebrows went up, which nobody had ever seen them do.

“Miss Lin,” he said.

“Bao,” said Evangeline. “Please. Him.” She didn’t lower the gun. “The one in the shirt. He’s from the north. He’s got a passport.”

Bao crossed the shop in four steps, and put his hand on the man in the pale shirt, and the man in the pale shirt went down onto the floor face first and stayed there.

Then the two men from the bridge came in through the broken door with their fishing rods still in their hands, and behind them the spring-onion seller in his two hats, who had run all the way from the middle of the bridge with his basket, and stood in the doorway gasping.

✦ ✦ ✦

She lowered the pistol.

She did it carefully, the way he’d taught her. She took her finger off the trigger and laid it along the side, and pointed it at the floor, and then she did something he hadn’t taught her, which was to stand there with it pointed at the floor and not move at all, for a while, while Bao and Zhao’s men did things around her.

Then she knelt down beside him in the broth.

She put the pistol on the floor, a little way off, out of reach of anyone. She put her hand on his face. He was looking up at her. His eyes were focusing now, a little, and finding her, and losing her, and finding her again.

“You,” he said. His voice came out of the bottom of the swimming pool. “You were supposed to stay behind me.”

“You were down,” said Evangeline.

“You should have run.” It came out slurred. He was trying to lift his head off the tiles. “The yard. The ladder. You know the way, we walked it, you should have—”

She bent down and kissed him.

Not hard. Lightly, on the mouth, on the floor of Nam’s wrecked shop, with broth soaking into her hem and his blood on her fingers. It stopped him the way nothing else in his life had ever stopped him talking.

“You’ve got a hole in your head,” she said against his mouth. “Stop talking.”

He stopped. He lay in the broth and looked up at her, and his face, under the blood and the grey, went red from the collar up, the way it had on the end of a camp bed over a towel folded wrong.

Her hand on his face was shaking. Not much. The first time he’d ever felt it shake.

He tried to lift his own hand to it, and couldn’t, and she took his hand instead and held it against her cheek.

“Nam,” he said.

“She’s alive.” Her voice was perfectly level. “She hit her head on the counter. Her wrist’s broken. She’s swearing at the cook.” Over by the counter, faintly, Old Nam was swearing at the cook. “Bao’s called Elara.”

“You shot him,” he said, and she told him where, and that she’d missed twice first. “I hit the ducks,” said Evangeline. “And the calendar.”

He started to laugh. It hurt his head so much that everything went white and sliding for a second, and he stopped, and lay there in the broth with her hand on his face, and his eyes filled up, and he didn’t know if it was the laughing or the pain or the other thing, the thing he’d felt when he opened his eyes and saw her feet planted on the tiles in front of his face.

“I’ve never,” he said. “Nobody. Not once in my whole life. Nobody’s ever stood in front of me.”

She bent down and put her forehead against his, in the wreck of Nam’s shop, with the boy still crying by the counter and the spring-onion man in the door and the broken glass all round them shining in the hot afternoon light.

“Get used to it,” said Evangeline.

chapters.title: After
chapters.desc: Staples in his scalp, a scan he doesn’t want, a detective who knows exactly who he is, and a man with a diplomatic passport who finds out what it’s worth. That night she shakes for an hour. He holds her the whole time.
chapters.epigraph: “A diplomatic passport is a document. Immunity is a status. You have the first. You don’t have the second.” — Inspector Song Wei Long
chapters.content:
Elara came at a quarter to three, in a taxi, in scrubs, with her hair falling out of its clip and a green bag over her shoulder that she’d taken from the emergency department without asking anyone.

She came through the broken door of Nam’s Noodles and stopped. She looked at the room. The duck cabinet. The calendar. The pipe at the foot of the counter. The boy with the shoulder, who Bao had sat against the wall with a tea towel pressed into it and who had stopped screaming and was just crying now, steadily, like rain. The man in the pale shirt face down by the window with one of Zhao’s men sitting on his back. Old Nam in a chair from the kitchen with her wrist in a cushion, swearing.

And her sister, kneeling on the wet floor in a pale blue dress with a man’s head in her lap.

“Oh, Ev,” said Elara.

Then she was a doctor.

✦ ✦ ✦

She did the boy first, because he was bleeding most. She knelt beside him and looked at the shoulder and said, in a voice that was nothing like her sister’s and nothing like the voice she’d used on the phone in February, “You’re going to be fine. It went through. It missed the bone. You’re very lucky the person who shot you is a terrible shot.” The boy stared at her. She packed the wound and taped it and told Bao he needed an ambulance in the next hour and not before, and Bao looked at the man on the floor by the window and said he’d see to it, and she didn’t ask what that meant.

She did Old Nam second. Old Nam told her she was fine. Elara told her she had a broken wrist and probably a concussion and was going to the hospital whether she liked it or not, and Old Nam gave her a long measuring look, the way she’d looked at Elowen a year ago, and said, “You’re the doctor one,” and let her splint it.

Then she knelt down beside her sister.

Jun Hyuk was awake. He’d been awake, more or less, for twenty minutes. He was lying on his side with his head on Evangeline’s knees and his eyes open, watching the room slide about, and he’d been sick once, onto the floor, which Evangeline had cleaned up with a tea towel without a word.

Elara looked at the back of his head. She parted his hair with gloved fingers, gently, and looked.

“Six centimetres,” she said. “Down to the bone. It needs closing. He’s been sick?”

“Once,” said Evangeline.

“Did he lose consciousness?”

“For about a minute. Maybe two.”

Elara looked down at him. “Do you know where you are?”

“Nam’s,” said Jun Hyuk. “On the floor. In the soup. Your sister shot a boy.”

“He’s oriented,” said Elara. “Rude, but oriented.” She sat back on her heels. “He needs a scan. Today. Now. A head injury with loss of consciousness and vomiting gets a scan, that’s not me being careful, that’s the rule. If there’s a bleed under the skull, it can look like nothing for six hours and then it can kill him.”

“No hospitals,” said Jun Hyuk.

“Then he dies on the floor of a noodle shop,” said Elara pleasantly, “and I’ll tell everyone it was his own fault.”

Evangeline looked at her sister.

“There’s a place,” said Evangeline. “On the hill. Above the old racecourse. It’s private.”

“The Crestview,” said Elara. “It’s the most expensive hospital in the city. It costs more for one night than I earn in a month. Rich men go there to have their knees done and not be in the newspaper.”

“They don’t ask questions,” said Evangeline, “of people who pay.”

Elara looked at her for a moment. Then at the big man on the floor with his head in her sister’s lap.

“Can he pay?” she said.

“Yes,” said Evangeline.

✦ ✦ ✦

Inspector Song Wei Long arrived at twenty past three, while Elara was closing the wound on Nam’s kitchen table with a staple gun from the green bag, because Jun Hyuk had refused to go anywhere with a hole in his head, and had said so, and had then been quietly sick again.

Wei Long came in through the broken door and stopped, the way everyone had stopped.

He looked at the room. At all of it. At the bullet holes, one in the wall above the counter and one in the duck cabinet, and the third that had gone through a boy and into the tiled floor behind him. At the man in the pale shirt, still face down, still with one of Zhao’s men sitting on him. At Old Nam. At the big man on the kitchen table with his head being stapled. At Evangeline Lin, standing beside the table with her hands folded in front of her, in a blue dress with broth soaked into the hem.

“Evangeline,” said Wei Long.

She inclined her head.

He looked at the small black pistol, which was lying on the counter now, on a clean tea towel, where she’d put it. He looked at her.

“Three shots,” he said.

She told him, in a few words, which one had hit the boy, and where the other two had gone.

Wei Long looked at the calendar on the floor, from a fish wholesaler, 2019, with a hole through the month of May. The corner of his mouth moved.

Then he went and crouched by the man in the pale shirt.

✦ ✦ ✦

The man in the pale shirt had a diplomatic passport.

He produced it, slowly, from the inside pocket of his jacket, when Zhao’s man let him sit up. It was dark red, with the heron on the front in gold. He held it out to Wei Long without a word, the way you’d hold out a ticket at a gate, and his grey face had got some of its colour back, and a little of its confidence.

Wei Long took it. He opened it. He read it, all of it, every page, with no expression whatsoever.

“You’ll find,” said the man in the pale shirt, in careful English, “that I have immunity. I am a member of His Highness’s household. I’m here on a private matter. You can’t arrest me. I’d like to call my embassy.”

Wei Long closed the passport.

“You’re welcome to call your embassy,” he said. “I’ll give you the number. I’ll dial it for you.” He turned the passport over in his long fingers. “But you’ll find that your embassy doesn’t know you’re here. You came in four days ago on a tourist visa, which you stamped into this. You aren’t on the diplomatic list. You aren’t accredited to anybody in this country. You aren’t attached to your mission. Your own ambassador, if I ring him, will tell me he’s never heard of you.” He held the passport up. “A diplomatic passport is a document. Immunity is a status. You have the first. You don’t have the second.”

The man in the pale shirt went still.

“So I’m going to arrest you,” said Wei Long, “for attempted kidnapping, conspiracy, assault, and whatever else I think of in the car. And then I’m going to ring your ambassador anyway. And then he’s going to ring your King. And I think your King,” he looked across the room at Evangeline, “is going to be very interested to hear what his uncle’s household was doing in a noodle shop on River Bridge Road on a Saturday afternoon.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He came to the kitchen table before he left.

Elara had finished. Jun Hyuk was sitting up now, carefully, on the edge of the table, with a dressing on the back of his head and his hands on his knees and his face grey. Wei Long stood in front of him. They were almost the same height, sitting and standing.

“Lee Jun Hyuk,” said Wei Long.

Jun Hyuk looked at him.

“Kuang Yaoming,” said Wei Long. “West Basin. October 2022. Tse, the river captain, 2019. A man called Hwang, who nobody has seen since October.” He said it all in exactly the same voice, as if he were reading a shopping list. “And forty-one pages from a school exercise book, signed by a dead judge, in an envelope addressed to me in capital letters.” He paused. “I’ve had nine arrests out of those pages. Two of them were judges. One was a police superintendent I used to like.”

Jun Hyuk didn’t say anything.

“I can’t prove any of the rest of it,” said Wei Long. “I know it, and I can’t prove it, and I’ve stopped trying, mostly, because every time I look, I find that the person who’s gone was somebody I’d been trying to arrest for ten years.” He looked at Evangeline, beside the table. Then back. “So I’ll say this once. Stop giving me reasons to try.”

He turned to go. At the broken door, he stopped.

“The Ferryman’s boat,” he said, without looking round. “The one with room for one in the hold. It was due at the old jetty below the bridge at four. We picked it up at half past two. The captain’s very talkative.” A pause. “I thought you’d want to know it’s gone.”

He went out.

Jun Hyuk sat on the edge of the kitchen table and stared after him.

“Well,” said Old Nam, from her chair, with enormous approval. “I like him.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The Crestview was on the hill above the old racecourse, and it looked like a hotel, and it treated Jun Hyuk like one.

They scanned his head at six. There was no bleed. There was a concussion, a bad one, and a fracture line in the skull that the doctor, a calm grey woman who looked at the stapled wound and then at Elara and said nice work, said would heal by itself if he didn’t do anything stupid for six weeks. She kept him until midnight, watching, waking him every hour to ask him the date. He told her it was the fifteenth of June, a Saturday, and that his fiancée had shot a man in a noodle shop, and the doctor wrote down oriented and didn’t ask anything else.

Evangeline sat by the bed the whole time in the chair, in her ruined blue dress, with her hands folded in her lap.

She hardly moved. She didn’t talk. She didn’t eat the sandwiches the nurse brought. She sat and watched him, and every hour when the doctor came in and woke him, she watched his face to see if he knew where he was.

At eleven, when the doctor had gone again, he turned his head on the pillow and started on her.

“Eat the sandwich,” he said. “You haven’t eaten since breakfast. You haven’t moved. You’re still in the dress. There’s soup on it. Bao can take you home, Elara can sit with me, she likes telling me off, you could sleep six hours and come back and I’d still be here, I’m not allowed to go anywhere, I’ve got a list—”

She got up out of the chair, and leaned over the rail of the bed, and kissed him.

He stopped in the middle of the word.

She stayed there, bent over the rail, with her mouth on his, until she felt him give up and his hand come up, slowly, to the back of her neck. A nurse came to the door with a tray, and looked, and went away again.

When Evangeline sat back down, she folded her hands in her lap.

“No,” she said.

He didn’t say another word about the sandwich. He lay and looked at her from the pillow with the dressing on the back of his head, and his ears had gone red, and every time the doctor came in after that and asked him the date, he got it right and then looked at Evangeline as if he expected to be marked.

At a quarter past midnight they let him go, with a list.

Bao drove them home.

✦ ✦ ✦

She started shaking at ten to one.

They’d come up the six flights of stairs slowly, because he wasn’t allowed to do stairs quickly, and she had walked behind him the whole way with one hand flat on his back. They’d come in through the three locks. She’d turned them behind him.

Then she’d stood in the middle of the long dark room, in the light from the harbour, and started to shake.

It wasn’t crying. It came up out of her from somewhere far down, from the place where she’d been keeping it since one minute past two in the afternoon, and it went through her like a ship’s engine, the way her father’s shaking had gone through him at the hospital in October. She stood in the middle of the room with her arms at her sides and shook, and couldn’t stop, and couldn’t speak, and couldn’t move her feet.

He came across the room to her.

He wasn’t supposed to lift anything. He wasn’t supposed to bend. He wasn’t supposed to do anything at all for six weeks except lie down. He put his arms round her and held her against his chest, and when her knees went, he went down with her, carefully, onto the floor of the long room, onto the concrete, with his back against the leg of the table and her in his lap, and held on.

She shook for an hour.

He knew it was an hour because the clock on the kitchen wall was in front of him, over her shoulder, and he watched it. Ten to one. One o’clock. A quarter past. Half past. She shook so hard that her teeth chattered, and her hands clutched at his shirt, and she made small sounds into his chest that weren’t words, and then, after a while, were.

“He screamed,” she said. “The boy. Like a child. He was somebody’s child.”

“I know.”

“I’m not sorry,” said Evangeline. Her voice was shaking with the rest of her. “I’m not sorry. He was going to hit you again. I’d do it again. I’m not sorry and I can’t stop shaking. I can’t stop. Why can’t I stop?”

“Because you’re a person,” said Jun Hyuk, into her hair. “That’s all. That’s what it is. It’s what happens to people. It happens to me.”

She was quiet, shaking.

“Still?” she said.

He thought about it. He wasn’t going to lie to her. Not tonight.

“Not like this,” he said. “Not any more. It stopped happening a long time ago. I think that’s worse.”

She pressed her face into his chest.

He held her. He didn’t talk much. He held her on the floor of the long room in the dark with the harbour lights on the ceiling, rocking her a little without meaning to, and at a quarter to two the shaking began to slow, and at ten to two it stopped.

She lay against him, limp, exhausted, with her eyes shut.

“You’re not allowed to lift things,” she said.

“I didn’t lift you. You fell on me. Different thing.”

She almost laughed. He felt it in his chest, the start of it, and then it went.

“Jun Hyuk.”

“Mm.”

“I’m not doing that again,” she said. “Ever.”

“You won’t have to,” he said. “I promise. You won’t ever have to. That was the last time.” His arms tightened round her. “I’ll make sure.”

She didn’t answer. She was asleep.

He sat on the floor of the long room with his back against the table leg and a fracture in his skull and her asleep in his lap in her ruined dress, and didn’t move until it was light. He was thinking about what it would take to keep a promise like that.

chapters.title: Raiden and the Paper Twin
chapters.desc: Her brother comes to draw the man who can’t lift anything for six weeks, and tells her the one thing he’s never told anyone. Then Jun Hyuk hears the name of a farm on the river road, in the winter of 2007, and goes very quiet.
chapters.epigraph: “In the morning there was a tin of peaches on the gatepost. I never found out who left it.” — Raiden Lin
chapters.content:
Raiden came on a Tuesday in July with a sketchbook, a box of pastries, his wife, and no warning.

“You can’t lift anything for six weeks,” he said, in the doorway of the long room, beaming, with Jinx behind him in a vest and leather trousers and grease on her forearms, carrying a toolbox. “Elara told us. So you’re sitting still. I’ve never once seen you sit still. Nobody has. So I’m going to draw you, while it lasts. It’s historic. It’s like drawing a comet.”

Jun Hyuk was on the long sofa by the windows, where he’d been since June, under orders. The sofa was new.
