He’d bought it the week after the Crestview, because Evangeline had said, in her flat voice, that if he was going to lie down for six weeks he would do it on something that didn’t creak, and he’d sent Bao to the most expensive furniture shop on Harbour Road with a tape measure and his height written on a card, and the thing that came back up six flights of stairs in four pieces, carried by four men, was long enough for him to lie on with his feet on it, which no piece of furniture in his life had ever been.

“You can draw me,” he said, “if your wife fixes the air conditioning. It makes a noise like a dying goat.”

Jinx looked up at the air conditioning unit over the windows. She looked at it for a moment, the way Zhao looked at people. Then she put down the toolbox, and opened it, and got out a screwdriver.

“Deal,” said Raiden, and sat down cross-legged on the floor with his sketchbook.

✦ ✦ ✦

They’d married in April, the two of them, at a registry office on a Thursday, with only Elowen and Zhao and Eliana there, and gone straight from the registry to a bike show in the north, in Jinx’s van, still in their good clothes. Raiden had told everyone about it for a month. Jinx had told nobody at all, and had started wearing a plain steel ring on a chain round her neck, because she said rings got caught in engines.

Evangeline liked her. She’d liked her since Jinx had nodded at her once across the room at Elowen’s wedding. They didn’t talk much. Jinx did things with her hands and Evangeline watched her do them, and that was enough for both of them.

Now Jinx was up a stepladder with her head inside the air conditioning, and Evangeline was holding the ladder, and Raiden was drawing.

He drew fast. He always had, since he came home from the borderland at ten, at the long kitchen table in the Walled City, on the backs of envelopes and the margins of homework and once, memorably, on the wall of the second landing, which their father had made him paint over and had then, years later, after Raiden had moved out, scraped back with a palette knife to find again. He drew Jun Hyuk on the sofa in four minutes. Then again from a different angle. Then just his hands, folded on his chest, the one with the missing fingertip on top.

“You’ve got good hands,” he said, not looking up. “Ugly, but good. They look like they know what they’re doing.”

“They do,” said Jun Hyuk. “Mostly.”

“And you’ve got the face,” said Raiden, “of a man who’s been lying on a sofa for four weeks being fed by my sister and is losing his mind.”

“Five weeks.”

Raiden laughed and kept drawing.

✦ ✦ ✦

Jinx fixed the air conditioning in forty minutes. It stopped making a noise like a dying goat and started making no noise at all, which none of them had heard it do before, and Jun Hyuk lay in the silence for a moment and then said that he would pay her anything she wanted, and Jinx said she wanted the stepladder, because it was a good one, and he said take it, and she did.

Then she went down to the van to put it away, and Evangeline went to make tea, and Raiden sat on the floor with his sketchbook on his knees and stopped drawing.

He sat looking at the last drawing for a while. Then he looked up, at the kitchen, where his sister was standing at the white enamel stove with her back to them, waiting for the water.

“Ev,” he said. “Can I tell you something?”

She turned round.

He had his cheerful face on. The one he’d had since he was ten, since he came back from the borderland, the useless-son face that made strangers believe he was a fool. But his hands on the sketchbook weren’t cheerful. They were holding it tightly.

She came and sat down on the floor beside him, with her back against the new sofa, near Jun Hyuk’s feet.

“I hated you,” said Raiden.

✦ ✦ ✦

He told it looking down at the sketchbook. He didn’t look at either of them.

“When I was in the freezer,” he said. “The night with the men on the road. When I was nine. I was in there for eleven hours, in the dark, and I counted to forty thousand, and somewhere around the fifteen thousands I started thinking about you. About you at home. In the Walled City. In my room.” He turned a page, blank. “I didn’t know why I’d been sent away. Nobody told me. But I knew there was a baby at home that was supposed to be me. I’d heard the women at the farm talking. A foreign baby, with my name on her papers and my birthday. And I sat in the freezer and hated you so much I stopped being frightened.”

Evangeline didn’t move.

“I hated you for years,” said Raiden. “When I came home, at ten. You were so quiet. And they’d taken you out of all the photographs, and they’d taken me out of all the photographs too, because we were supposed to be twins and nobody could have a picture with only one of us in it, and I thought, she’s even taken my pictures. I used to steal your things. Your hair ribbons. I threw them in the canal. Did you know that?”

“Yes,” said Evangeline.

He looked up at last.

“You knew?”

“I watched you do it,” she said. “From the second-landing window. Eleven ribbons.”

He stared at her. Then the cheerful mask slipped, and he laughed, a short broken laugh, and put the heel of his hand against one eye.

“Of course you did,” he said. “Of course you watched.” He put his hand down. “I stopped when I was fifteen. You were fifteen too. Obviously.” He almost smiled. “I came up to the attic one night to get a box of my old drawings, and you were up there, by the cedar chest. You had the blanket out. On your knees. With the gold heron on it. And you were crying. You didn’t make any noise. You never made any noise. But you were crying so hard you were shaking, and you didn’t know I was on the stairs.”

Evangeline’s hands had gone still in her lap.

“I went back down,” said Raiden. “I never told you I saw. I never told anyone. And I never stole anything of yours again.” He looked at the blank page. “I’d been thinking for six years that you’d taken my place. And I saw you in the attic and I understood that you didn’t have one either. Not really. You’d just been put in mine, like a stone in a hole, to keep it shaped.” He swallowed. “We were both the spare, Ev. They just hid us in different places.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t say anything for a while.

Jun Hyuk, on the sofa behind them, didn’t move. He lay with his hands folded on his chest and watched the back of her head, and the back of her brother’s, side by side against his sofa, a tall still woman and a man with a sketchbook, the same height, born two days apart to different mothers in different countries, given the same birthday by a man who’d needed a lie.

Then Evangeline reached out and took the sketchbook out of Raiden’s hands.

She turned it to the drawing of Jun Hyuk’s hands, the one with the missing fingertip on top. She looked at it. Then she turned to a blank page, and held out her hand for the pencil, and Raiden gave it to her, bewildered.

She drew a ribbon.

She drew it badly. She’d never been able to draw. It was a wobbly line with a loop in it, and she drew eleven of them, in a row, across the top of the page, and under them, in her small neat upright hand, she wrote: I knew. I didn’t mind. You were nine.

Raiden looked at it.

He put his face in his hands, and it was the boy underneath doing it, the one who had sat in a freezer for eleven hours and counted to forty thousand. He sat on the floor of the textile building with his face in his hands and his shoulders going, and his sister put her arm round him, without being asked, without thinking, the way she had at Elowen’s sink, and held on.

When Jinx came back up the stairs from the van, she stopped in the doorway, and looked at them, and went back down again, and sat in the van for twenty minutes with the radio on.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was later, with the tea, that he said the name of the farm.

He’d recovered. He was being Raiden again, mostly. He was telling Jun Hyuk, because Jun Hyuk had asked, about the safe house in the borderland where he’d grown up: an old farm on the river road, with a white water tower and a brick kiln, three hours north of the border town, run by a couple their father paid who’d been kind enough, in their way. He was telling it lightly, as a story, the way he told everything.

“The White Tower farm,” he said. “That’s what everyone called it. Near the old crossing at—oh, I can’t remember. A village with a broken bridge. The winter I was nine there was fighting on the far side of the river, and trucks on the road at night, and that’s what the freezer was. Men on the road. Trucks with their lights off. I could hear them through the walls of the freezer. And I thought they were coming for me.” He shrugged. “They weren’t, obviously. They went past. In the morning there was a tin of peaches on the gatepost. I never found out who left it. I ate the whole thing standing up in the yard.”

Jun Hyuk had stopped moving.

Evangeline felt it. She was sitting on the edge of the sofa beside his legs, and she felt him go still, all the way through, the way he went still when something got down to where there weren’t any words.

“What winter?” he said. His voice was strange.

Raiden looked at him. “I was nine. So—2007. December. Just before New Year.”

“The trucks,” said Jun Hyuk. “Did they have anything on the doors?”

Raiden thought about it, frowning.

“Lanterns,” he said slowly. “Painted lanterns. Grey. On the doors. I saw one through the crack in the yard gate when they went past. I’d forgotten that.” He looked at Jun Hyuk. “How did you—”

✦ ✦ ✦

“We were going to the crossing,” said Jun Hyuk.

He said it lying on his back, looking up, with his hands folded on his chest. His voice was low and rough.

“The Grey Lanterns. Sixty men in old trucks. December 2007. I was seventeen. We’d been hired to hold the crossing at the broken bridge for a week, over New Year, for a man who ran timber. We drove up the river road at night with the lights off, because there was shooting on the far bank. And we passed a farm with a white water tower. At dusk. And Old Ko—” He stopped. “Old Ko was driving the first truck. I was beside him. And he slowed down, at the gate, and looked at the house, and said, there’s a kid hiding somewhere in there. I can feel it. The dogs are barking at the wrong thing. And he told me to get out and leave something on the gatepost. So the kid would know we’d gone and it was all right.”

Raiden had gone white.

“It was the only tin we had,” said Jun Hyuk. “Peaches. He’d been saving it for New Year.”

Nobody said anything.

Outside, a ferry sounded its horn on the harbour. The air conditioning, which Jinx had fixed, made no sound at all.

“Nobody was coming for you,” said Jun Hyuk to Raiden. Gently now. “I’m sorry. I’m sorry you spent the night in the dark. Nobody was coming for you. We were just going past. And an old man who’d been shot four times and grew tomatoes in a tyre on the roof of his truck thought there might be a frightened kid in the farmhouse, and gave up his New Year peaches, and sent me out in the cold to put them on the post.”

Raiden put his hand over his mouth.

“I wanted you to know,” said Jun Hyuk. “That’s all. That it was somebody. That somebody saw.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Raiden stayed until dark.

He didn’t draw much more. He sat on the floor by the sofa and talked to Jun Hyuk about the borderland, about the river road and the broken bridge and the far bank, about places they’d both been ten years apart and never known it. Jinx came back up eventually and sat beside him with her shoulder against his and didn’t say anything, and Evangeline made dinner, and they ate it on the floor round the new sofa, because Jun Hyuk wasn’t allowed to get up.

At the door, Raiden stopped.

“Can I ask you something?” said Jun Hyuk, from the sofa, before he could go.

Raiden turned round.

“You design safe rooms,” said Jun Hyuk. “You make places safe without them looking safe. Zhao says you’re the best in the city and nobody knows it.”

“Zhao said that?”

“He said hm. Elowen translated.”

Raiden grinned.

“I want to buy her a house,” said Jun Hyuk. He wasn’t looking at Raiden. He was looking past him, at Evangeline, standing in the kitchen doorway with a tea towel in her hands. “A real one. Not a flat in a building nobody looks at. Not a room over a noodle shop. A house with a front door, and a garden, and a postbox with a name on it. And windows that open. I want it to be the safest house in this country, and I don’t want her ever to look at it and see that.” He paused. “And I want you to design it. I’ll pay whatever you ask. More than whatever you ask.”

Raiden looked at him.

Then he looked at his sister in the doorway, who was standing very still with the tea towel, and whose face hadn’t moved at all, though anyone who’d known her since they were ten could see how hard she was holding still.

“I’ll do it for nothing,” said Raiden. “No. I won’t. I’ll charge you a fortune, and I’ll give it to Jinx for a new workshop.” He tucked the sketchbook under his arm. “When do you want to see drawings?”

“Monday.”

“It’s Tuesday.”

“I know,” said Jun Hyuk. “I’ve waited long enough.”

✦ ✦ ✦

When the door had shut behind them, and the van had gone down the street, and the long room was quiet with the air conditioning making no sound at all, she came and stood by the sofa and looked down at him.

He looked up at her.

“A house,” said Evangeline.

“With a front door,” he said. “And a postbox. I was going to tell you properly. I had a plan. Raiden got there first.”

He didn’t wait for her to decide anything. He took her wrist and pulled, gently, and she came down onto the long sofa beside him, the one that didn’t creak, the length of her along the length of him, careful of his head, with her hand flat on his chest. He turned on his side to face her, which he wasn’t supposed to do, and kissed her.

Five weeks on a sofa. He kissed her as if he’d spent every hour of them thinking about it, which he had, slow and deep and not at all like a man who’d been told not to exert himself, with his hand spread on the small of her back holding her against him. She kissed the scar through his eyebrow, and the corner of his mouth, and his jaw, taking her time, while the ferries went back and forth with their lamps lit behind the windows and nobody got up to turn on a light.

“Nothing strenuous,” she said, against his throat.

“This isn’t strenuous,” said Jun Hyuk, and kissed her again, and the drawings could wait until Monday.

chapters.title: Jun Hyuk Takes a Job He Hates
chapters.desc: He doesn’t need the money. He needs a name that holds, a payslip, and a life nobody comes through the door for. So he goes to work for the man he likes least in the city, opening every container at the Iron Docks with his own hands.
chapters.epigraph: “Every box that comes through my docks gets opened. By you. I don’t care what it costs.” — Zhao Zhendong, the Iron Docks, August 2024
chapters.content:
He’d thought about the promise every day since the floor.

You won’t ever have to. That was the last time. I’ll make sure.

He lay on the long sofa through July with his head healing, and thought about what it meant. Wei Long had taken the boat. The man in the pale shirt had been put on a plane home by his own ambassador with a face like a slapped fish, and his master in the north was now, according to a very interesting letter that had arrived at Lin Jian’s office in the second week of July, in disgrace with his nephew the King. The Ferryman was still out there somewhere across the river, in a grey suit with an ivory toothpick.

But mostly he thought about himself.

People came through doors for him. They had for twenty years. He’d made sure of it. He’d spent nine years being the man that men like Hwang and Kuang and Gu Shanlin were afraid of, and the thing about being the man people were afraid of was that sooner or later they came through the door. And she’d be behind it. Or in front of it, now. With three bullets and the ducks.

He couldn’t stop being afraid of that. So he would have to stop being the other thing.

✦ ✦ ✦

“I need a job,” he told Evangeline, on the first of August, at the long table.

She looked at him over her tea.

“Not for the money,” he said. “I’ve got the money. I’ve got six crates and four caches and a building and a house with a fig tree and some tea. That’s not it.” He turned his cup round. “I need a name. A real one, on real papers, that a bank will open an account in and a lawyer will put on a house deed and a registry will put on a marriage certificate, and that a policeman can look up and find a man with a job and a payslip and a tax number and nothing else. I need to be boring. I need to be so boring that nobody ever comes through a door for me again.”

She put her cup down.

“I’ve never been boring,” he said. “I don’t know how. I’m going to need help.”

“Zhao,” said Evangeline.

He stared at her.

“He offered,” she said. She looked at him steadily. “He’s still got it.”

“I’m not working for Zhao Zhendong.”

She went back to her tea.

He lasted two days.

✦ ✦ ✦

The Iron Docks were at the eastern end of the harbour, behind high fences, under cranes the colour of old blood, and they had belonged to Zhao Zhendong for eleven years. For most of those years, a great deal of what had come through them had been the reason Jun Hyuk had a file on him. Now, for the last two, it had been mostly furniture, and frozen fish, and machine parts that really were machine parts, because a florist from the Walled City had said one word to her husband, and he had listened.

Zhao met him at the gate at seven in the morning, in a black suit, with Bao behind him.

“Hm,” he said.

“I’m here about the job,” said Jun Hyuk. “I want you to know I hate this. I want you to know I hate it very much. I’ve spent the whole drive here thinking of all the reasons I hate it, and there are eleven, and I’m going to tell you all of them, on the way to wherever we’re going.”

Zhao turned round and started walking. Jun Hyuk followed him and told him all eleven. It took them to the far end of the container yard, past the stacks, past the straddle carriers, to a long low shed with a steel door and a sign on it that had been painted that week. INSPECTION.

Zhao stopped outside it.

“Every box that comes through my docks gets opened,” he said. “Not scanned. Not sampled. Opened. Every door. Every one. By you, or by men you choose and train. You don’t answer to customs. You don’t answer to my managers. You answer to me.” A pause. “I don’t care what it costs. I don’t care how slow it makes us. If a box has a person in it, I want to know before it touches the ground. If it has a person in it and I didn’t know, I want you to tell me who packed it.”

Jun Hyuk looked at the shed. At the sign. At Zhao.

“Why?” he said.

Zhao didn’t answer straight away.

“Two hundred rifles,” he said. “To a man with boats.”

He went back towards the gate.

✦ ✦ ✦

Chen Si’s lawyer did the papers.

Her name was Ms. Fong, and she was small and grey and terrifying, and she had an office on the forty-first floor of a building on Harbour Road where the windows looked out over the whole city and the carpet was so thick that Jun Hyuk’s boots sank into it. She looked at him across a desk the size of a boat while he sat in a chair that was too small for him.

“Mr. Chen tells me,” she said, “that you would like to become a real person.”

“Yes.”

“And that you have, at present, a passport from a country you were not born in, in a name that isn’t yours, and an identity card from this one in a name that is, which you obtained in a back room in a border town in 2008 from a man called, I believe, Uncle Cardboard.”

“He was very good.”

“He was,” said Ms. Fong, “adequate.” She opened a file. “This will take four weeks. It will cost a great deal. When it’s finished, you’ll be Lee Jun Hyuk, born on the first of March 1990 in the border district, which I’m told is close enough. You’ll have a tax number, a bank account, a residence status that will survive a very hard look, and a clean record.” She looked up. “A clean record, Mr. Lee. Do you understand what that requires of you, from today?”

“Yes,” said Jun Hyuk.

“Good.” She closed the file. “Mr. Chen also asked me to tell you that he and his wife would like to come to the wedding. I told him I’d pass it on and that he shouldn’t hold his breath.”

“There are six people,” said Jun Hyuk. “She’s been very clear.”

“I’ll tell him,” said Ms. Fong, and for the first time she smiled, slightly.

✦ ✦ ✦

He opened his first container on the twelfth of August, at ten past six in the morning, with a bolt cutter and a torch.

Machine parts. Really machine parts, in wooden crates, with the right numbers stencilled on the right sides. He went through every crate. He knocked on the walls. He shone the torch into every corner and lay on his back on the floor of the container to look at the underside of the roof. Nothing.

He opened forty more that day. Furniture. Fish. Tiles. A container of children’s bicycles, all pink. A container of tinned pineapple. Nothing.

He’d hired four men by the end of the week. Not men he knew from before. Men Wei Long knew, quietly, from the station: two who’d retired early from the customs service because they’d been honest at the wrong time, one who’d been a fireman, and a big quiet woman called Mrs. Koo who’d spent twenty years searching cargo planes at the airport and could find a smuggled phone in a container of washing machines by the sound. He paid them three times what they asked. He trained them for a week. He taught them the things he knew that weren’t in any manual: where people hid, and how you could tell, and what the air smelled like in a box that had been shut on someone for two days.

He didn’t tell them how he knew.

✦ ✦ ✦

He hated it.

He hated it the way you hate cold water, for the first week. He hated getting up at five. He hated the yard, and the cranes, and the managers in the office who looked at him sideways and whispered about who he was. He hated Zhao, every time he saw him, which was every morning at seven, at the gate. He hated the payslip.

It came at the end of August, in an envelope, with his name on it. His real name, the one in the collar of a shirt he’d been wearing at seven years old. LEE JUN HYUK. A sum. A tax number. A pension contribution, which he had to ask Mrs. Koo the meaning of.

He sat in the inspection shed at the end of the day with the envelope in his hands and looked at it.

He’d been paid millions. In cash, in crates, in gold, in stones. By men with oil fields and men with mines and men who were frightened of their brothers. He’d been paid more for one week in 2013 than this envelope would pay him for a year.

He’d never once been paid in his own name.

✦ ✦ ✦

She brought him lunch.

He hadn’t asked. He’d never ask. She just appeared, the second week, at the gate of the Iron Docks at half past twelve, with Bao behind her, carrying a tiffin box of three stacked steel tins, the kind the dock workers’ wives had used fifty years ago, which she’d found at the market in the Walled City at the stall with the broken clocks.

The guard on the gate called the inspection shed. Jun Hyuk came across the yard at a run, in his overalls, which he’d never worn in his life before August, and stopped in front of her, breathing hard.

“What are you doing here?”

She held out the tiffin.

He took it. He didn’t know what to do with his face. Behind him, across the yard, he could feel four inspectors and two crane drivers and a man from the office watching.

“Rice,” said Evangeline. “Fish. Greens. Soup in the bottom. It’s still hot.”

He opened the top tin, there at the gate, in his overalls, with the whole yard watching. Steam came up out of it.

“You came all the way across the city,” he said, “to bring me lunch.”

“You’d have eaten instant noodles.”

He would have. They both knew it.

He bent down, in his overalls, at the gate of the Iron Docks, and kissed her. Quick and hard, with the tiffin held out to one side so the soup wouldn’t spill, in front of the guard and the man from the office and four inspectors who had never once seen him smile before nine in the morning. When he straightened up her ears had gone red. Her face hadn’t moved at all.

He ate it sitting on a crate outside the inspection shed, with her sitting beside him on another crate in her pale blue coat, very straight, with her hands folded, watching the cranes. Mrs. Koo came out and looked at them and went back in again. One of the crane drivers whistled. Zhao, who happened to be crossing the yard at that moment towards the office, stopped, and looked at the two of them for four seconds, and went on.

“He’s going to tell Elowen,” said Jun Hyuk, with his mouth full.

“Yes,” said Evangeline.

She came every Tuesday and Friday after that. The guard on the gate started opening it before she reached it. The crane drivers started calling the crate outside the shed the bench, and nobody else sat on it.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the twenty-seventh of August, at four in the afternoon, in the eleventh container of the day, Mrs. Koo put her ear to the wall and held up her hand.

Everyone stopped.

It was a forty-foot reefer, from a port in the south, carrying chilled squid. The refrigeration was running, set a few degrees above freezing, and someone had opened the fresh-air vent all the way. Mrs. Koo stood with her ear to the steel and her eyes shut. Then she looked at Jun Hyuk and pointed, precisely, at a spot two-thirds of the way down, behind the squid.

He opened it himself.

They had to move a lot of squid. Behind the last row of pallets, in a space about the width of a coffin that had been made by stacking the boxes cleverly and leaving a gap, there was a man. Twenty-five, perhaps. Thin. In a T-shirt and shorts, in a refrigerated box, curled up in a foil blanket with his knees against his chest. He’d been in there four days. He had a bottle of water, nearly empty, and a bag of bread, and he was so cold that he couldn’t speak, and his eyes, when the torch found him, were the eyes of a man who has decided he is going to die.

Jun Hyuk crouched down.

He made himself smaller. He put the torch down on the floor of the container, pointing away, so it wouldn’t be in the man’s face. He took his jacket off.

“Hello,” he said. Low and easy. “Hello. Listen to me. I’m not police. I’m not anybody. I open boxes, that’s all. And I’ve opened yours, and you’re going to be all right. We’re going to get you out and get you warm. Can you move your hands?”

The man stared at him.

“It’s all right,” said Jun Hyuk. “You don’t have to talk. I’ll talk. I’m very good at it. Here. Put this on. It’s big. Everything I own is big.”

He put the jacket round the man’s shoulders. Mrs. Koo was already on the phone for an ambulance. Behind him, the two retired customs men had gone quiet, and the fireman was standing in the door of the container with his hand over his mouth.

He got the man out. He carried him, in the end, because the man’s legs wouldn’t work, out of the reefer and across the yard to the inspection shed, wrapped in Jun Hyuk’s jacket and a foil blanket and a tarpaulin, and sat with him by the heater and talked to him about the weather until the ambulance came. The man didn’t say a word the whole time. But when the paramedics lifted him onto the stretcher, he reached out from under the blankets and caught Jun Hyuk’s sleeve, and held it, for a second, and let go.

Then Jun Hyuk went to find Zhao.

✦ ✦ ✦

He told him who’d packed it. A shipping agent in the south, and a name, and a payment, which Mrs. Koo had found in the paperwork and he’d found in the man’s pocket. Zhao listened, and picked up the phone on his desk.

“Wei Long,” he said into it. And then, after a while, three more words, which were more than Jun Hyuk had ever heard him say on a phone. “I have one.”

He put the phone down.

They looked at each other across the desk. Two big men, in an office over the container yard, with the cranes going past the windows.

“You did that well,” said Zhao.

Jun Hyuk opened his mouth to say something. He didn’t know what. Something about rifles, or dogs, or the eleven reasons. Nothing came.

“Hm,” he said instead.

Zhao looked at him. Then he smiled, slightly, at the corner of the mouth. Elowen had seen that nine times in four years. Jun Hyuk made it ten.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night, when he came home, the payslip was on the fridge.

She’d put it there with a magnet shaped like a fish, which she’d bought at the market for that purpose. It was the only thing on the fridge. She was at the stove with her back to him.

He stood in the kitchen doorway and looked at it. LEE JUN HYUK. His name, in print, on a piece of paper with a tax number, held to a fridge with a fish.

“You’re boring now,” said Evangeline, without turning round. “Very boring. I’m very proud.”

He came up behind her and put his arms round her waist and his face in her neck, in his overalls, smelling of the docks and squid and diesel, and didn’t say anything.

She leaned back against him and went on stirring.

Then she stopped stirring. She turned round in his arms, and wrinkled her nose at the squid, and kissed him anyway, with the spoon still in her hand and the soup ticking on the gas behind her. He lifted her up onto the counter beside the stove without taking his mouth off hers. The spoon went somewhere. Neither of them looked for it. She kept her knees either side of him and her hands on his face, and somewhere in the middle of it he started to laugh against her mouth, from pure astonishment, at being a man with a payslip on a fridge and the woman he was going to marry sitting on the counter, and she pulled him back by the collar of his overalls and made him stop.

He didn’t tell her that he’d been to see a house that afternoon, before he came home. Up in the hills to the north, at the end of a lane, with Raiden and a set of drawings and an estate agent who had stopped talking when she saw who was paying. A big old house, with a garden that went down to a stream, and a fig tree by the gate, and every window opening outwards onto the green.

He didn’t tell her he’d bought it, either, that afternoon, for cash, in his own name.

chapters.title: The Throne Lets Her Go
chapters.desc: The twenty-first floor of the Harbour Hotel, a notary, a pen, and a man of forty-four with her face round the eyes. He signs her free. Then he gives her three things that were never in any folder.
chapters.epigraph: “Our father asked about you once a year, on your birthday. He asked if the problem was still moved.” — the King, suite 2101
chapters.content:
The King came in September, without a flag.

He came on a Thursday, on an ordinary flight, in an ordinary suit, with four guards and the envoy and nobody from the newspapers, because nobody from the newspapers knew. He took the whole of the twenty-first floor of the Harbour Hotel, which had been arranged by the envoy with the Harbour Hotel’s manager in a series of phone calls the manager would remember for the rest of his career, and on Saturday the twenty-first of September at eleven in the morning, he sent a car to the Walled City.

The envoy had written to her in August. In the court language, by hand, three pages. The letter said that His Majesty had received her answer exactly as she had given it. It said that His Majesty had read it many times. It said that the events of the fifteenth of June, and His Majesty’s uncle’s part in them, had been discussed with His Majesty’s uncle, at some length, and that His Majesty’s uncle had retired to his estates in the north for his health and was not expected to return to court. It said that a document had been prepared, as she had offered. And it said that His Majesty would like, if she would permit it, to bring it to her himself.

He would like to see you once, the envoy had written at the end, in a different ink, as if he’d come back to it. I think you should let him. I think it would be good for both of you. But that is not my business, and you will decide.

She’d decided.

✦ ✦ ✦

Jun Hyuk went with her to the door of the suite.

Not inside. She’d asked him. The room, she’d said, at the long table in the textile building. Not by me this time. Outside. Please. He’d looked at her across the table and seen that she meant it, and understood why, more or less, and said yes, and then lain awake half the night not liking it.

So he walked her down the long carpeted corridor of the twenty-first floor of the Harbour Hotel, holding her hand, past two guards at the lift and two at the corner, to a pair of tall doors at the end with 2101 on them in brass, and two more guards outside.

One of them was Teo.

Teo saw him coming and his face lit up, and then he remembered where he was and put it away again, and stood very straight, and stared at a point on the wall. The other guard was the older one from the step in April. He looked at Jun Hyuk, and then, to Jun Hyuk’s great surprise, he gave a small nod, the kind you give a man who’s been right about something.

Evangeline stopped in front of the doors.

She was wearing the dark blue dress again, and the aquamarines, and her hair up, and a coat over her arm, the pale blue one. She stood in front of the doors of suite 2101 very straight, with her hands folded, and he could feel her shaking a little through her fingers, which were still in his.

He didn’t say anything. He’d thought about what to say all night, and in the car, and in the lift, and none of it was any good.

He lifted her hand and kissed the back of it, over the ring.

She looked up at him.

“I’ll be here,” he said. “Right here. I won’t move. If you want me, open the door, and I’ll be through it before it’s finished opening.”

“I know,” said Evangeline.

Teo opened the doors.

She went in.

✦ ✦ ✦

He waited an hour and forty minutes.

He didn’t sit down. There was a chair, a gold one with a striped seat, against the wall of the corridor, and Teo offered it to him twice, and he said no twice. He stood against the wall opposite the doors with his hands in his pockets and his eyes on the brass numbers, and he talked to Teo, because Teo wanted to talk and the older guard let him, about bees, mostly, and Teo’s mother’s bees, and the hills in the lake country where she kept them, which Teo said were the most beautiful hills in the world, and where the old families came from, and where the King’s grandmother had been born.

“And her mother,” said Teo. “The lady’s. My mother remembers her. Everybody in the lake country does. She played at the summer festival every year, by the water, when she was a girl. Before she went to the palace.”

Jun Hyuk stopped looking at the doors.

“What was she like?” he said.

Teo thought about it. “My mother says she didn’t talk much,” he said. “She said she let the instrument do it.”

Jun Hyuk looked at the doors again. He didn’t say anything for a while.

At the end of the corridor, by the corner, the older guard had taken his phone out and was showing a photograph on it to the guard beside him. A photograph of something small, in a pram. A grandson, probably. They were both smiling at it.

Jun Hyuk looked at the brass numbers and thought about a woman who didn’t talk much and let the instrument do it, playing by a lake in summer, before she went to the palace, and about how nobody had ever told her daughter that.

✦ ✦ ✦

Inside suite 2101, the King of a country she had never seen stood up when she came in.

He was forty-four. She knew that from the library. She had looked him up at sixteen, after the blanket, after the crest, after the country. She had looked at his photograph in the reference books and the newspapers for ten years, the way she had looked at the crest: a boy at a school in another country, a young man in a uniform, a husband at a wedding, a king in January in black. She had never once looked at him and thought he looked like anyone she knew.

He stood in the middle of the long bright room with the harbour behind him through the windows, in a grey suit, a tall thin tired man with grey coming in at his temples. And he looked at her, and she looked at him, and she saw it.

Round the eyes. Something in the shape of them. And the stillness. He was standing the way she stood, with his hands folded in front of him, very straight, his face giving nothing at all away.

He’d seen it too. She watched him see it.

“Evangeline,” said the King.

He said it carefully, the way Jun Hyuk had said it at the table with the peas.

“Your Majesty,” said Evangeline.

He flinched a little. Then he did something she didn’t expect. He crossed the room, and stopped in front of her, and held out his hand. Not to be kissed. To be shaken, like a man meeting someone at a business lunch.

She looked at the hand.

She shook it.

✦ ✦ ✦

The document was on the table by the window.

Ms. Fong had read it in August, every word, in both languages, with a translator Chen Si had flown in from a university abroad, and had said it was the cleanest instrument of its kind she’d seen in thirty years of practice. It renounced, for Evangeline Lin, born on the seventh of April 1998, any title, rank, precedence or claim of succession to which she was or might be entitled as a daughter of the late King’s House, absolutely and for ever. It acknowledged her, on the King’s side, as his father’s daughter. It released her from the care of the House. And it confirmed her inheritance: the house at the lake and all that it contained, and the sum from the late King’s private estate, in full, to be paid to her absolutely, with no conditions whatsoever.

She’d thought about the money, in August. She’d thought about refusing it. Then she’d thought about Nuo, at the bakery, with her nursing course paid for by a fund at a church that a man she loved had filled from the safes of men who sold people. She’d thought about Bik, who had a son, and the two women in the container who’d held each other and never said their names. She’d thought about what a sum like that could do, if it were put next to his, and given away carefully, by someone who’d been in a box.

She’d decided to take it.

There was a notary, a tidy man from the King’s embassy, and the envoy, and Ms. Fong, who’d come up the back stairs at ten and was sitting in the corner of the suite in black like a small grey crow. They watched her read it, all of it, in the court language, every page. They watched her pick up the pen.

She signed her name.

Not Lady anything. Not the name on the blanket. Just her own. Evangeline Lin. In her small, neat, upright hand.

The King signed after her. His signature took up half the page.

The notary pressed the seal. The envoy, standing by the window, looked out at the harbour for a while with his hands behind his back.

Ms. Fong collected her copy, and nodded once to Evangeline, and left by the back stairs.

✦ ✦ ✦

Then it was just the two of them. The King had sent the others out. He’d done it with a small movement of one hand, and they’d gone, the notary and the envoy and the guard by the inner door, and the doors had closed, and there was only the long bright room, and the harbour, and a man and a woman with the same eyes.

He sat down on the end of a sofa by the window, heavily, like a man who has walked a long way.

“I’ve three things for you,” he said. His English was good. Better than the envoy’s; less careful. “They weren’t in the folder. I didn’t let anyone put them in the folder.” He looked at his hands. “The first is a question you asked my envoy in April. I’m told you asked it before you asked anything else.”

She stood still.

He told her her mother’s name.

He said it in the court language, the old way, with the lake-country vowels. It was three syllables. It sounded, when he said it, like water going over stones. She had waited eleven years for it. She didn’t say it back. She stood in the middle of the long room with her hands folded, and her face didn’t move, and inside she felt it turning over and over like a stone in a river.

“She was twenty,” said the King. “From the lake country. A musician in the household orchestra. Viola. My mother said she was the best of them.” His voice was level. “She died of a fever when you were two. In a hospital in the capital. Nobody told her where you were. I don’t think she ever knew you were alive.”

Evangeline closed her eyes.

“I’m sorry,” he said. “That’s the worst of it. I thought you should have the worst of it from me, and not from a file.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The second thing was on the table by the sofa. A photograph, in a plain frame.

A young woman, by a lake, in summer, in a white dress, sitting on a wooden jetty with an instrument on her shoulder and the bow lifted, laughing at someone behind the camera. Dark hair, long, coming loose. A face that wasn’t carved, at all, because she was laughing. But round the eyes.

Evangeline picked it up and held it in both hands.

“Our father kept it,” said the King. “In a drawer. In his study. I found it in February.” He looked at the harbour. “He asked about you once a year. On your birthday. My mother told me, after he died. He’d ask his secretary if the problem was still moved.” He paused. “Every year. Twenty-six years. Is the problem still moved? And the secretary would say yes. And he’d put the photograph back in the drawer.”

She didn’t look up from the photograph.

“Did you know?” she said. “About me?”

“I found out when I was eighteen. I heard two of my mother’s women talking.” He was quiet a moment. “I looked for you. For two years. I wrote to people. I hired a man. I got as far as a city, and a man who moved cargo in a place called the Walled City, and then my father found out what I was doing and told me to stop.” He looked at his hands. “And I stopped. I was twenty. I’m not proud of it. I’ve been not proud of it for twenty-four years.”

She looked up at him.

He didn’t look away. He looked at her across the room with her own eyes, tired and grey and honest, and she understood that he had come all this way, without a flag, to say that.

✦ ✦ ✦

The third thing was in the bedroom of the suite, on the bed, and he went and got it himself.

It was a case. Old, black, scuffed at the corners, with brass catches and a handle worn pale by a hand. He brought it back into the long room and laid it on the table in front of her, and stood back.

She knew what it was before he said anything.

She knelt down on the carpet beside the table and undid the catches, one, two, and lifted the lid.

It lay in faded blue velvet, a dark honey-coloured wood, with a scroll at the top like a curled fern, and a bow clipped into the lid. There was a little cake of rosin in a compartment at the side, worn into a hollow in the middle, the way rosin wears when someone has used it every day for years. There was a hairpin in the compartment too. Plain, silver, bent a little, the kind you’d use to put your hair up in a hurry before you played.

“It was in the house at the lake,” said the King. “Nobody had opened the case since she died. My grandmother wouldn’t let anyone. It’s yours. It was always going to be yours. It’s in the will, under contents.” He was quiet for a moment. “I’m told you heard one played. On your birthday. Someone arranged it.”

She put her hand flat on the velvet beside the wood. Not touching it. Not yet.

“Yes,” said Evangeline.

“I’m told he paid the botanical gardens a great deal of money,” said the King, “and that the musician wouldn’t take a fee. And that you asked her to play it again.”

She looked up at him from the floor.

“My envoy,” said the King, “is very thorough.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They said goodbye at the doors.

It was short. She’d known it would be. He was a king, and he had a plane at four, and a country, and a wife and a council and an uncle in the north. And she had a man in the corridor who had been standing against a wall for nearly two hours, not sitting down.

He held out his hand again, at the doors, like a man at a business lunch. She looked at it. Then she didn’t shake it. She put her own hand flat on his chest, over his heart, for a second, the way she did when she came in through a door.

He went still.

“Goodbye,” said Evangeline, in the court language, with the lake-country vowels that she’d learned from no one. “Brother.”

The King of a country she had never seen looked down at her hand on his chest.

“Be happy,” he said. His voice wasn’t level any more. “Please. That’s all. I’m not allowed to order you to do anything now. You’ve just signed a paper to make sure of it. So I’m asking.” He took a breath. “Be happy, Evangeline.”

“I am,” she said.

She opened the doors.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was against the wall opposite, exactly where she’d left him.

He came off it before the doors had finished opening. Then he stopped, a step away, and looked at her.

At her face. At the photograph in its plain frame, held against her chest in one arm. At the old black case with the brass catches in her other hand, and the way she was holding it, carefully, by the handle that someone else’s hand had worn pale.

He didn’t say anything.

He didn’t say are you all right, or what happened, or what’s in the case. He just looked at her, and she saw that he’d understood, somehow, from standing against a wall all morning talking about bees with a boy whose mother remembered.

He took the case from her. Gently. He held it the way he’d held the honey from the hill village, in May, the first time he ever brought anyone anything.

Then he put his other arm round her, and the photograph, and walked her down the long carpeted corridor of the twenty-first floor of the Harbour Hotel, past Teo, who was looking at the wall hard with wet eyes, and past the older guard, who bowed, and past the two at the corner and the two at the lift, and none of them said anything at all.

In the lift, going down, she put her face against his shoulder.

“She laughed,” said Evangeline. “In the photograph. She was laughing.”

He held her.

“I know,” he said. “It’s all over your face.”

She lifted her face from his shoulder and kissed him. In the lift going down from the twenty-first floor, with the old black case between their feet and the photograph held flat between them, against his chest, by both their hands. He kissed her back, not carefully at all, against the mirrored wall, as if he’d stood against a wall for an hour and forty minutes holding his breath and had only now been let off, all the way down past the numbers lighting one after another, until the doors opened on the lobby and a man with a suitcase looked in at them and decided to wait for the next one.

chapters.title: A House With a Real Address
chapters.desc: No. 9, Fig Tree Lane. A front door, a garden that goes down to a stream, a glasshouse she didn’t know about, and windows that open. And a postbox with no name on it yet, because he’s waiting for her to choose.
chapters.epigraph: “Every window in this house opens. I checked them all. Twice.” — Lee Jun Hyuk, 12 October 2024
chapters.content:
He told her to bring her coat, and nothing else, and not to ask.

She didn’t ask. She never did. She put on the pale blue coat on the morning of the twelfth of October, a Saturday, and came down the six flights of stairs of the textile building behind him, and got into the truck, which he still drove, though he could have bought every truck in the city, because he said the black car made him feel like a minister.

He drove north.

Out of the city, past the towers, past the old ferry piers, onto the road that went up into the hills. Not the border road. The other one, the one that wound east of it through the reservoirs and the country parks and the villages that had been there before the city and had been left alone by it. It was a clear blue morning, the first cool one of the autumn. The hills were green.

He didn’t talk.

That was how she knew it was something. He’d talked to her every morning for two years, about the weather and the cats and the docks and Mrs. Koo and the crane drivers and the squid. He drove north for forty minutes with both hands on the wheel and his eyes on the road and didn’t say a single word, and every so often his right hand came off the wheel and found hers on the seat between them and held it, hard, and went back.

She left her hand on the seat after that, palm up, so he’d know where it was.

✦ ✦ ✦

The village was called Fig Tree Lane, though it wasn’t a lane, it was a village. The lane was one road, going up a valley between two green hills, with old houses on either side behind walls, and a stream at the bottom of the valley, and at the top, where the road stopped and turned into a footpath up the hill, a pair of iron gates in a long white wall, with a fig tree leaning over them.

He stopped the truck in front of the gates.

He turned off the engine. He sat there with his hands on the wheel. He didn’t look at her.

“This one,” he said.

She looked at the gates. Old iron, black, with a pattern of leaves in them. The white wall going away on either side under its tiles. The fig tree, big and old, with its grey trunk and its leaves going yellow at the edges for autumn, and three late figs still on it, dark purple.

On the wall beside the gates there was a number, in old blue and white tiles. 9.

And under it, set into the wall, there was a postbox. Green. Painted that week. With a brass slot, and a little brass frame on the front for a name.

The frame was empty.

✦ ✦ ✦

He took her in.

He didn’t carry her. She’d half thought he might, and been ready to be cross about it. He held her hand and walked her through the gates and up the path, between beds that someone had dug over and left bare, ready, and stopped at the bottom of four stone steps, and let her look.

It was a big house. Old, two storeys, white, with a roof of dark grey tiles and a long deep verandah along the front with wooden pillars and a wide wooden floor that someone had sanded and oiled until it shone. Big windows along the front, upstairs and down, with dark green shutters folded back. A heavy front door, the same green, with a brass knocker in the shape of a hand holding a ball.

It looked like a house in a book. Like the houses she’d seen on the hills from the bus when she was a girl, and wondered who lived in them.

“Raiden says it was built in 1931,” said Jun Hyuk, “by a man who made money in tea. Then his grandson lost it in the nineties, and it was empty for years, and then a family from the city had it and never came, and then I—” He stopped. “And now it’s yours.”

She turned and looked at him.

“Mine?” she said.

“Ours,” he said. “It’s in my name, because Ms. Fong said that was quickest. But the papers to put it in yours are on the kitchen table. Signed. You only have to sign under mine.” He was looking at the house, not at her. “I wanted you to have it whether or not. Whether or not anything. Whether or not you want me in it.”

She didn’t say anything. She went up the four stone steps, and across the shining verandah, and put her hand on the green front door.

It wasn’t locked.

✦ ✦ ✦

Every window in the house opened.

That was the first thing he showed her. Before the kitchen, before the stairs, before anything. He walked her into the big front room, empty, with its wooden floor and its fireplace and the light coming in long and gold across the boards, and went to the nearest window, and unlatched it, and swung it out. The air came in. Cool, green, smelling of the hill and the stream and the turned earth in the beds.

He went to the next one and opened that too. And the next. All four.

“Every window,” he said. “In the whole house. Thirty-one. I checked them all. Twice.”

She stood in the middle of the room with the air coming in from four windows at once.

“Raiden did the glass,” he said. “It’s the same as the textile building. Five layers. You could stand in the lane and shoot at it all day. But it opens. He found a man in another country who makes it in frames that open.” He shut one, to show her, and the latch made a heavy, soft sound, like a safe. “It’s the most expensive glass in this country. I don’t care. Nobody’s ever going to see it as anything but a window.”

“What else,” said Evangeline.

He looked at her.

“What else did he do,” she said. “Raiden. What else is in the house that I’m never going to see.”

He was quiet for a moment.

“I’ll show you,” he said. “All of it. Every door. Every room. Every way out. I’ll show you once, and then you can forget it, and you’ll never have to look at it again. But you should know.” He held out his hand. “You always know where the exits are.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He showed her.

The pantry under the stairs, which was a pantry, with shelves and jars and a sack of rice already in it, and which was also, when you pressed the third shelf in a particular way, a door, into a small room with a steel lining and its own air and water and a telephone that would ring at Inspector Song Wei Long’s desk. The cellar, with a second way out, through a tunnel Raiden had found that the tea man had built in 1931 for reasons nobody knew, that came up under a stone in the garden by the stream. The walls, which looked like old plaster and weren’t. The front door, which looked like old wood and wasn’t. The gates.

“And this,” he said, at the back of the house, at the end of a flagged passage past the kitchen, and opened a door.

It was a glasshouse.

It wasn’t a steel box on a ledge this time. It was a real glasshouse, Victorian in shape, built onto the back of the house where the sun came all day, with an iron frame painted white and a curved glass roof, and slatted wooden benches down both sides, and a stone floor with drains in it, and a deep sink at her height with a brass tap, and shelves, and hooks, and a long table for potting. It was empty. All of it. Waiting.

At the far end, on the last bench, in their pots, in the sun, were nine plants.

Basil, two kinds. Mint. Coriander. Chives. Thyme, and lemon thyme. Rosemary, flowering blue. And a pot of white orchids.

She stopped in the door.

“I brought them up on Thursday,” he said, behind her. “From the box. In the truck. Very slowly. I put the seatbelt round the orchids.” He was trying to sound as if it was a joke. His voice wasn’t managing. “The strawberries are on the verandah. Half the leaves went brown on the way up. Mrs. Bae next door says they’ll be fine. She says she’s been growing strawberries on this lane for fifty years and she’s never seen anybody wash their leaves with soap.”

Evangeline walked down the length of the glasshouse to the nine pots.

She stood looking at them. The basil that had come up in nine days on the sixth floor of a textile building, behind five layers of glass. The rosemary that had come through the winter under its lid. The orchids. She put out her hand and touched one of the white flowers, lightly, the way she’d touched the ring, the first night.

Then she turned round.

He was standing in the door at the other end, filling it, with his hands at his sides.

She came back down the glasshouse to him. Not fast. She never moved fast. She came down between the empty benches, through the light, and stopped in front of him, and took his face in both her hands, and pulled it down.

She kissed him in the door of the glasshouse and took her time about it.

When she drew back, he didn’t open his eyes. He stood with his forehead against hers and his hands at her waist, breathing.

“You did all of this,” she said, “since July.”

“Since June,” he said. “Since the floor.” He opened his eyes. “I’m making sure.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They had lunch on the verandah, on the steps, because there was no furniture yet. Bread and cheese and figs from the tree by the gate, which he climbed, at her request, in his good shirt, and nearly fell out of, and came down from with three figs in his teeth. She laughed so hard she had to sit down on the step. Fourteen, he thought, spitting out figs. Fourteen.

Afterwards, she went down the garden on her own.

He let her. He sat on the top step of the verandah and watched her go, a tall figure in a pale blue coat going down between the empty dug beds, slowly, looking at everything. The old wall. The stream at the bottom, brown and quick over its stones. The stone by the stream, which she looked at for a moment and didn’t step on. The fig tree. She went right round the garden, along every wall, the way she’d learned the house in the Walled City at seven, every stair and every door and every place the sound carried.

When she came back up the path, she didn’t come to the verandah.

She went to the gate.

He watched her open it and go out into the lane and stand in front of the white wall, by the blue and white 9, looking at the green postbox with the empty brass frame on the front.

He got up and went after her.

✦ ✦ ✦

“What do you want on it?” he said.

She didn’t turn round. She was looking at the empty frame.

“Anything,” he said. “Lin. Lee. Both. Neither. Your mother’s name. A picture of a heron. A picture of a duck, for the duck cabinet. Nothing. You can leave it empty forever and the postman will still come, Mrs. Bae says, because he’s been coming to this gate since he was nineteen.” He put his hands in his pockets. “I didn’t want to choose. It’s the first address you’ve ever had that was yours. I didn’t want to put my name on the front of it before you’d said.”

She was quiet.

She thought about the tall house in the Walled City, where her name had never been said at dinners. About the cedar chest and the blanket and the gold heron. About the court language and the lake-country vowels and three syllables like water over stones. About a piece of paper on the twenty-first floor of the Harbour Hotel with Evangeline Lin on it, in her own hand, that had made her nobody’s, absolutely and for ever.

And a payslip on a fridge, with a magnet shaped like a fish.

“Have you got a pen?” said Evangeline.

He had a pencil. He always had a pencil, a short one, for the rabbit book. He gave it to her.

There was a card in the brass frame already, blank, cream, waiting. She took it out. She held it against the white wall, flat, and wrote on it, in her small, neat, upright hand, in capitals, so that the postman would be able to read it from the lane.

Three letters.

She slid it back into the frame.

LEE.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t say anything.

He stood in the lane in front of the white wall and looked at the card in the brass frame on the green postbox, and his face went still and stayed that way, and she watched it, and waited, the way she’d learned to wait.

“We’re not married,” he said at last. Barely a sound.

“Not yet,” said Evangeline.

“You could put Lin. You could put your own. You’ve never had your own. I don’t—you don’t have to—”

“I know,” she said. “I chose.”

She turned round and looked up at him in the lane, under the fig tree, with the autumn light coming down through the yellowing leaves onto both of them.

“You’ve had a name in your collar since you were seven,” she said. “Nobody ever put it on a door.”

He put his hand over his eyes.

She took his other hand, the one with the missing fingertip, and held it, and stood beside him in the lane in front of their house, at the top of Fig Tree Lane, where the road stopped and turned into a path up the hill, and waited for him to be able to take his hand away from his face.

It took a while. She didn’t mind.

Up the lane, at the gate of the house next door, a small old woman in a cardigan and gardening gloves had come out to see who was talking, and stood looking at them, and then went back inside and shut her door, and came out again twenty minutes later carrying a cake.

chapters.title: The Neighbours Bring a Cake
chapters.desc: Mrs. Bae from next door arrives with a chestnut sponge. He checks it for explosives. She eats a slice in front of him. Then a week of buying furniture with a man who never looks at a price, and a cedar chest her father carries up four stone steps on his own.
chapters.epigraph: “I’ve lived on this lane fifty years. Nobody’s ever checked my cake before. I’m very flattered.” — Mrs. Bae, No. 7
chapters.content:
Mrs. Bae was seventy-one, small and round, and talked more than anyone Jun Hyuk had ever met, including himself.

She came through the gate of No. 9 at half past three, carrying the cake on a plate with a tea towel over it, in her gardening gloves, which she had forgotten to take off. She was talking before she reached the steps. She was talking about the fig tree, which she said had been planted by the tea man’s wife in 1932 and had never once failed to fruit. She was talking about the family from the city, who had owned the house for six years and come twice and never once said good morning. She was talking about the stream, and the postman, and her husband’s chillies, and the cat, which was hers, technically, but which went where it liked, and which had been sitting on the wall between the two gardens since noon watching them, and which she said had very good judgement.

“I saw you at the postbox,” she said, reaching the bottom of the steps. “With the card. I’m sorry. I’m terribly nosy. Everybody on the lane will tell you I’m terribly nosy, so you might as well hear it from me.” She held up the plate. “So I made you a cake. Chestnut. With cream. It’s the only one I’m good at. Welcome to Fig Tree Lane.”

Evangeline came down the steps and took it.

“Thank you,” she said.

Mrs. Bae beamed at her. Then she looked up the steps at Jun Hyuk, who was standing at the top of them, by the green front door, with his hands in his pockets, and her beam widened.

“Goodness,” she said. “Aren’t you big. My husband will be thrilled. He’s been trying to find someone to carry his compost for three years.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He checked the cake.

He didn’t mean to. It wasn’t a decision. It was something his hands did, the way they found the exits in a room, the way they’d checked the walls of every container at the Iron Docks. Evangeline brought the plate up onto the verandah and set it on the top step, between the three of them, and took the tea towel off, and he was already crouching beside it.

He looked at it. He picked up the plate and felt the weight of it, and tilted it a little to the light. He put his nose close to it and smelled it: chestnut, and cream, and butter, and sugar, and nothing else. He took the knife Evangeline had brought out from the kitchen and cut a thin slice from the side, and looked at the inside of it, the sponge and the cream and the sponge, layer by layer, the way Mrs. Koo looked at a pallet of squid.

He put the knife down.

Then he looked up and saw both women looking at him.

Mrs. Bae had her gloved hand over her mouth. Her eyes were bright.

“I’m sorry,” said Jun Hyuk. He’d gone red from the collar up. “I’m sorry. It’s a—I’ve got a habit. From work. I didn’t mean—it’s a lovely cake. It’s a beautiful cake. I don’t think you’re trying to blow us up. I didn’t think that. My hands did it on their own.”

Mrs. Bae took her hand away from her mouth.

“I’ve lived on this lane fifty years,” she said. “Nobody’s ever checked my cake before. I’m very flattered.”

Evangeline picked up the thin slice he’d cut.

She held it up, so he could see it. Then she ate it, in front of him, slowly, the whole thing, on the top step of the verandah of their house, with her eyes on his face the entire time. When she’d finished, she licked the cream off her thumb.

“Good,” she said.

Mrs. Bae laughed so hard she had to sit down on the steps.

✦ ✦ ✦

Mr. Bae came round an hour later to see what the noise was.

He was a tall, stooped, silent man of seventy-five who had been, Mrs. Bae said, the headmaster of the village school for thirty years, and who had said about nine words a day since he retired, and most of those about his chillies. He shook Jun Hyuk’s hand and looked up at him. He looked at Evangeline. He looked at the card in the postbox.

“Lee,” he said.

“That’s us,” said Jun Hyuk.

Mr. Bae nodded, as if something had been settled, and went to look at the fig tree.

The four of them ate the rest of the cake on the verandah steps as the sun went down behind the hill, while Mrs. Bae talked about everyone on the lane, which took some time, and Jun Hyuk talked back, because he couldn’t help it, and Mr. Bae and Evangeline sat side by side on the bottom step not saying anything, in perfect contentment, like two old men fishing off the same pier.

The cat came down off the wall at dusk and walked along the verandah and stopped in front of Jun Hyuk and stared at him.

It was ginger, and enormous, and missing half an ear.

“That’s Pudding,” said Mrs. Bae. “Don’t let him in. He’s a terrible thief.”

The cat looked at Jun Hyuk. Jun Hyuk looked at the cat. Then the cat climbed into his lap, turned round twice, and lay down.

“Oh dear,” said Mrs. Bae, delighted. “Now you’ve done it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They moved in on the Saturday after, the nineteenth.

They didn’t bring much. That was the strange part. Two years of living together, in a karaoke flat and a textile building, and when it came to it, everything they owned went up the four stone steps of No. 9 in an afternoon: the lamp with the paper shade, the teapot that remembered things, the rice cooker, the knives, the two cups that didn’t match, the jar of salted lemons, the long sofa from Harbour Road, which took four men again. The towels. The menu from Nam’s Noodles, with ten rules on it, which she took off the inside of the textile building’s door carefully with her fingernail and taped to the inside of the green front door at her eye height.

And the old black case with the brass catches, which he carried up himself, last, the way you’d carry something asleep.

The rest they had to buy.

He let her choose. He’d decided that in August, before he even bought the house, standing in the empty rooms with Raiden and the estate agent. Every chair and every table and every cup and every curtain, she would choose, and he would carry. So they spent a week in the furniture shops on Harbour Road and in the old town and in a warehouse by the docks that sold things out of old houses, and she walked slowly along every aisle the way she walked along the orchid stalls, looking at the joints and the backs and the undersides, turning things over, and he walked behind her and didn’t look at a single price.

“You’re not looking,” she said, on the third day, in a shop full of old wooden tables.

“No,” he said.

“This one costs more than the truck.”

“Everything costs more than the truck. The truck cost eleven hundred dollars in 2014 and the man who sold it to me cried with happiness.” He put his hand on the table. It was long and dark and old, with a crack running down the middle that someone had mended with a butterfly of brass. “Do you like it?”

She looked at the mend.

“Yes,” she said.

“Then it’s ours.” He nodded to the man behind the counter, who had been watching them for twenty minutes and had gone pale when he heard the word truck, and went to pay.

✦ ✦ ✦

She chose a bed on the fourth day.

It took her the whole morning. She lay on eleven of them, one after another, in a shop on Harbour Road with a carpet so thick his boots disappeared, under the eyes of a saleswoman who had stopped trying to sell anything somewhere around the fifth and was now simply watching, like a woman at a play. Evangeline lay on each bed on her back, straight, with her hands folded, and looked at the ceiling. Then she got up and moved to the next one.

On the eleventh, she lay down and didn’t get up.

She lay there. Then she turned her head on the pillow and looked at him, standing at the end of it with his hands in his pockets.

He understood. He lay down beside her.

It was the first bed he’d ever lain on that was longer than he was. His feet stopped before the end. His arm didn’t hang off the side. There was room, on either side of the two of them, for another two of them. He lay on his back in the middle of a furniture shop on Harbour Road, in front of the saleswoman, with Evangeline beside him, and looked at the ceiling, and didn’t say anything for a while.

“This one,” said Evangeline.

He nodded. He couldn’t say anything for a moment.

Then he rolled onto his side, in the middle of a furniture shop on Harbour Road, and kissed her. On their bed, which they hadn’t paid for yet, with his hand flat on the pillow beside her head and his weight on one elbow over her. Evangeline didn’t move away. She put her hand on the back of his neck and kept him there until he’d finished, and then a little after.

The saleswoman, at the end of the aisle, put her hand over her heart.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her father came on the Sunday, with Elowen and Zhao and Raiden and Jinx and Elara and Eliana, in three cars, which was the first time all of them had come up the lane at once and which Mrs. Bae watched from her gate with a cup of tea and enormous satisfaction.

Lin Jian got out of the first car last.

He stood in the lane in his funeral suit and looked at the white wall, and the blue and white 9, and the fig tree, and the green postbox with the card in the brass frame.

He looked at the card.

Then he went round to the back of Raiden’s van, and opened it, and took something out.

It was the cedar chest. From the attic of the tall house in the Walled City. Old, reddish, heavy, with brass corners and a lock that hadn’t worked since the nineteen-seventies. It was the chest she’d found the blanket in when she was fifteen. It was the chest that had sat in the attic for twenty-six years with her secret folded inside it.

He carried it up the path on his own. He wouldn’t let anyone help. He was sixty, and heavy, and grey in the face by the bottom of the steps, and Raiden started forward and Elowen put a hand on his arm and he stopped. Lin Jian carried the cedar chest up the four stone steps one at a time, breathing hard, and across the verandah, and set it down in front of his daughter, at the green front door.

He straightened up.

“It’s inside,” he said. “The blanket. And the papers. Both birth certificates. And the photograph of the blanket, that was in my drawer.” He was breathing hard. “I don’t want any of it in my house any more. It isn’t mine. It never was. It’s yours.” He looked at her. “Do what you want with it. Burn it. Keep it. Put it in the stream. I don’t care. I’m not asking you to keep it. I’m asking you to have it.”

She looked at the chest. Then at him.

She thought about what Elowen had told her in July: that their father had sat in the attic every evening for a week, after the letter from the palace, with the chest open, going through it, and that he had cried, and that when Elowen went up to bring him tea he had said, I kept the wrong thing.

“Thank you, Baba,” said Evangeline.

He nodded. He didn’t trust himself to say anything else. He went past her into the house, fast, and they heard him in the front room, admiring the windows, loudly, to Jinx.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night, in the new bed, in the big room at the front of the house with two of the windows open to the hill, she couldn’t sleep.

Neither could he. He lay on his back in the middle of the bed that was longer than he was and listened to the house. It was a different kind of quiet from the textile building. No printing works. No harbour. No ferries. An owl, somewhere up the hill. The stream at the bottom of the garden, faint. The fig tree moving against the wall.

And no door in front of him.

The bedroom door was across the room, on the far side, in the dark. He couldn’t see it from the bed. He’d been lying there for an hour, still, not looking at it.

She knew. She’d known since they lay down.

At midnight she got up. She went across the room in the dark, barefoot, to the cedar chest, which they’d put at the foot of the bed because neither of them could think where else to put it. She opened the lid. He heard her take something out. Silk, rustling.

She came back to the bed with the blanket.

It was small. He hadn’t expected that. A baby’s blanket, white silk gone the colour of old ivory, with a border of gold thread and a heron in one corner, standing over three peaks, and a date sewn under it in numbers he couldn’t read. She shook it out over the bed, over the two of them, where it covered almost nothing, a square of silk on a bed for giants.

Then she lay back down and put her head on his chest and her hand over his heart.

“There,” she said.

He lay still under the little blanket, with her on his chest, in their bed, in their house, with the windows open and the owl on the hill.

“What does that mean?” he said. “There.”

She considered it.

“It means it’s been used for something,” said Evangeline. “Now.”

He put his hand on her hair.

After a while she lifted her head and kissed him, in the dark, under a blanket the size of a tea towel. He kissed her back, and turned them both until she was under him and the little square of silk had slid off onto the floor, and for a while, in the new bed with the owl on the hill, neither of them thought about the door at all.

He didn’t sleep, much. But he didn’t look at the door, either.

chapters.title: He Doesn’t Know How to Sleep Without a Weapon
chapters.desc: Everything he used to keep under the bed is locked in a steel room behind the pantry now. So he lies awake facing a door he can’t see. She moves to his side of the bed, between him and the door, and stays there for a month.
chapters.epigraph: “You watch the door. I’ll watch you. That’s fair.” — Evangeline, No. 9 Fig Tree Lane, November 2024
chapters.content:
He’d put it all away on the first day.

That had been the plan, and he’d kept to it. On the twelfth of October, before he brought her up the lane, he’d driven up alone with the long canvas case and the bag and everything else he’d carried for twenty years, and gone into the pantry under the stairs, and pressed the third shelf the way Raiden had shown him, and put all of it inside the small steel room behind, on a rack Raiden had built for exactly that, and closed the door, and pressed the shelf back.

It was there. He could get to it in eleven seconds from the bed. He’d timed it, twice.

He couldn’t sleep.

✦ ✦ ✦

The house was the safest place he’d ever lived in, by a long way; he’d helped Raiden make it so. The lane was quiet and the owl was only an owl. The trouble was the bed.

For twenty years, wherever he’d slept, there had been something within reach. Under a pillow. Beside a chair. Down the side of a seat in the cab of a truck. He’d slept with it the way a child sleeps with a hand on a blanket, and he hadn’t known that was what it was for until it wasn’t there.

He lay on his back in the big bed in the front room, in the dark, with the windows open and Evangeline asleep against his shoulder, and his right hand moved, every few minutes, without his permission, to the edge of the mattress, and found nothing there, and came back.

By the end of the first week, he’d stopped pretending to sleep. He’d wait until she was breathing slowly, and then he’d get out of bed carefully, and go and sit in the armchair by the window, the one she’d chosen in the warehouse by the docks, facing the bedroom door across the room, and stay there until it was light.

On the eighth night she woke up and found him there.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t say anything at first. She lay in the bed and looked at him across the dark room, sitting in the armchair by the open window with his hands on his knees, facing the door, the way he’d sat in the chair in the karaoke flat on the first night, in November, two years ago.

“Jun Hyuk,” she said.

“Go back to sleep. I’m fine.”

She sat up.

“It’s not the house,” he said, before she could say anything. “The house is good. The house is the best house in the world. It’s me. I can’t—” He stopped. He looked down at his right hand on his knee, which had moved, while he was talking, to the arm of the chair, and found nothing there. “I’ve always had something. At night. In reach. Since I was eleven. I put it all away, because I promised. Because you shouldn’t have to sleep next to it. And now I can’t sleep without it.” He laughed, without any breath in it. “I’m thirty-four. I’ve been shot three times and blown off the back of a truck. And I can’t sleep without a—without my blanket.”

She didn’t laugh.

She got up out of the bed and came across the room to him, in the dark, barefoot. She didn’t take his hand. She looked at him in the chair, and then at the door, across the room, and he watched her work something out.

Then she went back to the bed and picked up her pillow, and his, and swapped them.

He stared at her.

She’d always slept on the side by the window. He slept on the side by the door, because he always had, wherever he’d slept, since he was nine, so that whatever came through it would come to him first. She put his pillow on the window side. She put hers on the door side. She got into the bed on the door side, between the empty half of it and the door, and lay down, on her side, facing across the room.

Facing the door.

“Come to bed,” she said. “Your side’s by the wall now.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He came. He didn’t know what else to do. He got into the bed on the window side, against the wall, with her between him and the room, and lay on his back, and looked at the ceiling.

She lay on her side with her back against him and her face to the door. Her hair was on his pillow. He could feel her breathing.

“You can’t see it,” he said, after a while. “From there. In the dark.”

“I don’t need to see it,” said Evangeline. “I can hear it.”

He was quiet.

“I’ll know if anything comes through that door,” she said. She reached back with one hand, without turning round, and found his arm, and pulled it over her, round her waist, and held it there. “You watch the door. I’ll watch you. That’s fair.”

“That’s not how it works,” he said. His voice had gone. “I’m the one who—it’s supposed to be me, in front. I’m the one who stands—”

“Not any more,” said Evangeline.

She didn’t say anything else. She lay with his arm round her and her face to the door, and after a while her breathing slowed, and he lay behind her in the dark, against the wall, with the window open over him and the owl on the hill, and found that his right hand was on her waist, and that it had been there for some time, and had stopped looking for anything else.

He slept for three hours.

It was the most he’d slept since they came up the lane.

✦ ✦ ✦

She slept between him and the door for a month.

Every night. She never said anything about it. She just went to the door side of the bed when she got in, and lay facing the room, and pulled his arm round her. Some nights he slept three hours. Some nights four. On the twentieth night he slept six, and woke at seven in the morning with the sun on the ceiling and her still on her side in front of him, awake, watching the door, with her hand over his on her waist, and realised that she’d been awake for an hour, keeping it, letting him sleep.

He didn’t say anything. He pulled her back against him and put his face in her hair and lay there until she turned round.

On the thirty-first night, he slept eight hours. He didn’t wake up once. He didn’t know it until she told him, in the morning, at the long dark table with the brass butterfly in it, over tea. Eight hours and eleven minutes. She’d counted, of course. He sat and stared at her, and she drank her tea.

✦ ✦ ✦

The days were different too. He went to the docks at half past five every morning in the truck, and opened containers with Mrs. Koo until four, and came home up the lane at five with the sun going down behind the hill, and she was always somewhere he could find her.
