In the glasshouse, mostly. She’d filled it in a fortnight. Orchids along one side, in rows, white and pale yellow and one striped one Mrs. Bae had given her from her own window. Herbs on the other. Seedlings on the potting table under glass covers. She’d bought a book about grafting and a pair of secateurs from the knife man in the Walled City, and on Saturdays she went down the lane with Mrs. Bae to a nursery in the next village and came back with things in pots that he had to carry up from the car.

And in the music room.

That was what Raiden had called it on the drawings. A small square room at the back of the house, off the passage to the glasshouse, with a north window and wooden walls, that the tea man’s wife had used for sewing in 1932. Raiden had panelled it, and put in a window seat, and a chair with no arms, and a music stand that he’d found in a market and repaired himself. He’d done it without being asked. He’d shown Jun Hyuk the drawing in August and said, She’ll want somewhere. She won’t say so.

She opened the old black case on the table in the music room on the first Sunday in November, and looked at the instrument inside for a while.

Then she rang Mrs. Lai.

✦ ✦ ✦

She was very bad at it.

That was the first thing Mrs. Lai said, in the first lesson, on the second Tuesday in November, sitting in the chair with no arms in the music room with her own viola on her knee. She said it kindly, and honestly, in the voice of a woman who had taught the instrument for thirty years and had never once lied to a pupil.

“You’re very bad,” said Mrs. Lai. “Everyone is, at the beginning. It’s a difficult instrument. It doesn’t want to be played. You have to persuade it.” She watched Evangeline’s hands on the bow. “Your hold is good. Your posture is good. Your ear is very good. Your sound is terrible. That will change. It takes about a year to make a sound you can bear and about ten to make one anyone else can.”

Evangeline drew the bow across the open string, carefully, the way she’d been shown.

It made a noise like a cat being stepped on.

From the kitchen, where he had been pretending to make tea for twenty minutes so he could listen, Jun Hyuk made a sound he turned into a cough.

Mrs. Lai didn’t look round. “Again,” she said.

Evangeline did it again.

It was worse.

“Good,” said Mrs. Lai, and Evangeline looked up at her, and Mrs. Lai smiled. “That’s what good sounds like, for the first month. Now. Again. I’m going to make you do it until you hate it, and then you’ll do it a hundred more times, and then one day you won’t hate it. That’s all it is.”

She practised every day after that. Half an hour, before he came home. He could hear it from the bottom of the lane when he got out of the truck: long, slow, scraping notes coming out of the open north window of the music room, one after another, the same four notes, over and over, terrible, patient. Mrs. Bae said she could hear it from her kitchen and that it made her cry, though not, she said, for the reason he’d think.

He never told her it sounded like a cat. He stood at the bottom of the garden every evening with his bag over his shoulder and listened to all of it, every scraping note, until she stopped. Then he went up the path.

✦ ✦ ✦

The fund was her idea.

She told him one evening in the second week of November, at the long table, plainly, the way she told him everything that mattered.

“I’ve asked Ms. Fong,” she said. “To make it properly. A foundation. With my money. The money from the lake. And yours, if you want. The money from the safes.” She turned her cup. “For people who come out of boxes. For school. Nursing. Rent. Lawyers. Doctors. For whatever they need, for as long as they need it. Not a church fund. Not an anonymous envelope. A real one, with a name on it, and an office, and a woman who answers the phone.”

He sat still.

“I’ll run it,” said Evangeline. “Ms. Fong says I’ll need a board. I’ve asked Elowen. And Nuo, when she qualifies. And Mrs. Koo.” She looked at him. “And you.”

He didn’t say anything for a while.

“What will you call it?” he said.

She’d thought about it. He could see that she’d thought about it.

“The Open Door,” said Evangeline.

He got up from the table and went out onto the verandah and stood there in the dark, with his hands on the rail, looking down the garden at the stream, for some time. She didn’t follow him. She knew he’d come back in.

When he did, his eyes were red, and he sat down across from her, and put both his hands flat on the table on either side of his cup.

“All of it,” he said. “Everything in the crates. Everything in the caches. Take all of it. I don’t need any of it. I’ve got a payslip.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On a Sunday afternoon at the end of November it rained, a soft steady grey rain off the hill, and she shut the music room window after her practice and came and found him in the bedroom, where he’d gone to fetch a jumper and had stayed, sitting on the end of the bed, looking at the rain on the glass.

She stood in the doorway.

He looked round. She was in a grey cardigan, the one from the karaoke flat, which she still wore, and her hair was down, and she was looking at him the way she’d looked at him over the candles on the night of the typhoon.

She closed the bedroom door behind her.

Not all the way. A hand’s width. The way she’d always left her door at home, so she could hear the stairs. Then she crossed the room to him, and stood in front of him where he sat on the end of the bed, between his knees, and put her hands on his shoulders.

He looked up at her.

“It’s the middle of the afternoon,” he said, as if somebody ought to point it out.

“Yes,” said Evangeline, and he took her by the waist and pulled her down into his lap and kissed her before she could bend to him.

There was no hurry in it this time, and no fear, and no candle burning down. There was grey rain on thirty-one windows that opened, and a bed that was longer than he was, and the whole afternoon, and nowhere either of them had to be. She undid his shirt slowly, button by button, the way he’d once undone hers, and he let her, and watched her face the whole time.

He didn’t check, this time. That was what she noticed. He touched her face the way he always did, eyebrows, nose, cheekbone, jaw, and then he didn’t stop to press two fingers to her pulse, to make sure. He knew. He’d stopped needing to make sure somewhere between the Glass Pavilion and the green postbox, and she felt the difference in his hands, which were slow and sure and warm and not shaking at all.

He talked to her. Low, against her skin, the way he had the night of the typhoon. Things about the house, and the rain, and her, mostly her. That he’d heard her from the bottom of the lane on Tuesday and had to stand by the gate for ten minutes before he could come up. That she was beautiful when she was concentrating. That he wanted to grow old in this bed, with her, and complain about his knees, and hear her play badly for ten years until she played well. She held his head against her and listened, and pulled him down, and the rain went on against the glass, and neither of them hurried, and neither of them stopped.

Afterwards, they lay under the little silk blanket, which covered nothing, and the big ordinary one, which covered everything, and watched the rain.

“Your side,” she said, after a while. “You’re on my side.”

He looked. He was. He’d ended up on the door side of the bed, between her and the room, the way he used to, without noticing.

“Do you want to swap?” he said.

She thought about it.

“No,” said Evangeline. “I want you to stay where you are.”

He stayed. He lay on his side of the bed that had been her side for a month, facing the door, with her against his back, and her arm round him, and her hand over his heart. And he looked at the door, a hand’s width open, the way she liked it, and listened to the rain, and wasn’t afraid of it at all.

chapters.title: The Last Target
chapters.desc: Old Nam rings on a Thursday night. The Ferryman is back on the river after nine years, with a boat and thirty people and a Saturday. Jun Hyuk goes into the pantry under the stairs, and she sits across the table every night and watches him clean the rifle.
chapters.epigraph: “He’s back. Gu. The grey suit and the toothpick. Saturday the seventh. The old jetty below the bridge.” — Old Nam, on the phone with the cord
chapters.content:
The wedding was set for the twenty-first of December.

She’d chosen it. In the first week of November, at the long dark table, with a calendar from Mrs. Bae that had pictures of chillies on it. She’d turned the pages to December and put her finger on the twenty-first, a Saturday, and said, “This one.”

“Why that one?”

“It’s the longest night of the year,” said Evangeline. “After it, the nights get shorter.”

He’d looked at her across the table. Then he’d got up and come round it and pulled her up out of her chair and kissed her, there, beside the chilli calendar, with both hands in her hair, hard enough that she had to hold on to his shirt, until the calendar was on the floor and her back was against the dresser and the cups on it were rattling. Then he’d gone out onto the verandah again and stood there in the dark with his hands on the rail, which was getting to be a habit, and Mrs. Bae had seen him from her kitchen window and come round with soup.

So it was set. Six people. The garden. Herbs from the glasshouse in her hands, she’d decided, instead of flowers, because Elowen would have done flowers so well that she couldn’t bear to ask her to do them, and because she wanted Elowen sitting down, for once, being a guest. Elara would be on a night shift and would come when she could. Old Nam had been invited, and had said she didn’t go to weddings and would send noodles. Mr. and Mrs. Bae would watch from over the wall, which Mrs. Bae said was how all the best weddings on the lane had been watched for fifty years.

He’d bought her nothing for it. She’d made him promise. She said she had a ring already and a house already and a coat already and didn’t need anything else, and he’d said everyone needs something else, and she’d looked at him, and he’d promised.

He’d been planning something anyway, of course. She knew. She could see it on his face every evening when he came up the path. She didn’t ask.

✦ ✦ ✦

Old Nam rang on the twenty-eighth of November, a Thursday, at ten past nine at night.

On the landline in the hall of No. 9. It had come with the house, an old cream telephone on a little table under the stairs, and it had rung four times since October: Mrs. Bae twice, Elowen once, and a man selling insurance, whom Jun Hyuk had kept on the line for twenty minutes asking questions about the policy until the man hung up.

He answered it. Evangeline was at the long table with her tea and the chilli calendar.

She watched him listen.

He stood in the hall under the stairs with the cream receiver against his ear and didn’t say anything. Not one word. She’d never once seen him on a phone without talking. He stood there and listened for two minutes, with his free hand flat on the wall, and his face went still, and stayed there.

“Thank you, Nam,” he said at last. His voice was perfectly ordinary. “Yes. I know. I know. Look after your wrist.”

He put the phone down.

He stood in the hall with his hand still on the receiver.

“Who was it?” said Evangeline.

He didn’t turn round.

“Gu,” he said. “Gu Shanlin. He’s back.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He told her at the table. He always told her. He’d promised in May, in a car, and he’d kept it every day since.

The Ferryman had been gone for eight years. Not gone: across the river, on the far side, in the hills where there were no flags and nobody to arrest anyone. Running his boats from there. Since 2016, since a judge had let him walk out of court at four in the afternoon, he hadn’t once set foot on the near bank. He was too careful for that.

But in June, the man in the pale shirt from the north had paid him for a boat, and the boat had been taken at half past two by Inspector Song Wei Long, and its captain had talked, a great deal. And since then, Old Nam said, the Ferryman’s business had been going badly. Two more boats taken in September. A warehouse in the south closed in October, after a man was found in a container of squid at the Iron Docks and a shipping agent was arrested. People on the river had stopped trusting his crossings. People who used to pay him had started paying someone else.

So he was coming across himself. To fix it.

“He’s in the border town,” said Jun Hyuk. “Since Tuesday. At the hotel by the old checkpoint, under another name. Nam’s cousin’s girl cleans the rooms.” He turned his cup. “There’s a boat on Saturday the seventh. Thirty people, from the far side. They’ve paid. He’s crossing them himself, to show the river he still can. The old jetty below the bridge, after midnight.” He was quiet for a moment. “Nine days.”

She didn’t say anything.

“He’ll be on the jetty,” said Jun Hyuk. “Himself. He has to be. That’s the point. Everyone on the river has to see him there.” He looked at his hands on the table. “I’ve been waiting nine years for him to be somewhere I could see.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He went into the pantry that night.

She heard him. She was upstairs, in the bedroom, getting ready for bed, and she heard him go along the hall under the stairs, and the pantry door, and then, faintly, the sound of the third shelf being pressed. A click. The steel door behind it.

He was in there a long time.

When he came up, he got into the bed on the window side, the way he had for a month, and she got in on the door side and lay facing the room and pulled his arm round her. And they lay there in the dark, and neither of them slept, and neither of them said anything about it.

In the morning, the long canvas case was under the bed.

✦ ✦ ✦

He cleaned it every night that week.

At the long dark table with the brass butterfly in it, after dinner, on the old grey towel he’d brought from the truck two years ago and had never thrown away. The way he’d done it every night in the karaoke flat and in the textile building, piece by piece, slowly, in silence, the way Old Ko had taught him at eleven by the light of a hurricane lamp in a tent.

Except that he hadn’t done it since October. Not since the pantry. Not once in seven weeks.

She sat across from him and watched.

She’d always watched. She’d watched him do it a hundred times. She’d learned to push the cloth across the table to where his hand would be before he reached for it. She’d learned not to talk. She’d sat with it the way you sit with someone praying.

This was different.

He cleaned it as if he were saying goodbye to something. Or hello. She couldn’t tell which, and she didn’t think he could either. His hands were slow and sure, and his face in the lamplight didn’t change all evening, and he didn’t talk, not at dinner, not after, not in bed. On Friday he came home from the docks at five and didn’t stop at the bottom of the garden to listen to her practise. He came straight up the path.

She heard him not stop.

She put the bow down in the middle of a note and sat in the chair with no arms in the music room with the instrument on her knee and didn’t play anything else.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Saturday, while he was at the docks, she went to see Wei Long.

She didn’t tell him. It was the first thing she’d ever done in two years that she didn’t tell him first, and she knew it, and did it anyway. She took the bus into the city, because Bao would have told Zhao and Zhao would have told Elowen, and walked from the bus station to police headquarters, and asked at the desk for Inspector Song, and sat on a plastic chair in the lobby with her hands folded for forty minutes until he came down.

He looked at her from the bottom of the stairs.

“Evangeline,” he said.

He took her to a café across the road. Not an office. He seemed to understand that she wouldn’t talk in an office. He bought her a cup of tea she didn’t drink, and himself a black coffee, and sat across from her at a small table in the window, and waited, the way he’d waited at the hospital, and in her father’s kitchen when she was eleven.

“Gu Shanlin,” said Evangeline.

His face didn’t change. But he put his coffee down.

“If you arrested him,” she said. “If you had him. What would it take? For it to stay? Not like last time. Not a judge letting him walk out in a week.” She looked at him. “What would you need?”

Wei Long was quiet.

“Everything,” he said at last. “Every boat. Every truck. Every payment. Every name. Every person who ever got into one of his boxes, and where they were taken, and who paid, and who signed. Years of it. Dates and places and amounts, in one place, that a prosecutor could put in front of a court and walk through, step by step, so that no judge alive could look at it and say unreliable.” He turned his cup. “I’ve been building it for eleven years. I’ve got about a third. I’ve got what Lo gave me. I’ve got what the captain in June gave me. It isn’t enough.” He looked at her. “It would take someone who’d been watching him longer than I have. And writing it down.”

She didn’t move.

She thought about an exercise book with a cartoon rabbit on the cover, in a go-bag, in a karaoke flat, two years ago. About the boxes in the corner of the textile building, under a tarpaulin, that weren’t money. About the shelf in the steel room behind the pantry, under the rack where the long canvas case had been, where there were nine more exercise books, the same kind, with different cartoons on the covers. Rabbits, and ducks, and a cat in a hat. Nine years of them. In pencil. In big square capitals.

Wei Long watched her face.

“Evangeline,” he said. Very gently, for him. “Has he got it?”

She stood up.

“Thank you for the tea,” she said.

She hadn’t drunk any of it. She left the café and walked back to the bus station, and he watched her go through the window, a tall straight figure in a pale blue coat going away up the street, and didn’t follow, and sat afterwards with his black coffee going cold.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was cleaning it again that night when she came and sat down across from him.

He didn’t look up. He had the last piece in his hands. He was working the cloth over it, slowly, the way he always did at the end, and the lamplight was on his hands and the scar across his knuckles and the missing fingertip.

She’d thought about it all the way home on the bus. What she’d say. She’d written it in her head, and crossed it out, and written it again, the way she’d written her answer to the envoy at five in the morning on her birthday. She had it ready. All of it. Every word.

She didn’t say any of it.

She put her hand over his.

Over his hand, and the cloth, and the piece of the rifle he was holding. She laid her palm flat on the back of his hand and held it still, and he stopped.

He went still. The cloth didn’t move. He didn’t look up.

They sat like that, at the long dark table with the brass butterfly in it, under the lamp. Neither of them said anything. Outside, the owl was on the hill. In the music room, the old black case was open on the table with the instrument in it, where she’d left it in the middle of a note on Friday when she heard him not stop at the bottom of the garden.

Then she said it. Not what she’d written on the bus. Something else, that came up out of her the way the court language had come up out of her in her mother’s front room, from somewhere she hadn’t known was there.

“You’ve spent your whole life,” said Evangeline, low, “punishing the world for its sins, Jun Hyuk.”

He didn’t move.

“For eleven women in a truck,” she said. “For a barrier you lifted. For a box you didn’t open.” Her hand stayed on his. “Just once. Stay here. And let me show you that you’re allowed to be forgiven.”

He looked at her hand on his.

He didn’t say anything. He couldn’t. She watched him not be able to. His face had gone somewhere she’d never seen it go, somewhere far down and dark, and his hand under hers on the cloth was shaking.

He didn’t put the rifle down.

But he didn’t pick the cloth up again, either. He sat with her hand on his and the last piece in his fingers, and looked at the table, and the lamp burned, and the owl called on the hill, and neither of them moved until midnight.

At midnight she lifted her hand off his. She bent and kissed the back of it, where her palm had been, the old white scar across the knuckles, once. Then she went up to bed and left the lamp on for him.

He came up an hour later. He got in on the window side without a word, and she pulled his arm round her and faced the door, and after a while she felt him put his mouth against the back of her neck and leave it there, and breathe.

chapters.title: Evangeline Asks Him Not to Go
chapters.desc: She has asked him questions, and asked him to teach her, and asked him to come here. She has never once asked him for anything for herself. On the Friday night before the boat, she does.
chapters.epigraph: “Don’t go.” — Evangeline, 6 December 2024, the first thing she has ever asked for
chapters.content:
He told her on Friday morning, at a quarter to five, before the docks.

He’d been awake since two. She knew, because she’d been awake since two as well, on the door side of the bed with his arm round her, both of them lying still in the dark pretending, the way they’d pretended every night that week. At half past four he got up, and she heard him dress, and go downstairs, and the kettle, and she lay there and listened, and then she got up too.

He was at the long table with his coffee, three sugars, looking at nothing.

She sat down across from him in her cardigan.

“Tomorrow night,” he said. He didn’t look up. “I’m going up to the border tomorrow afternoon. I’ll be at the jetty by eleven. The boat comes over after midnight.” He turned his cup. “I’ll stop the boat. The thirty people will be all right. Nam’s got a place for them, and Wei Long’s people will be at the bridge by one, because I’m going to ring him at half past twelve and tell him there’s a boat. And Gu will be on the jetty.”

She didn’t say anything.

“I’m going to finish it,” said Jun Hyuk. “That’s all. Nine years. He’ll be standing on a jetty in the dark with thirty people coming off a boat behind him, and I’ll be on the bank, and I’ll finish it.”

He looked up at last.

“Then I’ll come home,” he said. “Sunday morning. I’ll come up the lane by eight. And I’ll never do anything like it again, as long as I live. I’ll open boxes at the docks and carry Mr. Bae’s compost and listen to you play the same four notes until you can play five. I promise you.” His voice cracked on the last word, and he made it stop. “This is the last one.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t ask him not to go then.

She sat across the table from him at a quarter to five in the morning and looked at his face, and saw that he meant every word, and saw what it had cost him to say them, and saw the thing behind them too. The thing she’d seen on the night of the twenty-second of June, in the dark, when he’d told her about the river road. The barrier that never went back down.

She got up and made him breakfast. Eggs. Rice. The last of the salted lemons from Elowen’s mother’s tree, sliced thin, beside the eggs, because she’d put them by in a jar in July last year for when you’re ill, and she thought this counted.

He looked at the lemon on his plate.

He ate it.

At half past five, at the green front door, he stood and she put her hand flat on his chest, and he put his over it, and she felt his heart going hard under her palm, the way it had against the steel door in December two years ago, the night he stopped kissing her carefully.

He went down the path. She heard the truck start in the lane.

She stood at the green door until she couldn’t hear it any more.

✦ ✦ ✦

She practised that morning. Half an hour. The four open strings, one after another, the way Mrs. Lai said, over and over, long slow bows. They were getting better. Mrs. Bae said so, over the wall; she said the cat had stopped leaving the garden when they started. Evangeline drew the bow and listened to the long scraping notes come out of the instrument her mother had played by a lake, and thought about nothing at all, on purpose, for thirty minutes.

Then she put the bow down and went into the glasshouse and stood among the orchids and shook.

It wasn’t like the night on the floor. It lasted a few minutes, while she stood between the benches with her hands flat on the potting table, very hard, so that the little clay pots rattled, and then it stopped, and she stood there breathing.

She’d never asked him for anything.

She’d thought about that all week. She’d asked him questions, at first, and then fewer, because he told her everything before she could ask. She’d asked him to teach her to shoot. She’d asked him who, once, at a table, before he went across the river. She’d asked him to come here, in the dark, on a camp bed, and lie down. But she’d never once in two years asked him for anything for herself. Not to stay. Not to stop. Not to be anything but what he was.

She’d been so careful.

She’d grown up in a house where she was a secret and a burden and a thing worth more than the house, and she’d learned, before she could read, that the way to be allowed to stay was to need nothing. To ask for nothing. To take up no room. She’d been doing it so long she’d stopped knowing she was doing it. And she’d brought it with her, up the stairs of a karaoke flat, and through a steel door, and into every room she’d ever shared with him: I’ll follow every rule. I’ll never ask. I’ll never be the thing that stops you.

She stood in the glasshouse with her hands on the table and understood that she was going to break it.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came home at five, the same as every day.

He came up the lane in the truck and parked it by the fig tree and got out, and stood at the bottom of the garden with his bag over his shoulder. She was in the music room. She’d been sitting there with the instrument on her knee since half past four, waiting, not playing.

When she heard the truck door, she played.

The four strings. Long and slow and terrible, one after another. She heard him stop at the bottom of the garden. She heard him stand there. She played all four, twice, as well as she could, which was not well, and then she stopped, and put the bow down, and sat with her hands in her lap.

He came up the path.

She heard him on the verandah. The green door. His bag going down in the hall. His feet on the floorboards, along the passage to the glasshouse, and stopping at the door of the music room.

She looked up.

He was standing in the doorway, filling it, the way he always did. He was looking at her sitting in the chair with no arms with her mother’s viola on her knee. His face broke a little at the edges, the way ice breaks on a puddle when you put your foot on it.

“You played,” he said. “When I got out of the truck. You waited.”

She put the instrument back in its case, carefully, and closed the lid, and did up the brass catches, one, two.

Then she stood up and crossed the room to him.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t put her hand on his chest.

She stopped in front of him, in the doorway of the music room, close, and looked up at his face, which was a long way up, and had been since the container. She looked at the scar through his eyebrow, and his mouth, and his eyes, which were dark, and wet, and frightened.

He knew. She saw that he knew what she was going to say.

“Don’t go,” said Evangeline.

He closed his eyes.

“Don’t go,” she said again. Her voice was shaking. She let it. “Please. Jun Hyuk. Don’t go tomorrow. I’ve never asked you for anything. You know I haven’t. Not once, in two years. I followed every rule. I didn’t touch the bag. I didn’t wait up, except when I did. I didn’t ask who, or where, or why. I washed your hands and I didn’t ask. I never asked you to stop being what you are, because I thought if I asked, you’d—” She stopped. She swallowed. “I’m asking now. I’m asking for me. Not for him. Not for the thirty people. For me. Don’t go.”

He opened his eyes.

“Evangeline,” he said. Barely a sound.

“I don’t care if it’s right,” she said. “I don’t care if he deserves it. He does. I know he does. I was in his box. I know better than anyone in this city what he deserves.” The tears were running down her face now. She didn’t wipe them. She’d never cried in front of him. Not in the container, not at the hospital, not in the shower in October with his hands, not on the floor of the long room in June. She’d cried at fifteen, in an attic, with the blanket, and not since. “But if you go up there and stand on that bank and finish it, you’ll come home on Sunday morning at eight and you’ll walk up the lane. You’ll have done it for them. For the eleven. For the barrier. And it won’t put the barrier down. You told me. It never goes back down.” Her voice broke. “And you’ll carry it up the lane, and up the steps, and in through the green door. Into our house. And I’ll have to watch you carry it. For the rest of our lives.”

He was crying too. She hadn’t seen him start.

“I’m asking you to put it down,” said Evangeline. “Not him. It. I’m asking you to let somebody else finish it. Just once.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“There isn’t anybody else,” he said.

He said it the way you’d say it to a doctor, with nothing left in his voice to argue with. Just the fact.

“There’s never been anybody else,” he said. “That’s the whole point. That’s why I started. Because there was a judge, and a court, and a witness, and it didn’t matter. He walked out at four in the afternoon. If I give it to the police and it goes wrong again—if there’s another judge, another Lo, another week—then Gu walks out again, and goes back across the river, and the next box he fills—” He couldn’t finish. “I can’t. I can’t stand on that bank and watch him walk away again. Not after you. Not after I found you in one of his boxes.”

“Then don’t give it to the police,” said Evangeline. “Give it to Wei Long.”

He stared at her.

“I went to see him,” she said. “Last Saturday. While you were at the docks. I didn’t tell you. I’m sorry. I’m telling you now.” She wiped her face, at last, with the heel of her hand. “I asked him what it would take. For it to stay. For no judge to be able to say unreliable. He said everything. Every boat. Every truck. Every payment. Every name. Years of it, written down, by someone who’d been watching longer than he had.” She held his eyes. “He asked me if you had it.”

He didn’t move.

“There are ten books,” said Evangeline, “on the shelf in the steel room.” Her voice was low. “You’ve been building the case against him since the day after the judge. You just never gave it to anyone. Because you never thought anyone would finish it but you.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He stood in the doorway of the music room.

She didn’t touch him. She’d asked. She’d said it. She stood in front of him with her face wet and her hands at her sides and waited, the way he’d waited at West Basin, with his hand in the air, for her to decide.

Outside, it was getting dark. The owl started up on the hill. Next door, through the wall, faintly, Mrs. Bae’s radio was playing.

“I have to go,” he said at last.

Something in her face closed.

“No. Listen. Listen to me.” He reached out and took her face in his hands, both of them, the way he had in the door of the glasshouse. His hands were shaking. “I have to go. Tomorrow. To the border. Because the boat’s still coming, Evangeline. Thirty people. On a river, in the dark, in December, in one of his boats. They’ve paid. They’re coming whether I’m there or not. Somebody’s got to be on that bank when they land. Somebody who knows what they’ll be getting off into.” His thumbs moved on her cheeks. “I’m not going to leave thirty people in the dark on a jetty because I’ve decided to be a good man. I can’t. You wouldn’t want me to. You stood in front of four women in a box.”

She looked up at him.

“I don’t know what I’ll do,” he said. “When I’m there. When he’s on the jetty. I don’t know. That’s the truth. I’ve never lied to you and I’m not going to start now, the night before.” His voice cracked. “But I heard you. I heard every word. And I’ll take it with me. All of it. Up the road and onto the bank.”

She didn’t say anything.

Then she put her hands up over his, on her face, and held them there.

“Ring me,” said Evangeline. “When you get there. Whatever you decide. Ring me.”

“I promise,” said Jun Hyuk.

He bent his head and kissed her. Her face was wet, and so was his, and it wasn’t a good kiss: it was salt and shaking, with his thumbs still on her cheeks and her hands still over his, and she held on to his wrists and kissed him back as if she could keep him in the doorway of the music room with it, if she didn’t stop.

Later, while he was in the shower, she went into the hall, where his bag was waiting by the green door. She had never once touched it. Rule five. She knelt and opened it and put in a flask of the ginger soup, wrapped in one of the white towels, and the first-aid box from under the sink, and did it up again exactly the way it had been.

That night she didn’t sleep on the door side. She lay on her own side, by the window, and he lay between her and the door, the way he used to, the way he had for twenty years. She held his arm round her all night. And neither of them slept at all, and at some point in the dark, late, he said into her hair, so quietly she almost didn’t hear it, that nobody in his whole life had ever asked him to stay.

chapters.title: He Goes Anyway — Then Turns Back
chapters.desc: The bank above the old jetty, eleven at night, a rifle, and a bag with ten exercise books in it. A boat comes across the river with thirty people on it. A man in a grey suit stands on the jetty counting money. At twelve forty-one, with the man in the scope, he rings her.
chapters.epigraph: “I can see him. I’ve got him. I can’t hear anything but you.” — Lee Jun Hyuk, the north bank, 12:41 a.m., 8 December 2024
chapters.content:
He packed the books last.

He’d packed everything else on Friday night, while she lay awake upstairs on her side of the bed, the window side, which she hadn’t slept on for a month. The rifle in its long canvas case. The bag. The things he’d carried for twenty years, out of the steel room behind the pantry, on the rack Raiden had built. He’d laid them out on the long dark table and checked them and packed them, the way he always had.

Then, on Saturday afternoon, at two, standing in the steel room with the light on, he’d looked at the shelf under the rack.

Ten exercise books. In a row. A rabbit, a rabbit, two ducks, a cat in a hat, a dog with a bone, a bear, a rabbit, a frog with an umbrella, a rabbit. The cheapest kind, from the stationery shop by the border bus station, which had only ever sold four designs. Nine years. Every boat. Every truck. Every name.

He’d stood there a while.

Then he’d taken them off the shelf, all ten, and put them in the bag with everything else, without deciding why.

✦ ✦ ✦

She came to the green door when he left.

She didn’t say anything. She’d said it. She put her hand flat on his chest, the way she always did, and he put his over it. She looked at the long canvas case on his shoulder, and the bag. She didn’t look away from them.

She didn’t say ring me. She’d said it last night, and he’d promised, and she knew he kept promises. She just looked at him.

He bent down and kissed her. On the doorstep, under the brass knocker, with the long case on his shoulder knocking against the frame. She put her other hand on the back of his neck and kissed him back, hard, the way she had with her back against a steel door two years ago, and when he lifted his head she was the one who let go first, because one of them had to.

She took her hands away. He went down the path and out of the gate past the fig tree and the green postbox with LEE on it, and got into the truck, and didn’t look back, because if he’d looked back he’d never have gone, and the boat was still coming, and the thirty people on it hadn’t asked anybody for anything.

He watched her in the mirror instead. Standing at the gate in her pale blue coat. Until the lane bent.

✦ ✦ ✦

Old Nam was behind her counter, in her purple jacket, with her wrist still in the splint that Elara had put on it in June and that she refused to take off because she said it made people give her their seats on the bus.

She looked at him come in. At the long canvas case. At his face.

“The quiet girl,” she said. “She asked you not to come.”

He stopped in the middle of the shop.

“How do you—”

“Because you’ve got a face like a man who’s been asked something,” said Old Nam, “for the first time in his life.” She put down her chopper. “So why are you here?”

“The boat,” said Jun Hyuk.

Old Nam looked at him.

“I’ve got the back room ready,” she said at last. “Blankets. Soup. My cousin’s girl and her mother. The doctor one, the little sister, she’s coming up at one with her green bag. Thirty, you said?”

“Thirty.”

“Then I’ll need more soup,” said Old Nam, and went into the kitchen, and he heard her start to chop.

✦ ✦ ✦

The old jetty was below the bridge on the near bank, at the end of a track behind the boat sheds, where the river was wide and slow and black and the far bank was a line of darker black against the hills with no lights on it at all. Nobody used the jetty any more. It had been a ferry landing before the bridge was built, in the sixties, and now it was rotten planks on rotten posts, and a lamp on a pole at the end that someone had rigged to a battery and that came on, Nam’s cousin’s girl said, when a boat was coming.

There was a bank above it. A steep one, with scrub on it and a stand of bamboo at the top, forty metres from the end of the jetty, looking straight down.

He was in the bamboo by eleven.

He lay on his stomach on the cold ground the way he’d lain on the roof of a container at West Basin, two years and two months ago, and set up, and checked everything, and then lay still. He didn’t talk. There was nobody to talk to. He lay in the bamboo with the river below him and the cold coming up through his jacket and the long canvas case open beside him, and waited.

He didn’t think about anything. He’d learned that at seventeen. You didn’t think. You lay still and waited for the second car.

He thought about her anyway.

He thought about her standing at the green gate. About her face, in the doorway of the music room, wet, the first time he’d ever seen it wet. I’m asking for me. About four long scraping notes coming out of an open window into the dark when he got out of the truck, because she’d sat there for half an hour waiting to play them for him.

He moved his shoulder, which had gone numb.

✦ ✦ ✦

The lamp on the end of the jetty came on at eleven minutes past midnight.

Then the car. A dark saloon, very clean, coming down the track behind the boat sheds with its lights off, and stopping at the landward end of the jetty, and three men getting out. Two big ones with torches. One small, neat, in a long grey coat over a grey suit.

He walked down the rotten planks to the end of the jetty, under the lamp, without hurrying, and stood there with his hands in his coat pockets, looking out at the black river.

Jun Hyuk looked at him through the scope.

Nine years.

Gu Shanlin was older. Of course he was. He’d been fifty-two in 2016, in the dock, in a grey suit, with an ivory toothpick he turned in his fingers. Now he was sixty, and his hair had gone white, and he was thinner. But it was the same face. Soft, pleasant, patient, like a man waiting for a bus. And when he took his right hand out of his coat pocket, there it was, between his fingers. The toothpick. Ivory, gone yellow. Turning.

Jun Hyuk breathed out.

He’d seen that face every night for nine years. Not in dreams. On purpose, in the dark, before he slept, along with the smell of the box. He’d made himself see it, so he wouldn’t forget.

He had him.

He’d had him since he stepped under the lamp. Forty metres. No wind. A man standing still at the end of a jetty in the light, looking out at the water. He could have done it at eleven years old, in a tent, by a hurricane lamp. Old Ko would have done it with his eyes shut.

He didn’t move.

✦ ✦ ✦

The boat came out of the dark at twenty-five past twelve.

A long low wooden river boat, the kind they used for sand, with an engine at the back going quietly and no lights, coming across the black water from the far bank. It came in slowly. It nudged up against the end of the jetty under the lamp, and a man at the back threw a rope, and one of Gu’s big men caught it.

And they came up out of the hold.

Thirty people. Climbing up out of the dark inside the boat, onto the deck, one at a time, slowly, the way people climb out of a place they’ve been sitting in for hours. Men in jackets. Women with bags. An old man in a blanket, helped by two others. They came up into the light of the lamp on the end of the jetty and stood on the deck, blinking, holding on to each other, looking at the near bank, at the country they’d paid to get to.

Gu Shanlin stood under the lamp and watched them come, and counted them, with his toothpick, pointing it at each one as they came up, the way you’d count sheep into a pen.

Jun Hyuk lay in the bamboo with his eye to the scope and his finger along the side, not on it, and watched him count.

He thought: That’s how I counted them. At West Basin. In the back of the truck.

He’d touched each one on the shoulder as he counted. To make sure.

✦ ✦ ✦

At twelve thirty-one he rang Wei Long.

He did it one-handed, without taking his eye from the scope, the way he’d planned. Two sentences. There’s a boat at the old jetty below the bridge. Thirty people, landing now. Wei Long didn’t ask who it was. He said twenty minutes, and hung up.

Twenty minutes.

Gu would be gone in ten. He knew that. He’d watched him for nine years. Gu Shanlin didn’t stay anywhere long enough for a police car to cross a bridge. He’d count them, and take the second half of the money from whoever was waiting for them on this side, and get back in the clean dark saloon, and go back to the hotel by the old checkpoint, and in the morning, across the river, to the hills where there weren’t any flags. And the river would know he’d crossed a boat himself and walked away again. And the next boat would be full.

Ten minutes.

His finger moved from the side of the rifle to where it went.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t know, afterwards, how long he lay there like that.

A minute. Two. With Gu in the scope under the lamp, turning his toothpick, and the thirty people on the deck behind him in the light, and the river black and slow, and his finger where it went. Everything was still and clear, the way it always was at the end.

He thought about the barrier. The handle. Forty-one degrees.

He thought about eleven names in the back of a book with a rabbit on the cover.

He thought about a box with holes drilled in the roof, and a woman standing in the middle of it with her hands open, between the door and the people she’d decided were hers.

And then, clearly, the way you’d hear a voice in the next room, he heard her. Not in his head. In the bamboo, beside him, the way she’d been beside him on the floor of Nam’s shop with the pistol in both hands. You’ll carry it up the lane, and up the steps, and in through the green door. Into our house.

I’m asking you to put it down.

He took his finger off.

He laid it back along the side of the rifle, flat, the way he’d taught her on the range in the hills. Then, with his other hand, without moving his eye from the scope, he took his phone out of his jacket and rang her.

✦ ✦ ✦

She answered before the first ring finished.

She’d been at the long dark table. He knew it the way he knew his feet on her stairs. She’d been sitting at the table with the lamp on and the phone in front of her and her hands folded, since he left.

“Jun Hyuk,” she said.

He couldn’t say anything for a second.

“I’m on the bank,” he said at last. His voice came out of him low, like something being dragged. “Above the jetty. The boat’s in. They’re all off. Thirty. They’re standing on the deck in the light. They’re all right.” He breathed. “And he’s on the jetty. Under the lamp. I can see him. I’ve got him. I’ve had him for twenty minutes.”

She didn’t say anything. He could hear her breathing.

“I can’t hear anything but you,” he said.

His voice broke. He let it.

“I’ve waited nine years,” he said. “Nine years for him to stand somewhere I could see. And he’s there. And I’ve got him. And I can’t hear anything but you, in the doorway, in the music room. Asking.” He was crying. He didn’t stop. “Nobody ever asked me. In my whole life. Nobody ever asked me to stay.”

On the other end of the line, in the house at the top of Fig Tree Lane, she was quiet.

“Come home,” said Evangeline.

She didn’t say please, or don’t, or let him go. She’d said all of that already.

“Come home,” she said again.

He lay in the bamboo with his eye on the man under the lamp.

Then he took his eye away from the scope.

✦ ✦ ✦

He did it slowly, the way he did everything at the end. He took his eye away. He took his hand off the rifle. He rolled onto his back in the bamboo and lay looking up at the sky through the leaves, where there were stars, a great many, because there were no lights on the far bank and very few on this one, and the phone was still against his ear, and he could hear her breathing.

“I’m coming home,” he said.

He heard her breathe out. A long breath, like a door opening.

“I’ve got to do something first,” he said. “Two things. Then I’m coming home. I’ll be there before it’s light. Not eight. Before it’s light.”

“What things?”

“The thirty people,” said Jun Hyuk. “They’re about to be put in a truck. I’m going to go down there and stand at the end of the jetty with my hands in my pockets, and talk to them about the weather, very loudly, until the police come. Gu won’t wait to see who I am. He’ll get in his car and go. Let him.” He wiped his face with the back of his hand. “And then there’s a man at the bridge with a long face who’s going to need some books.”

She didn’t say anything for a while.

“Rabbits,” she said. “And ducks.”

“And a frog with an umbrella,” said Jun Hyuk. “I’d forgotten the frog.”

He heard her laugh. On the phone, in the dark, from two and a half hours away, small, with tears in it. Fifteen.

✦ ✦ ✦

He went down the bank.

He left the rifle in the bamboo, in its case, closed, and went down the scrub on his heels with the bag over his shoulder, and walked out along the rotten planks of the old jetty towards the lamp, not hurrying, with his hands in his pockets, the way Gu had. The two big men with torches turned round and saw him coming, and saw the size of him, and looked at each other.

Gu Shanlin turned round.

He looked at the man walking towards him down the jetty. The torchlight went over Jun Hyuk’s face, the scar through the eyebrow, and Gu’s own face, pleasant and patient, changed. Not much. A flicker, at the eyes. A man who has heard a description of somebody for nine years, in back rooms, on the river, and has finally seen the face.

The toothpick stopped turning.

“Good evening,” said Jun Hyuk. “Cold, isn’t it. Clear, though. You can see every star. You don’t get that in the city.” He stopped at the end of the jetty, ten metres from Gu, under the lamp, between Gu and the boat, and turned his back on him, and looked at the thirty people standing on the deck in the light. “Hello,” he said to them. Low and easy. “Hello. Listen to me. I’m not with him. I’m not with anybody. There are some police coming in about fifteen minutes, and they’re going to take you somewhere warm, with soup. A lady called Nam has made you soup. Don’t get in any truck. Stay where you are, on the boat, with me. That’s the only rule. It’s easy.”

An old woman at the front of the deck was looking at him.

“What’s your name, auntie?” said Jun Hyuk.

Behind him, he heard Gu Shanlin say something low to the two big men. He heard feet on the planks, going away, fast. Car doors. An engine, starting, on the track behind the boat sheds. A clean dark saloon going away up the track with its lights off, back towards the hotel by the old checkpoint.

He didn’t turn round.

He stood at the end of the old jetty under the lamp, with his back to the bank and his face to the thirty, and talked to them about the weather, and the stars, and the soup, until he heard the sirens on the bridge.

chapters.title: Staying
chapters.desc: Ten exercise books handed through a car window at the bridge. A rifle carried down a bank for the last time and given away. Two and a half hours of road, and a woman standing at a green gate at four in the morning in her coat. The night he stays.
chapters.epigraph: “Put it in whatever room you put things in. I don’t want to know where.” — Lee Jun Hyuk, to Inspector Song Wei Long, 8 December 2024
chapters.content:
Wei Long was on the bridge at ten past one, standing beside his car in the light of the checkpoint, with his long face and his long coat, watching his people bring the thirty up from the jetty in blankets.

Jun Hyuk walked up the track from the boat sheds with the bag over his shoulder and stopped in front of him.

They looked at each other for a while. The river went past under the bridge, black and slow. Behind them, on the track, Elara was kneeling beside the old woman from the front of the deck, whose name was Auntie Lian, with her green bag open, and Old Nam was standing at the top of the track in her purple jacket and her splint directing the police officers to her back room as if they were her staff.

“He’s gone,” said Wei Long. “Gu. Back to the hotel, my people say. He’ll cross in the morning.”

“I know.”

“You let him.”

“Yes,” said Jun Hyuk.

Wei Long looked at him with nothing at all in his face. Then he looked at the bag.

✦ ✦ ✦

Jun Hyuk took the books out one at a time and put them on the bonnet of the car, in a row, under the checkpoint light.

A rabbit. A rabbit. Two ducks. A cat in a hat. A dog with a bone. A bear. A rabbit. A frog with an umbrella. A rabbit.

Wei Long looked at them.

He picked up the first one, the rabbit from 2016, with its cover gone soft and grey at the edges from nine years in a go-bag, and opened it. The first page, in pencil, in big square capitals, pressed so hard the pencil had nearly gone through: LO WING-HANG. HIGH COURT. GU SHANLIN TRIAL, OCTOBER 2016. DISMISSED DAY 6. And under it, a list. Names. Dates. Sums. Companies. Harmony Pacific. Blue River Holdings.

He turned the page. And the next. He stood on the bridge at a quarter past one in the morning in December, in the cold, under the light, and read, and didn’t say anything, and his long face went still, the way a man’s face goes still when he’s been looking in the same drawer for eleven years and the thing is suddenly in his hand.

“Every boat,” said Jun Hyuk. “Every truck. Every payment I could find. Every name. Where they were taken and who was waiting and who signed and who looked the other way. Nine years. There’s a list at the back of the last one of everyone in the city who’s ever taken money from him. Some of them you’ll know.” He looked at the books on the bonnet. “There’s nothing in there about me. I was very careful about that. You’ll have to take my word for it.”

Wei Long closed the book.

“Why?” he said. “Tonight. After nine years.”

Jun Hyuk looked at the river.

“Somebody asked me,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

Wei Long put the ten books in the boot of his car himself, one at a time, as if they were made of glass.

When he shut the boot, he stood with his hand on it for a moment.

“I’ll need you,” he said, without looking round. “At the trial. To say where these came from. In a court. With your name. Your real one.”

“Ms. Fong says I’ve got one now.”

“Ms. Fong,” said Wei Long, “is the only lawyer in this city I’m afraid of.” He turned round. “It’ll be a year. Maybe two. He’ll have very good lawyers. They’ll go through every page. They’ll go through you.”

“Let them,” said Jun Hyuk. “I’m boring now. I’ve got a payslip.”

Wei Long looked at him. And then, for the first time in all the years Jun Hyuk had known of him, the corner of his long mouth lifted into what was, unmistakably, a smile.

“Go home, Lee,” he said.

“One more thing.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He went back down the track, past the boat sheds, and up the steep bank in the dark to the stand of bamboo.

The rifle was where he’d left it, in its long canvas case, closed. He knelt beside it in the bamboo for a moment. Then he picked it up, and put the strap over his shoulder, and stood, and looked down at the old jetty below him, empty now, with the lamp on the end of it still burning on its battery, and the river black beyond it, and the far bank darker, and the stars.

Forty metres.

He’d lain here for an hour and twenty minutes with his finger along the side of it.

He carried it down the bank. Not on his shoulder. In his arms, the way he’d carried the jar of honey from the hill village, and the viola in its case down the corridor of the Harbour Hotel. Down the scrub, on his heels, slowly. Along the track. Up to the bridge, under the light, where Wei Long was standing beside his car, watching him come.

He held it out.

Wei Long didn’t take it at first. He looked at it. Then at Jun Hyuk’s face.

“I can’t take that,” he said. “It’s not evidence. You haven’t done anything with it.”

“I know,” said Jun Hyuk. “That’s why. Put it in whatever room you put things in. I don’t want to know where.” His arms were shaking a little. “I’ve had one since I was eleven. Every night. In reach. I don’t want it in my house any more. I don’t want it in the steel room behind the pantry, where I can get to it in eleven seconds from the bed. I want it somewhere I can’t get to at all.” He held it out further. “Please.”

Wei Long looked at him.

Then he took it.

He took it the way Jun Hyuk had carried it down the bank, in both arms, carefully. He opened the back door of the car and laid it on the seat, and shut the door, and stood with his hand on the roof.

“I’ll put it somewhere,” he said. “I won’t tell you where.”

“Thank you,” said Jun Hyuk.

He turned round and walked to his truck and got in and sat in the driving seat with both hands on the wheel and didn’t start it for a while.

His hands were empty. He kept looking at them.

✦ ✦ ✦

He drove home.

Two and a half hours. South from the border town on the old road, then east, onto the reservoir road, up into the hills. No lights on it. No other cars. The reservoirs black and flat on either side, with the stars in them. He drove with both hands on the wheel at exactly the speed limit, the way he’d driven four women to a hospital two years and two months ago, and he didn’t talk, because there was nobody to talk to, and then he found he was talking anyway. Out loud. To her. Telling her about the stars in the reservoirs and the old woman called Auntie Lian and Wei Long’s face when he opened the first book.

He came up Fig Tree Lane at ten past four.

The lane was dark. Every house was dark. The Baes’ was dark, and the one below, and the one below that, all the way down to the stream. The fig tree was a black shape against a sky going faintly grey at one edge, behind the hill.

And at the gate of No. 9, in the dark, there was a light.

✦ ✦ ✦

She was standing at the gate.

She had the lamp from the long table. The little one with the paper shade, from the karaoke flat, that she’d left on for him every night for two years so he’d see it from the top of the stairs. She’d run the cord out through the front door and along the verandah and down the path, all of it, three extension leads from the drawer, so that she could stand at the gate in the lane with it in her hands, lit, at four in the morning, in December, in her pale blue coat.

He stopped the truck.

He sat there with the engine running and looked at her through the windscreen: a tall still woman at a green gate under a fig tree, holding a lamp.

She wasn’t waiting up. He’d made a rule about that, on the back of a menu. She’d followed it, mostly. She was standing up. That was different.

He turned off the engine and got out.

He walked round the front of the truck to the gate, and stopped in front of her, and looked at her in the light of the lamp, which made her face gold and her eyes dark.

Neither of them said anything.

She looked at him. At his face first. Then down. At his shoulder, where the strap of the long canvas case had been every time he’d ever come home to her. At his hands, empty, at his sides.

She looked at his empty hands.

Then she put the lamp down on top of the green postbox, carefully, beside the brass frame with LEE in it, and stepped into him, and put her arms round him, all the way round, as far as they’d go, which was not far, and held on.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t let her go up the path. He picked her up.

He did it the way he had on the fifth of May, the first time he came back to her from across the river. The whole length of her, off her feet, against him. Her arms round his neck. Her face in his collar. He carried her through the gate and up the path between the dug beds and up the four stone steps and across the verandah, and the cord of the lamp trailed behind them from the postbox, all three extension leads of it, and he didn’t notice, and she didn’t care.

The green door was open. She’d left it open.

He carried her in. He kicked it shut behind them. On the inside of it, at her eye height, the menu from Nam’s Noodles, with ten rules on it, moved in the draught and was still.

He didn’t put her down in the hall. He carried her up the stairs.

✦ ✦ ✦

He told her everything. In the dark, in the big bed, under the little silk blanket that covered nothing and the big ordinary one that covered everything, with the window open to the hill and the grey coming up at the edge of the sky.

The bamboo. The lamp on the jetty. The toothpick, turning. The thirty people coming up out of the hold. Gu counting them, pointing at each one, the way he’d counted the women at West Basin. Twenty minutes with his finger along the side. The moment his finger moved.

Her voice in the bamboo.

She lay with her head on his chest and her hand over his heart and listened to all of it, every word, the way she’d listened to the weather on the other side of the river two years ago in a dead little room with painted windows. She didn’t say anything.

“I gave him the rifle,” he said at last. “Wei Long. On the bridge. I don’t know where he’ll put it. I asked him not to tell me.”

Her hand on his chest didn’t move.

“There’s nothing left,” he said. “In the pantry. In the steel room. On the rack. There’s nothing. I’ve never in my life slept in a house with nothing.” He was quiet. “I don’t know how.”

She lifted her head.

She found his face in the grey half-dark, the way he always found hers, and held it.

Then she said something. In the court language, low, with the lake-country vowels. Four or five words. He knew them. She’d taught him in April, in the textile building, laughing into the pillow while he said them wrong on purpose.

You are my home.

He said them back.

He said them properly, this time. Every sound. Not perfectly, nobody born on a river road in a border war could say them perfectly, but properly, slowly, the way he’d said her name for the first time at a table with a bowl of peas, as if he’d been practising. Because he had. In the truck. On the reservoir road. For two hours, out loud, with the stars in the water.

She went still against him.

Then he kissed her, before she could move.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was slow. Everything was slow, that night, that morning, because there was nowhere at all that either of them had to be, and nothing on the rack in the steel room, and nothing at the edge of the mattress, and nothing at all between him and the door but her. He touched her face, and didn’t check. She undid the buttons of his shirt, one by one, and he let her, and when she put her mouth on the old scar across his ribs he made the sound he’d made on the night of the typhoon, low and broken, like something giving way, and this time he didn’t stop it.

He cried. Not much. Not like the shower in October. He cried the way the rain had come off the hill on the Sunday at the end of November: steadily, without any fuss, the whole time, with his face in her neck. She held his head and didn’t say anything, and didn’t stop, and neither did he.

He talked to her. Of course he did. Low, against her skin, the whole time, her name and the court words and the stars in the reservoirs and the frog with the umbrella. That he’d been afraid of the door since he was nine. That he wasn’t afraid of it now. That he’d lie in this bed with her and grow old and complain about his knees and listen to her play the same four notes until she played five, and then six, and then something by a lake that he wouldn’t know the name of. She listened to all of it. She pulled him closer.

Afterwards, the sun came up behind the hill.

It came in through the open window, low and gold, across the big bed and the little silk blanket and the two of them under it, and across the floor to the bedroom door, which was open a hand’s width, the way she liked it.

He looked at the door.

He was on the door side. He’d ended up there again, without noticing. Between her and the room.

He didn’t move.

“I want you to stay,” said Evangeline, low, against his chest.

“I’m staying,” said Jun Hyuk.

He slept until noon. She lay awake beside him the whole morning, with the sun moving across the room, and her hand over his heart, and watched the door for him.

Nothing came through it at all.

chapters.title: Someone Else Finishes It
chapters.desc: Friday the thirteenth of December, six in the morning, a farmhouse on the far side of the river that is in the book with the frog on the cover. He watches it on a television in the inspection shed at the Iron Docks, on the bench, with her beside him and her lunch going cold.
chapters.epigraph: “Gu Shanlin, I’m arresting you.” — Inspector Song Wei Long, 6:04 a.m., 13 December 2024, on every channel by noon
chapters.content:
He went back to work on Monday.

He didn’t know what else to do. He’d slept until noon on Sunday and woken with the sun on the floor and her beside him, awake, watching the door, and lain there not knowing what day it was, and not minding. On Sunday afternoon he’d carried Mr. Bae’s compost. On Sunday evening he’d stood at the bottom of the garden and listened to her play four notes, and then, carefully, a fifth.

On Monday at half past five, he got up, and got dressed, and drove to the Iron Docks, and opened containers with Mrs. Koo until four.

Frozen fish. Tiles. Furniture. A container of pink bicycles again, the same company, the same pink. Nothing.

He didn’t ring Wei Long. Wei Long didn’t ring him. He didn’t look at the news. On Tuesday, Evangeline brought lunch in the tiffin and they sat on the bench outside the inspection shed and didn’t talk about it. On Wednesday Mrs. Koo asked him if he was all right and he said yes and found that it was true. On Thursday night he slept seven hours.

On the jetty he’d handed it to somebody else and walked away, and he didn’t know what would happen to it. That had been the point. Not knowing was harder than the bamboo had been.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Friday at half past twelve, she came through the gate of the Iron Docks with the tiffin and Bao behind her, the way she did every Friday, and the guard on the gate didn’t open it for her.

He came out of his box instead, fast, and held it open, and said something to her that Jun Hyuk couldn’t hear from across the yard, and pointed at the inspection shed.

Then Mrs. Koo came out of the shed and looked for Jun Hyuk, and found him at the far end of the stacks with a bolt cutter, and shouted his name. Not loudly. Mrs. Koo never shouted anything loudly. But she’d never shouted his name before at all.

He put the bolt cutter down.

✦ ✦ ✦

The television in the inspection shed was small and old and lived on top of the filing cabinet, and nobody ever turned it on except the fireman, for the horse racing on Saturdays. It was on now. Mrs. Koo had turned it up. The two retired customs men were standing in front of it with their arms folded. The fireman was sitting on the edge of a crate with his hand over his mouth.

Evangeline was standing just inside the door with the tiffin in both hands.

He came in and stood beside her.

On the screen, a reporter in a padded jacket was standing on a track in the hills with her breath smoking in the cold, in front of police tape and a white farmhouse with a red tin roof, and behind her, police cars. A great many police cars. The words along the bottom of the screen said Major trafficking arrests and then, as he watched, Suspected network head detained at dawn.

“—where, at four minutes past six this morning, officers from the city’s serious crimes unit, working with police from across the border for the first time in a joint operation of this kind, arrested a sixty-year-old man believed by investigators to have run one of the region’s largest people-smuggling networks for more than two decades. The man, named by police as Gu Shanlin, was—”

And there he was.

They’d filmed it. Of course they had. Wei Long would have made sure, Jun Hyuk thought afterwards. A man who’d watched a judge let someone walk out of court in a week would want the whole region to see this one walk out of a farmhouse.

The front door of the white farmhouse with the red tin roof. Six in the morning, still dark, floodlights. Two officers in vests. And between them, small and neat, in a grey suit with no tie, with his white hair uncombed and his hands behind his back, Gu Shanlin.

He looked smaller. On the jetty, under the lamp, through the scope, he’d been a man standing still in the light with all the time in the world. On a television in a shed at the Iron Docks, between two officers, in the floodlights, with his hands behind him, he looked like what he was. An old man in a suit who’d been woken up.

Behind them, coming out of the farmhouse door, very tall, in a long coat, with a face like something made of winter: Song Wei Long.

The camera found him. It held on him for a second as he stopped on the step and looked round, at the cars, at the cameras, at the dark. His face did nothing at all.

Then he said something to the officers, and they walked Gu Shanlin down the steps to the car, and as they reached it, something small fell out of the old man’s jacket pocket onto the frozen ground. The camera didn’t follow it. Nobody on the screen noticed.

Jun Hyuk did.

A toothpick. Ivory, gone yellow. Lying on the ground in the floodlights by the wheel of a police car.

✦ ✦ ✦

“—investigators say the arrests, which took place simultaneously at eleven addresses on both sides of the border, were made possible by evidence described by a senior source as extraordinarily detailed and covering, quote, every boat, every truck, and every payment for nine years. Fourteen further arrests have been made in the city this morning, including—”

Names. Faces. A shipping agent from the south. A man who owned a chain of massage parlours in the eastern district. A retired customs officer. A businessman in a good coat being led out of a tower on Harbour Road with his jacket over his handcuffs. A deputy director of something.

Jun Hyuk knew every one of them. He’d written every one of them down, in pencil, in capitals, at the back of the book with the frog on the cover.

He sat down on the crate by the door, the one the crane drivers called the bench, which someone had carried inside, and put his hands on his knees and watched the television.

Evangeline sat down beside him.

She didn’t put the tiffin down. She held it in her lap, the three stacked steel tins, the soup in the bottom still hot. She didn’t say anything. She sat beside him on the bench in her pale blue coat, very straight, with her shoulder against his arm, and watched with him.

✦ ✦ ✦

The farmhouse was in the frog book.

He’d written it down in April 2022, six months before West Basin. White farmhouse, red tin roof, end of the track past the second ford. Gu sleeps here when he crosses. Never more than two nights. Dogs. Back door to the orchard. He’d sat in a hill above it for three days that April and watched, and never got closer, because there were always dogs, and men, and Gu never stayed more than two nights.

Gu had gone back across the river on Sunday morning, after the jetty. To the farmhouse. Because it was safe, and he’d always been safe there, and there had never been anybody on the far bank who could arrest him for anything.

And Wei Long had read the frog book on Sunday. And on Monday he’d driven across the bridge to the far bank with three of the ten books in a briefcase and sat for four days in rooms with policemen from the other side who had been trying to arrest Gu Shanlin for longer than he had, and shown them the pages. And on Friday at four minutes past six, while Jun Hyuk was driving down the reservoir road to the docks after seven hours’ sleep, they’d gone up the track past the second ford together.

He hadn’t been there.

He watched it on a television on a filing cabinet in a shed, six hours later, sitting on a crate.

Somebody else had finished it.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the screen, the car with Gu Shanlin in it pulled away down the track into the dark, and the reporter turned back to the camera, and started to talk about the river, and the boats, and the people who’d died in them over twenty years. A number came up on the screen. It was a big number.

Then, for a moment, a photograph. Old, grainy, from a newspaper, nine years ago. A white refrigerated truck in a lay-by on a river road, with police round it and the back doors open. August 2015. Eleven women were found dead in a lorry abandoned near the border.

Jun Hyuk made a sound.

It wasn’t a word. It came up out of him the way it had in the shower in October, from somewhere far down, and he put his hand over his face.

Evangeline put the tiffin down on the floor.

She took his other hand, the one on his knee. She held it in both of hers in her lap. She didn’t say anything. In the shed, nobody said anything. Mrs. Koo reached up and turned the television off, and the two customs men went outside, and the fireman got up off his crate and followed them, and Mrs. Koo stood for a moment looking at the big man on the bench with his hand over his face and the tall woman holding his other one. Then she went outside too, and shut the door behind her gently.

They sat there.

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhao came at one.

He opened the door of the inspection shed without knocking and stood in it, in his black suit, with the yard and the cranes behind him, and looked at the two of them on the bench for four seconds.

Then he came in and shut the door and stood in front of them.

He didn’t say anything. He looked at Jun Hyuk’s face, which was wet and which Jun Hyuk didn’t bother to hide. He looked at Evangeline, holding his hand. He looked at the dead television on top of the filing cabinet.

“Hm,” he said.

He reached into the inside pocket of his jacket and took something out and held it out. A flask. Silver, old, dented, with the engraving on it worn nearly smooth.

Jun Hyuk looked at it.

“Old Zhao’s,” said Zhao. “He gave it to me the day I got out. For days like this.”

Jun Hyuk took it.

He didn’t drink. He held it. Zhao Zhendong stood in front of him a moment longer, and then put his hand on Jun Hyuk’s shoulder, once, briefly, heavily, the way you’d put a hand on a horse, and turned round and went out again, and shut the door.

Evangeline looked at the door. Then at him.

“That,” she said, “is the most I’ve ever heard him say.”

He laughed. It came out of him wet and broken and astonished, and he put his forehead down on her shoulder and laughed into her coat, and she put her hand on the back of his neck and held him there.

When he lifted his head she kissed him. In the inspection shed, on the bench, with the dead television on the filing cabinet and Zhao’s flask in his fist and the soup going cold in the tiffin at their feet. His face was still wet. She didn’t mind. He kissed her back slowly, as if there were all the time in the world now, which there was, and when Mrs. Koo opened the door ten minutes later to see if they wanted the heater on, she shut it again without a word.

✦ ✦ ✦

He read her the names that night.

In the garden, at the bottom, by the stream, in the dark, with the lamp from the long table on the end of its three extension leads, sitting on the flat stone that was the end of a tunnel from 1931. He’d brought the first book home. The rabbit. Wei Long had given it back on Thursday, by courier, with a note: I’ve copied it. You’ll want this one. He opened it to the last page.

Eleven names. In pencil, in capitals. Found out one by one, over two years, from families and villages and a woman at an aid station who’d kept a list.

He read them out, every one, slowly, with their ages, where he knew them, and where they’d come from. The youngest was sixteen.

Evangeline sat beside him on the stone and listened.

When he’d finished, she got up, and went up the garden to the glasshouse, and came back with a tray.

Eleven small pots. Rosemary. Cuttings she’d taken from the plant that had come through the winter on the ledge of the textile building and flowered blue in the spring, that she’d been rooting on the potting table since October without telling him why.

She knelt in the bed along the bottom wall, by the stream, in the lamplight, and dug eleven holes with the trowel Mrs. Bae had given her, and planted them, in a row, one by one.

He knelt beside her and helped.

“Rosemary,” she said, when the last one was in. “For remembrance.”

He looked at the eleven small plants in a row in the dark along the bottom wall of their garden, by the stream, at the top of a lane where nobody had ever come through a door for him.

“Will they grow?” he said.

“Rosemary always grows,” said Evangeline. “You can’t stop it. It’s the hardest thing in the garden to kill.”

He put his arm round her and kissed her temple, and then her mouth, cold, with soil on both their hands and the eleven small plants in a row beside their knees, and they knelt there in the cold earth, side by side, until the lamp on the end of its long cord flickered, and she said they should go in, and he said in a minute, and they stayed a while longer.

chapters.title: A Wedding With Six Guests
chapters.desc: The longest night of the year, a garden in December, herbs from the glasshouse in her hands, six guests and a seventh in scrubs. She talks. He can’t. And her wedding present to him is something nobody has been able to give him since he was seven.
chapters.epigraph: “You said if you came back, I was yours. You came back.” — Evangeline Lee, 21 December 2024
chapters.content:
The morning of the twenty-first was cold and clear, and the sky over the hill was the colour of her earrings.

He was up at five. He couldn’t help it. He went down to the kitchen in the dark and made coffee, three sugars, and stood at the back door with it, looking down the garden at the frost on the dug beds and the stream at the bottom going quick and dark between white stones and the row of eleven small rosemary plants along the bottom wall, which had not died, which were standing up straight in the cold as if they’d been told to.

She came down at six, in her cardigan, and stood beside him.

“You’re not supposed to see me,” she said. “Mrs. Bae says. Not before.”

“It’s six in the morning. You’re in a cardigan.”

“Mrs. Bae says it counts.”

He looked at her. Her hair was down. Her face was perfectly still. Behind the stillness she was so happy he could hardly look at her.

“I’ll go and stand in the glasshouse,” he said, “with my eyes shut.”

She took his coffee out of his hand and drank some of it, which she never did, because she said it tasted like syrup with a grudge, and made a face, and gave it back.

“Go on,” said Evangeline.

He went and stood in the glasshouse among the orchids with his eyes shut for twenty minutes, because she’d asked, and because he’d have stood anywhere she asked, with his eyes shut, for as long as she liked.

✦ ✦ ✦

They came up the lane at eleven.

Six. She’d said six, at the orchid stall in November a year ago, with her forehead against his, and he’d held her to it, and so had she.

Her father first, in his funeral suit, which was the only suit he owned and which he’d had cleaned and pressed for the occasion so that it looked, Raiden said, like a funeral suit that had won something. Then Elowen, in green, with a camellia in her hair, and Zhao beside her in black, who stopped at the gate and looked at the white wall and the fig tree and the green postbox with LEE in it for four seconds before he came in. Then Raiden, in a silver waistcoat he’d made himself, and Jinx, in a leather jacket over a red dress, with the steel ring on its chain. Then Eliana, in a hoodie, because she’d refused to wear anything else and nobody had the energy to argue, carrying a laptop and a wedding present in a box with too much ribbon.

Six.

Elara had a night shift. She’d sent a message at four in the morning:

Elara: On a twelve-hour. Two crash calls already. Will come when I can. Start without me. DON’T START WITHOUT ME.

Old Nam had sent noodles. Her cousin’s girl brought them up from the border on the first bus in two enormous pots wrapped in towels, with a note in Nam’s terrible handwriting: I don’t go to weddings. Long life noodles. Don’t cut them. Don’t let him cut them. He’ll cut them.

And Mr. and Mrs. Bae watched over the wall, standing on two chairs in their own garden, the way all the best weddings on the lane had been watched for fifty years, with Pudding the cat sitting on the wall between them like a ginger usher.

✦ ✦ ✦

There was no arch. No flowers, except the camellia in Elowen’s hair. The garden in December was bare beds and frost and the fig tree with no leaves and the stream at the bottom, and Evangeline had wanted it exactly like that.

The celebrant was a small brisk woman with a briefcase, recommended by Ms. Fong, who said she had married people on boats and on mountains and once in a lift, and that a garden was very restful. She stood at the bottom of the path with her back to the stream and her papers on a music stand from the music room.

He stood beside her. In the good shirt, the one Evangeline had sewn a button on in the karaoke flat two years ago, and a black suit that Elowen had taken him to buy in November in a shop on Harbour Road where they’d measured him for an hour and he hadn’t looked at the price. With his hands clasped in front of him, because he didn’t know what else to do with them.

He was looking at the house.

From an open window at the back, the north window of the music room, faintly, someone began to play.

He hadn’t asked. He’d promised her he wouldn’t get her anything. But he’d rung Mrs. Lai a week ago and asked, and Mrs. Lai had said she’d been waiting to be asked since the Glass Pavilion, and that she wouldn’t take a fee for this either, and that she would sit in the music room with the window open and not come out, so that nobody could say she was a seventh guest.

It was the same piece. The old slow one, low and warm and sad, from the night of her birthday.

The green door opened.

✦ ✦ ✦

She came down the four stone steps on her father’s arm.

She was wearing white. Not a wedding dress.
