A plain long white dress, simple, high at the neck, with long sleeves, that she’d chosen herself in a shop in the old town after trying on a great many, and the aquamarines, and her hair up, with a plain silver pin in it. Bent a little. The kind you’d use to put your hair up in a hurry before you played. And in her hands, instead of flowers, a bunch of herbs from the glasshouse, tied with a strip of white silk: rosemary, and thyme, and mint, and bay, and one white orchid in the middle.

He stopped breathing.

Behind him the stream went over its stones, and over the wall Mrs. Bae said oh loudly and was hushed by her husband, and from the music room window the viola went on, low and slow, and his bride came down the garden path towards him between the frosted beds on her father’s arm.

Lin Jian stopped halfway.

He’d done that before, at a flower shop. Elowen had told her. He stopped halfway down the path and turned to his daughter and said something to her, low, that nobody else heard. Evangeline listened. Then she nodded. And her father bent his heavy grey head and kissed her forehead, which he had never once done in twenty-six years, and they walked the rest of the way.

He put her hand into Jun Hyuk’s.

He held them both together for a moment between his big swollen-knuckled hands. He looked up at the man who had once held a knife to his throat.

“I’m asking you,” said Lin Jian. His voice was rough. “To make her happy. I’m asking. Not telling.”

“I know,” said Jun Hyuk. “I heard.”

Lin Jian nodded, and let go, and went and stood beside Raiden, who put his arm round him without looking.

✦ ✦ ✦

The celebrant said what celebrants say. He didn’t hear a word of it. He was holding her hand and looking at her face, and she was looking back, smiling at him openly in front of everyone.

Then the celebrant said they could say something to each other, if they’d like.

He opened his mouth.

He’d written it. Of course he had. He’d written it in the truck, and on the bench at the docks, and in the glasshouse that morning with his eyes shut. It was long. It had the container in it, and the hospital, and the towels, and the menu, and a great many other things, and he’d practised it out loud in the truck.

Nothing came.

He stood in his garden in December with her hand in his and his mouth open, and nothing at all came out. Not one word. The man who’d talked to everyone about everything for thirty-four years stood in front of six people and a celebrant and two neighbours on chairs and a ginger cat, and couldn’t.

His face went still.

She watched it happen, and her own face went soft and fierce at once, and she took his other hand too, so she was holding both, and she spoke instead.

✦ ✦ ✦

“You opened the door,” said Evangeline.

Her voice was low and level and carried, in the cold clear air, all the way to the wall.

“In a container. At West Basin. I was standing in the middle of it, and you opened the door, and you crouched down so you wouldn’t frighten anyone. And you said stay behind me.” She held his hands. “I did. For two years. Behind you in the stacks, and on the roofs, and on the stairs, and at my father’s office, and on my mother’s step. I followed every rule you ever wrote. Except one. I came back.”

Over the wall, Mrs. Bae had her hand over her mouth.

“You said if you didn’t come back, I’d have somewhere to go,” said Evangeline. “A house with a fig tree, and a name that wasn’t mine. And if you did come back, I was yours.” She looked up at him. “You came back. Every time. From across the river, and from Kiln Street, and from the floor of Nam’s shop, and from the jetty, with your hands empty.”

He was crying. He didn’t stop it.

“I’ve never had anything that was mine,” she said. “Not a name. Not a birthday. Not a room nobody could take me out of. You gave me a ring with a way out in it, and then you gave me a reason not to use it.” Her voice shook, once. She let it. “I’m not behind you any more. I’m not in front of you, either. I’m beside you. That’s where I’m staying.”

She stopped.

The viola, from the open window, had stopped too. Nobody in the garden moved.

“You can talk now,” said Evangeline, low, just to him.

He couldn’t. He tried. He opened his mouth and what came out was her name, the whole of it, all four syllables, the way he’d said it at a table with a bowl of peas.

“Evangeline,” he said.

That was the whole of his speech, in the end, and everybody in the garden knew it was enough.

✦ ✦ ✦

He put the ring on her finger. Not a new one. The same plain silver band, with the coordinates inside, that she’d taken off for the first time since April last year that morning, and given to Raiden to hold, and that Raiden had kept in his top pocket all through the service and checked every few minutes. She put a ring on his: plain, silver, the same as hers, from the jeweller on Harbour Road who had a broken necklace in the window, which Aurelia had made herself and sent up the lane by courier on Thursday with a card that said No charge. Don’t argue. — A. Inside it, engraved small, there were coordinates too.

He looked at them. He didn’t know where they were.

“Here,” said Evangeline. “The gate.”

The celebrant said the rest. Nobody heard that either.

When he kissed her, under the bare fig tree in front of six people and two neighbours on chairs, Raiden cheered so loudly that Pudding fell off the wall.

✦ ✦ ✦

Elara came at a quarter to two, in scrubs, with her hair falling out of its clip and her hospital lanyard still round her neck, at a run up the lane from the taxi, shouting I said don’t start without me, and found them all at the long dark table in the front room with the windows open, eating Old Nam’s long-life noodles, uncut, with the viola case on the window seat and the white silk from the herbs tied round the neck of the jar of the last salted lemons.

She stopped in the doorway.

She looked at her sister, at the head of the table, in white, with the bent silver pin in her hair, laughing at something Jinx had said. Laughing out loud. With her whole face.

Elara burst into tears.

“Seventh guest,” said Raiden, and pulled out a chair for her.

✦ ✦ ✦

She gave him his present at dusk.

He’d thought there wasn’t one. She’d made him promise, so he’d assumed she’d promised herself. At five o’clock, when the light was going and the others were in the kitchen arguing about who’d washed which pot, she took him by the hand out onto the verandah, and sat him down on the top step, in the cold, and put an envelope in his hands.

Old, brown, soft. With a stamp on the front of an aid organisation that had worked on the river road in the nineties, and a typed label: Records. Station 4. 1998.

He looked at it. He didn’t understand.

“Wei Long,” said Evangeline. “In October. I asked him if the aid stations on the river kept records. When they took people in. He found the organisation. They’d moved everything to a warehouse across the border. A woman there looked for six weeks.” She sat down beside him on the step. “Open it.”

He opened it.

There was one card inside. An admission card, the kind they’d had at the aid stations, printed in three languages, filled in by hand. The ink had gone brown. The card was soft as cloth with age.

The name at the top was a woman’s. A name he hadn’t heard since he was seven years old, since a tent by a river, since the last time anyone had said it. His mother’s.

And under it, in the space for dependants, in a different hand, a careful, small, frightened hand, the handwriting of a woman writing her son’s name for a stranger in a language she didn’t speak well:

Lee Jun Hyuk. Boy. Born 23 November 1990. The first snow.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t move.

He sat on the top step of his verandah, in his wedding suit, at dusk, with the card in his hands, and didn’t move at all.

“Your birthday,” said Evangeline. “Your real one. Your mother wrote it down.” She put her hand on his back. “You were thirty-four last month. You didn’t know.”

His breath went out of him.

He bent over the card on his knees, in the cold, and held it in both hands as if it were the only warm thing left in the world, and she put her arms round him from the side and her face against his shoulder and held on, and from the kitchen, behind them, through the open window, they could hear Raiden telling everyone loudly that he had definitely washed the big pot.

“You found my mother’s handwriting,” he said, at last. Barely a sound.

“You found my mother’s music for me,” said Evangeline. “I wanted to find you something back.” She held him tighter.

He turned and put his face in her neck, in her white dress, with the card held against his chest, and stayed there until the light was gone and the lamp in the front room came on behind them, and the owl started on the hill, and over the wall Mrs. Bae, who had never got down off her chair, blew her nose loudly and went in to start the dinner.

chapters.title: Forgiven
chapters.desc: Epilogue. Three years later, the longest night of the year. Eleven rosemary bushes as high as the wall, a viola that sounds like a viola now, and a young woman in a nurse’s uniform at the gate with a letter.
chapters.epigraph: “I hold the hair now. Every shift. I wanted you to know.” — Nuo, at the gate of No. 9, 21 December 2027
chapters.content:
The rosemary was as high as the wall.

He noticed it every morning now, at five, when he stood at the back door with his coffee and looked down the garden. Eleven bushes in a row along the bottom wall by the stream, grey-green and thick and woody at the base, so big that Mrs. Bae said they’d have to be cut back in the spring or they’d have the wall down. They flowered blue every year in March. The bees came from all over the valley for them. Evangeline cut sprigs from them for the kitchen, and for the jar on the long dark table, and once a year, on the thirteenth of December, for a small bunch tied with string that she left on the flat stone by the stream at the end of the tunnel from 1931, and that he never asked about and always found.

Rosemary always grows, she’d said, the night they planted it. You can’t stop it.

He drank his coffee, three sugars, and went to work.

✦ ✦ ✦

He ran the whole harbour now.

Not the Iron Docks. All of it. In the spring of 2025, after the arrests and the newspapers and a long meeting in a room in the Department of Trade with eleven men in suits who did not want to be in a room with him, the city had made a law, the first of its kind in the region, that every container coming into every port in the city would be opened. Not scanned. Opened. And somebody had to be in charge of opening them, and Inspector Song Wei Long had sat at the end of the table in his long coat and said a name, and the eleven men had looked at each other, and then at Zhao Zhendong, who was sitting at the other end in black and said nothing at all, and then hm.

So now he had a hundred and forty inspectors, in five ports, in grey overalls with a small open door embroidered on the pocket, which had been Mrs. Koo’s idea. Mrs. Koo ran the training. The two retired customs men ran the night shifts. The fireman had married one of the crane drivers. They had found, in three years, two hundred and nine people in boxes, and every one of them had come out alive, because the boxes had been opened in time.

He opened one himself, every morning, the first one, at six. He’d never stopped. Nobody asked him to. It was just the first thing he did, after the coffee, before anything else: the bolt cutter, the bar, the door, the torch.

If there was ever anybody in there, he wanted the first voice they heard to be his.

✦ ✦ ✦

He’d testified.

In March of 2026, in the High Court, for eleven days, in his real name, in a suit Elowen had made him buy, about every page of ten exercise books with cartoons on the covers. Gu Shanlin’s lawyers had gone through every page. They’d gone through him. For eleven days they’d asked him who he was and where he came from and what he’d done and where he’d been on certain nights in certain years, and he had stood in the witness box and answered every question that was about the books, plainly, in his rough border voice, and to every question that wasn’t, the prosecutor had stood up and said objection, and been upheld, while Ms. Fong sat on the bench behind him, small and grey and terrifying, and wrote it all down.

Evangeline had sat in the public gallery every day. At the back. In her pale blue coat. Watching the door.

On the twentieth of March, a Friday, at four in the afternoon, the jury came back.

Gu Shanlin was sixty-two. He’d die in prison. The judge said so, at the sentencing, in plain words, in a voice with nothing in it. Wei Long, in the front row, didn’t move a muscle. Afterwards, on the steps of the High Court, with the cameras, he said eleven words to the reporters, which was more than anyone had ever heard him say to a reporter, and then walked down the steps to his car.

Jun Hyuk had gone out of the back of the court, with her, and Bao had driven them home, and he’d stood at the bottom of the garden by the rosemary for an hour in the dark without saying anything, and she’d stood beside him, and then they’d gone in.

He hadn’t felt what he’d thought he’d feel. Nine years he’d waited to feel it. It didn’t come. What came instead, standing by the rosemary, was something much quieter and much stranger, that he didn’t have a word for. It felt like putting down something he’d been carrying so long he’d forgotten it was there, and finding that his arms didn’t know what to do.

He’d asked her about it, in bed.

“Tired,” said Evangeline. “It’s called tired. You’ve been carrying it a long time.” She put her hand over his heart. “You’re allowed to be tired now.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He talked for both of them, at parties.

That had happened without either of them deciding it. In the spring of 2025 the invitations had started coming, the way they did once your name was in the newspapers for something good: galas, dinners, openings, the Chen Foundation’s spring gala, where Aurelia had looked at him across a room full of people in silk and said to Evangeline, your husband is the only man here who’s asked the waiter’s name. And Evangeline hated them. She always had. She hated rooms full of people who wanted to talk, and cameras, and being looked at, and small talk, most of all small talk, which she said was like being made to eat sand one grain at a time.

So he talked. He talked to the ministers and the bankers and the wives of the bankers and the man from the newspaper. He talked about the weather and the harbour and the container ports of the south and the price of tea. He talked so much and so cheerfully and so endlessly that nobody ever noticed that the tall still woman on his arm, in pale blue, with a face like something carved, hadn’t said a single word all evening. He talked enough for both of them. She stood beside him with her hand on his sleeve and watched the exits and watched the people, and every so often, when someone was particularly awful, she’d move her thumb on his arm, once, and he’d know, and steer them away.

Aurelia had kept count. Evangeline had said eleven words to her in their first five years, and not one since, and Aurelia said so at every New Year, in the tall house in the Walled City, and then lost to her at mahjong, and called it a moral victory.

✦ ✦ ✦

She played now.

Three years. Mrs. Lai still came on Tuesdays. Mrs. Lai said that she was not good yet, and would not be for some time, and that it didn’t matter, because she was no longer bad. That was the whole difference. The sound that came out of the music room window in the afternoons was a viola’s sound now. Low and warm. A little rough at the edges. Not a cat being stepped on any more. A voice in the next room that you knew and couldn’t quite hear.

She’d learned one piece all the way through. Only one. An old one, from the lake country, simple, that Teo’s mother had written out for her from memory in a letter in the first year, because she said it was the one the girl by the lake had played at the summer festival every year, before she went to the palace.

They’d been to the lake. In the summer of 2025, with the King’s permission and without his guards. They’d stayed a week in the house that had been her mother’s, which was small and white and stood at the edge of the water with a wooden jetty going out from it, and she’d sat on the end of the jetty in the evenings with the photograph beside her and looked at the water and the hills going down into it, and he’d sat behind her on the boards with his back against a post, and watched her, and not talked, for a whole week. On the last evening she’d got up off the end of the jetty and come back along the boards to him and sat down in his lap, against the post, with the photograph left face up on the planks and the water going dark all round them, and kissed him until the frogs started up in the reeds and he’d forgotten every word he knew. Teo’s mother had brought honey. The King had sent a letter, in his own hand, the first one. It said I’m told you’re happy. I’m glad. And under it, smaller: I’m told he talks.

She’d laughed until she cried at that, on the jetty. He’d stopped counting at sixty.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was the twenty-first of December, 2027. A Tuesday. Their third anniversary. The longest night of the year.

He came home from the docks at five and got out of the truck, which he still drove, which Jinx had rebuilt twice and refused to let him replace, and stood at the bottom of the garden with his bag on his shoulder, and listened.

The piece from the lake. All the way through. A little rough at the edges, the way it always was. He stood by the gate and listened to the whole of it, every note, coming out of the open north window of the music room into the cold dusk, and didn’t go up the path until it had finished.

Then he turned round, because there was somebody at the gate.

✦ ✦ ✦

She was about twenty-four.

Small, with short hair, in a dark coat over a pale blue nurse’s uniform with the badge of Harbourside General on the pocket, and white shoes, and a lanyard round her neck. She was standing in the lane by the green postbox with LEE on it, holding an envelope in both hands, looking up at the house as if she weren’t sure she was allowed to be there.

He’d have known her anywhere.

“Nuo,” he said.

She jumped. She turned round and saw him, and her face crumpled the way it had once before, in the back of a truck, in October five years ago, when he’d handed her a bottle of water the size of her head.

“I’m sorry,” she said. “I’m sorry. I didn’t know if I should. She gave me the address. Years ago. She said I could come any time. I never did. I didn’t know what I’d say.” She was holding the envelope tightly. “I qualified. In the summer. And I’ve been on the emergency department since September, the night shifts, the same one, the same corridor. And last night—” She stopped.

He didn’t say anything. He waited.

“Last night they brought a girl in,” said Nuo. “Nineteen. From the docks. From a box. One of yours found her. In a container of tinned pineapple. Four days.” Her voice wobbled. “She was sick in the toilet. Like I was. And I sat with her on the floor. And I held her hair.”

He stood still.

“I hold the hair now,” said Nuo. “Every shift. I wanted you to know.” She held out the envelope. “I wrote it down. Because I knew I’d cry. I’ve written it a hundred times since I was nineteen. I never sent it. I didn’t know your name, at first. And then when I did, I didn’t know how to start.”

He took the envelope.

✦ ✦ ✦

He read it standing in the lane by the postbox, in the dusk, with the light going behind the hill and the lamp in the front room of No. 9 coming on behind the windows.

It was one page. In a young woman’s handwriting, round and careful, in blue ink. It didn’t say very much. It said that she’d been in a box with four other women for two days in October 2022 at West Basin, and that the door had opened, and that a man had crouched down in it so he wouldn’t frighten them, and said hello, and listen to me, and stay behind me. It said that she had been going to die in that box, and had known it, and had stopped being afraid of it, which was the worst part. It said that she was alive. It said that she was a nurse. It said that she had a cat, and a flat with two other nurses, and a boyfriend who worked in the hospital pharmacy and was very kind and bad at cooking. It said that every time a frightened person was brought into her department, she crouched down so she wouldn’t frighten them, and said hello, and listen to me, and that she’d learned it from him.

And at the bottom, in the same round careful hand, smaller, as if she’d come back to it later:

I’ve been angry with God for a lot of things. Not that.

Whatever you did before that night, you opened the door. You don’t owe anybody anything any more. Not me. Not anyone. I wanted to tell you that. I hope somebody already has.

He read it twice.

Then he stood in the lane by the green postbox with the letter in his hand and didn’t move, with the cold coming down off the hill, and Nuo standing in front of him in her white shoes, crying, and not wiping it.

✦ ✦ ✦

The green door opened behind him.

He didn’t turn round. He heard her on the verandah. On the steps. On the path between the beds, which weren’t bare in December any more but full of the things she grew: winter greens, and herbs, and the dark glossy leaves of the camellia Elowen had given them for the second anniversary. On the gravel by the gate.

She stopped beside him.

She looked at Nuo. Nuo looked at her. And Evangeline Lee, who had said eleven words to Aurelia Chen in five years and never once in her life said anything she didn’t mean, crossed the lane to the young woman in the nurse’s uniform, and put her arms round her, without being asked, the way she’d held Elowen at a sink and Raiden on a floor, and held on.

Over her shoulder, she looked at him.

At his face, in the dusk. At the letter in his hand.

She saw it. She saw what had happened. She’d always been able to see what happened to him, since the first night, by the third post at West Basin, when he came back from the tower and didn’t talk. She saw it go through him now, standing in the lane outside his own house with a letter in his hand from a girl he’d given a bottle of water to.

He’d been told before. By her, in the dark, on the twenty-second of June. You opened mine. By the silence of a dying man in a hospital bed in a flat below the Peak, with a yellow face who’d asked him to stay until he slept. By ten exercise books in the boot of a police car, and a jury, and a judge. By eleven rosemary bushes that wouldn’t die. By a payslip on a fridge with a fish.

He’d heard all of it. He’d never once let himself believe it.

He stood in the lane in the last of the light, on the longest night of the year, and let himself.

✦ ✦ ✦

Nuo stayed for dinner. Of course she did. Mrs. Bae came round with a chestnut cake as soon as she saw a stranger at the gate, which was how Mrs. Bae always found out who people were, and Mr. Bae came round behind her and shook Nuo’s hand and said nurse, and nodded, as if something had been settled. Pudding sat on Nuo’s lap all evening. Nuo said she’d never been chosen by a cat before. Jun Hyuk said you got used to it.

She left at ten, in a taxi he’d paid for and she’d tried to pay for and he’d won.

They stood at the gate, the two of them, and watched the taxi’s lights go away down Fig Tree Lane, past the Baes’ and the house below and the house below that, all the way down to the stream and round the bend and gone.

It was cold. The sky over the hill was black and full of stars. The longest night of the year.

“After this,” said Evangeline, “the nights get shorter.”

“I know,” he said.

She leaned against him.

He put his arm round her. She was wearing the pale blue coat. Her hair was coming loose from its pin, the bent silver one, the one you’d use to put your hair up in a hurry before you played.

“Jun Hyuk,” she said.

“Mm.”

“Come inside with me.”

He looked down at her, at her face in the light from the lamp in the window behind them, carved and still and not still at all.

“Yes,” he said.

He kissed her first. At the gate, in the cold, under all those stars, three years married, the way he’d once kissed her at a bus stop on River Bridge Road in front of a woman with a chicken in a basket: as if he’d been doing it for years. Then not like that at all. She put both hands inside his coat and held on, and he leaned her back against the white wall by the green postbox, and kissed her until the lamp in the window behind them was the only light left on the lane.

They went up the path together, side by side, between the winter beds, and up the four stone steps, and across the verandah, and in through the green door. On the inside of it, at her eye height, the menu from Nam’s Noodles moved in the draught: ten rules, in two hands, in pencil, gone soft and grey at the folds.

He looked at it as he shut the door. He did, every time. Seven. DON’T COME BACK. She had broken that one more times than either of them could count.

He turned the lock. There was only the one now. Then he followed her in.

chapters.title: A Princess at the Supermarket
chapters.desc: November 2022. She is twenty-four and has never once bought her own groceries. He follows her round the biggest supermarket in the border town at a distance of six metres, pretending not to, until the vegetable scales defeat her.
chapters.epigraph: “You have to weigh them first. Over there. And then it prints a sticker. Nobody tells you. I didn’t know for years either.” — Lee Jun Hyuk, aisle four
chapters.content:
The cook had always done it. For twenty-four years, in the tall house in the Walled City, food had arrived. Fish came in the mornings, wrapped in newspaper. Vegetables came in baskets. Rice came in sacks that two men carried up from a van. Evangeline had stood in the cook’s kitchen at night with her mother and learned to make soup and dumplings and steamed egg and salted fish rice, but she’d never once in her life been the person who went out and got the things you made them with.

She’d decided to.

It was the third week of November, and she’d been coming up to the karaoke flat for a month, and the fridge in it, which was a small white box under the counter that hummed, had in it three cans of coffee and a bottle of soy sauce that had gone solid. She’d been bringing food from home in flasks. It wasn’t enough. It wasn’t hers.

So on a Thursday, after she’d put her phone in the jar at Nam’s, she walked down River Bridge Road to the big supermarket by the bus station, which she’d seen from the bus every time she came, and which had a sign over the door with a smiling cartoon carrot on it.

She didn’t know he was behind her until the automatic doors.

✦ ✦ ✦

He hadn’t meant to follow her.

He’d been at Nam’s counter when she came in through the back with her canvas bag, and he’d watched her put the phone in the jar, and then, instead of going up the alley to the steel door, she’d gone out of the front of the shop and turned left, down the road, towards the bus station.

He’d looked at Nam.

Nam had looked at him with an expression of great patience and gone on chopping.

So he went after her. Not close. Six metres. On the other side of the road. With his cap pulled down. In case. It was the border town and she was a woman who’d been in a box five weeks ago, and he told himself that was the reason, and he believed it for about as long as it took her to walk up to the supermarket with the cartoon carrot on it and stop in front of the doors.

The doors slid open.

She jumped.

She stood in front of them, very straight, with her canvas bag over her shoulder, and looked at them, and they slid shut again. She took a step forward. They slid open. She stood still. They waited. She went in, quite fast, the way you’d go past a dog that might bite.

He stood on the other side of the road and put his hand over his mouth.

Then he crossed it, and went in after her.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was a very big supermarket. It was the only big one in the border town, and on a Thursday afternoon it was full of everybody: the vegetable sellers buying what they didn’t grow, the men from the building sites buying beer and noodles, the women from both sides of the river with their trolleys and their lists, and a great many children.

She stood just inside the doors and looked at it.

He stood behind a tower of tinned pineapple, six metres away, and looked at her looking.

Her face didn’t move. It never did. But she was holding her canvas bag with both hands, the way you’d hold a rail on a boat, and she’d stopped in the middle of the entrance where people had to go round her, and a woman with a trolley said something sharp, and she didn’t hear.

Then she saw the baskets.

He watched her see them. A stack of red plastic baskets by the door, with handles. He watched her look at them, and at the other people taking them, and at her own canvas bag, and work it out. She took a basket. She held it the way the others held them, on her arm. She looked down at it as if it had been handed to her by a stranger at a station and she wasn’t sure what was in it.

She went down the first aisle.

✦ ✦ ✦

It took her forty minutes to do what would have taken anybody else ten.

She read everything. Of course she did. She picked up every packet she was going to buy and turned it over and read the back, all of it, the way she read the labels on medicine and the instructions on seed packets. She compared things. She stood in front of the rice for six minutes with two bags in her hands, one in each, reading them, and a small boy stopped beside her and stared up at her as if she were a statue that had come to life.

She put both bags back and took a third.

In the aisle with the tins, she stood in front of the soy sauce for ages and then took one of every kind.

In the aisle with the towels and the household things, which was at the back, next to a section with pots and pans and a sign that said HOME, she stopped for even longer. He watched her pick up a towel, a thin white one, the cheapest kind, and feel it between her fingers, and put it back. And another. And put it back. And then walk all the way along the aisle to the end, where there was a shelf of better ones in plastic, and stand there, and read the labels, and choose three.

He didn’t know why she was buying towels. He didn’t own towels. He thought perhaps they were for her.

He’d find out on Friday.

✦ ✦ ✦

The vegetables defeated her.

He’d known they would. They defeated everybody. In the big supermarket by the bus station, you didn’t take your vegetables to the till. You put them in a plastic bag from a roll and took them to a scale at the end of the aisle, with a screen, and you pressed the picture of the right vegetable on the screen, and the scale weighed them and printed a sticker, and you put the sticker on the bag. Nobody told you. There was no sign. It was the kind of thing you were supposed to have always known.

She went straight past the scale to the till with a bag of spring onions and a bag of ginger and a bag of greens.

The woman at the till looked at the bags. Then at her.

“They’re not weighed,” she said.

Evangeline looked at her.

“You have to weigh them,” said the woman, in the voice of a woman who said it forty times a day. “Over there. At the scale. And then it prints a sticker. Then you bring them back.”

Evangeline looked at the bags in her basket. Then over her shoulder, at the end of the aisle, at the scale with the screen. Then at the queue behind her, which was six people long and growing, and was looking at her.

Her face didn’t move at all.

But her ears had gone red.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came round the end of the tinned pineapple.

He’d been standing behind it for forty minutes telling himself that he was going to stay there, out of sight, the whole time, and walk out after her and follow her back up River Bridge Road and never mention it. And then her ears went red.

He came round the pineapple and up the side of the queue and stopped beside her at the till.

“Here,” he said. “Give them to me.”

She turned round.

She looked at him. At his cap. At his face under it. She didn’t look surprised. She looked, for a second, like a woman who’d known exactly where he was for forty minutes and had been waiting to see how long he’d last.

He took the three bags of vegetables out of her basket.

“You have to weigh them first,” he said. “Over there. And then it prints a sticker. Nobody tells you. I didn’t know for years either. I used to just take them to the till and the woman would sigh at me.” He nodded to the woman at the till. “Sorry, auntie. Two minutes.”

The woman at the till looked at him, all of him, and decided to wait.

He took the vegetables to the scale. He weighed the spring onions and pressed the picture of spring onions and the scale printed a sticker. He weighed the ginger. He weighed the greens, and there were four pictures of greens that all looked the same, and he stood there for some time pressing them, and the wrong sticker came out, and he said a word he’d learned at ten, and pressed another one.

When he turned round, she was standing behind him.

She’d left the queue. She’d left the basket at the till. She’d come all the way down the aisle to watch.

“Show me,” said Evangeline.

✦ ✦ ✦

He showed her.

She weighed the greens again herself, to see how it worked. She pressed the right picture. She looked at the sticker that came out with an expression of great seriousness, as if it were a document, and stuck it on the bag, very straight.

Then she took the bag back to the till, past the queue, and put it in her basket, and the woman at the till scanned everything, and Evangeline took her mother’s card out of her purse, the one she’d never once used until October, and held it out.

The woman at the till looked at the card. Then at her.

“You tap it,” she said. “On there. The machine.”

Evangeline looked at the machine.

Behind her, Jun Hyuk reached past her shoulder and tapped the machine twice with one finger, to show her where, without touching her hand, and she held the card to it, and the machine beeped.

She looked down at it.

“Good,” she said.

The woman at the till laughed. She couldn’t help it. She was a tired woman of fifty in a supermarket in a border town at four in the afternoon, with a queue of six, and she laughed out loud at the tall still young woman with red ears, and at the enormous man behind her who’d turned her card round, and then she put her hand over her mouth and said sorry, sorry, dear, and gave them their receipt.

✦ ✦ ✦

He carried the bags.

She didn’t let him at first. She picked up all four of them herself, at the end of the till, and he stood and watched her try to work out how to carry four heavy bags and a canvas bag and her purse with two arms, and then she put them down again and looked at him.

He picked them up.

They walked back up River Bridge Road together in the late afternoon, not six metres apart now, side by side, him with the four bags and her with the canvas one, past the bus station and the pharmacy and the man who sold spring onions on the bridge, who looked at the bag of spring onions from the supermarket in Jun Hyuk’s hand with deep reproach.

“You followed me,” said Evangeline.

“I didn’t.”

She looked at him.

“I was in the area,” he said. “There was some pineapple I wanted to look at. For a long time.”

She didn’t say anything. But at the steel door at the side of the karaoke bar, with the four bags at his feet while he found his key, she put her hand flat on his arm, for a second, above the elbow, lightly. And then took it away.

He stood there with the key in his hand.

Then he turned round. He hadn’t meant to. She was right behind him, closer than she’d ever stood, in the narrow space by the steel door with the alley at her back, and she didn’t step away. She looked up at him. He looked at her mouth, and knew she’d seen him do it, and couldn’t stop.

It would have taken nothing. Half a step he didn’t have room for, and his head bent, and the rest.

He didn’t touch her. He’d made himself a rule in October, outside a hospital, with her hand on his sleeve: she would decide. Every time. She’d come to him or she wouldn’t, and he’d never once put a hand on her first, and he wasn’t going to start in an alley because her ears had gone red at a till.

“The greens,” he said. His voice came out wrong. “They’ll wilt.”

Her eyes changed. She might have been laughing at him. It might have been something else entirely.

She stayed exactly where she was for one second longer than she needed to. Then she stepped back, and he let them in, and she put the shopping away, every single thing, in the cupboard and the little humming fridge, in rows, with the labels facing out. The soy sauce, all seven kinds. The rice she’d spent six minutes choosing.

The towels she didn’t unpack. She put them, still in their plastic, in her canvas bag, and took them home on the six o’clock bus.

He didn’t ask.

On Friday she brought them back, washed, and folded in thirds, and rolled.

chapters.title: Lee Jun Hyuk Tries to Cook Breakfast
chapters.desc: November 2024, Fig Tree Lane. He wants to bring her breakfast in bed, once, like a husband in a film. The smoke alarm was not consulted.
chapters.epigraph: “I’ve cleaned a rifle in the dark in four minutes. I can make an egg.” — Lee Jun Hyuk, 6:12 a.m., before the egg
chapters.content:
He’d seen it in a film.

Years ago, in a hotel room in a port city in the south, at three in the morning, waiting for a man who never came. The television had been on with the sound off. A man in a striped apron carrying a tray up a staircase: orange juice, a flower in a glass, eggs, toast in a rack. A woman in a white bed sitting up and laughing. He’d watched the whole thing without the sound, with his back against the door, and thought it was the stupidest thing he’d ever seen.

He’d thought about it, on and off, for nine years.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the third Sunday in November, at ten to six in the morning, he got out of bed carefully, so as not to wake her, and went down to the kitchen of No. 9 in his bare feet.

He had a plan. He always had a plan. Eggs, two, the way she liked them, with the edges gone crisp. Rice from the rice cooker, which he’d set the night before. Greens. Tea in the dark clay teapot that remembered things. And a flower in a glass, because the man in the film had a flower in a glass, and there were white orchids in the glasshouse, and he’d cut one.

He’d never cooked anything in his life that wasn’t instant noodles or a tin. She’d cooked every meal he’d eaten for two years. He’d watched her do it every day. He knew how.

He’d cleaned a rifle in the dark in four minutes. He could make an egg.

✦ ✦ ✦

The rice was fine. The rice cooker had done it.

The greens he washed, the way she did, three times, and put in a pan with garlic and oil, the way she did, and turned up the heat, the way he thought she did, and turned round to cut the orchid.

When he turned back, the garlic was black.

He looked at it. He took the pan off the heat and looked at the black garlic for a while, and then threw it away, and started again, and this time he didn’t turn round. The greens went limp and bright and smelled almost right, and he put them on a plate and stood back from them, breathing hard, as if he’d defused something.

Then the eggs.

He cracked them into the pan the way she did, one-handed, against the edge. The first one went in. The second one went mostly in, and partly down the front of the stove, and partly on his foot. He looked at his foot. He looked at the pan, where one egg was sitting in the oil and starting to go white at the edges, and a second egg was a great deal of shell.

“No,” he said, under his breath. “No, no, no.”

He started picking out shell with his fingers.

The oil was hot. He’d turned the gas right up, because she always got the edges crisp, and crisp meant hot, he’d reasoned, and he was a big man and believed in doing things properly. He burnt two fingers. He said the word he’d learned at ten. He got most of the shell out. The edges of the first egg were going from white to golden to brown to something else, and the oil had started to smoke, and he looked round for the spatula, and it wasn’t where she kept it, because he’d put it somewhere else at half past five when he got the plates out, and he didn’t know where.

The smoke alarm went off.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was a good smoke alarm. Raiden had chosen it. It was the loudest smoke alarm Jun Hyuk had ever heard, and he had been in buildings that were on fire. It screamed. It screamed in the hall and the kitchen and the stairwell and the bedroom, because Raiden had linked them all, and up the hill an owl that had been settling for the day took off from the fig tree in alarm, and next door, at No. 7, a light came on.

He turned off the gas. He opened the back door. He opened every window in the kitchen, all four, which opened outwards, onto the cold grey November morning. He stood under the alarm in the hall in his bare feet with egg on one of them and flapped a tea towel at it.

It went on screaming.

He heard her on the stairs.

✦ ✦ ✦

She came down in her nightdress and the grey cardigan from the karaoke flat, with her hair all down her back, and stopped at the bottom of the stairs, and looked at him.

At him standing under the alarm, flapping a tea towel. At the smoke coming out of the kitchen door in a soft grey river along the hall ceiling. At the front door, which was opening, because Mrs. Bae was coming through it in her dressing gown and her gardening gloves with a fire extinguisher she’d had since 1987 held out in front of her like a lance.

“Where’s the fire?” shouted Mrs. Bae.

“There isn’t one!” shouted Jun Hyuk, over the alarm. “It’s an egg!”

Mrs. Bae lowered the extinguisher.

Evangeline went past both of them into the kitchen.

✦ ✦ ✦

He followed her in.

The kitchen was full of smoke. All four windows open and the back door open and the cold coming in, and the smoke going out through them in long grey ribbons, and on the stove the pan with the egg in it, which was black, and a second egg, which was mostly shell, and down the front of the white enamel, slowly, a third egg that he hadn’t known about.

On the long table, in the middle of it all, there was a tray. On the tray: a bowl of rice, steaming. A plate of greens, slightly limp, almost right. A cup and the dark clay teapot. A glass, with water in it, and in the glass, a single white orchid, cut that morning in the glasshouse in the dark, standing straight in the smoke.

She looked at it.

The alarm stopped. Mr. Bae, from the hall, had found the button. In the silence, the owl came back and landed in the fig tree.

She turned round and looked at him.

He was standing in the kitchen door with the tea towel in one hand and two burnt fingers and egg on his foot, red from the collar up, the way he’d been red on the camp bed in November two years ago with a towel folded wrong.

“It was going to be breakfast in bed,” he said. “I saw it in a film. A man with a tray. On some stairs. There was a flower.” He looked at the tray. “I’ve cleaned a rifle in the dark in four minutes. I thought I could make an egg.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t laugh.

She came across the kitchen to him through the last of the smoke, and took the tea towel out of his hand, and put it down. She took his hand, the burnt one, and turned it over and looked at the two red fingers. Then she took him to the sink and ran the cold tap and held his fingers under it, in her own hand, the way she’d held them under warm water in a bathroom in October a year ago, and didn’t say anything.

He stood at the sink with his fingers under the tap and her beside him in her nightdress.

“I wanted to,” he said. “Just once. Do it for you. You’ve done it every day for two years. Every single meal. I wanted you to wake up and it’d be there, and you wouldn’t have done it, somebody else would have.” He looked at the black pan on the stove. “I’m very bad at it.”

She turned off the tap.

She looked up at him, a long way up, in the grey morning light coming in through four open windows, with the smoke going out over her head.

Then she reached up, and took his face in her wet cold hands, and he did what he always did now when she looked at him like that. He didn’t wait. He bent down and kissed her, right there at the sink, in the smoke, with his burnt fingers in her hair, long and slow and not at all sorry, until she was up on her toes and holding on to his shirt.

In the hall, Mrs. Bae said oh my goodness and went out of the front door, taking her husband and the fire extinguisher with her, and shut it.

✦ ✦ ✦

They ate breakfast in bed.

She made him. She made the eggs again, two, with the edges crisp, in about four minutes, while he sat at the table holding his fingers in a bowl of cold water and watching her do it as if it were a magic trick. Then she put everything on the tray, the rice and the greens and the eggs and the tea and the orchid in its glass, and picked it up, and held it out to him.

“You carry it,” said Evangeline. “It was your idea.”

He carried it.

Up the stairs, slowly, with both hands, with her walking behind him with one hand flat on his back, the way she walked behind him on stairs. Into the bedroom. She got back into the bed, on the door side, which was hers that month, with her hair down, and sat up against the pillows, and he put the tray across her knees.

She looked at it. The orchid in its glass. The greens that were almost right.

“There,” he said. “Like the film.”

She picked up a piece of the greens he’d made, the slightly limp ones, with her chopsticks, and ate it, and looked at him.

“Yours are better,” she said.

He sat down on the edge of the bed beside her with his fingers throbbing and watched her eat every single thing on the tray, including all of his greens, and thought that the man in the film had had no idea what he was doing.

✦ ✦ ✦

Pudding the cat came in through the open kitchen window at No. 9 while they were upstairs, and walked along the long dark table, and down onto the stove, and ate the burnt egg out of the pan.

Mrs. Bae said afterwards that he’d been sick on her doorstep at ten and had looked, she said, enormously pleased with himself.

chapters.title: The Neighbour’s Cat Chose Him
chapters.desc: Winter 2024. A ginger cat with half an ear, a terrible thief, decides that the biggest man on Fig Tree Lane belongs to him. The biggest man on Fig Tree Lane says he doesn’t like cats. Nobody believes him.
chapters.epigraph: “I don’t like cats. I’ve never liked cats. Cats are a liability.” — Lee Jun Hyuk, with a cat asleep on his chest
chapters.content:
“I don’t like cats,” said Jun Hyuk.

He said it on the verandah on the second Saturday in December, sitting on the top step with a cup of coffee, while Pudding, the ginger cat from No. 7, sat on his left boot and washed one enormous paw.

“I’ve never liked cats,” he said. “Cats are a liability. They knock things over. They make noise at night. They get under your feet when you’re carrying something heavy. In the Grey Lanterns we had a cat for two weeks in 2006 and it got into the ammunition truck and had kittens in a box of grenades and Old Ko had to move them one at a time with a soup ladle.”

Evangeline, on the step beside him, looked at the cat on his boot.

“He’s on your foot,” she said.

“I know he’s on my foot. I didn’t ask him to be on my foot.” He drank his coffee. He didn’t move his foot.

✦ ✦ ✦

Pudding had been coming over the wall since October.

At first he came for the verandah, which was warmer than his own because it faced the morning sun, and for the glasshouse, where he liked to sleep among the orchids on the slatted bench under the potting table, and where Evangeline let him, because he never knocked anything over. Then he came for the kitchen, through the window over the sink, which was always open an inch, and stole things. A prawn. Half a fish. The burnt egg, in November, which Mrs. Bae still talked about.

Then he came for Jun Hyuk.

Nobody knew why. Mrs. Bae said he had never in nine years chosen anybody. He tolerated Mrs. Bae, because she fed him, and Mr. Bae, because Mr. Bae was quiet and let him sit on the compost, and otherwise he walked the length of Fig Tree Lane every evening like a small ginger landlord, looking at everyone and liking nobody.

He liked Jun Hyuk.

He liked him the first afternoon, on the verandah, when he climbed into his lap and turned round twice and lay down. He liked him every afternoon after that. He waited for the truck at five, on the white wall by the green postbox, and when Jun Hyuk got out of it he came down off the wall and walked up the path in front of him, slowly, with his tail up, like an escort. He sat on Jun Hyuk’s boots. He sat on Jun Hyuk’s newspaper. He sat, once, on Jun Hyuk’s head, when Jun Hyuk was lying on the long sofa from Harbour Road with his eyes shut, and Jun Hyuk lay still with eight kilograms of cat on his face and said, muffled, that he didn’t like cats.

✦ ✦ ✦

The trouble was the nights.

He’d been sleeping better. Since the jetty. Since the bridge, and the rifle in the back of Wei Long’s car, and the empty rack in the steel room behind the pantry. Six hours some nights. Seven. Once, the night before the wedding, nine.

But some nights he still woke at three and didn’t know where he was, and his right hand went to the edge of the mattress, and found nothing, and he lay in the dark with his heart going and the door across the room and couldn’t get back.

On one of those nights, the second week of December, he felt something land on the bed.

He went still.

Something heavy. Walking up the blanket, from the foot of the bed, deliberately, over his legs, over his stomach. Stopping on his chest. Turning round twice. And lying down, all of it, eight warm kilograms, on his breastbone, right over his heart, and beginning, loudly, to purr.

He lay in the dark with his eyes open.

The window was open an inch, the way she liked it in winter. The cat had come in over the verandah roof. He’d have to tell Raiden. He’d have to do something about the verandah roof.

He didn’t do anything. He lay there. The purr went down through him like an engine idling. The weight was warm.

Beside him, on her side, facing him, Evangeline opened her eyes.

She looked at the cat on his chest. Then at his face, in the dark.

She didn’t say anything. She put her hand on the cat, lightly, beside his own hand, which had come up, without his deciding, and was resting on the ginger fur.

He was asleep in ten minutes.

✦ ✦ ✦

“He’s yours,” said Mrs. Bae, on the twentieth of December, at the gate, with a bag of cat food and a basket with a cushion in it. “Take him. He’s made up his mind. I’ve been feeding him nine years and he’s never once slept on my chest. My husband’s very relieved. He says he can have the compost back.”

“I don’t like cats,” said Jun Hyuk.

“I know, dear,” said Mrs. Bae. “Everyone on the lane knows. Mrs. Tam at No. 3 saw you carrying him across the road on Thursday so he wouldn’t get wet.”

He took the basket.

He took the bag of cat food.

He went up the path with both of them, and the cat walked in front of him, slowly, tail up, like an escort, into the house.

✦ ✦ ✦

He named him Sergeant.

He didn’t mean to. It was a joke at first. The cat would sit on the top step every evening at five, upright, with his half an ear and his scarred ginger face, and watch the truck come up the lane like an officer inspecting troops, and Jun Hyuk would get out and look at him and say Sergeant, the way Old Ko’s men used to say it when Old Ko came out of his tent in the morning.

After a week the cat answered to it. He’d never once answered to Pudding.

Mrs. Bae said it was hurtful and that she was going to sulk about it until New Year, and then brought round a chestnut cake.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came home late on a Thursday in January. The docks had had a ship in from the south with three hundred containers on it and he’d opened the first of them himself, at six, and the last of them with Mrs. Koo at nine at night, and found nothing, and driven home in the dark with his eyes stinging.

The house was dark except for the lamp in the front room.

He let himself in. He took his boots off in the hall. He went into the front room and stopped in the doorway.

She was asleep on the long sofa from Harbour Road, under the blanket, with a book open on her chest. And on top of the book, on top of her, curled into a ring of ginger fur with his nose under his tail, was the cat.

The cat opened one eye and looked at him.

He stood in the doorway in his socks, with his bag still on his shoulder, and looked at the two of them in the lamplight for a while.

Then he put the bag down, and crossed the room, and knelt down on the floor beside the sofa, and carefully, without waking her, put his arms round both of them. His wife, and the cat on his wife. He put his face against her shoulder, in her hair, with the cat’s warm side against his cheek, and stayed there, on his knees on the floor, breathing her in.

She woke up.

She didn’t move, because of the cat. She turned her head on the cushion and looked at him, close, in the lamplight, his face in her hair and his arms round her and the cat.

“You don’t like cats,” she said, low.

“I don’t,” he said. “I’ve never liked cats.”

He turned his head and kissed her, slowly, with eight kilograms of ginger cat purring between them, and didn’t stop, and the cat, who had very good judgement, stayed exactly where he was.

chapters.title: Evangeline Learns to Shoot
chapters.desc: February 2024, a range in the hills that belongs to a man who owes him a favour. She asked him to teach her. She is very, very bad at it, and so serious about being bad at it that he can’t concentrate on anything else.
chapters.epigraph: “Again.” — Evangeline, after missing the target entirely for the fourteenth time
chapters.content:
She asked him on a Tuesday, at the long table in the textile building, while he was cleaning his things.

She waited until he’d finished. She always did. She waited until the last piece was back where it went, and the cloth was folded on the grey towel, and his hands were flat on the table on either side of it. Then she said, without looking up from her tea:

“I want you to teach me.”

He looked at her.

He didn’t ask what. He knew what. He’d seen her watching his hands for a year and a half, the way she watched everything, as if she might be asked to do it herself one day and wanted to get it right. He’d known she’d ask, sooner or later. He’d been dreading it since the email with the heron on it.

“No,” he said.

She looked up.

“No,” he said again, and heard how it sounded, and didn’t care. “You don’t need it. You’re never going to need it. That’s what I’m for. That’s the whole point of me.” He put his hand over the folded cloth. “I’m not putting one of these in your hand. I’ve seen what they do to people who hold them. I’m not having it in your hand.”

She looked at him across the table.

“There’s an email,” she said, “with a heron on it.” Her voice was perfectly level. “And you’re one man. And you sleep.”

He didn’t say anything.

“I don’t want to hurt anyone,” said Evangeline. “I want to know how. In case. So that if it’s ever the two of us in a room, it’s two.” She turned her cup. “So teach me.”

He looked at her. He thought about West Basin, and the woman standing in the middle of a dark box between the door and the people she’d decided were hers, with her hands open, and nothing in them.

He thought: she’s always going to stand there. Whatever I do. She’s going to stand in front of the door.

“Sunday,” he said. His voice had gone rough. “Seven in the morning. Wear boots.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The range belonged to a man called Mr. Yuen, who had served with the Grey Lanterns for six months in 2004 and now ran an orchard in the hills to the north-west, and kept a long flat strip of ground at the back of it with earth banks at the end, for reasons he didn’t discuss. He owed Jun Hyuk a favour from 2004 that neither of them discussed either. He met them at the gate on Sunday at seven with a flask of tea, looked at Evangeline, looked at Jun Hyuk, and went back to his trees.

It was cold. February in the hills, frost on the grass, the mist still lying in the valley below. She wore boots, and the pale blue coat, and a pair of ear defenders he put on her himself, carefully, settling them over her ears and moving her hair out of the way with his fingers, and then standing there with his hands on either side of her head for longer than he needed to.

She looked up at him.

He took his hands away.

✦ ✦ ✦

He taught her the way Old Ko had taught him, at eleven, by a hurricane lamp. Slowly. Everything in order. How to stand. How to hold it. How to breathe. How never, ever, for any reason, to point it at anything you weren’t prepared to lose.

She learned all of it perfectly the first time. Of course she did. She stood exactly the way he showed her, feet apart, weight forward, arms straight. She held it exactly right. She breathed exactly right. She listened to every word, with the total attention she gave to medicine labels and seed packets and the court language in a library, and repeated it back to him, once, in order, so that he’d know she had it.

Then she fired, and missed the target entirely.

Not the middle. The target. The whole of it. A paper sheet the size of a newspaper on a wooden frame at ten metres. The shot went into the earth bank somewhere to the left and threw up a little spurt of frozen dirt.

She lowered it, the way he’d shown her. She looked at the target. She looked at the spurt of dirt.

“Again,” said Evangeline.

✦ ✦ ✦

She missed it thirteen more times.

He’d never seen anything like it. She did everything right. Every single thing. Her stance was better than half the men he’d served with. Her hands didn’t shake. She breathed out and squeezed and didn’t flinch at the noise, and every time, every single time, the shot went somewhere else. Left. Low. High and left. Into the bank. Into the frost. Once, inexplicably, into Mr. Yuen’s compost heap, fifteen metres to the right.

From the orchard, faintly, Mr. Yuen could be heard laughing.

She didn’t laugh. She didn’t get angry. She didn’t throw it down or say it was stupid or that she’d never be any good. She lowered it, every time, exactly the way he’d shown her, and looked at where it had gone with an expression of total, grave, scientific concentration, as if the shot were a patient with a symptom she couldn’t yet explain, and said, “Again.”

He stood behind her and watched, and couldn’t concentrate on anything.

That was the problem. He was supposed to be watching her hands and her stance and the target. He was watching the back of her neck, under the ear defenders, where her hair had come loose. The line of her shoulders in the pale blue coat. The way she breathed out, slowly, before every shot, the way she breathed out over a pot of tea. Her face, in profile, frowning at the frozen earth bank as if it had personally offended her.

He’d never wanted anyone so much in his life. On a firing range. In February. At ten past eight in the morning.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the fifteenth shot, he stepped in behind her.

He didn’t ask. He put his chest against her back and his arms along hers, his hands over her hands on the grip, and she went still, not the old stillness, not the one from the tall house, a different one, and he felt her breath catch.

“You’re closing your eyes,” he said, low, against her ear, under the edge of the ear defender. “At the last second. Just before. You don’t know you’re doing it.”

She didn’t move.

“Keep them open,” he said. “Look at it. All the way. Even when it’s loud.” His hands tightened over hers. “You never close your eyes. Not in the box. Not at the hospital. You’ve looked at everything that ever frightened you, your whole life, straight on. Don’t stop now.”

She breathed out.

She kept her eyes open.

The shot hit the paper. The edge of it, the top left corner, a hand’s width from the frame. But the paper.

✦ ✦ ✦

She lowered it. She looked at the hole in the corner of the target.

Then she turned round inside his arms, with the thing pointed carefully at the frozen ground the way he’d taught her, and looked up at him, with the ear defenders on and her face pink with cold, and her eyes blazing.

“The paper,” she said.

He took it out of her hand. He put it down on the bench beside them, carefully, the right way. Then he took the ear defenders off her, both sides, and dropped them on the bench too, and put his hands in her cold hair, and kissed her.

On a firing range, in February, at quarter past eight in the morning, with frost on the grass and the mist in the valley and Mr. Yuen in his orchard very loudly not looking. He kissed her as if she’d done something wonderful, and as if he’d been waiting through fourteen misses to do it, which he had, and she held on to the front of his jacket with both hands and kissed him back until neither of them could feel the cold at all.

“You’re terrible,” he said against her mouth. “You’re the worst shot I’ve ever seen in my life. You hit a compost heap.”

“Kiss me again,” said Evangeline, “and stop talking about the compost.”

He laughed, helplessly, into her hair.

✦ ✦ ✦

They went every Sunday for six weeks.

She got better. A little. By the end of March she could hit the paper two times in three at five metres, and one in three at ten, and she never once closed her eyes again. Mr. Yuen gave her a bag of oranges on the last Sunday and said, gravely, that he’d been shot at by worse.

At three metres, at the end, Jun Hyuk stood her close to the target and watched her put three in a row into the paper, near the middle, one after another, steady, eyes open.

“Three’s enough,” he said. “Three is a room. Three is all you’ll ever need.” He took it out of her hands. “You’ll never need it. I promise. But if you do, three.”

She looked at the three holes in the paper.

She looked at him.

“I know,” said Evangeline.

He kept the paper. The one from the first day, with the single hole in the top left corner. He folded it small and put it in the back of the rabbit book, behind the eleven names, where nobody would ever find it but him.

chapters.title: He Learns Her Favourite Colour
chapters.desc: October 2023, a year to the week after West Basin. He has bought her aquamarines and a pale blue coat and has never once asked. When he finally does, she doesn’t say blue.
chapters.epigraph: “Orange.” — Evangeline, the textile building, October 2023
chapters.content:
He’d been sure.

That was the embarrassing part, afterwards. He’d been completely sure, the way he was sure of a lock or a route or a man’s hands. A year of looking at her every day, and in that year she had worn pale blue more than anything else: the dress at Elowen’s wedding, the cardigan she mended in, a scarf, a ribbon, a pair of socks. He’d noticed, the way he noticed everything. He’d taken Aurelia Chen’s tray of earrings and watched her face not move for sapphires and diamonds and move for aquamarines the colour of the sky before anyone was awake. He’d gone into a shop on Harbour Road with one coat in the window and said, she likes pale blue but she’d never say it, and come out with a pale blue coat that came down to her ankles.

He was sure. So he’d never asked.

It was Eliana who made him.

✦ ✦ ✦

She came to the textile building on the first Thursday in October, with Elowen, in her hoodie, with her laptop, to show him something about a man who’d been asking questions on the river, and she stayed for dinner, and halfway through the fish she looked across the table at him and said, “What’s her favourite colour?”

He looked at her.

“Jie’s,” said Eliana. “What’s her favourite colour? You must know. You know everything about her. You know which way she folds towels.” She pointed her chopsticks at him. “Go on.”

“Blue,” said Jun Hyuk. “Pale blue.”

Elowen, beside her sister, put down her bowl.

Eliana’s eyes went slowly wide. She looked at Elowen. Elowen looked at the ceiling.

“Oh no,” said Eliana.

“What?”

“Oh no,” said Eliana, with deep delight. “You don’t know. A whole year and you don’t know.” She turned to her sister. “He doesn’t know!”

Evangeline, at the end of the table, went on eating her fish.

“Ma dressed her in pale blue,” said Elowen, kindly, the way you’d break bad news to a large dog. “From when she was a baby. For twenty years. Because it went with her eyes, Ma said. Ev’s just never stopped.” She picked up her bowl again. “It’s not her favourite. It’s just what she’s always worn.”

He looked down the table at Evangeline.

She looked back at him with a perfectly straight face and laughing eyes.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t ask her that night.

He didn’t ask her the next night, either, or the one after. He was a man who had walked into rooms with guns in them and asked the men holding the guns what they had for breakfast. He couldn’t ask her a question about a colour. He kept opening his mouth to do it, at the table, in bed, at the window box, and shutting it again.

It had taken him a year to get this wrong. He wasn’t going to get it wrong twice.

On the fifth night he gave up waiting for a good moment and made one.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came home from the city at nine with a box.

A big flat white one, from a shop in the old town that sold nothing but cloth. He put it on the long table in front of her, where she was sitting with her tea and the mending, and sat down across from her, and folded his hands.

“There are twelve things in there,” he said. “Scarves. Silk. Every colour the woman had. I asked her for one of everything.” He didn’t look at the box. He looked at her. “I’m not going to guess. I’ve already guessed and I was wrong, in front of your sister, and Eliana’s going to tell that story at our funeral. So I’m asking.” He took a breath. “What’s your favourite colour?”

She looked at the box. She didn’t open it.

She looked at him.

“Orange,” said Evangeline.

✦ ✦ ✦

He sat still.

Of all the colours in the world, he thought later, he’d have put orange last. She didn’t own anything orange. She’d never once, in a year, worn anything orange or bought anything orange or looked twice at anything orange in a shop. There was nothing orange in the textile building at all except the bottles of chilli oil and the lights of the cranes across the harbour at night.

“Orange,” he said.

She nodded.

“Since when?”

She turned her teacup a quarter turn on the table. He’d learned that it meant she was deciding how much to say.

“West Basin,” said Evangeline.

He didn’t move.

“The floodlights,” she said. “In the stacks. They were orange. When the lock went, and the door opened, the light came in. All the way to the back. Orange.” She looked at the cup. “I’d been in the dark for two days. Counting the holes in the roof. And then the door opened and the light came in, and it was orange, and there was a man in it.” She was quiet for a moment. “I’d never thought about colours before. I’d never had a favourite anything. I wasn’t allowed to want things.” She looked up at him. “And then the door opened. And I thought, that one.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t say anything.

He couldn’t. He sat across the long table in the textile building with the box of twelve silk scarves between them and looked at her, and couldn’t find a single thing to say.

Then he got up.

He came round the table. He didn’t wait for her to stand. He took her face in his hands and tipped it up and kissed her, hard, the way he’d kissed her against the steel door that first December, and pulled her up out of the chair and into him, all the way, her mending going on the floor, and kept kissing her until she was holding on to his shirt to stay upright.

“Orange,” he said, against her mouth. It came out cracked down the middle. “You never said. A whole year. You never once said.”

“You never asked,” said Evangeline.

He laughed, shakily, into her hair. Then he kissed her again, because once wasn’t nearly enough.

✦ ✦ ✦

She opened the box when he finally let her.

Twelve scarves, in tissue, folded. Red and green and gold and purple and white and black and three kinds of blue, because the woman in the cloth shop had known nothing about anybody’s favourite anything and had assumed, like him, that it was probably blue.

And one orange. Not bright. A deep warm burnt orange, like the floodlights at West Basin on wet steel at two in the morning.

She took it out and held it.

She put it on.

She wore it with the pale blue coat the next morning, to the market, and to Nam’s on Saturday, and to Elowen’s on Sunday, where Eliana took one look at her sister and the orange scarf and the man behind her and put her face in her hands and said oh, that’s so much worse.

He found more things that week without being asked. An orange teapot cosy from a stall in the market. A tin of orange tea from the shop with the mountains on the tin. A string of orange paper lanterns for the window, which she hung over the hatch so that at night they glowed on the inside of the five layers of glass. And on the fourteenth of October, a year to the day after he’d left her at a hospital with a note and no name, a single orange tulip, out of season, flown in from somewhere, in a glass on the long table when she came up the stairs.

She stood looking at it with her coat still on.

He was standing by the window, waiting to see her face.

She took off the coat. She took off the orange scarf, and hung it on the back of the chair, and crossed the room to him, and put her hands flat on his chest, and he picked her up before she could say anything at all.

chapters.title: The Borderland Boy
chapters.desc: Spring 1999. A boy of eight with a name written inside his collar, an aid station on a river road, and a sergeant with one spoon who decides, against every rule his unit has, to take him along.
chapters.epigraph: “That’s a big name for a small boy.” — Sergeant Ko Baek-san, reading a collar, 1999
chapters.content:
His mother had written his name inside his collar.

He didn’t remember her doing it. He remembered the shirt. Grey, too big for him, with a frayed edge at the cuffs where he chewed them, and inside the back of the collar, on a strip of white cotton she had sewn there, in black ink, in a careful, small, frightened hand: three words he couldn’t read.

He couldn’t read anything. He was seven. There hadn’t been a school in the village since he was five, when the men came across the river the first time and the teacher went away and didn’t come back.

He remembered the aid station. A long white tent on the river road with a red mark painted on the roof so that the planes would see it and not drop anything on it, which mostly worked. He remembered a woman in a white coat who spoke a language he didn’t know and held his mother’s hand. He remembered being told to wait outside. He remembered waiting outside for a long time, on a bench, in the heat, watching the road. He remembered the woman in the white coat coming out at last and crouching down in front of him, so she wasn’t taller than him, and saying something he didn’t understand, gently, and holding out his mother’s bag.

That was the first time anyone had ever crouched down for him.

He didn’t remember anything else about that day. He’d tried, later. It was gone.

✦ ✦ ✦

He stayed at the aid station for a year.

Nobody knew what else to do with him. There were a lot of children on the river road in 1998, and the aid station had a list for them, and a tent at the back with mattresses in it, and a woman from a church who came on Thursdays with books. He learned to carry water. He learned to fold the bandages they washed and boiled and dried on lines between the tents, in thirds, and then rolled, because the woman in the white coat said that was how you kept them clean. He learned forty words of the language the woman in the white coat spoke, mostly thank you and wait and don’t touch that.

He didn’t learn to read. The woman from the church tried. He couldn’t sit still.

He watched the road instead.

That was what he did, all that year, when he wasn’t carrying water. He sat on the bench outside the long white tent where he’d sat on the day his mother died, and watched the river road. The trucks going past. The people walking, with bags on their heads. The soldiers, sometimes. He learned to tell from a long way off whose soldiers they were by the way they drove, and whether to go inside. He learned to count them. He learned that if you sat very still on a bench by a road, people stopped seeing you.

He was very good at it by the time the Grey Lanterns came.

✦ ✦ ✦

They came in the spring of 1999, in nine old trucks with grey paper lanterns painted on the doors, and stopped at the aid station because one of their men had a hole in his leg.

The boy on the bench watched them come.

They didn’t drive like anybody’s soldiers. They drove like men who’d been driving the same road for a very long time and knew where every pothole was and didn’t care whose side the road was on. They parked in a row by the river. Men got out, a lot of them, big and loud and dirty, carrying things, laughing, and one of them on a stretcher, swearing.

The last man out of the first truck was old.

That was what the boy thought, anyway. He was perhaps fifty. Grey hair cut short, a face like a walnut, a body like a sack of rice tied in the middle, and a cigarette, and a tyre on the roof of his truck with something green growing in it. He didn’t go into the tent with the others. He stood by his truck and lit his cigarette and looked at the aid station, and the river road, and the bench.

He looked at the boy on the bench.

Then he walked over and sat down on it, at the other end, and smoked his cigarette, and didn’t say anything.

✦ ✦ ✦

They sat there for an hour.

The boy didn’t move. He’d learned not to. The old man didn’t move either. He smoked three cigarettes, one after another, and watched the road, the way the boy watched it, and every so often he said something, low, in a rough voice, in a language the boy knew, the border language, the one his mother had spoken.

He talked about the road. About the trucks that went past and whose they were and where they were going. About the river, which was low that spring, and the crossing at the broken bridge, which was going to be bad when the rains came. About the tomatoes in the tyre on the roof of his truck, which he’d been growing for two years and driving through a war, and which were, he said, the only thing in the Grey Lanterns that had never once let him down.

He didn’t ask the boy anything. He just talked. On and on, low and easy, about nothing, as if it didn’t matter at all whether anyone was listening.

The boy listened to all of it.

After an hour, the old man stubbed out the third cigarette on the bench and turned his head.

“You’re good at sitting still,” he said. “Who taught you?”

The boy didn’t say anything.

“Nobody, eh?” said the old man. “Me neither.” He held out his hand, flat, palm down, slowly, the way you’d offer it to something wild. “Ko. Ko Baek-san. Sergeant, they call me. I don’t know why. Nobody ever made me one. What’s your name?”

The boy looked at the hand.

He didn’t know how to say it. He’d heard his mother say it, a hundred times, a thousand. He’d never once had to say it to anyone himself.

So he did the only thing he could think of. He turned round on the bench, and pulled the back of his grey collar down, and showed him.

✦ ✦ ✦

The old man leaned over and read it.

He read it slowly. His lips moved. He could read, it turned out, though not well, and not that alphabet often. He read it twice. Then he sat back on the bench and looked at the boy with an expression the boy didn’t understand at all and would understand, much later, the first time he looked at a woman standing in the middle of a dark box with her hands open.

“Lee Jun Hyuk,” said Sergeant Ko.

The boy had never heard it in anyone’s voice but his mother’s.

“That’s a big name for a small boy,” said Ko. He looked at the boy’s thin arms and his chewed cuffs and his feet in shoes that were too big for him, stuffed with paper. “You’ll have to grow into it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The Grey Lanterns stayed three days, while the man with the hole in his leg got better.

On the third night, the boy heard the old man arguing with someone behind the trucks. The commander, a younger man with a gold tooth, who said that the Lanterns didn’t take children, had never taken children, it was the one rule they had, they were a unit not a nursery, and what was he going to do with it, feed it to the tomatoes?

“He can carry water,” said Ko. “He can fold bandages. He sits still for an hour and watches the road and counts the trucks and knows whose they are. Half your men can’t do that drunk or sober.”

“He’s eight.”

“Then he can carry tea,” said Ko, “and run messages, and sleep in my truck, and never once go anywhere near the front of anything. Never. Not while I’m alive. And when I’m not alive, you can do what you like.” A pause. “Or you can leave him on a bench by a road for the next lot to find. Your choice. I know what I’d want, if it was me on the bench.”

There was a long silence behind the trucks.

“On your head, Ko,” said the commander, and walked away.

✦ ✦ ✦

The old man came round the trucks and found the boy sitting in the dark on the bench, where he’d been listening, and sat down beside him.

He took something out of the top pocket of his jacket. A spoon. A plain tin one, bent a little at the neck.

“This is everything I own,” he said. “In the world. I keep it here.” He tapped his top pocket. “You own something, you have to go back for it. So I don’t own anything but this.” He held it out. “You’ll want one. For the soup. I’ll get you one at the next town. Till then, we share.”

The boy looked at the spoon.

He took it. He held it in both hands, in the dark, by the river road, outside the tent where his mother had died, and didn’t say anything at all. He didn’t know how to say anything. He’d never needed to.

“That’s all right,” said Ko. “You don’t have to talk. I’ll talk. I’m very good at it.” He lit a cigarette. “When people are scared, you keep talking, so they hear a voice that isn’t scared, and they follow the voice. That’s the whole trick. I’ll teach you.” He breathed out smoke at the stars. “One day you’ll be the one talking. You’ll see.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“And you were,” said Evangeline.

It was a Sunday night in January, 2025, at the long dark table at Fig Tree Lane, with the lamp on and the cat asleep on the window seat. He’d told it to her across the table, slowly, from the beginning, because she’d asked, and because nobody ever had.

“I was,” he said. “Every day. For thirteen years. Until his heart stopped on a Tuesday on the way to buy cigarettes.” He looked at his hands. “He never once let me go near the front. Not while he was alive. He kept his word.”

She got up.

She came round the table to him, and he turned his chair before she reached it, so that he was facing her, the way he always did now, and pulled her down into his lap before she could do anything else, and held on. She put her arms round his neck. She put her face against his.

“He’d have liked you,” he said, into her hair. “He’d have talked at you for an hour and you’d have listened to every word. He’d have been unbearable about it.”
