“I’d have liked him,” said Evangeline.

He kissed her, slowly, at the long table, with the lamp on.

Behind them, on the shelf above the stove, in a small glass dish of its own, there was a spoon. Old, silver, worn thin at the neck. She’d given it to him on the first of March, two years ago, when he didn’t know his birthday. He took it out of the dish every morning, and put it in his top pocket, with a coin from a dumpling, and every night he put them back.

chapters.title: Paper Twins
chapters.desc: April 2025. For seventeen years Raiden has said he’s the older twin, because he’s louder. Now there’s a king’s signature that says otherwise. He doesn’t accept it. So they have a party on the eighth, the day in between.
chapters.epigraph: “Paper beats silk. Everybody knows that.” — Raiden Lin, wrongly
chapters.content:
Raiden had said he was older since the spring he came home from the borderland, when they were ten.

It was the first thing anyone at the long kitchen table in the Walled City remembered about the two of them: a thin loud boy just home from the borderland, with his chin up, and a silent girl beside him, the same height, on the same birthday, the ninth of April, and the boy saying, to anyone who’d listen, that he was older. By eleven minutes. He’d made the number up. He’d never once been told it. He said it so often and so firmly that by the time they were twelve the whole family believed it, including their father, who knew perfectly well that the two of them had been born two days apart to different mothers in different countries, and who had never once corrected him.

Evangeline had never argued.

She’d known since she was fifteen, from a date sewn into the corner of a silk blanket in numbers she’d taught herself to read. She’d been born on the seventh. She was two days older. She’d never said so. She’d sat at the end of the table every ninth of April for seventeen years and let him blow out the candles first.

Then a letter came from a palace with the seventh of April in it in black ink, and a king signed a paper on the twenty-first floor of the Harbour Hotel that said so too.

Raiden read the paper at Lunar New Year, at the long kitchen table, over Ms. Fong’s shoulder, and went quiet.

“That’s a forgery,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t accept it.

He said so all through February and March, to anyone who’d listen. He said paper beat silk, and that his own birth certificate, which was real, said the ninth, and hers, which was a lie, also said the ninth, and that two pieces of paper beat one foreign king. He said the blanket could have been wrong. He said the king could have been wrong. He said that even if she had technically been born first, he had been louder first, which was more important, and that she’d never once objected in seventeen years, which was legally binding.

Jinx said he was being an idiot. Elowen said he was being an idiot. Elara, on the phone between operations, said he was being an idiot with great conviction and that she was proud of him. Eliana made a spreadsheet.

Evangeline didn’t say anything at all.

She let him talk. She’d been letting him talk since they were ten. And every time he said paper beats silk at the long kitchen table in the Walled City, she turned her teacup a quarter turn, and looked at him, and he could see, across the table, that she was laughing at him inside so hard he had to look away.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was Jun Hyuk who settled it.

He did it the way he did most things now, without asking anyone. In the second week of March he came home from the docks and sat down at the long dark table at Fig Tree Lane across from her and said, “There’s going to be a party.”

She looked up.

“For your birthday,” he said. “Your real one. The seventh. The first one you’ve ever had in your own house.” He put his hands flat on the table. “Last year I had six hours and a glasshouse at the botanical gardens. This year I’ve had a month. There’s going to be food, and your family, and the Baes, and Nam if she’ll come, and Nuo, and Mrs. Lai, and a cake that isn’t chestnut, I’m sorry, Mrs. Bae, it’s going to be a cake from Nuo’s bakery with your name on it. Your name. Not anyone else’s.”

She looked at him.

“What about Raiden?” she said.

“Raiden can come on the seventh and be wrong in person.”

“He won’t come on the seventh.”

He stopped.

She was right. He knew it at once. Raiden would sooner eat his own sketchbook than come to a birthday party on the seventh of April. It would be admitting it. And she wouldn’t have a birthday without him. She hadn’t had one without him since she was ten. They’d been sharing candles ever since.

“Then the ninth,” said Jun Hyuk.

“No,” said Evangeline, quietly and firmly. It was the first time he’d ever heard her sound like a little girl who’d had her candles blown out first for seventeen years and had just found out she didn’t have to.

He looked at her across the table.

“The eighth,” he said. “The day in between.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The party was on the eighth of April, a Tuesday, at No. 9 Fig Tree Lane, from six until whenever, and Raiden came up the lane at ten past six with Jinx and a cake of his own, a big one, from a shop on Harbour Road, with icing on top in blue that said HAPPY BIRTHDAY RAIDEN (THE OLDER ONE).

He put it on the long dark table beside Nuo’s cake, which said Evangeline in orange, and nothing else.

He looked at the two cakes. He looked at his sister, at the head of the table, in pale blue with an orange scarf.

“I’m not admitting anything,” said Raiden.

“No,” said Evangeline.

“I’m here on the eighth, which is neutral. Like Switzerland. Or a ceasefire.”

She inclined her head.

He sat down beside her. He always had. At the long kitchen table in the Walled City, at every birthday since they were ten, they’d sat side by side at the end with two cakes or one cake or no cake at all, the year the power went off in the whole Walled City. He sat down beside her now, at a different table, in a different house, with her husband at the other end of it carving a duck, and put his elbow on the table and his chin in his hand, and looked at her sideways.

“You let me,” he said. Low. Just to her. “Every year. You knew. You let me blow them out first.”

She looked at him.

“You were loud,” said Evangeline. “You needed it more.”

He looked at her. Then he put his arm round her shoulders and pulled her against him, hard, and kissed the top of her head, the way he had when they were eleven and she’d fallen down the stairs at the Walled City and not cried, and he’d cried for her instead.

“Two days,” he said into her hair. “That’s nothing. That’s a weekend.”

“It’s forty-eight hours,” said Evangeline. “And eleven minutes.”

He burst out laughing. Down the table, Jinx put her face in her hands. Lin Jian, at the other end beside Jun Hyuk, laughed too, a big rusty sound nobody had heard much from him in twenty years, and then stopped, and looked at his two paper twins side by side at the end of the table, and had to go out onto the verandah for a minute.

✦ ✦ ✦

They blew the candles out together.

Both cakes, at once, side by side, with everyone counting. Nobody went first. Eliana filmed it, so that there could be no argument afterwards, and posted it to the group chat with the caption DRAW (OFFICIAL), which Raiden contested for a week.

Afterwards, when the family had gone down the lane in their three cars and the Baes had gone back over the wall and Nuo had gone home in the taxi he’d won, and the dishes were done, and the cat was asleep on the window seat, Jun Hyuk found her on the verandah, on the top step, in the dark, with the orange scarf round her shoulders, looking down the garden at the rosemary.

He sat down beside her. He didn’t wait for her to lean on him. He pulled her into him, his arm round her, her head on his shoulder, and she let him.

“First birthday in your own house,” he said.

“Second,” said Evangeline. “Yesterday was the first. You made pancakes.”

“I made pancakes,” he agreed. “Nobody died.”

She almost laughed. He felt it in his shoulder, the start of it.

“Was it all right?” he said. “The eighth. The day in between. I didn’t know what else—you’d never have had it without him. And he’d never have come on the seventh. So I thought—”

She turned her face up and kissed him.

Not carefully. On the top step of the verandah, in the dark, in the cold April air with the stream going at the bottom of the garden and the smell of the rosemary coming up the path. He kissed her back the way he always did now, like a man who’d never once stop being surprised by it, and pulled her into his lap, orange scarf and all, and didn’t stop until the owl started up on the hill.

“It was perfect,” said Evangeline, at last, against his mouth. “You made me a day. Nobody’s ever made me a day.”

He held her on the step and couldn’t say anything at all.

In the kitchen behind them, on the long dark table, under a tea towel, the last slice of Raiden’s cake sat on its plate. Someone had scraped off the word OLDER with a knife, neatly, and left the rest.

chapters.title: He Talks for Both of Them
chapters.desc: The Chen Foundation Spring Gala, May 2025, as seen by Aurelia Chen. Elowen’s quiet sister has said eleven words to her in five years. Her husband has said several thousand to everyone else in the room, and has not let go of her hand once.
chapters.epigraph: “Your husband is the only man here who’s asked the waiter’s name.” — Aurelia Chen, to Evangeline Lee, who didn’t answer
chapters.content:
Aurelia Chen had been to two hundred galas, give or take, and she knew exactly how they went.

You arrived at eight, not before. You stood near the stairs for the first half hour, because everyone had to come up them and everyone had to see you. You let men who wanted something from your husband tell you about their wives. You let their wives tell you about your necklace. You counted, quietly, who spoke to whom, and for how long, and who left early, and who arrived with someone they shouldn’t have, and by ten o’clock you knew more about the city than its government did, and by eleven you were bored, and touched your left earring, and Chen Si came and got you.

It was the Chen Foundation’s spring gala, at the Harbour Hotel, on the seventeenth of May. It was the third one she’d hosted. She’d invited four hundred people. She knew three hundred and eighty of them already.

At a quarter past eight, Evangeline Lee came up the stairs on the arm of her husband, and Aurelia stopped counting.

✦ ✦ ✦

She’d seen them before, of course. At the Lins’, at New Year, every year since the wedding. At Elowen’s flower shop, once, in the winter, buying white orchids. She’d seen him at the Harbour Road boutique in 2023 in a mended shirt and a cap, paying for a pair of aquamarines with a black card without looking at the price, which was the moment Aurelia had decided she liked him.

She hadn’t seen them at anything like this. They didn’t go to things like this.

Evangeline was in pale blue, plain and long, with the aquamarines and a narrow orange silk scarf round her throat, which shouldn’t have worked with the blue and which, Aurelia saw at once with a jeweller’s eye, worked perfectly. She came up the stairs very straight, with a face like something carved, and her hand on her husband’s arm, and her eyes, Aurelia noticed, going to the doors. Every door. The ones to the terrace, and the ones to the kitchens, and the fire exit behind the orchestra. All of them, in order, before she reached the top step.

And him.

He was enormous. Aurelia had forgotten, or had stopped noticing, the way you stop noticing a mountain behind a house. In a black dinner suit that had plainly been made for him by someone who’d needed a stepladder, he filled the top of the stairs. He had a scar through one eyebrow and a face like a good-tempered dock worker’s, and he was smiling at everybody.

He was already talking.

✦ ✦ ✦

He talked to everyone.

Aurelia watched him do it for an hour, from her place by the stairs, and found she couldn’t stop. He talked to the minister for trade about the container ports of the south. He talked to the head of the Harbour Board about the tides, at length, with his hands, until the head of the Harbour Board was nodding and taking notes on the back of a menu card. He talked to Mrs. Lu, who was eighty-four and had been widowed in March, about her late husband’s bonsai trees, for twenty minutes, while she held his arm and cried a little and laughed a great deal. He talked to a young waiter who’d dropped a tray of glasses by the bar, and was on his knees picking up the pieces, red in the face, with the head waiter coming. Jun Hyuk crouched down beside him on the floor in his dinner suit and helped, and asked him his name, and how long he’d been working there, and told him that he’d once dropped a tray of forty cups of tea on a sergeant in 2001 and the sergeant had made him clean every boot in the unit with a toothbrush, and by the time the head waiter arrived they were both laughing.

He talked enough for both of them, and after the first half hour Aurelia saw that this was the point. He was so loud and so cheerful and so easy, so endlessly interested in tides and bonsai and broken glasses, that nobody in the room had noticed that the tall still woman on his arm hadn’t said a single word to anyone. Not one. People came up to them, and he talked, and Evangeline stood beside him with her hand in his and her face perfectly composed and her eyes on the doors, and people went away again thinking they’d had a lovely conversation with the Lees.

He was doing it for her.

He’d taken every word in the room that might have been aimed at her, and caught it, like a man catching rain in his hands so it wouldn’t land on someone.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t let go of her once.

Aurelia noticed that next. She was good at noticing hands; you were, in her trade. He never let go. Not when he shook the minister’s hand; he shook it with his left. Not when he helped the waiter; he’d brought her down with him, and she’d crouched on the floor beside him in her pale blue dress and picked up glass, carefully, with her other hand. Not when he ate. He held a plate in one hand and her fingers in the other and ate one-handed and didn’t seem to notice he was doing it.

And every so often, in the middle of a sentence about tides, he’d stop, and look down at her, just for a second, the way you’d glance at a clock to make sure of the time. And something would go across his good-tempered dock worker’s face that wasn’t good-tempered at all. Something hungry and fierce and so naked that Aurelia, who had been married for six years to a man who looked at her like that across boardrooms, had to look away.

“He’s very in love with her,” said Chen Si, at her elbow, with a glass of something.

“He’s out of his mind,” said Aurelia.

“Yes,” said her husband, mildly. “It’s very restful to watch somebody else for once.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At half past nine, the minister’s son tried his luck.

He was twenty-eight, the minister’s son, and handsome, and had been to a university abroad and come back with an accent he worked hard on, and he’d been watching Evangeline across the room for twenty minutes the way men like him watched things in shop windows. When Jun Hyuk was pulled away by the head of the Harbour Board to settle an argument about moorings, and let go of her hand for the first time all evening, only for a second, to draw something on a napkin, the minister’s son crossed the room.

He stopped in front of her with two glasses of champagne and a smile.

“You’re Elowen Zhao’s sister,” he said. “The quiet one. I’ve always wanted to meet you. They say you don’t talk. I don’t believe it.” He held out a glass. “Let me be the one who makes you.”

Evangeline looked at the glass. She didn’t take it.

She looked at him. And Aurelia, ten metres away, saw her do something with her face that she’d seen Evangeline do across a mahjong table at New Year: nothing at all, very precisely, in a way that made the person on the other side of the table understand that they had made a serious error and would be some time finding out what it was.

The minister’s son kept smiling. He leaned in.

Then a hand came down on his shoulder.

✦ ✦ ✦

Jun Hyuk hadn’t hurried. Aurelia would remember that. He’d put down the napkin and the pen in the middle of the argument about moorings and walked across the room, not fast, the way the tide comes in, and by the time anyone had noticed he’d gone, he was there, with one big hand on the minister’s son’s shoulder, and the other already round his wife’s waist, pulling her in against his side.

He was smiling. He was still smiling. That was the frightening part.

“Hello,” he said pleasantly. “You’ve met my wife.”

The minister’s son turned round and looked up. Quite a long way up.

“She doesn’t drink champagne,” said Jun Hyuk. “And she doesn’t talk to people she doesn’t like, which is nearly everyone, which is very sensible of her, and which I’d have thought a man who went to such a good university could work out from her face.” His hand on the minister’s son’s shoulder hadn’t moved. It hadn’t tightened. It was simply there, the size of a dinner plate. “She talks to me. That’s the arrangement. I talk to everyone else.” He smiled down at him. “So you can talk to me. About anything you like. For as long as you like. Shall we start with why you’ve been looking at her for twenty minutes?”

The minister’s son said something about the bar, and went.

Jun Hyuk watched him go. Then he turned his head and looked down at his wife, pressed against his side, with her hand flat on his chest, and the smile went right off his face, and what was underneath it made Aurelia, ten metres away, put down her glass.

He bent his head and kissed her.

In the middle of the ballroom of the Harbour Hotel, in front of four hundred people and a minister for trade, a short, hard, entirely unapologetic kiss, his hand in the small of her back, as if there had been nobody else in the room at all. Then he straightened up, and took her hand again, and went back to the head of the Harbour Board and his napkin, and finished his sentence about moorings exactly where he’d left it.

Evangeline’s face hadn’t moved.

But her thumb, on the back of his hand, was moving, slightly, back and forth. Aurelia saw it. And she saw him feel it, mid-sentence, and stop talking for exactly one second.

✦ ✦ ✦

At eleven, Aurelia found herself beside Evangeline at the bar.

Just the two of them. Their husbands were across the room, standing side by side by the wall with Zhao, all three of them with their hands in their pockets, not speaking, which was apparently what they did now. Jun Hyuk was talking. The other two were listening, with the faces of men who had been listening for some time and expected to go on.

Aurelia looked at Elowen’s sister. Evangeline was holding a glass of water. She was looking at the doors.

“Your husband,” said Aurelia, “is the only man here who’s asked the waiter’s name.”

Evangeline didn’t answer.

She turned her head and looked at Aurelia with that carved still face. Then she looked across the ballroom at the big man by the wall in the dinner suit made by someone with a stepladder, talking with both hands to two of the most frightening men in the city, who were, Aurelia could see from here, trying hard not to laugh.

And she smiled.

It was the first time Aurelia had ever seen her smile. It went right across her face, all of it, and stayed there.

Then she put down her glass of water and walked across the ballroom to him, through four hundred people, straight, and he saw her coming and stopped talking mid-word and held out his hand before she reached him.

Aurelia watched them go. She took out her phone, and opened her notes, and looked at a line she’d kept since 2020. Evangeline. Words to me: 11.

She didn’t change it.

She added, underneath: Smiles: 1.

chapters.title: The Silver Ring Engraving
chapters.desc: May 2026. Two lines of numbers inside a silver band, worn for three years and never once looked up. A boat that goes twice a week from a harbour nobody watches. A stone house with a fig tree, a wall behind a stove, and a way out that neither of them needs any more.
chapters.epigraph: “If I don’t come back, this ring has the coordinates to a life where no one can find you.” — the ring, April 2023. “Show me anyway.” — Evangeline, May 2026
chapters.content:
She’d never looked them up.

Three years she’d worn the ring. Every day, every night, in the bath and in the glasshouse and at the range in the hills with ear defenders on, under a white silk tie at her wedding. She knew the numbers inside it by heart; she’d read them a thousand times, tipping the band to the light. Two lines. Degrees, minutes, seconds. She’d never once typed them into anything.

She hadn’t wanted to know. That was the truth of it. As long as she didn’t know where the place was, it wasn’t a place. It was only a door. And she’d never needed the door, because he’d come back every time.

It was Serafina’s wedding that did it.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the twenty-fifth of April, in a garage under a railway bridge, with trains going over every eleven minutes, Serafina Song married a quiet man with a precise face who had once made people disappear for a state, and Evangeline stood at the back in pale blue and watched, and beat Aurelia at the toast-glass game in four minutes, and said nothing at all.

Afterwards, at three in the morning, on the drive home up the reservoir road, she said, looking out of the window at the black water, still thinking about the wedding, “He gave her a building.”

Jun Hyuk glanced across at her.

“The arch,” she said. “In both their names. So nobody could ever move her.” She turned the ring on her finger.

He drove for a while.

“Do you want a building?” he said. “I’ll buy you a building. I’ll buy you the street. Name it.”

“No,” said Evangeline. She was looking at the ring. “I want to go and see the one you gave me.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It took four days to get there.

A plane south, to a city on the coast of a country she had never been to. A train along the coast, slow, through rice fields and limestone hills. A night in a hotel in a fishing town where nobody spoke a language either of them knew and the owner fed them grilled fish on the roof and wouldn’t take money for the beer. And at six in the morning on the fourth day, from a small stone harbour at the end of a road nobody watched, a boat.

It went twice a week. It was wooden and blue and smelled of diesel and fish, and the captain was an old man with no teeth who looked at Jun Hyuk for a while, and then at the woman beside him, and then nodded once, as if he’d been expecting them for nine years, which he had.

“He knew,” said Evangeline, on the deck, with the wind in her hair.

“I paid him years ago,” said Jun Hyuk. “To take whoever came. No questions. Every year since. He thought I’d forgotten.” He looked at the old man at the wheel. “I’m the first one who’s come.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The island was small and green and steep, with a white beach on one side and cliffs on the other and a single village of stone houses climbing the hill above a harbour the size of a swimming pool. Goats. Fishing nets drying on walls. A church with a bell. Nobody looked at them at all.

The house was at the top of the village, at the end of a path that turned into steps and then into a track, on its own, with the whole sea below it.

It was old. Grey stone, two rooms, a red tile roof patched with tin, blue shutters peeling in the salt wind. A walled yard in front with a well in it. And by the gate, so big it leaned over the wall and half the yard, a fig tree, grey-trunked, broad-leaved, with the first small green figs of the year on it.

She stopped at the gate.

He stopped behind her.

She didn’t go in. She stood in the gate with her hand on the warm stone of the wall and looked at it. The well. The shutters. The fig. A table under the tree, an old one, with a bench, weathered silver. Somebody had swept the yard. The old man on the boat, probably. Or his wife. Every year, for nine years, for someone who’d never come.

“You built this,” she said, “for you.”

“For me,” he agreed. “In case I ever needed to stop being me.” He was quiet for a moment. “I used to think about it at night. On roofs. In the bamboo. A stone house with a fig tree at the end of the world, where nobody knew my name. I thought it was the only place I’d ever be allowed to stop.” He looked at the back of her head. “And then I gave it to you. Across a table. In case I didn’t come back.”

She turned round.

“You came back,” she said.

“Every time,” he said.

She took his face in her hands, there in the gateway, and pulled it down to hers.

✦ ✦ ✦

The money was behind the stove.

He showed her. Of course he did; he’d promised her the night he gave her the ring, and he kept promises. In the back room, an old iron stove with a flue going up through the roof, and behind it, if you lifted out three loose stones in the wall, a space, and in the space, wrapped in oilcloth, a box.

He lifted it out and put it on the table under the fig tree and opened it.

Money, in plastic, in the currency of the country, a great deal of it. Gold, a little. And papers. A passport, two passports, with photographs that had been taken in a back room in a border town in 2016: one of him, younger, with his hair longer, and one with a space where a photograph should be, and a name in it that wasn’t anyone’s. Birth certificates. A bank book. An identity card for an island in the south, for a woman who’d never existed.

She picked up the passport with the space where the photograph should be.

She looked at the name in it.

“I was going to be her,” she said.

“If you’d needed to be.”

She looked at him across the old table under the fig tree with the sea behind him, and he looked back, steadily, the way he’d looked at her across a table in a karaoke flat when he put a ring beside her teacup.

“I don’t need to be,” said Evangeline.

“No,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

They burned the papers that evening.

In the old iron stove, with the door open, one by one. The passport with the space in it. His, from 2016, with the long hair. The birth certificates. The bank book. The identity card for the woman who’d never existed. They sat on the stone floor of the back room in front of the stove, side by side, with their shoulders touching, and fed them in, and watched them go.

When the last one had gone, she put her head on his shoulder.

“I wanted to see it,” she said, “before I didn’t need it. So I’d know what you gave me.”

He put his arm round her.

“What did I give you?” he said.

She took her time.

“A way out,” said Evangeline. “In case.” She turned her face into his neck. “And I never once wanted it.”

He didn’t say anything. He turned his head and kissed her, on the stone floor in front of the stove, with the last of the papers going to ash, slowly, and then not slowly, and then he stood up and lifted her with him, all the way up, off the floor, and carried her out of the back room and through the front one and out of the blue door into the yard, where the light was going gold over the sea.

“Where are we going?” she said, against his shoulder.

“Swimming,” said Jun Hyuk.

✦ ✦ ✦

He carried her all the way down the steps and the track and the path to the white beach on the far side of the island, in the last of the sun, with the goats watching, and didn’t put her down until the water was round his knees.

She’d never swum in the sea. She told him so, standing in it up to her waist in her cotton dress with her hair coming down, astonished, with the water going gold and green round her and small fish going past her ankles.

“I know,” he said. “You told me once. You said you’d always wanted to and nobody had ever taken you.”

She looked at him.

“I remember everything you’ve ever told me,” said Jun Hyuk. “Every word. There aren’t very many. I’ve kept all of them.”

She went under. On purpose. She sank down into the warm gold water until it closed over her head, and came up again with her hair streaming and her face open, all of it, laughing out loud in the sea at the end of the world, and he waded in after her with his clothes on and caught her round the waist and lifted her up against him, both of them soaked, and kissed her with the salt on her mouth until the sun went into the water behind them.

✦ ✦ ✦

They stayed nearly two weeks.

They slept in the stone house with the shutters open to the sea, in an old iron bed the old man’s wife had made up for them with sheets that smelled of sun. They ate figs off the tree, and fish from the harbour, and bread from the woman at the bottom of the village who made one batch a day and sold out by eight. He mended the roof. She swept the yard, every morning, though it didn’t need sweeping, because it was hers.

On the last morning, at the gate, she stopped and looked back at it. The fig, the well, the blue door, the table under the tree.

“We’ll come back,” she said. Not a question.

“Every year,” said Jun Hyuk. “If you want.”

“Not because we need to,” said Evangeline. “Because we want to.”

He looked at her in the gateway with the sea behind her.

“Then that’s what we’ll do,” he said, and kissed her hand, over the ring with the numbers in it, and carried her bag down to the boat.

chapters.title: Clean Towels
chapters.desc: October 2025. She goes to the lake country for four days with Mrs. Lai to play at the summer festival’s autumn concert, and he stays home with the cat and every towel in the house. When she comes back up the lane, they are all folded her way. Except one.
chapters.epigraph: “She does it in two seconds. It took me until four in the morning.” — Lee Jun Hyuk
chapters.content:
She’d never been away from him.

Not once. Not overnight. Not in three years. He’d been away from her: across the river for thirteen days in 2023, to Kiln Street for four, up to a bamboo stand on a riverbank for one long night. But she’d never once been the one to go. She’d been the one at the table under the lamp, with her coat on, not waiting up.

In October 2025 Teo’s mother wrote from the lake country.

The letter came by post to No. 9, in the court language, in a round careful hand, with a pressed flower in it and a jar of honey in a separate parcel. It said that the autumn concert at the lake, which was held every year on the jetty by the old summer house, for the families of the lake country, was in two weeks. It said that a viola teacher from the city had written to the festival committee in the spring, a Mrs. Lai, about a pupil. It said the committee would be honoured if the daughter of the girl who used to play on the jetty every summer would come and play one piece. Only one. The old one, from the lake, that Teo’s mother had written out from memory.

It said: Your mother was younger than you are now when she last played here. Some of us who heard her are still alive. We would like to hear it again.

Evangeline read it at the long dark table four times.

Then she looked across the table at him.

He was already nodding. He’d been nodding since the second line.

“Go,” he said. “Of course go. Four days. I’ll be fine. I’ll be absolutely fine. I’ve got the cat.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He was not absolutely fine.

He knew it the first night. He came home up the lane at five from the docks and got out of the truck and stood at the bottom of the garden with his bag on his shoulder and listened, the way he did every evening, and there was nothing. No four notes. No old piece from the lake coming out of the north window of the music room, rough at the edges. The window was shut. The house was dark.

He stood there anyway, listening to nothing.

Sergeant came down off the wall and walked up the path in front of him, tail up, like an escort, and stopped at the green door and looked back at him, as if to say: well?

He went in.

✦ ✦ ✦

He tried to cook. He’d learned four things since the smoke alarm: rice, which the rice cooker did; greens, which he could now do without blackening the garlic about two times in three; an egg; and a soup Mrs. Bae had taught him in the spring, which took two hours and which he made on the first night and ate standing at the stove, the way Zhao used to eat before Elowen, and then sat down, because he could hear her voice in his head telling him to.

He went to bed at ten. He lay on the door side of the bed that was longer than he was, alone in it for the first time since October last year, with the window open and the owl on the hill and the cat on his chest, and didn’t sleep.

At two in the morning he got up, and found himself in the bathroom at the end of the landing, in the dark, with the light on, standing in front of the cupboard where the towels were kept. She’d bought a lot of towels since the three from the supermarket by the bus station. White ones, all of them, thick, from a shop in the old town, because she said white was the only colour you could boil. There were twenty-two in the house. He knew. He’d counted, once, the way he counted exits.

They were all folded her way. In thirds, lengthwise, and then rolled, tight, like cakes. In rows. Stacked.

He took one out and unrolled it.

He stood in the bathroom at two in the morning in his bare feet, holding a white towel, and looked at it. Then he laid it flat on the edge of the bath, and folded it in thirds, slowly, the way she’d shown him on the end of a camp bed in November three years ago with her hand over his. And rolled it.

It came out a little loose at the end.

He unrolled it and did it again.

✦ ✦ ✦

He did all twenty-two.

He didn’t know why. He couldn’t have explained it to anyone, and he didn’t try. He took every towel out of the cupboard and every towel off every hook and the two from the kitchen and the one from the glasshouse that she used for drying her hands after potting, and carried them all into the bedroom and put them on the bed in a heap, and sat down cross-legged in the middle of the big bed in the middle of the night with the cat watching him from the windowsill, and unrolled every single one, and folded it again. In thirds. Then rolled.

The first ten were bad. He knew they were bad. The ends stuck out. The thirds weren’t even. He did them again.

Somewhere around the fourteenth, he stopped thinking about how and started thinking about her. About her hands on the end of a camp bed, folding. About her voice, the first word she’d ever said to him at a hospital, name, and the first thing she’d ever asked, who was Old Ko?, with a towel in his lap. About her standing at a sink in a textile building with her hands in the water and her eyes shut, saying you’re not patient. About her tomorrow, and the next day, and the day after, sitting on the end of a wooden jetty in the lake country where her mother had played every summer, in front of the people who’d heard her, with her mother’s viola on her shoulder.

He’d wanted to go. She’d asked him not to. Not unkindly. I want to do it on my own, she’d said at the long table. The first time. So I’ll know I can. And he’d understood, and said yes, and meant it, and he still meant it.

He folded the fifteenth towel and it came out perfect.

✦ ✦ ✦

By four in the morning, they were all done.

Twenty-two white rolls on the bed, in rows, tight, even, every one of them in thirds and then rolled, exactly her way. He looked at them in the light from the bedside lamp. Then he picked up the last one, the twenty-second, the one from the glasshouse that she dried her hands on after potting, and unrolled it a little at the end.

Just a little. So the end was loose. So it wasn’t quite right.

He put them all back. The cupboard, the hooks, the kitchen, the glasshouse. All of them perfect, except that one.

Then he went back to bed and slept until seven.

✦ ✦ ✦

She came home on the fourth day, at six in the evening, up the lane in a taxi from the airport, in her pale blue coat with the orange scarf, with the old black case in her hand.

He was at the gate. He’d been at the gate since half past five.

She got out of the taxi and stopped and looked at him. He looked at her. She looked tired, and windblown, and her eyes were red at the rims, and there was something in her face he’d never seen there before, something wide open and settled at once, like a field after rain.

“How was it?” he said.

She came through the gate and put the viola case down carefully on the path, and put her hand flat on his chest.

“An old man cried,” said Evangeline. “In the front row. He was ninety-one. He said he’d heard her play it in 1995, on the same jetty, and he’d never thought he’d hear it again.” Her voice was perfectly level and her eyes were filling up. “He held my hands. He said I played it worse than she did. He said it was the best thing he’d heard in thirty years.”

He didn’t say anything.

He picked her up.

Right there on the path, in front of the Baes’ kitchen window, with the taxi still pulling away down the lane. The whole length of her, off her feet, against him, her arms round his neck, her face in his collar, and he held her and turned round, once, slowly, in the path between the beds, the way he’d held her the night he came back from across the river in 2023 with a jar of honey.

“Four days,” he said into her hair. “Four days, Evangeline. I’ve never been so bored in my life. The cat’s sick of me. Mrs. Bae’s brought round three cakes. I made the soup twice.” He put his mouth against her neck, just below her ear. “Don’t ever go anywhere without me again.”

“I’m going back next year,” said Evangeline.

“Then I’m coming,” he said. “I’ll sit at the back. I won’t say a word. I’ll cry in the front row with the ninety-one-year-old.”

She laughed against his shoulder.

He carried her up the four stone steps and in through the green door, and kicked it shut, and kissed her in the hall under the stairs, with the menu from Nam’s Noodles moving on the inside of the door, for long enough that the cat gave up and went back out through the kitchen window.

✦ ✦ ✦

She found the towels that night.

She went into the bathroom at the end of the landing at ten to wash her face, and opened the cupboard, and stopped.

He was lying on the bed. He heard her stop. He heard her not move.

Then she came along the landing and stood in the bedroom doorway, in her nightdress, with a white towel in her hands, rolled tight, perfect, in thirds.

She looked at him.

“All of them?” she said.

“All twenty-two,” said Jun Hyuk.

She didn’t say anything. She stood in the doorway with the towel, and her eyes were so bright he had to look away.

She went downstairs. He heard her in the kitchen, at the hooks. In the passage. In the glasshouse.

When she came back up, she was holding a different towel. The one from the glasshouse, that she dried her hands on after potting. The twenty-second. With the end a little loose.

She held it up.

“You did that on purpose,” she said.

He looked at her from the bed.

“I wanted you to have something to fix,” he said. “When you came home. So you’d know it was still yours.”

She stood in the doorway.

Then she came and sat down on the edge of the bed beside him, and unrolled the towel on her knees, and folded it in thirds, and rolled it, slowly, tight, perfect, the way she had on the end of a camp bed in November 2022 with her hand over his.

She put it down on the bedside table.

Then she lay down beside him, on the door side, and pulled his arm round her, and faced the room.

“I missed you,” said Evangeline.
